# Jagannatha-Puri

## Preface

This book is decidedly slanted. Its primary intent is to bring the experience and history of the land of Jagannath to those who have some sympathy for the vision of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, the golden incarnation, and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati Thakur, who revived Lord Chaitanya’s movement in the 20thcentury.

His Holiness Srila Bhakti Promode Puri Maharaj, the first president of the World Vaishnava Association and founder of the Gopinath Gaudiya Math, revealed his own deep relation with the land of Purushottam Kshetra by choosing to enter the eternal pastimes here. His long-standing love for Puri inspired him to write in 1967: “The land or Kshetra of Lord Jagannath is the spiritual world on earth. Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu chose this land as the place to spend the last twenty-four years of his life. Ever since that time, Gaudiya Vaishnavas have had an unbreakable relationship with Puri.”

In that same article, Puri Maharaj expressed his intention to write occasional articles in glorification of Puri Dham. He did indeed write some twenty such articles in *Chaitanya Vani* between 1965 and 1990, which were the point of departure for this book. Indeed, it was our original intention to produce a book exclusively out of Puri Maharaj’s articles, but it soon became evident that this would not be possible.

Many of these Puri Maharaj’s articles are specific to certain years (e.g., the Nava Kalevara of 1969, the Rathayatras of 1968 and 1983) while others contain material that is supplementary in nature – isolated legends or details about particular events. Furthermore, many of these articles duplicate each other.

On another occasion, Puri Maharaj asked his disciples to translate Sundarananda Vidyavinoda’s book *Śrī Kṣetra* into English so that people from all over the world could learn to appreciate this land with its unique spiritual heritage. Thus, in order to do full justice to Maharaj’s desire, we decided to integrate his articles into the broad outlines presented by Sundarananda’s *Śrī Kṣetra.*

Both Puri Maharaj and Sundarananda also gave much information about other holy spots in Orissa that are of interest to Gaudiya Vaishnavas. The editors of this volume decided, however, that including this material in this book would have excessively increased its length and so decided to save them for a later work.

Several of Puri Maharaj’s articles express some important aspect of Gaudiya Vaishnava theology as it relates to Sri Purushottam Kshetra. These have been left in their entirety so that the full force of His Grace’s message could shine forth. These chapters are clearly indicated in the table of contents and in the text.

*Śrī Kṣetra*, though a goldmine of information about the land of Puri, has the single greatest flaw of being outdated. It was first published in 1951 and has never been updated. Sundarananda Vidyavinoda’s research was done in the late 1940’s, and though it is for the most part irreproachable, many changes have taken place in the half-century that have followed its publication. Most notably, Indian independence resulted in many changes in the way the Jagannath temple is managed as well as in the fortunes of many of the maths. It may be added that the increased presence of the disciples and grand-disciples of Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati is one of the striking transformations that the town has gone through in the last fifty years.

All these factors made added research necessary to update the information found in this book. Many people assisted in providing bits of information or materials that enriched this book, which nevertheless seems to be nothing more than a beginning in touching on the innumerable aspects of Jagannath Puri.

In giving thanks, it should be noted that H. H. Puri Maharaj gave credit to Sri Gati Krishna Das Adhikari as the source of the information he was reproducing. Gati Krishna Prabhu was an Orissan bhakta who hailed from a village near the Nila Madhava temple in the Daspalla area. He was initiated by His Grace Bhakti Dayita Madhava Goswami Maharaj and later became editor of the Orissan edition of *Chaitanya Vani,* the monthly journal of the Chaitanya Gaudiya Math. Gati Krishna Prabhu was also the official guide to pilgrims from the Chaitanya Gaudiya Math who came to Puri city. He possessed a great fund of knowledge about the city, its history and its legends.

Special thanks must go to Madhavananda Das, Bhaktarupa Das and Fakir Mohan Das of Iskcon Bhubaneswar, who sent many materials such as maps and books, and who personally looked into many questions of fact by going on the spot. They proved to be a great fund of knowledge and a great resource. Madhavananda Prabhuji is to be especially thanked, as he in particular took a great deal of time away from his many other services to help out. I pray that all the members of the Gaudiya guru-varga be especially kind to these devotees.

I would also like to thank Bhakti Bibudh Bodhayan Maharaj, the current acharya of the Gopinath Gaudiya Math, Akinchan Das Bhakti Ballabha Tirtha Maharaj’s disciple, who made relevant portions of Bhakti Dayita Madhava’s biography available to me, Professor Joseph O’Connell, who sent me the biographies of Ram Das Babaji and Charan Das Babaji, and His Holiness Bhaktivedanta Tripurari Swami, who advised on several points of siddhanta.

It must be admitted that this work is nothing more than a beginning. In a city as rich in spiritual history as Jagannath Puri, there is a legend behind every nook and cranny. There are also many theological questions that devotees may one day be called on to answer and stories they will be asked to explain. Some of the most salient controversies have been addressed herein, but we sincerely hope that in the future, others will come and expand this work for the greater glory of Lord Jagannath, Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu and Their devotees.

## Chapter 1 - Pilgrimage to Sri Kshetra

## The concept of sacred space

Nowadays, the Indian and Orissan governments look towards the West and its ever-growing hunger for offbeat travel destinations as a lucrative source of foreign currency. As part of that program, their tourist departments are busily engaged in a process of transforming Hinduism’s ancient holy places of pilgrimage into exotic hot spots for the world tourism map. Rather than immediately crying “sacrilege!” however, we should remember that there is a common thread between the concepts of vacation travel and pilgrimage.

The adventurous tourist wants want to step outside his normal existence to encounter nature in the wild or some strange and wonderful manifestation of human culture – in the hope of being transformed in some way. Even the less adventurous vacationer still wants to come away from his holiday feeling refreshed and renewed, the accumulated stresses of daily life forgotten. Aren’t these part of the promise of pilgrimage -- freedom from sin and transcendence of the empirical self?

Tourism can thus be seen as a secular version of the search for spiritual perfection. But, of course, pilgrimage is much more than a momentary relief from day-to-day cares or a titillating new experience of the exotic.

All human beings, secular or religious, have some awareness of sacred time and place. What American does not feel some degree of awe when standing in the Lincoln Memorial or before Mount Rushmore, great testimonials to the ideals on which the American nation was founded? The aura of sacredness, even in such secular places of pilgrimage, comes from a combination of factors, but is more than any one of them alone. It is more than the man-made monument itself, impressive though it may be, more than the ideals that inspired it, more even than the hundreds of thousands of pilgrims who have trekked there year after year, leaving their accumulated feelings of reverence to permeate the ground below and the atmosphere above.

The overall effect is that any individual who enters such a place and pauses to reflect cannot help but be touched by the spirit of the sacred and the fundamental meaning that it communicates – something that transcends individual human experience and bears testimony to a higher purpose for human life. From the time of the pyramids, through the great cathedrals of the European middle ages, to the great secular monuments of the modern day, human beings have sought out or created such sacred places and designated sacred times – moments of silence, festivals, memorials, times of prayer and remembrance – as ways of orienting their lives to a higher purpose.

## Places of Pilgrimage: Tirtha, Kshetra and Dham

India, the home of Hinduism, is a land where pilgrimage has always played a large role in the religious life of the people. There are many great sites that are visited by pilgrims in their thousands – Hardwar, Prayag and Ganga Sagar are some of the most ancient holy places situated on sacred bodies of water. The ocean, rivers, lakes -- even man-made ones -- that have been invested with the sacred are called tirthas. The name *tīrtha* or “ford” comes from the idea of “crossing over” the ocean or river of material suffering. Since this quality has been attached to all holy places, the term tirtha has come to be used in a generic manner for any such spot, and *tīrtha-yātrā* for all pilgrimage.

Jagannath Puri is situated on the ocean, the “great tirtha,” and also has four other prominent bathing spots, together known as the five tirthas, Pancha Tirtha. Devotees come to these places to perform the timeless rituals of bathing, saying prayers and offering oblations while standing in the sacred waters. As they do so, they feel that not only are they cleansing the body, but also being cleansed of sin. They are thus crossing over from this world into the next. This “crossing over” can be figurative or real – for many pious Hindus consider it to be the ultimate act to go to Benares or Jagannath Puri to die – or failing that, to simply lie by the banks of the Ganges to breathe their last. Failing that, they try to have their funeral rites carried out there, so that their ashes may be sprinkled in the holy water. One of the customary duties of the Hindu pilgrim is to make offerings to the ancestors (*śrāddha*) in such a holy place.

There are other sacred places in India that have been centers of worship for centuries, where there are temples in which the deity is considered to be particularly “awake” or *jāgrata,* i.e., where the deities have historically blessed their devotees, often through miraculous displays of compassion. These too often have roots deep in prehistory.

Some of them are the sites connected to Lord Shiva, like Benares or Bhubaneshwar, and the Goddess, like Kamakhya. Vishnu temple cities like Nathdwar, Tirupati, Venkateshwar and Jagannath Puri are also significant pilgrimage centers in this category.

Some of these temple cities have arisen out of ancient rituals of the pre-Aryan peoples of India, like Jagannath Puri where the Lord of the Universe became manifest to the Shabara, Vishwavasu. This epiphany – where the truth of a supreme person, lord of the universe, was revealed to a humble and uncultured man – made Puri the seat of a great culture, where the entire kingdom dedicated itself to the service of God in wooden form. Through the ages, the members of different faiths – whether Jain, Buddhist, Shaiva, Shakta or Vaishnava – all came to accept that Jagannath was their God, regardless of their own sectarian beliefs. They celebrated the festivals connected with their God, festivals of sacred time, interpreting them according to their understanding of the religious function and the meaning of worship itself.

When an extended area is viewed as having a sacred character of this kind, it is often called a “kshetra” (*kṣetra*).

Another term used to designate holy places is dham (*dhāma*). The term was first used in connection with Jagannath Puri when Sankaracharya established one of his four great preaching centers or maths here. He called the four places where he founded these maths – Bhadrinath in the north, Dvaraka in the west, Rameshwar in the south, and Jagannath Puri in the east – the four dhams of India.

The word *dhāma* means “dwelling place.” According to the Pandas in Jagannath Puri, Badrinath Dham originated in the Satya Yuga when Lord Jagannath was in deep meditation; Rameshwar is connected to the Treta Yuga when Lord Jagannath took His bath; Dwaraka Dham arose in the Dwapara Yuga when the Lord's activity was sleeping or taking rest. Finally, Puri Dham in the Kali Yuga is the place where Lord Jagannath eats His meals. Therefore, Badrinath is called the Lord’s place of meditation, Rameshwar His bathing place, Dwaraka His bedroom, and Puri His dining room.

Vaishnavas, however, generally use the word dham specifically to refer to the places where Krishna made His home during His incarnation, His “dwelling place.” Mathura-Vrindavan and Dwaraka are the places where Krishna had His pastimes; Ayodhya is the birthplace of Lord Rama, and Gaudiya Vaishnavas also consider Nabadwip, the birthplace of Lord Chaitanya, to be such a sacred land. *Dhāma* means “effulgence” in Sanskrit, and it indicates the concept of the sacred place as an extension of the divine presence, non-different from the Supreme Person Himself.

Gaudiya Vaishnavas also consider Jagannath Puri to be a dham, primarily because it was inundated with the mercy of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu chose Puri to spend the last twenty-four years of His life. The entire land of Puri is permeated with reminders of this time, when Mahaprabhu’s *rādhā-bhāva* was the most intense and He made His most significant revelations.

Pilgrims invest a further level of sacredness in places where great saints were born, practiced their spiritual life, experienced the Divine, attained perfection or died. For Vaishnavas in the line of Bhaktivinoda Thakur, Jagannath Puri is particularly significant, for it was in the holy atmosphere of Sri Kshetra that the Thakur’s devotion to the Supreme Lord blossomed, and it is here that Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati Goswami Prabhupada appeared in the world to further the mission of Lord Chaitanya in the world. For those who follow in their line, the words of the *Padma-purāṇa – hy utkale puruṣottamāt* – “The religion of devotion to Vishnu will spread from the town of Purushottam in Orissa” have particular significance on account of these events.

Siddhanta Saraswati himself established the Purushottam Math in the vicinity of Tota Gopinath, but in 1950, there were still no other Gaudiya Maths in the town. Since then, many of his disciples have come and settled here to do bhajan and to establish centers for their followers, including most notably Bhakti Dayita Madhava Maharaja, who reclaimed the birthplace of Siddhanta Saraswati near the Narayan Chata Math on the Grand Road, and the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, which now runs the Bhakti Kuti where Bhaktivinoda Thakur spent many of the last years of his holy life engaged in bhajan. Both these places are of great historical importance for the followers of Bhaktivinoda Thakur and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati Thakur Prabhupada.

Saintly persons of other spiritual traditions have also established monasteries in Puri and so their followers give the town the same sort of veneration. For the disciples of Srila Bhakti Promode Puri Goswami, Purushottam Kshetra will forever be of special significance, as it is here that he lived out his last days and entered into the eternal companionship of the Lord.

## Pilgrimage in the 19th century

With all these layers of spiritual significance, Puri has always been a great magnet to the people of India, who left their homes at great personal sacrifice, often spending their entire life’s savings just for the chance to see Lord Jagannath and bathe in the ocean tirtha. The Chaitanya Charitamrita describes the annual pilgrimages made by Mahaprabhu’s followers, who would walk the 500 kilometers from Bengal. Mahaprabhu’s dear associate Shivananda Sena would supervise the trip, taking care of travel arrangements, accommodations, border crossings, river crossings, and tolls for the several hundred pilgrims who would go to see Mahaprabhu every year during the Rathayatra. These times were often troubled and Shivananda had to make full use of his extensive diplomatic skills to negotiate through the various difficulties.

W. W. Hunter, writing at the time Bhaktivinoda Thakur was assistant magistrate in Puri, describes the armies of pilgrims that came each year to Puri. His eyewitness account, which evokes both the color and the hardship of the pilgrimage to Puri, is worth repeating here:

Day and night throughout every month of the year, troops of devotees arrive at Puri, and for three hundred miles along the great Orissa road every village has its pilgrim encampment. The parties consist of from twenty to three hundred persons. At the time of the great festivals these bands follow so close as to touch each other; and a continuous train of pilgrims, many miles long, may often be seen on the Puri high road.

They march in orderly procession, each party under its spiritual leader. At least five-sixths, and often nine-tenths of them, are females. Now a straggling band of slender, diminutive women, clothed in white muslin, and limping sadly along, announces a pilgrim company from Lower Bengal; then a joyous retinue with flowing garments of bright red or blue, trudging stoutly forward, their noses pierced with elaborate rings, their faces freely tattooed, and their hands encumbered with bundles of very dirty cloth, proclaims the stalwart female peasantry of Northern Hindustan. Ninety-five out of a hundred are on foot.

Mixed with the throng are devotees of various sorts, some covered with ashes, some almost naked, some with matted, yellow-stained hair, and almost all with their foreheads streaked with red or white, a string of beads round their necks, and a stout staff in their hands.

Every now and then, covered wagons drawn by the high-humped bullocks of upper India, or by the smaller breed of Bengal, according to the nationality of the owner, creak past on their wooden wheels. Those from the Northern Provinces still bear traces of the licentious Mussalman rule by being jealously shut up. The Bengali husband, on the other hand, keeps his women good-tempered and renders pilgrimage pleasant by piercing holes in the wagon-hood, through which dark female eyes constantly peep out.

Then a lady in colored trousers, from some village near Delhi, ambles past on a tiny pony, her husband submissively walking by her side, and a female domestic, with a hamper of Ganges water and a bundle of dirty cloth, bringing up the rear.

Next a great train of palankeens, carrying a Calcutta banker and his ladies, sweeps past. I met one consisting of forty palankeens, with 320 bearers and about fifty luggage-carriers, whose continuous chant made itself heard far off in the silent night.

But the greatest spectacle is a north country Raja with his caravan of elephants, camels, led horses, and swordsmen, looking resigned and very helpless in his sedan of state, followed by all the indescribable confusion, dirt, and noises of Indian royalty.

Even in the days before the railway (which only connected Calcutta to Puri in 1901), thousands of pilgrims annually made their way to Jagannath Puri. The Rathayatra regularly attracted the largest crowd, with as many as 100,000 people assisting at the great festival in a normal year. The incredible hardship that these pilgrims faced in making the a trip of five hundred to a thousand kilometers on foot stands as a testimony to the intensity of their devotion and the repute and glory of Jagannath Puri.

It was not an easy trip by any standard. During their stay in Puri pilgrims would be badly lodged in overcrowded and unsanitary housing. The temple held a monopoly on providing food, and pilgrims were forbidden to cook for themselves. Despite the glories of Maha Prasad being edible even when old or rotten, over-consumption of

prasad in such a state caused problems to travelers whose health was often weak due to the long journey.

In those days, drainage and sanitation in the town were poor. In the heat and humidity that characterized Puri weather during the season of the Rathayatra, the oven-like heat of the overcrowded small rooms combined with improper sanitation made Puri a breeding place for cholera. Epidemics of the disease were a regular occurrence, causing up to 10,000 pilgrim deaths a year. In some years, the picture was one of incredible desolation. One writer described the city in the epidemic year 1841:

Corpse-fields lay around the town, in one of which, the traveler counted between forty and fifty bodies besides many skeletons which had been picked by vultures. The birds were sitting in numbers on the neighboring sand-hills and trees, holding carnivorous festivity on the dead; and the wild dogs lounged about full of the flesh of man.\[1\]

In the rains, the return journey was even more difficult than the first part of the pilgrimage. The legendary rapacity of the Puri priests and lodging-house keepers often left the pilgrims at the end of their resources. Traveling conditions during the rainy season were notoriously bad in eastern India before the introduction of asphalted roads. There was no way of crossing the swollen rivers other than at the whims of greedy ferrymen who held the travelers hostage. Floods would turn the entire Mahanadi delta into a malarious swamp. The inadequacy of shelter on the road made travelers facile prey for disease, whether cholera or malaria.

Hundreds died on the roadside from sheer exhaustion. Overcrowding along the way created artificial famines in small village that could not provide for the surging crowds passing through. As if all this were not enough, conditions were made even more dangerous by roadside criminals who preyed on the weakened travelers by kidnapping women pilgrims to sell into prostitution or into Muslim zenanas.

During the 19thcentury, British government took many steps to improve the situation -- the construction of better roads and the railway had an immense effect on easing the difficulties of the journey. Besides the improved ease of traveling, medical science, pilgrim hospitals and sanitation have all made the tragedies of the past a distant memory. Since Independence, the Orissan and Indian governments have taken great steps to improve conditions for pilgrims at the modern Rathayatra festival, which may now attract as many as 800,000 visitors from all over the world.

## Criticisms of Tirtha Yatra

In view of all the troubles that people went to on pilgrimage journeys, it is not surprising that many spiritual leaders called the institution itself into question. In the 15thand 16thcenturies, in particular, the Sants leveled a spirited critique of formal religion and corrupt priesthood in both Hinduism and Islam, which extended to houses of worship and pilgrimage.

The argument they gave was the following: If the ultimate goal of spiritual practice is to see God everywhere, in everything, is it not misleading for us to pinpoint any one place as being especially sacred? Guru Nanak criticized both Hindus and Muslims for showing special veneration for particular places, whether Mecca or Benares, as holy. He asked, “If God is everywhere, then why venerate an idol? Indeed, by placing limits on God in this way, do we not become blind to the universal presence of God?”

Narottam Das Thakur, the second-generation follower of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, expressed a similar sentiment with great force in his *Prema-bhakti-candrikā:*

*tīrtha-yātrā pariśrama kevala maner bhrama*  
*sarva-siddhi govinda caraṇa*

**Making great efforts to visit the holy places is nothing but illusion. All perfection can be found at Lord Krishna’s lotus feet.**

The point is a valid one: it has been made in the Bhagavatam and should be held in mind by every pilgrim. A pilgrim is not a tourist who simply comes to swim in the sea, gawk at some exotic buildings and buy a few souvenirs. He comes precisely because he recognizes that he is incapable of seeing God everywhere and needs to inundate his mind with aids to remembering Him.

The Vaishnava approach is to see God in His concentrated form – as present in the Holy Dham and His deity form -- and through such absorption, to come to see Him everywhere. The holy land is a place where the spiritual energy is concentrated. Most importantly, it is a place where the company of spiritually advanced people can easily be found. The holy land thus acts like a strong medicine, giving pilgrims a concentrated dose of the sacred that they can then carry with them back into their own everyday lives. A pilgrim does not simply make a physical journey, but an internal one.

## How a Gaudiya Vaishnava performs pilgrimage

In a 1967 article about the Chaitanya Gaudiya Math pilgrimage to Jagannath Puri,\[2\] Srila Bhakti Promode Puri Maharaj summarized the speech given by His Divine Grace Bhakti Dayita Madhava Maharaja to the assembled devotees on the first evening of their arrival at Dudhwala Dharma Shala:

According to our most worshipable Srila Prabhupada’s teachings, performing the Dham parikrama is a way in which a devotee can easily practice the five most powerful acts of devotional service: associating with devotees, chanting the Holy Name, hearing the Bhagavatam, residing in Mathura (or the Holy Dham) and serving the deity form of the Lord.

*sādhu saṅga nāma kīrtana bhāgavata śravaṇa*  
*mathurā vāsa śrī mūrtira śraddhāya sevana*  
*sakala sādhana śreṣṭha ei pañca aṅga*  
*kṛṣṇa prema janmāya ei pāṅcera alpa saṅga*  
*eka aṅga sādhe keha sādhe bahu aṅga*  
*niṣṭhā haile upajaya premera taraṅga*

**One should associate with devotees, chant the holy name of the Lord, hear Srimad Bhagavatam, reside at Mathura and worship the Deity with faith and veneration. These five limbs of devotional service are the best of all. Even their brief performance awakens love for Krishna. Whether a person executes only one or several of these processes of devotional service, the waves of love of Godhead will well up as a result of his or her fixed determination or** ***niṣṭhā*****. (CC** [**2.22.214-5**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/22.128)**,** [**219**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/22.134)**)**

*durūhādbhuta-vīrye 'smin*  
*śraddhā dūre 'stu pañcake*  
*yatra svalpo 'pi sambandhaḥ*  
*sad-dhiyāṁ bhāva-janmane*

**Each one of these five devotional activities is possessed of extraordinary power. Even without faith, if a pure-hearted person has the slightest connection to such activities, he will quickly develop deep feeling for Krishna. (*****Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu*** [**1.2.238**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/rupa-brs1/1.2.238)**)**

Since we have had the good fortune to come to this auspicious place, we should not stop chanting the Lord’s name, qualities, or pastimes for even a moment while we are here. Such activities are always auspicious, but when in the Holy Dham, they become even more powerful and effective. They quickly give results in that Krishna’s blessings come more quickly to His devotees in the Dham. This is part of the surrendering process: to believe firmly that Krishna will be merciful.

When in the Holy Dham, one should avoid discussing mundane topics or gossip, but make every effort to concentrate on the Lord’s name, form and pastimes. This is a sign of true intelligence. The topmost form of worship is the worship of the Lord’s holy name:

*bhajanera madhye śreṣṭha nava vidhā bhakti*  
*kṛṣṇa prema, kṛṣṇa dite dhare mahā śakti*  
*tāra madhye sarva śreṣṭha nāma saṅkīrtana*  
*niraparādhe laile nāma pāya prema dhana*

**Of the many ways of executing devotional service, there are nine that are considered to be the best, for they possess a great capacity to deliver love for Krishna and thus Krishna himself. Of these nine processes of devotional service, the most important is the chanting of the Lord=s holy name, for if one chants without committing offences he will obtain the treasure of love for the Lord. (CC** [**3.4.70-1**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-antya/4.70)**)**

The great benefit of coming to a holy place is that it is the place where people dedicated to the spiritual life make their home. Therefore, Bhaktivinoda Thakur says,

*tīrtha phala sādhu-saṅga sādhu-saṅge antaraṅga*  
*śrī-kṛṣṇa-bhajana manohara*  
*jathā sādhu tathā tīrtha sthira kari nija citta*  
*sādhu-saṅga kara ataḥpara*

**The real fruit of visiting the Holy Dham is the association of saintly devotees. In such intimate association, the worship of the Lord is very pleasing. A place is considered holy if saintly devotees are present there. Remember this always and forever associate with devotees. (*****Kalyāṇa-kalpa-taru*****, 14)**

This instruction should be our guideline whenever we go to a holy place. We should all be careful to seek out real devotional treasures when visiting the Holy Dham, making sure that we get the company of devotees who will make our visit there worthwhile. Association with devotees is the root cause of bhakti, and without their mercy, there can be no advancement in devotional service.

*mahat-kṛpā vinā kono karme bhakti naya*  
*kṛṣṇa-bhakti dūre rahu saṁsāra nahe kṣaya*

**No one can achieve bhakti without the blessings of the great devotees. You cannot even attain liberation from material entanglement, what to speak of devotion. (CC** [**2.22.51**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/22.51)**)**

“Taking shelter of Your abode”

Residing in the Holy Dham is part of the fundamental process of devotional service – taking shelter of the Lord or *śaraṇāgati.*

*tavāsmīti vadan vācā*  
*tathaiva manasā vidan*  
*tat sthānam āśritas tanvā*  
*modate śaraṇāgataḥ*

**One who has taken shelter makes use of his body to reside in a holy place connected to the Lord. With his words, he says, “O Lord, I am Yours.” And he uses mind to think of himself as belonging to the Lord. In this way, he enjoys spiritual bliss. (*****Hari-bhakti-vilāsa*** [**11.677**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/hbv/11.677)**)**

Anyone who comes to the Holy Dham of Purushottam Kshetra should daily sing the following bhajan written by Bhaktivinoda Thakur, which illustrates this way of taking shelter:

*ki jāni ki bale tomāre dhāmete*  
*hainu śaraṇāgata*  
*tumi dayāmaya patita-pāvana*  
*patita-tāraṇe rata*

**I don’t know what I have done to deserve this, but here I am, taking shelter of Your abode. O savior of the sinful, You have so mercifully dedicated Yourself to saving the fallen.**

*bharasā āmāra ei-mātra nātha*  
*tumi to karuṇāmaya*  
*tava dayā-pātra nāhi mora sama*  
*avaśya ghucibe bhaya*

**My only hope, O Lord, is that You are compassionate. This makes me the most worthy recipient of Your mercy, so You will surely erase all my fears.**

*āmāre tarite kāhāro śakati*  
*avanī-bhitare nāhi*  
*dayāla ṭhākura ghoṣaṇā tomāra*  
*adham pāmare trāhi*

**No one in this world can save me, so sinful am I. Yet You have vowed loudly and clearly to kindly deliver the lowest and most sinful of humankind.**

*sakala chāṛiyā āsiyāchi āmi*  
*tomāra caraṇe nātha*  
*āmi nitya-dāsa, tumi pālayitā*  
*tumi goptā, jagannātha*

**I have given up everything to come here and fall down at Your feet, O Lord. I am Your eternal servant, O Jagannath, and I make You my protector and maintainer.**

*tomāra sakala āmi mātra dāsa*  
*āmāre taribe tumi*  
*tomāra caraṇa karinu varaṇa*  
*āmāra nahi to āmi*

**Whatever I have is Yours. I am only a servant and You will take care of me. I have accepted Your lotus feet as everything in my life, I make no claim even over my very self.**

*bhakativinoda kāṅdiyā śaraṇa*  
*layeche tomāra pāya*  
*kṣami aparādha nāme ruci diyā*  
*pālana koro he tāya*

**I, Bhaktivinoda, cry as I take shelter of Your lotus feet. Since I have done so, forgive me my offenses; give me a taste for chanting Your holy name and protect me always. (*****Śaraṇāgati*****)**

## Seeing the Dham with transcendental eyes

One often hears criticism of Lord Jagannath’s sevaks, the temple priests, whether it be for their exploitation of pilgrims, the laxity of their spiritual practices, the insincerity of their faith, or some other transgressions, real or imagined. Bhaktivinoda Thakur himself addressed this issue in his short work, *The Temple of Jagannath at Puri* (1871). It is clear from the Thakur’s career and statements that he sympathized with reformist tendencies that sought to eliminate corruption from the religious life of India.\[3\]

A devotee is naturally troubled to see a holy place not being treated with the proper dignity by the people who live there or those who visit it. This is expressed in the idea of *dhāmāparādha,* or “offences to the Holy Dham.” The primary offense to the Holy Dham is considering its residents as ordinary people. Proper Vaishnava behavior is to treat all the Dham’s residents as residents of the spiritual world, as is repeatedly stated in the Puranas.

*aho kṣetrasya māhātmyaṁ*  
*samantād daśa-yojanam*  
*diviṣṭhā yatra paśyanti*  
*sarvān eva caturbhujān*

**How glorious is this land, eighty miles across from one end to the other.\[4\] The demigods look down on this land and see that all its residents have four arms like those of Vaikuntha. (BRS** [**1.2.106**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/rupa-brs1/1.2.106)**, from Brahma Purana)**

*kṣetraṁ tad durlabhaṁ vipra samantād daśa-yojanam \|*  
*tatrasthā dehino devair dṛśyante ca caturbhujāḥ \|\|*  
*praviśantas tu tat kṣetraṁ sarve syur viṣṇu-mūrtayaḥ \|*  
*tasmād vicāraṇā tatra na kartavyā vicakṣaṇaiḥ \|\|*

**When the gods look down on this rarest of lands, which is twenty miles across, they see that everyone who lives there has a four-armed form. Even those who simply visit that land take on spiritual forms like that of Vishnu. Therefore one should be careful to never judge its residents. (*****Padma-purāṇa*** **7.11.5-6)**

*se sthānera prabhāve yojana daśa bhūmi*  
*tāhāte basaye jata jantu kīṭa kṛmi*  
*sabāre dekhaye caturbhuja deva-gaṇe*  
*bhuvana-maṅgala kari kahiye je sthāne*  
*nidrāteo je sthāne samādhi-phala haya*  
*śayane praṇāma phala jathā vede kaya*  
*pradakṣiṇa phala pāya karile bhramaṇa*  
*katha-mātra jathā haya āmāra stavana*  
*hena se kṣetrera ati prabhāva nirmala*  
*matsya khāileo pāya haviṣyera phala*

**By My holy influence, the gods see every single living being in the ten yojanas of this territory, even including the worms and insects, as four-armed beings. I have made everyone there a source of good for the entire world. By the holy potency of Jagannath Puri, even one who spends his time there sleeping gets the benefits associated with samadhi; one who just lies down gets the fruits of paying obeisance; one who walks about that land gets the fruits of circumambulating the deity; simply by talking, one gets the results of offering praises to the Lord; and even someone who eats fish in this holy land gets the fruit of eating** ***haviṣyānna.***

*nija-nāme sthāna mora hena priyatama*  
*tāhāte jateka baise se āmāra sama*  
*se sthāne nāhika yama-daṇḍa-adhikāra*  
*āmi kari bhāla-manda vicāra sabāra*

**This land has been named after Me because I love it so much. All those who live here are equal to Me. The Lord of Death has no right to come here to punish the residents of this land. I am the only one who judges their good or bad actions. (Cbh** [**3.2.371-7**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cb-antya/2.371)**)**

This means that for the Western mind, there are occasionally sensibilities that are offended and experienced as cultural clash. Hypocrisy, greed, and uncleanliness are some of the flaws that may spring to the eyes.

In 1990, when a piece of masonry fell from an arch on the Jagannath temple, Bhakti Promode Puri Maharaj wrote, “These events have caused people to make all kinds of speculations and criticisms \[of the temple priests\]. Of this we say that Lord Jagannath is the master and controller of the universe. He is the life of every living being’s life. It is incorrect to blame a handful of Lord Jagannath’s direct servants for defects in His service while making a hypocritical show of piety oneself.”\[5\]

Anyone who believes in the concept of Jagannath’s sacredness and in the idea of reincarnation as explained in the Bhagavad Gita must recognize the fundamental venerability of anyone who is born or takes up residence in a holy land like Puri. This requires a special effort to recognize how the sacred is manifest there. Though this may at times be difficult, cultivation of this attitude should be considered an integral part of any pilgrimage. One who wishes to make the most of his or her visit to the Holy Dham should take care to remain in the company of pure devotees. This is the starting point for all spiritual advancement.

On the other hand, there is no reason that devotees from whatever part of the world cannot work to the greater glory of the Dham without offending those who live there, by performing various kinds of selfless service.

## Chapter 2 - Sri Kshetra: Land of the Lila Purushottam

*dūrād adarśi puruṣottama-vaktra-candro*  
*bhrājad-viśāla-nayano maṇi-puṇḍra-bhālaḥ*  
*snigdhābhra-kāntir aruṇādhara-dīpti-ramyo’*  
*śeṣa-prasāda-vikasat-smita-candrikāḍhyaḥ*

**From afar I saw the moon-like face of Lord Purushottam, with His immense eyes and jeweled tilak on His forehead. The color of His body was that of a shining cloud and bright red lips beautified His face. His unlimited blessings were revealed by the moonlight of His smile. (*****Bṛhad-bhāgavatāmṛta*** [**2.1.167**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bb/2.1.167)**)**

The Supreme Person appears in His deity form (*arcāvatāra*) as Jagannath, the lord of the three worlds, and the land where He appears is known as Purushottam Kshetra, or the “Supreme Person’s holy land.” Because it is His own city, it is called Jagannath Puri, or just Puri. It also goes by other names, such as *bhauma vaikuṇṭha,* because it is the divine abode on earthly soil, and Nilachala or Niladra (“blue mountain”) because it is the horizon on which the sun in the form of the Lord Nila Madhava first appeared.

In the Chaitanya Bhagavata, the glories of Sri Puri Dham are explained by Krishna while speaking to Lord Shiva about Bhubaneswar:

*sei vāraṇāsī prāya suramya-nagarī*  
*sei sthāne āmāra parama gopya purī*  
*sei sthāna śiva āji kahi tomā-sthāne*  
*se purīra marma mora keha nāhi jāne*  
*sindhu-tīre baṭa-mūle nīlācala nāma*  
*kṣetra śrī-puruṣottama ati ramya sthāna*  
*ananta-brahmāṇḍa kāle jakhana saṁhāre*  
*tabu se sthānera kichu karite nā pāre*  
*sarva-kāla sei sthāne āmāra basati*  
*prati-dina āmāra bhojana haya tathi*

**This beautiful city is the equal of Benares in holiness. This place is my most secret abode. O Shiva! I am telling you now that no one knows the mysteries of this holy place. This land, known as Nilachala, stands at the foot of a banyan tree on the seashore. Also known as the holy land of Sri Purushottam, it is a most beautiful place. Even when the time comes for universal destruction, this land is not affected. I live here for all time and take My meals here every day. (**[**3.2.366-70**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cb-antya/2.366)**)**

In the *Utkala-khaṇḍa* (1.12-13)*,* Jaimini Rishi glorifies Sri Kshetra as follows: “This is a most wonderful and delightful place, sovereign among all holy places. Eighty miles long (ten *yojanas*), it is surrounded by the sands that have come out of the ocean and beautified by the blue mountain that stands in its center.”

The Lord himself says, “The land to the north of the seashore and to the south of the Maha Nadi (“the Great River”) gives all other holy places in the world their powers. The land becomes holier with every step one takes southward from Bhubaneswar (Ekamra Forest) to the ocean. The land by the ocean, where the blue mountain stands, is the most secret of holy places, unobtainable by even Brahma.” (*Utkala-khaṇḍa*, 1.33-35)

As the above verse indicates, Sri Kshetra is ten yojanas or 80 miles wide, which includes the entire Puri district from Bhubaneswar to the sea. The town of Jagannath Puri itself is only five kros or ten miles wide. This smaller area has the shape of a conch shell, so it is sometimes called Shankha Kshetra.

*pañca-krośam idaṁ samudrasyāntar-vyavasthitam*  
*dvi-krośaṁ tīrtha-rājasya taṭa-bhūmau sunirmalam*  
*suvarṇa-bālukākīrṇaṁ nīla-parvata-śobhitam*  
*sīmā pratīcī kṣetrasya śaṅkhākārasya mūrdhani*  
*śaṅkhāgre nīla-kaṇṭhaḥ syād etat krośaḥ sudurlabhaḥ*  
*paramaṁ pāvanaṁ kṣetraṁ sākṣān nārāyaṇasya vai*  
*śaṅkhasyodara-bhāgas tu samudrodaka-samplutaḥ*

**The holy place is ten miles wide and the two miles closest to the ocean are extremely holy. The shape of Puri is usually compared to a conch shell, tapering off to the east and round in the west. The belly of the conch is in the ocean, while the blue-throated Shiva makes his home in the narrow portion. (UK 3.52-3, 4.5-6)**

The *Mādalā-pañjī*, however, says that Sri Kshetra is ten miles across and is the navel of the larger Purushottam Vaikuntha, which is shaped like a conch shell eighty miles across

## Purushottam Kshetra

The earliest name of the land surrounding Lord Jagannath’s temple is Purushottam Kshetra. It is given this name because it is the abode of the Supreme Person, or *puruṣottama*. The Padma Purana says:

*lavaṇāmbho-nidhes tīre puruṣottama-saṁjñakam*  
*puraṁ tad brāhmaṇa-śreṣṭha svargād api sudurlabham*  
*svayam asti pure tasmin yataḥ śrī-puruṣottamaḥ*  
*puruṣottamam ity uktaṁ tasmāt tan-nāma-kovidaiḥ*

**O best of the Brahmins, this city of Purushottam on the banks of the salt-water ocean is more rare than the heaven worlds. It has been wisely named Purushottam because the Supreme Person personally resides there. (*****Padma-purāṇa*** **7.11.3-4)**

In the *Bhagavad-gītā*, the Lord reveals that He is the Supreme Person, or *puruṣottama:*

*yasmāt kṣarād atīto=ham*  
*akṣarād api cottamaḥ*  
*ato 'smi loke vede ca*  
*prathitaḥ puruṣottamaḥ*

**Since in my essence I am beyond both the fallible individual soul and My infallible manifestations as Brahma or Paramatma, this personal manifestation of Mine is supreme. For this reason I am known in both the Vedic literature and among the people of the world as the Purushottam. (Gita** [**15.18**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/15.18)**)**

This Krishna is further known as Lila Purushottam, because He manifests His perfection as the Supreme Person by engaging in various diversions known as lilas. Not only are the creation, maintenance and destruction of the universe extensions of His desire for play, but in the intimacy of His own internal potency, He engages in human-like activities that show the perfection of the dance of love. This is the meaning of the Vedanta, *lokavat tu līlā-kaivalyam* – “Like a human being, the Lord displays His perfection exclusively in play.”

*svayaṁ bhagavān āra līlā-puruṣottama*  
*ei dui nāma dhare vrajendra-nandana*

**The Lord, son of the king of Vraja, is known both as the original Personality of Godhead (*****svayaṁ bhagavān*****) and as Supreme Person engaged in various pastimes (*****līlā-puruṣottama*****). (CC** [**2.20.240**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/20.240)**)**

Jagannath Puri has also been given the name of *daśāvatāra-kṣetra,* because it is the root source of the creation, destruction and maintenance of the universe. According to the *Utkala-khaṇḍa,* the Lord appears here in His incarnations first before going off to other places to complete His work. Once these incarnations have completed their mission, they return again to Purushottam where they remain, merging into the form of Lord Jagannath. Thus, one can get the same results that would come of seeing Matsya and the other incarnations of the Lord simply by coming to Sri Purushottam.\[6\]

The *Śrī-Vaiṣṇava-tantra* indicates that in His form as Lord Jagannath, Krishna engages in the pastimes of all His worldly abodes – Mathura, Dwaraka and Vraja.

*mathurā-dvārakā-līlā yāḥ karoti ca gokule*  
*nīlācala-sthitaṁ kṛṣṇas tā eva carati prabhuḥ*

**Here in Nilachala, Krishna performs all the very same pastimes that He enjoys in Mathura, Dwaraka and Gokula.**

Vraja is manifest in the land of Purushottam in the deities beloved to all the Gaudiya Vaishnavas -- Govinda, Gopinath and Madan Mohan; Vrindavan is represented by Sundarachala and Radha Kund by Rohini Kund; Govardhan Hill is there in the form of the sand dunes (*caṭaka parvata*) by the sea*,* Vamshi Bata in the Akshaya Bata, the Yamuna River in the ocean. Barshana is represented by the place where Hari Das Thakur had his pastimes and Gopishwar is there in the form of Advaita Acharya.

## The Lord’s abode on earth

Sri Kshetra is known as Bhauma Vaikuntha or “the Lord’s abode on earth.” The Lord often appears on earth in different forms, accompanied by his associates and abode. Sometimes, the Lord remains in permanence on this earth in different *arcā* forms and thus the Lord’s abode accompanies Him in each of these cases.

The Lila Purushottam, the Supreme Person who engages in wonderful pastimes, is the original manifestation of the Godhead, Vrajendranandan. He wears the clothing of a cowherd and thinks of himself as a cowherd. He sports eternally in the land of Vraja, a divine land of cow pastures. His first expansion or *svayaṁ prakāśa* form is Balaram, who also thinks of himself as a cowherd in Vraja. The same two personalities appear in Dwaraka and Mathura where they think of themselves as warrior kings, or Kshatriyas.

*svayaṁ-rūpera gopa-veśa gopa-abhimāna*  
*vāsudevera kṣatriya-veśa āmi kṣatriya-jñāna*  
*vraje gopa-bhāva rāmera pure kṣatriya-bhāvana*

**In his original form, the Lord dresses like a cowherd boy and thinks Himself to be one. When He appears as Vasudeva, the son of Vasudeva and Devaki, He dresses like a Kshatriya and thinks of Himself as one. Balaram also thinks of himself as a cowherd boy in Vrindavan and Kshatriya in Dwaraka. (CC** [**2.20.177**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/20.177)**,** [**187**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/20.187)**)**

Krishna and Balaram have their first series of four expansions or *catur-vyūha* in Dwaraka. These four forms are Vasudeva, Sankarshan, Pradyumna and Aniruddha. The second *catur-vyūha* manifests in the spiritual world. These four expansions of the Lord have another twenty forms that go by the name of *vilāsa* forms. Altogether, these twenty-four forms reside eternally in the eternal abode of Vaikuntha. These same forms appear within the material world in twenty-four different places as *arcā* incarnations, or worshipable deity forms. These twenty-four deity incarnations are self-manifesting, that is, they appear as they are in the world without any human intervention. Lord Jagannath in Puri is one such eternally self-manifest form of the Lord.

The Lord exercises His pastimes by appearing within this world in different times and places in different manners. When He does so, He appears with His abode and His eternal associates. This also holds true when He appears as the *arcā avatāra.*

*Krishna Das Kaviraja explains this as follows:*  
*jadyapi paravyoma sabākāra nitya-dhāma*  
*tathāpi brahmāṇḍe kāro kāṅho sannidhāna*

**Even though all these forms of the Lord have their eternal residence in the spiritual world of Vaikuntha, some of them also make their homes here and there within the material universes. (CC** [**2.20.212**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/20.212)**)**

*ei-mata brahmāṇḍa-madhye sabāra parakāśa*  
*sapta-dvīpe nava-khaṇḍe jāṅhāra vilāsa*  
*sarvatra prakāśa tāṅra bhakte sukha dite*  
*jagatera adharma nāśi dharma sthāpite*

**The Lord is situated in different spiritual manifestations within the within, sporting on its seven islands and nine lands. The Lord appears in this way throughout the universe in order to bring pleasure to His devotees. In this way, He also destroys irreligion and establishes the eternal religious principles.(CC** [**2.20.218-9**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/20.218)**)**

*mathurāte keśavera nitya sannidhāna*  
*nīlācale puruṣottama jagannātha nāma*  
*prayāge mādhava mandāre śrī-madhusūdana*  
*ānandāraṇye vāsudeva padmanābha janārdana*  
*viṣṇu-kāñcīte viṣṇu hari rahe māyāpure*  
*aiche āra nānā mūrti brahmāṇḍa-bhitare*

**Lord Keshava eternally resides at Mathura, and Lord Purushottam, known by the name Jagannath, eternally resides at Nilachala. At Prayag, the Lord is situated as Bindu Madhava, and at Mandara Mountain, the Lord is known as Madhusudan. Vasudeva, Padmanabha and Janardana reside in the Ananda Forest. In Vishnu Kanchi, the Lord is known as Vishnu, while in Hardwar, he is known as Hari. There are many other such forms throughout the universe. (CC** [**2.20.215-7**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/20.215)**)**

## Daru Brahma

Lord Jagannath, the *arcā avatāra* of the Supreme Person, is frequently referred to by the name “Daru Brahma” (*dāru-brahma*), the incarnation of God in wood. Verses in the *Padma-purāṇa, Bṛhad-viṣṇu-purāṇa*, and *Tattva-yāmala* all refer to Lord Jagannath as the *dāru brahma*--

*samudrasyottare tīre āste śrī-puruṣottame*  
*pūrṇānanda-mayaṁ brahma dāru-vyāja-śarīra-bhṛt*

**In the land of Purushottam on the north shore of the sea, Brahma, the full manifestation of joy, plays at taking a wooden body.**

*nīlādrau cotkale deśe kṣetre śrī-puruṣottame*  
*dāruṇy āste cidānando jagannāthākhya-mūrtinā*

**In the land of the blue mountain in Orissa, in the holy place known as Sri Purushottam, the supremely joyful spirit manifests in a form of wood, known to the world as Jagannath.**

*bhārate cotkale deśe bhū-svarge puruṣottame*  
*dāru-rūpī jagannātho bhaktānām abhaya-pradaḥ*  
*nara-ceṣṭām upādāya āste mokṣaika-kārakaḥ*

**In the land of Bharata, in the province of Orissa, in the place known as Purushottam, the heaven on earth, the Lord of the Universe has appeared in a wooden form to remove the fears of His devotees. Though He acts like a human being, He is the one and only cause of salvation.**

Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu gave different instructions to Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya and his brother Vidya Vachaspati, telling one of them to serve Jagannath in Puri, the other to remain in Nabadwip to serve the aqueous form of Brahma, the Ganges River. Krishna Das Kaviraj reports these instructions in the following words:

*sārvabhauma vidyā vācaspati dui bhāi*  
*dui jane kṛpā kari kahena gosāñi*  
*dāru jala rūpe kṛṣṇa prakaṭa samprati*  
*daraśana snāne kare jīvera mukati*  
*dāru brahma rūpe sākṣāt śrī puruṣottama*  
*bhāgīrathī hana sākṣāt jala brahma sama*  
*sārvabhauma kara dāru brahma ārādhana*  
*vācaspati kara jala brahmera sevana*

**Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu mercifully blessed the two brothers, Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya and Vidya Vachaspati. He said, “In this Age of Kali, Krishna is manifest in two forms – one of wood, the other of water. Through this mercy, the conditioned souls can become liberated simply by the acts of looking and bathing. Lord Jagannath is the Supreme Lord Himself in the form of wood, and the River Ganges is the Supreme Lord Himself in the form of water. Sarvabhauma, you should worship the Lord as the wood Brahma, and Vachaspati, you should worship Him as the water Brahma.” (CC** [**2.15.133-6**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/15.133)**)**

The first reference to the Supreme Spirit (Brahman) appearing in a wooden form (*dāru*), is found in the world=s oldest book, the Rig Veda*.* The following text is found in its Tenth Mandala (10.155.3):

*ado yad dāru plavate sindhoḥ pāre apūruṣam*  
*tadārabhasva durhaṇo tena gaccha parastaram*

The British scholar Ralph T. H. Griffiths translated this verse as follows:

**“Yon log that floats without a man to guide it on the river’s edge – seize it thou thing with hideous jaws and go thou far away thereon.”**

This translation is obscure and does not follow the famous commentator of the Veda, Sayana Acharya, who lived in the 14th century. This is Sayana’s explanation of the above hymn:

*ado viprakṛṣṭa-deśe kartumānam apūruṣaṁ nirmātrā puruṣeṇa rahitaṁ yad dāru dārumayaṁ puruṣottamākhyaṁ devatā-śarīraṁ sindhoḥ pāre samudra-tīre plavate jalasyopari vartate tad dāru he durhaṇo duḥkhena hananīya kenāpi hantum aśakya he stotaḥ ārabhasva ālambasva upāssvety arthaḥ tena dārumayena devenopāsyamānena parastavam atiśayena taraṇīyam utkṛṣṭaṁ vaiṣṇavaṁ lokaṁ gaccha*

**“Present in a distant place (*****ado*****), the creator who is beyond the perception of the senses, the Self-born who is without any human element, exists in a wooden form and is named Purushottam. O immortal panegyrist, take shelter of that wooden form of the Lord, and through His worship go to the supreme abode of Vishnu.”**

Some of these words require further explanation. The words *viprakṛṣṭa-deśe* mean “the supreme place.” The dictionary also defines the word *viprakṛṣṭa* as meaning “distant” or “not present.” In this case we should understand that it means, “beyond the perception of the jiva’s material senses.” This is stated in the *Īśopaniṣad*, where it is said that “though the Lord is distant, He is very close to us all” (*tad dure tad v antike*). The word *apūruṣa* means that the Lord is uncreated, that He is not a product of human activity.

In the *Sāṅkhyāyana-brāhmaṇa*, a variant of the Rig Veda verse is found --

*ādau yad dāru plavate sindhoḥ pāre apūruṣam*  
*tad ālambasva durdūno tena yāhi paraṁ sthalam*

**You who are afflicted by life in this world, take hold of that piece of wood, not fabricated by any human, which floats across the ocean from the beginning of the creation, and go to the supreme abode.**

The above is a literal translation of this verse, which is nevertheless more explicit than the earlier version. It has been further explained in the *Sāṅkhyāyana-bhāṣya* commentary:

*ādau viprakṛṣṭa-deśe vartamānaṁ yad dāru dāru-mayaṁ puruṣottamākhyaṁ devatā-śarīraṁ plavate jalasyopari vartate apūruṣam nirmātṛ-rahitatvena apūruṣaṁ tad ālambhasva durdūno he hotaḥ tena dārumayena devana upāsyamānenaiva paraṁ sthalam vaiṣṇavaṁ lokaṁ gacchety arthaḥ*

**“The self-created supreme person who is beyond the perception of the senses, who is self-born and beyond all mortal limitations, exists in a wooden form on the ocean’s shores where He is known as Purushottam. O performer of the sacrifice, worship this form of the Lord and, in so doing, go to the supreme abode of Vishnu.”**

The influence of the Rig Veda is also found in a verse of the *Utkala-khaṇḍa* (21.3):

*ya eṣa plavate dāruḥ sindhu-pāre hy apauruṣaḥ*  
*tam upāsya durārādhyaṁ muktiṁ yāti sudurlabhām*

**One who venerates the transcendental piece of wood that floated to the ocean shore, which is so hard to worship properly, will attain the rarest form of salvation.**

## Puri: the Lord’s capital city

Puri means “city.” It is the capital city of the Lord of the Universe. As such, it is considered a manifestation of God’s majesty or supreme opulence. This is natural, as it is the usual way one thinks of the Supreme Person – as a supreme ruler, the king of kings. For Gaudiya Vaishnavas, it is thus reminiscent of Dwaraka, where Krishna spent the last part of His life, leading the life of a king.

Sanatan Goswami has written the following glorification of Jagannath Deva in his *Bṛhad-bhāgavatāmṛta:*

*dāru brahma jagannātho bhagavān puruṣottame*  
*kṣetra nīlācale kṣārārṇava-tīre virājate*  
*mahāvibhūtimān rājyam autkalam pālayan svayam*  
*vyañjayan nija-māhātmyaṁ sadā sevaka-vatsalaḥ*  
*tasyānnaṁ pācitaṁ lakṣmyā svayaṁ bhuktvā dayālunā*  
*dattaṁ tena svabhaktebhyo labhyate deva-durlabham*  
*mahāprasāda-saṁjñaṁ ca tat-spṛṣṭaṁ yena kenacit*  
*yatra kutrāpi vā nītam avicāreṇa bhujyate*  
*aho tat-kṣetra-māhātmyaṁ gardabho caturbhujaḥ*  
*yatra praveśa-mātreṇa na kasyāpi punarbhavaḥ*  
*praphulla-puṇḍarīkākṣe tasminn evekṣite janaiḥ*  
*phalaṁ syād evam aśrauṣam āścaryaṁ pūrvam aśrutam*

**The Supreme Lord Jagannath, the wooden form of the Param Brahma, resides in the holy land known as Purushottam-Nilachala by the shores of the salt ocean. He lives there in great opulence, personally ruling over the kingdom of Orissa, revealing His glories to all and protecting His servants. He personally eats the food that is cooked by Lakshmi Devi herself and then kindly blesses His devotees with His remnants, which are unobtainable by the gods. These remnants are named “Maha Prasad” and can be honored without any consideration, no matter if they have been touched by an unclean person or carried over long distances. Not only is Lord Jagannath’s Maha Prasad glorious, but His abode Sri Kshetra is also glorious beyond compare. Even a donkey in that land has a four-armed Vishnu form. As soon as one enters that land, he is assured of never taking birth again. And if one looks upon the blooming lotus-eyed form of Jagannath, then he attains rewards that are amazing beyond anything ever before heard. (*****Bṛhad-bhāgavatāmṛta*** [**2.1.159-64**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bb/2.1.159)**)**

Lord Jagannath is naturally the life and soul of the people of Orissa. They believe that the Supreme Lord has appeared in the town of Purushottam Kshetra on the shores of the blue sea in the wooden form of Jagannath Deva in order to give them the shelter of His lotus feet, the source of freedom from lamentation, fear and mortality. As a result, in all their daily actions, they display a consciousness of Lord Jagannath’s presence. All of life’s major events, from the giving of the first solid food to a child (*anna-prāśana*) to the initiation of young Brahmins (*upanayana*) and marriage, incorporate the worship of Lord Jagannath and include praying to Him for His permission and blessings. When a couple is to be wed, the first guest invited to the wedding feast is Lord Jagannath, who is sent an official invitation. The last rites of *śrāddha* are conducted with Lord Jagannath’s prasad. In this way, all the rites of passage are executed with some connection to the Lord.

Orissa has no king other than Lord Jagannath Himself. No separate coronation ceremony was ever held for the Gajapati king, for he considered himself to be nothing more than a representative of the Lord. He would administer the affairs of state on behalf of the Lord, thinking himself to be the Lord’s servant. He clearly showed this every year when he swept the ground in front of Lord Jagannath’s car at the beginning of the Rathayatra festival. Even now, with the end of monarchies in democratic India, Lord Jagannath still remains the symbolic center and Puri the spiritual capital of the Orissan people.

Many times in history, foreigners and people belonging to other faiths attempted to attack and destroy Lord Jagannath’s temple, knowing that whoever controlled the temple would easily be able to extend his control over the whole of Orissa. Throughout the ages, the Orissan people put their own lives at risk to protect the Lord, to hide Him from His attackers, for the destruction of Jagannath would have meant the setting of the sun of their national pride and the end of the main inspiration of Orissan culture and identity from the Vedic age to the present day.

Though Puri thus resembles Dwaraka as the city of divine majesty and opulence, there is a secret spirit of sweetness in Puri as revealed by a verse of Umapati Dhara:

*ratna-cchāyā-cchurita-jaladhau mandire dvārakāyā*  
*rukmiṇyāpi prabala-pulakodbhedam āliṅgitasya*  
*viśvaṁ pāyān masṛṇa-yamunā-tīra-vānīra-kuñje*  
*rādhā-kelī-parimala-bhara-dhyāna-mūrcchā murāreḥ*

**In His house in Dwaraka, on the shores of the sparkling ocean sprinkled with gems, as Krishna Murari embraced His queen, Rukmini, He remembered the fragrance of the ecstasies He had enjoyed with Radha in the reeds by the banks of the black Yamuna waters; the hairs on His body stood on end and He fainted. May that faint protect you always.\[7\]**

In other words, though Puri is externally Dwaraka, it is the Dwaraka where Krishna’s memory of Vrindavan’s superiority flows like a powerful undercurrent. This is the mood of Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu and His followers, as shown in Sanatan’s *Bṛhad-bhāgavatāmṛta.*

## Sri Kshetra

Jagannath Puri has also been called Sri Kshetra since great antiquity. The word *śrī* refers to Vishnu’s *svarūpa-śakti*, Lakshmi Devi, the goddess of fortune. This means that the Lord’s opulence is fully manifest here. It also means that this land is under the influence of the Lord’s internal potency, as Lord Purushottam is never separated from His energies.

One can take the meaning of the word Sri even further to mean Srimati Radharani, who is the root of all the Lord’s internal energy. The entire land of Puri is permeated with memories of Lord Chaitanya’s last twenty-four years on this planet, when his *rādhā-bhāva* was the most intense. Ever since that time, Gaudiya Vaishnavas have had an unbreakable relationship with Puri. Devotees who worship the Lord in the conjugal mood, *madhura-rasa*, see that this land has been manifested out of her power and generosity.

Gadadhar Pandit is the form Radharani took to participate in Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s pastimes. Gadadhara Pandit took Kshetra sannyas in this holy land and committed himself to remain in Sri Kshetra without ever leaving it. Thus he lived at the Tota Gopinath temple, where he would read and give discourses on the Bhagavata to Lord Gaurasundara, the Supreme Person in the form of the person Bhagavata.

Orissa’s King Prataparudra surrendered himself completely to the moon of Nabadwip, Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. The King’s right-hand man, Raya Ramananda, was the first to have a direct vision of the united effulgence of the personification of “the highest perfection of divine love” (*mahā-bhāva-svarūpiṇī*) or Radha and “the king of sacred rapture” (*rasa-rāja*), Krishna, in Gaura Hari.

Jagannath Puri was inundated with the mercy of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, who is the combined form of Radha and Krishna in the age of Kali. Svarupa Damodar and Ramananda Raya were like His alter egos, who expanded His pastimes, which are like an appendix to the pastimes that the Supreme Lord performed in Vrindavan as Krishna. Lord Chaitanya is also the Lila Purushottam, or Supreme Person manifested in His pastimes, the holy land of Puri is also the highest of all the Lord’s abodes. For this reason it is also called Sri Purushottam.

After taking sannyas, Lord Gaurasundara took the name Sri Krishna Chaitanya. Then He displayed the most ecstatic and confidential aspects of this epilogue to Krishna’s pastimes in Sri Kshetra. Svarupa Damodar, Ramananda Raya, and their friends Rupa, Sanatan and Hari Das, their followers Raghunath, Sri Jiva and Krishna Das Kaviraj, all chose Gaurasundara as their *abhīṣṭa-deva* or worshipable deity. For this reason, the Gaurasundara who lived in Puri in the company of Svarupa Damodar and Ramananda Raya is considered to be a more wonderful and special manifestation than the one that appears in Nabadwip.

## Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, the mobile Jagannath

*śrīmac-caitanya-deva tvāṁ vande gaurāṅga-sundara*  
*śacīnandana māṁ trāhi yati-cūḍāmaṇe prabho*  
*ājānu-bāho smerāsya nīlācala-vibhūṣaṇa*  
*jagat-pravartita-svādu-bhagavan-nāma-kīrtana*  
*advaitācārya-saṁślāghin sārvabhaumābhinandaka*  
*rāmānanda-kṛta-prīta sarva-vaiṣṇava-bāndhava*  
*śrī-kṛṣṇa-caraṇāmbhoja-premāmṛta-mahāmbudhe*  
*namaste dīnadīnaṁ māṁ kadācit kiṁ smariṣyasi*

**O blessed Chaitanya Deva, I worship You who have appeared in a beautiful golden form. Deliver me, O son of Sachi, O master, O topmost member of the sannyas ashram. You have the physical features of greatness: Your long arms reach your knees and Your face is decorated with a smile. You are the ornament of the land of Nilachala. You have appeared in this world to inaugurate the chanting of Your relishable holy names. You are accompanied by Advaita Acharya Prabhu and You bring joy to Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya. You are delighted by the service rendered by Ramananda and are the friend of all the Vaishnavas. You are the great ocean of ambrosial love for the lotus feet of Sri Krishna. I bow down to You and beg You to remember me, some time or another, for I am the most wretched of the wretched.**  
**(Sanatan Goswami’s** ***Līlā-stava*** **104)**

Sanatan calls Jagannath the “beloved of Chaitanya” (*caitanya-vallabha*) in his *Līlā-stava*. In the same work, he gives Mahaprabhu the epithet, “ornament of the land of Nilachala” (*nīlācala-vibhūṣaṇa*). Vrindavan Das Thakur, who is sometimes called the Veda Vyasa of Mahaprabhu’s incarnation, called Lord Chaitanya the “mobile Jagannath” (*sacala-jagannātha*).

*mahānande sarva-loka jaya jaya bale*  
*āilā sacala-jagannātha nīlācale*  
*āpane śrī-jagannātha nyāsi-rūpa dhari*  
*nije saṅkīrtana-krīḍā kare avatari*

**In great ecstasy, all the people began to cheer, saying, “The moving Lord Jagannath has arrived in Nilachala. Lord Jagannath himself has taken the appearance of a sannyasi, incarnating in order to enjoy the pastime of singing His own holy names.” (Cbh** [**3.5.126**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cb-antya/5.126)**,** [**165**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cb-antya/5.165)**)**

Thus according to Gaudiya Vaishnava theology, Jagannath is the wooden, unmoving form of the Supreme Lord (*dāru-brahma*). His moving manifestation, the jewel of Nilachala, is Lord Sri Chaitanya Deva. When overcome by the mood of Radharani, Chaitanya Mahaprabhu would see Jagannath Deva as none other than the son of Nanda, the blue-black form of the Lord that enchants even Cupid. We should follow in His footsteps. It is thus perfectly natural that the devotees who follow Lord Chaitanya should hold Lord Jagannath and His land, Purushottam Kshetra, particularly dear. In particular, those devotees who worship the lord in the conjugal mood find that this land inspires their intimate feelings of love for the Supreme Lord and His consort.

*jagannātha hana kṛṣṇera ātma svarupa*  
*kintu ihāṅ dāru brahma sthāvara svarūpa*  
*tāṅhā saha ātmatā eka rūpa hañā*  
*kṛṣṇa eka tattva rūpa dui rūpa hañā*  
*saṁsāra tāraṇa hetu yei icchā śakti*  
*tāhāra milana kari ekatā yaiche prāpti*  
*sakala saṁsārī lokera karite uddhāra*  
*gaura jaṅgama rūpe kailā avatāra*  
*jagannāthera darśane khaṇḍāya saṁsāra*  
*saba deśera saba loka nāre āsibāra*  
*śrī kṛṣṇa caitanya prabhu deśe deśe yāñā*  
*saba loke nistārilā jaṅgama brahma hañā*

**There is no difference between Lord Jagannath and Krishna, but here Lord Jagannath is fixed as the Absolute Person appearing in wood. Therefore He does not move. Thus Lord Jagannath and Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, although appearing as two, are in fact one because They are both Krishna, who is One without a second. The supreme desire to deliver the entire world meets in both of Them, and for that reason also They are one and the same. To deliver all the materially contaminated people of the world, that same Krishna has descended, moving as Lord Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. By visiting Lord Jagannath one is freed from material existence, but not all men of all countries can come or be admitted here in Jagannath Puri. Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, however, moves from one country to another, either personally or through His representative. As the moving Brahman, He thus delivers all the people of the world. (CC** [**3.5.148-53**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-antya/5.148)**)**

Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya, a contemporary resident of Nilachala and the greatest logician and Vedanta scholar in India at the time recognized Gaura Hari as the *sacala-brahman*, “the moving form of Brahman.”

Of the twenty-four years after Mahaprabhu took sannyasa,

*aṣṭādaśa-varṣa kevala nīlācale sthiti*  
*āpani ācari jīve śikhāila bhakti*

**Mahaprabhu remained exclusively in Nilachala for the last eighteen years. There He practiced devotional service, teaching the world by His personal example. (CC** [**2.1.22**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/1.22)**)**

In the first six of these last years, Lord Chaitanya was based in Nilachala, but undertook several long pilgrimages. Thus, during this entire period, fortunate people were able to have the vision of both the moving Brahman (Mahaprabhu) and the non-moving Brahman (Jagannath). Devotees from all over India came to Mahaprabhu in Nilachala, just like rivers flow to the sea.

Reminders of Mahaprabhu’s career in Purushottam are found everywhere throughout the Puri temple. For instance, the paved area around the main temple and within the inner surrounding wall known as the Kurma Berha is known as the Sri Chaitanya Mandap or the Sri Chaitanya Mandal. This is how the people of Puri commonly refer to it when talking to each other.

The entire town of Puri is filled with reminders of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s pastimes. The temple of Jagannath is still known as *gaura-bāṭa* and the surrounding neighborhood is called Gaurbat Sahi. Besides this, even now, amidst the ruins of the old palace, worship of deities of the dancing forms of Gauranga and Nityananda that have been there since the time of Prataparudra is still conducted.

In an Orissan work dating from the time of Mahaprabhu named *Śūnya-saṁhitā*,\[8\] it is said that Lord Chaitanya had 12,000 followers in Orissa during His lifetime. Throughout Orissa, Bhagavata readings are always preceded by kirtans glorifying Gaura-Nitai and a great number of maths of Gaudiya sadhus can be found everywhere in Orissa.

There is probably not a single village in the entire state where there is no temple of Chaitanya Deva. According to Nagendranath Basu, there are more than 800 temples in Orissa in which a deity of Gauranga is worshiped.\[9\] One Western-educated Indian scholar has written, “Orissa was Chaitanya and Chaitanya was Orissa. The king, the subjects, the high and the low – all were mad after him.”\[10\] M. T. Kennedy writes in his *The Chaitanya Movement*: “Orissa became such a stronghold of the Chaitanya faith that today the name of Gauranga is more commonly reverenced and worshiped among the masses in Orissa than in Bengal itself.”\[11\]

The town of Jagannath Puri is thus the home of both the non-moving Brahman, Lord Jagannath, and the moving Brahman, Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu.
