## Chapter 3 - The Nila Madhava Legends

## The Nila Madhava legends

Many accounts are given of Lord Jagannath’s appearance, both in popular oral traditions as well as in the more authoritative Puranic texts. The most popular and widely accepted version is found in an Orissan book called *Deula-tolā* (“The building of the temple”), written by Shishu Krishna Das in the 18thcentury. It combines the legends of the *Utkala-khaṇḍa* and *Mādalā-pāñjī*. What follows is based on that account:

In the first half of the creator god Brahma’s life (*parārdha*), the Lord of the Chaturvyuha took the form of Nila Madhava and appeared in Shankha Kshetra in order to give His blessings to the most fallen sinners of this world.

In the second *parārdha*, in the first Satya Yuga of the first Manvantara, a king named Indradyumna took birth in the Solar Dynasty. He ruled over the land of Malwa, making his capital in Avanti (Ujjain). Being a great devotee of Vishnu, Indradyumna became very eager to have a direct vision of the Lord. One day, Lord Vishnu sent a messenger to Indradyumna’s court to tell him about Nila Madhava’s glories. On hearing about Nila Madhava, the king sent many Brahmins out to look for Him. These Brahmins traveled to the four corners of India, but failed in their attempts to find the Lord in His Nila Madhava form. After some time, they had all returned to the capital city empty handed and only Indradyumna’s royal priest, Vidyapati, was left still looking for the elusive deity.

Vidyapati had traveled to a great many places before he came to the land of a non-Aryan tribe known as the Shabaras. One of these tribal people, whose name was Vishwavasu, took him in as a guest in his home. Vishwavasu’s daughter Lalita personally served Vidyapati and eventually Vishwavasu asked him to accept her as his wife.

Vidyapati observed that Vishwavasu left the house every evening and did not return until noon the next day. When he came back, he smelled of camphor, sandalwood and incense. Vidyapati asked his wife Lalita where her father went and she answered that he went to worship Nila Madhava. Vidyapati became excited at the prospect of finally finding Nila Madhava and begged his father-in-law to allow him to see the Deity. Finally, Lalita convinced Vishwavasu to take Vidyapati with him, but first the suspicious Shabara blindfolded the Brahmin so that he would not remember the path they were to take.

Before they left, however, Lalita cleverly wrapped some sesame seeds in her husband’s cloth. Vidyapati dropped these seeds on the path as he was being led through the woods. When they arrived in a clearing before Nila Madhava, Vishwavasu untied the blindfold and Vidyapati was able to drink in Nila Madhava’s beauty through his eyes. He began to recite prayers and praises and dance in ecstasy.

The Shabara left Vidyapati alone to pray to Nila Madhava while he went deeper into the forest to look for suitable fruits, roots and flowers to offer his Deity. While he was gone, the Brahmin saw a crow fall from a tree into a nearby lake and die. Amazingly, he saw the bird immediately take on a four-armed Vishnu form and ascend to Vaikuntha, gaining the liberation known as *sārūpya* in the very instant that it gave up its body. Feeling the great spiritual potency of the place, Vidyapati thought that he should do the same thing. He climbed the same tree and was about to jump into the lake when he heard a disembodied voice say, “O Brahmin! Before you die, you must first tell Indradyumna Maharaj that you have found Nila Madhava.”

Soon afterward, the Shabara Vishwavasu returned with fruits and flowers from the forest and started to do Nila Madhava’s puja. Nila Madhava then spoke to him, saying, “Dear Vishwavasu, long have I accepted your forest fruits and flowers with great pleasure, but now I wish to enjoy the regal opulence that only King Indradyumna can afford Me.”

Blind with grief at the prospect of losing his service to Nila Madhava, Vishwavasu locked his son-in-law in his house to prevent him from going to see the king. However, after repeated requests from his daughter, the Shabara finally accepted the divine will and released Vidyapati. The Brahmin immediately went to the court of King Indradyumna and told him that he had found Nila Madhava. In great joy, the king assembled a party to bring the Deity back to Avantipur.

The king’s party was able to follow the trail of mustard plants that had grown from Vidyapati’s seeds, but when they came to its end, they found nothing there. Nila Madhava was gone. The enraged King immediately laid siege to the Shabara village and arrested Vishwavasu, but a voice from the sky said, “Stop harassing the Shabaras. Build a temple on the blue mountain for the worship of the Daru Brahma. You will never see Me as Nila Madhava, but rather You will have a vision of Me in My wooden form.”

Indradyumna built a temple of stone. In order to transport the stone, he had a road built from a quarry in Baula Mala to Nilachala. He constructed the temple in the navel of the conch shell of Sri Kshetra. The temple was built with a foundation 90 feet deep and the tower rose 180 feet above the ground. At the top of the temple tower, he had a pinnacle fashioned in the shape of a water pot (*kalaśa*) with Lord Krishna’s chakra above it. He had the entire temple covered in gold. Indradyumna also founded the Brahmin village of Ramakrishnapur for the temple servants.

When the time came to inaugurate the temple, Indradyumna went to Brahmaloka to ask Lord Brahma to perform the ritual sacrifices and ceremonies. He appointed Suradeva and Gala Madhava to act as his regents over the kingdom in his absence. Indradyumna had to wait a long time to see Lord Brahma and during this time, the temple he had built sank into the sand. Gala Madhava had the temple pulled out, but falsely claimed to have built it himself.

However, on the sacred fig tree by the temple was a crow named Bhushandi, who age after age chants the name of Rama and witnesses everything that transpires. The crow testified, “It was Indradyumna who built this temple. It sank into the sands during his absence and Gala Madhava came and lifted it out.” Because Gala Madhava had lied, Lord Brahma condemned him to remain outside the temple, to the west of Indradyumna Sarovar.

Indradyumna requested Lord Brahma to ritually consecrate the temple. In response to his request, Brahma said, “This land of Sri Kshetra has been manifested by the Supreme Lord and His internal potencies. He Himself is self-manifest, so there is nothing I can or need to do in order to consecrate this temple. Lord Jagannath and His holy abode are eternally manifest within this material world purely by His mercy. Nevertheless, I will place a flag on the very top of the temple pinnacle. Those who see this flag from a distance and pay their respects to the Lord will easily attain liberation.”

## The Lord appears in His wooden form

King Indradyumna became so discouraged at not being able to see Nila Madhava that he lay down on a grass mat, determined to fast to the death. Lord Jagannath then appeared to him in a dream and said, “Do not worry. I am floating on the sea and will soon be arriving at the place known as Banki Muhana.”

The next day, the King went with his army to the beach and there saw the Daru Brahma, a huge log marked with the four symbols of Vishnu – the conch, lotus, club and discus. The King was very powerful, but even with the help of all his elephants and foot soldiers was unable to move the log. Again Jagannath appeared to the King in a dream and said, “You must go and fetch My servant Vishwavasu, who used to worship Me in My Nila Madhava form. Bring him and a golden chariot and place them in front of the Daru Brahma.”

The King did as he was told. The Shabara Vishwavasu stood on one side of the Daru Brahma*,* the Brahmin Vidyapati on the other. All around them, everyone began chanting the holy names of the Lord. The King himself went to the foot of the Daru Brahma log and prayed to Him to get on the golden chariot. Then, the Daru Brahma consented to be lifted by Vidyapati and Vishwavasu alone.

The King had the chariot pulled to a predetermined place and there Lord Brahma started the performance of a sacrifice. Narasingha Deva himself was present on the sacrificial altar. It is said that this sacrifice was performed at the Gundicha temple and that the Nrisingha deity in the adjoining temple there is said to be this original Narasingha Deva murti.\[12\]

Indradyumna Maharaj called together many expert craftsmen to transform the Daru Brahma into a worshipable murti, but none of them was able to lay even a finger on the divine piece of timber. Every time they tried, their tools would break. Finally, the Lord himself came to the King, disguised as an old wood worker named Ananta Maharana. He gave the King his word that if he could work uninterrupted behind closed doors, he would complete the work in a mere twenty-one days. He also told the king that all the other carpenters who were there should be engaged in building three cars to carry the deities when they were finished. The King had the divine piece of wood placed inside the temple and the doors were locked with Ananta Maharana inside. The King promised not to open them before the twenty-one days were up.

After only two weeks, however, the temple fell silent. The sounds of chisels, hammers and saws that had been heard regularly up till then stopped. The King became so worried that he consulted with his queen about what to do. She told him to open the temple doors and see what was happening. The King’s ministers repeatedly advised him against doing so, but he ignored them and forced the locked doors open.

When the King looked inside, he found that the old craftsman had disappeared but that he had left behind three murtis carved out of the Daru Brahma*.* When he came closer, he observed that the deities’ hands had no fingers, and that they had no feet. One of his senior ministers turned to the King and said, “This craftsman was none other than Lord Jagannath Himself. Because you broke your promise and opened the door a week ahead of time, He has appeared to you in this unfinished form.”

The King felt as though he had committed a great offense. In order to expiate himself of the sin, he once again lay down on the grass mat, intending to fast to the death. Once again Lord Jagannath appeared to him and said, “Listen, my dear King. This is the imperishable form of the Daru Brahma named Purushottam, who lives in this land of Nilachala for all eternity. I appear in this world in twenty-four different places in My deity incarnation (*arcāvatāra*). In each of them, I descend with My own holy abode.

*apāṇi-pādo javano grahītā*  
*paśyaty acakṣuḥ sa śṛṇoty akarṇaḥ*  
*sa vetti vedyaṁ na ca tasyāsti vettā*  
*tam āhur agryaṁ puruṣaṁ mahāntam*

**“Though the Lord has neither hands nor feet, He takes and He runs. He sees without eyes and hears without ears. He knows all that is to be known, but nobody knows Him. This is the one they call the original and greatest being, the Purushottam. (*****Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*****,** [**3.19**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sveta-bs/3.19)**)**

“According to this verse of the Upanishads, I have no material hands or feet and yet I accept the service and offerings of My devotees with spiritual hands and feet that are invisible to ordinary people. In this way, I have come to do good for all the world.

“I have descended to fulfill My promise. I have tricked you into breaking your promise to create a sweet, memorable pastime surrounding My appearance. When devotees whose eyes are smeared with the salve of love look upon Me with the desire to relish My sweetness, I will appear to them in My form as Shyamasundar. Since you wish to worship Me in great opulence, you may occasionally decorate Me with hands and feet made of silver or gold. Still, I remind you that My body is itself the ornament of all ornaments.”

The king felt that the purpose of his life had been fulfilled by the Lord’s words and so he prayed to Him as follows: “May the descendants of the elderly craftsman who carved these three deities be engaged in building their cars for all time to come. May their generations never dwindle!”

Lord Jagannath smiled and said, “So be it.” Then the Lord continued, “The descendants of Vishwavasu, who served Me so faithfully in My form as Nila Madhava, will henceforth be known as Dayitas and will continue to serve Me in My Jagannath form. The descendants of Vidyapati through his Brahmin wife will be My pujaris, and those who are his descendants through Lalita will be My cooks and will be known as *sūārs* or *sūpakāras*.”

Indradyumna said to Jagannath, “Please grant me one other boon. I wish that Your temple remain closed for only three hours a day, so that people can come at almost any hour of the day or night to see You. And I also wish that You should be given offerings of food all day long, so that Your divine hands are never dry!”

Jagannath again said, “So be it.” And then, “Now ask for something for yourself.”

The King said, “I ask that no one ever be able to claim Your temple as his own personal property. I therefore wish to die without any children to carry on my line.”

Once again, Lord Jagannath agreed to grant the King this boon.

## Other accounts from the scriptures

These are the broad outlines of the story as told in the *Deula-tolā*, but other details are found in many other texts, such as the *Atharva-veda, Brahma-purāṇa, Skanda-purāṇa (Utkala-khaṇḍa*)*, Kūrma-purāṇa, Padma-purāṇa, Bhaviṣya-purāṇa (Puruṣottama-māhātmya*), *Nīlādri-mahodaya,* and *Viṣṇu-rahasya.* These books all contain sections glorification of Sri Kshetra and Lord Jagannath. The land of Purushottam is also mentioned in the *Matsya-purāṇa, Varāha-purāṇa, Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa,* and other Puranic texts.

In the *Utkala-khaṇḍa* of the *Nārada-purāṇa* (52.12) we find the following verse in which the Lord answers a question by Lakshmi Devi:

*pratimāṁ tatra tāṁ dṛṣṭvā*  
*svayaṁ devena nirmitam*  
*anāyāsena vai yānti*  
*bhavanaṁ me tato narāḥ*

**In the great holy place known as Purushottam, which has no equal in the three worlds, there is an image of the Lord that was carved by the Lord Himself. Anyone who beholds that form easily goes to My abode.**

In this same section of the *Nārada-purāṇa* (54.22-65), it is said that Indradyumna was a devotee who came to Sri Kshetra in order to worship Lord Vishnu. On coming, he performed an Ashvamedha sacrifice, gave land and cows to the Brahmins and built a palace-like temple. He was quite troubled about what deity should be installed there. In a dream he was told that he should go look on the seashore and he would find what he was looking for. When he came to the beach, he saw that a magnificent tree had washed ashore. Standing beside the tree was the Lord Himself in the form of a Brahmin boy accompanied by the divine craftsman, Vishwakarma. On the Lord’s orders, Vishwakarma carved the three images of Jagannath, Balaram and Subhadra from the divine piece of timber. These three images were then installed in Indradyumna’s temple in the midst of a great kirtan festival.

A lengthy version of the legend is given in the *Skanda-purāṇa’s Utkala-khaṇḍa* (chapters 1-19): After creating the world of moving and unmoving beings, Lord Brahma wondered what opportunities he could provide for these beings to be liberated from the threefold miseries. He took shelter of Lord Vishnu, who said to him, “In this world, I eternally reside in the land of Purushottam Kshetra on the blue mountain by the ocean, a secret place unknown even to the gods. Any living being who sees Me there will immediately find salvation.”

Lord Brahma went to Nilachala. He was watching a crow bathe in Rohini Kund and drink its water. He was amazed to see that as soon as the crow looked on the Lord’s murti, it immediately attained *sārūpya-mukti* and became an eternal associate of the Lord.

Yamaraj heard about this and came to Nilachala to see for himself. Lakshmi Devi told him kindly that anyone who left his body in Purushottam Kshetra would be outside of his jurisdiction. Lakshmi told Lord Yamaraj that for the entire first *parārdha*, she would stay with Nila Madhava in a murti made of black stone, but by the Svayambhuva Manvantara of the Shweta-varaha-kalpa of the second *parārdha*, during the rule of King Indradyumna, a fifth generation descendant of Lord Brahma himself, they would have disappeared.

In due course of time, Indradyumna was born in the city of Avanti. From his childhood, he wondered where on earth he would be able to see God Himself with his mortal eyes. He asked this question of everyone he met, until finally one sadhu pilgrim told him to go to Sri Kshetra where he could have darshan of Nila Madhava. Indradyumna gave his priest’s brother, Vidyapati, the responsibility of finding this deity.

Vidyapati came to Nilachala and learned that a certain Vishwavasu lived on the nearby island of the Shabaras and worshiped Lord Nila Madhava. He sent a message to King Indradyumna with this information. Indradyumna set off for Nilachala, but before he could get there, he heard that both the blue mountain and the deity, Nila Madhava, had disappeared into the sand.

In Nilachala, Indradyumna received instructions from Narada Muni, who told him to go establish a temple for Adi Narasingha in order to eliminate all obstacles to his objectives. Vishwakarma built this temple beside Nilakantha Shiva. The King then performed a thousand Ashvamedha sacrifices in front of this temple for the satisfaction of the Lord who holds a mace in His hand. Immediately upon completion of these sacrifices, Indradyumna heard that an extraordinary tree marked with the Lord’s conch and discus had appeared on the shore. This tree was in fact a transformation of one of the hairs that had fallen from the body of Lord Vishnu in Shwetadwip.

Indradyumna had a dream in which he saw that the Lord’s deity form would come from this piece of timber. Narada told Indradyumna to place the piece of wood on a great altar and worship it while a sankirtan festival was underway. As Indradyumna carried out this instruction, a disembodied voice ordered him to lock a certain old carpenter in the altar room with the divine piece of wood for fifteen days. Indradyumna followed this instruction and on the full moon day of Jyeshtha, opened the door to see Balaram, holding the mace, club, discus and lotus, Subhadra, holding a lotus flower signifying peace and blessings, and Lord Jagannath, holding the conch, discus, mace and lotus.

The *Kapila-saṁhitā* version of the legend follows the *Utkala-khaṇḍa* almost exactly.

The *Nīlādri-mahodaya* (chapter 4) gives somewhat different details, though the broad outline remains the same. There is said that after fifteen days, the Lord Himself manifested on the altar in seven different forms (*saptadhā-mūrti*) as Janardan, Baladeva, Bhadra, Sudarshan, Vishwadhatri, Lakshmi and Madhava. Indradyumna found these seven wooden deities in the workshop, but no craftsman.

The *Nīlādri-mahodaya* describes the deities as Indradyumna beheld them. Lord Jagannath had the color of a dark cloud, with eyes like large, blooming lotus flowers. He stood on a lotus seat with His arms held up, but His hands were hidden. Lord Balaram had a seven-headed snake over his head, his color was the white of a conch shell and his eyes were like lotus flowers. He also stood on a lotus seat and held up his arms, though his hands were hidden. The beautiful Subhadra, maintainer of the devotees, was similar in form, except that her arms were by her sides and her color was that of kunkum.

The other deities are described as follows: Sudarshan appears like a column. Madhava is a small murti. The smiling Lakshmi Devi appears with four arms; two of them hold lotus flowers, the other two are held in the gestures of giving blessings and bestowing fearlessness. She sits on a lotus pedestal and is surrounded by four elephants that constantly bathe her from jugs held in their trunks.

The goddess Vishwadhatri also stands on a lotus pedestal. Her right hand is in the gesture of knowledge (*jñāna-mudrā*), while the left hand holds a lotus flower. Her color is an effulgent white.

In the *Padma-purāṇa,* the following description is found: After ruling over the kingdom of Kanchi for many, many years, Ratnagriva finally became indifferent to worldly wealth and power. One night, he saw a Brahmin ascetic in a dream, and indeed, the very next day, a Brahmin of exactly the same appearance came to his court. This Brahmin told the King of the glories of Purushottam Kshetra, where even the tribal archers, the Bhils, had attained four-armed forms and liberation.

Once a Bhil youth named Prithu climbed a jambu tree in order to pick the fruits, but from that vantage point he saw a temple made of gold and jewels. The boy went inside the temple and beheld the Lord with his symbols of mace, conch, discus, lotus and Sharnga bow. He picked up a bit of the Lord’s prasad that had fallen to the ground and tasted it. When he looked again at the Lord, he immediately took a Vishnu-like four-armed form. The other Bhils heard from him how it had happened and they immediately did as he, taking prasad and gazing at the Lord. They all thus attained four-armed Vishnu forms. Since Prithu had discovered the temple, the rest of the Bhils worked together to salvage it from the jungle and reestablish its former glory. Thus the *Padma-purāṇa* (*Pātāla-khaṇḍa,* 9) also talks about the salvaging of an already built temple.

## Sarala Das’ version of the story

There is another version of the legend of Lord Jagannath’s origins that is popular in Orissa. Sarala Das, the author of the 15th century Orissan translation of the Mahabharata, made a connection between Lord Krishna's disappearance and the appearance of Lord Jagannath.

In his *Muṣalī-parva,* Sarala first establishes on the basis of scripture that Krishna left behind a seemingly material body upon completion of His manifest pastimes. Cited is the account of Krishna being cursed by the sage Durvasa Muni that all the parts of His body would be impervious to any weapon except the soles of His feet,\[13\]where He was finally “shot” by the hunter Jara.\[14\]

Sarala Das then goes on to write that Krishna’s body did not entirely burn in the cremation fire despite the best efforts of the Pandava brothers,\[15\] but left a piece of unburned tissue around His navel. Adivine voice from the heavens instructed them to set the unburned flesh afloat in the ocean. This remnant of Krishna’s body floated around India from Dwaraka until it washed ashore in Puri at the Chakra Tirtha. The tribal chieftain, Jara Shabara, found these remains and worshiped them as Nila Madhava. According to popular belief, this unburned portion of Krishna’s body still remains inside Lord Jagannath’s body as the Nabhi Brahma, being transferred from the old Jagannath into the new at the time of the Nava Kalevara.

In the 16th century, Atibori Jagannath Das followed Sarala Das in his *Dāru-brahma Gīta*. He wrote there that after Lord Krishna’s demise, His dead body was carried by the Pandavas to Nilagiri on a sandalwood stretcher, the wood from which they used to cremate it. Though the fire burned for five days, all that burned of Krishna’s body wer His hands and feet. A heavenly voice then told the Pandava brothers to set the remains afloat in the sea, which they did. Krishna's half-burned body floated ashore at the Banki Muhana where it was rescued by Basu Shabara, who placed it under the banyan tree by Rohini Kund and began to worship it. From this point on, both Sarala Das and Jagannath Das resume the story of Nila Madhava as given above.

Vaishnavas have good reasons for not accepting Sarala Das’ version, for not only does he interpolate unauthorized stories of his own invention in the Mahabharata, but his explanation for why Krishna’s navel did not burn is totally unacceptable to Vaishnava siddhanta. In several places in his Mahabharata, Sarala Das shows a misunderstanding of Krishna’s relations with the Vraja gopis, the young married girls of Vrindavan. Here again, he attributes the failure of Krishna’s body to burn to sinful reactions incurred from engaging in illicit sexual behavior. Like so many other people who have been deprived of the mercy of the pure devotee, Sarala Das takes Krishna’s loving exchanges with His devotees to be the adulterous activities of a lusty human being with no moral sense. In fact, Krishna’s activities with the gopis are a transcendental manifestation of His divine loving play with His pure devotees.

Sarala Das’ version of the origins of Jagannath is evidently well-known in Orissa, but it is not approved by the followers of the Bhagavatam. In 1969, Srila Bhakti Promode Puri Maharaj wrote a lengthy article responding to a statement based on the above account that was published in connection with the Nava Kalevara ceremonies of that year: \[16\] “The legend says that the navel of Lord Krishna did not burn fully during cremation of His dead body and came floating on the sea in the shape of a log of wood. The image of Lord Jagannath was built from this log of wood.”

In response to this statement, Puri Maharaj wrote,

The Supreme Personality of Godhead is the embodiment of eternity, absolute knowledge and unlimited transcendental bliss. His form is eternal, the manifestation of absolute reality; it is indestructible and ever bereft of any material qualities. However, we observe that the materially conditioned living entities are often put into confusion about this fact.

In the *Mausala-parva* of the Mahabharata, the *mausala-līlā* or Apastime of the club@ is described. There it is said that after Lord Krishna left His body, Arjuna performed the cremation ceremony and other connected rituals. Nevertheless, to understand this topic and grasp its esoteric conclusion, one must approach a pure devotee and self-realized soul. Srila Krishna Das Kaviraj Goswami writes in the Chaitanya Charitamrita:

*tabe sanātan sab siddhānta puchilā*  
*bhāgavata-siddhānta gūḍha sakali kahilā*  
*hari-vaṁśe kahiyāche goloke nitya-sthiti*  
*indra āsi karila jabe śrī-kṛṣṇere stuti*  
*mausala-līlā, ār kṛṣṇa-antardhān*  
*keśāvatār, ār jata viruddha vyākhyān*  
*mahiṣī-haraṇ ādi, sab māyāmay*  
*vyākhyā śikhāila jaiche susiddhānta hay*

**Sanatan Goswami then inquired from Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu about all the different conclusions of the revealed scriptures, and the Lord explicitly communicated to him the true position of the Bhagavatam. He told him about the descriptions of the eternal spiritual planet of Goloka Vrindavan found in the** ***Hari-vaṁśa*****, as given by Lord Indra in his glorification of Lord Krishna after the Govardhana lila. Mahaprabhu explained pastimes such as the destruction of the Yadu dynasty (*****mausala-līlā*****), Lord Krishna=s disappearance, Lord Krishna and Balaram=s appearance from Kshirodakashayi Vishnu=s black and white hairs, the kidnapping of the Queens of Dwaraka, etc., in conformity with the correct scriptural conclusions. (*****Chaitanya Charitamrita*** [**2.23.115-118**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/23.115)**)**

My merciful spiritual master, His Divine Grace, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati Prabhupada explains this in his *Anubhāṣya* commentary: AThe *mausala-līlā* pastime in the Mahabharata, Lord Sri Krishna=s disappearance, the incarnation of the hairs, the kidnapping of His queens and so on are fictitious stories; they are not eternal, transcendental pastimes. They have been narrated for the express purpose of deluding the foolish, the gross materialists, atheists, and demoniac forces antagonistic towards the Supreme Lord.@

The Krishna sun never truly sets. He is free from all material influences, the fully independent, self-willed Supreme Personality of Godhead. When He chooses to manifest His multifarious pastimes of birth, the *rasa-līlā*, the slaying of Kamsa, marrying Queen Rukmini and so on, to be seen by one and all in a particular material universe (*brahmāṇḍa*), He does so primarily for the transcendental pleasure of His pure, self-realized devotees. Yet when He withdraws these pastimes, disappearing from public vision, these unalloyed devotees are plunged into an ocean of grief. Both the Lord=s permanent pastimes in the spiritual world, which are categorized according to the times of day even though they have no connection to material time, as well as His nativity pastimes and so on within the material world, are eternal. The former, however, are called the *aprakaṭa*, or Aunmanifest@ lila*,* while the latter are called the *prakaṭa* or Amanifest@ pastimes. When the eternal *prakaṭa* pastimes, beginning with the Lord=s birth, are withdrawn and disappear from one particular material universe, they simultaneously begin in another material universe, just as when the sun sets in one part of the world, it is dawning in another.

Sri Krishna is the controller of time and is thus never subjected to the cycle of birth and death. So any stories of His cremation and the floating of His half-burned body in the ocean must be considered figments of the imagination.

## Another legend about how Lord Jagannath took His form

The following is a popular story about the appearance of Lords Jagannath, Baladeva and Subhadra. It is not found in any Purana that I know of, \[17\] but as it illustrates the mood of Krishna in Dvaraka when feeling separation from Vrindavan, it suits the mood of the Gaudiya Vaishnavas.

Once upon a time, Rukmini Devi noticed that Krishna was crying in His sleep and calling out the name of Radha.

*ratna-cchāyā-cchurita-jaladhau mandire dvārakāyā*  
*rukmiṇyāpi prabala-pulakodbhedam āliṅgitasya \|*  
*viśvaṁ pāyān masṛṇa-yamunā-tīra-vānīra-kuñje*  
*rādhā-kelī-parimala-bhara-dhyāna-mūrcchā murāreḥ \|\|*

**On the shores of the ocean, sprinkled with sparkling gems, in His palace in Dvaraka, the hairs on His body stood on end in the embrace of none other than Rukmini; Krishna Murari remembered the fragrance of ecstasies He had enjoyed with Radha in the reeds by the banks of the black Yamuna waters and fainted. May that faint protect you always.**

Rukmini was concerned and awakened her husband. She asked Him what was wrong, but He gave no clear answer. He said, “I don’t remember” and went back to sleep. It became a matter of some concern to the 16,000 queens, who thought, “We are in no way inferior to any woman in the world, in beauty, culture or nobility. How then can our beloved husband be thinking of some other woman in His dreams? Who is this woman?”

Satyabhama said, “I believe that there was a cowherd girl named Radha in Vrindavan who was once our husband’s beloved.”

The queens of Dvaraka then went to Rohini Devi to find out more about Krishna’s pastimes with Srimati Radharani in Vraja. Since Rohini had been living in Vraja during Krishna’s youth, she could tell them what had transpired there. At first, however, Rohini was reluctant to answer their questions. She said, “I was in Vrindavan when all these things happened, and so I know all about them. Even so, Krishna is like my own son, so how can I talk about His love affairs? If He or Balaram should walk in, I would be terribly embarrassed.”

Nevertheless, the queens insisted and Rohini was unable to deny them their request. So they made Subhadra stand guard at the entrance to the queens’ quarters and, while Krishna was holding court, Rohini began to describe the Lord’s wonderful activities with Radha and the other gopis.

Krishna always appears wherever His pastimes are being described and, sure enough, He and Balaram left the royal court and hurried to the inner chambers. When the divine brothers saw their sister Subhadra standing at the door, they stood beside side her and began listening intently to the descriptions given by Rohini Devi.

The queens were so absorbed in listening themselves that they did not even notice the arrival of Krishna and Balaram. Rohini’s storytelling was so sweet and engaging that Krishna, Balaram and Subhadra lost all consciousness of the external world. In their ecstasy, their arms and legs withdrew into their bodies until they took the forms that they have in Puri. Krishna’s Sudarshan Chakra was also so ecstatic that he melted and was transformed into a staff.

At this moment, Devarshi Narada appeared on the scene and, seeing the wonderful forms their Lordships had taken, became overwhelmed with amazement and joy. His voice cracked with emotion as he said, “Oh my Lord! What wonderful new pastime have You devised today? I have never seen such a beautiful and wonderful form in my life. I like it so much that I pray You never to let it disappear from the face of this earth. May it remain somewhere for all time as a testimony to the wonders of the gopis’ love for You.”

The Supreme Lord is always sympathetic to the wishes of His devotees and could not leave Narada’s request unfulfilled. He said, “My dear Narada, so be it. King Indradyumna performed austerities for so long and Brahma has asked Me to fulfill his desire by appearing in Nilachala in a wooden form. And Bimala Devi has also been engaged in penances that have pleased Me. I have agreed to appear in Nilachala to distribute My remnants to all and sundry. Now I have a third reason to appear in Nilachala, in this particular form.” So this is why Lord Krishna manifested these very forms again in Nilachala.

Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, always absorbed in the mood of Radharani, saw Jagannath as Radha’s lover, Shyamasundar. This caused Him to experience the ecstasies of divine love. And just as Krishna became totally absorbed in listening to Rohini’s description of His own pastimes with the gopis, Chaitanya Mahaprabhu would forget the world whenever He heard these subjects being discussed. The ecstatic reactions on His body caused him to sometimes take on a form like that of a tortoise, with its head and limbs withdrawn. Sometimes the opposite would happen and all His limbs would become distended and His body would appear to lengthen. Krishna Das Kaviraj Goswami has described all these amazing ecstasies in the Chaitanya Charitamrita in the [17th chapter](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-antya/17) of the *Antya-līlā.*

*anudghāṭya dvāra-trayam uru ca bhitti-trayam aho*  
*vilaṅghyoccaiḥ kāliṅgika-surabhi-madhye nipatitaḥ*  
*tanūdyat-saṅkocāt kamaṭha iva kṛṣṇoru-virahād*  
*virājan gaurāṅgo hṛdaya udayan māṁ madayati*

**Without opening the three doors, Gauranga managed to get past the three walls and fell down amongst the Tailanga cows; His body shrunk and His limbs retracted into His body making Him look like a tortoise. This is how Gauranga acted under the influence of intense separation from Krishna. This memory rises in my heart and drives me mad with separation from Him. (*****Gaurāṅga-stava-kalpa-taru,*** **5)**

## Chapter 4 - The Jagannath Trinity

*śrī-jagannātha nīlādri-śiro-mukuṭa-ratna he*  
*dāru-brahman ghana-śyāma prasīda puruṣottama*  
*praphulla-puṇḍarīkākṣa lavaṇābdhi-taṭāmṛta*  
*guṭikodara māṁ pāhi nānā-bhoga-purandara*  
*nijādhara-sudhā-dāyinn indradyūmna-prasādita*  
*subhadrālolana-vyagra rāmānuja namo=stu te*  
*guṇḍicā-rathayātrādi-mahotsava-vivardhana*  
*bhakta-vatsala vande tvāṁ guṇḍicā-ratha-maṇḍanam*  
*dīna-hīna-mahā-nīca-dayārdrīkṛta-mānasa*  
*nitya-nūtana māhātmya-darśin caitanya-vallabha*  
*namaḥ*

**O Lord Jagannath! O crest-jewel of the blue mountain! O wooden form of Brahman! O dark-skinned Lord! Supreme Person! Be merciful to me. You have blooming lotus eyes; You relish your residence on the shores of the salt ocean; You have a pot belly from relishing all the various kinds of food offerings. Deliver me. You bestow the nectar of Your own lips to all; You were satisfied by the service of King Indradyumna; Obeisance to You, the younger brother of Balaram, always eager to accept the sisterly affection of Subhadra, You increase everyone’s joy with the annual festivals in the Gundichatemple and on the Rathayatracart; I worship You, who take care of Your devotees, who adorn the chariot that takes You to Gundicha. Your mind is moist with compassion for all the most fallen and most wretched; You are ever new; You reveal your glories; You are the beloved of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. I bow down to You. (*****Līlā-stava*****103)**

## The transcendental nature of the Lord’s deity form

The transcendental, non-dual supreme truth never appears within the limits of material time or place. The Vedic literature calls him the Inconceivable. The empiricists, researchers and historians who are unable to understand this truth attribute a beginning to that which is beginningless. They try to find the Param Brahma, who is outside history and immeasurable, within the parameters of unreliable historical data. They thus fall into guesswork and speculation. Is it any wonder, then, that they deceive themselves and others, falling away from the path of the truth? The Vedic literature repeatedly advises us to give up the attempt to know the beginnings of the beginningless and to understand the material history of that which is transcendental to history. We must listen to the instructions of the scripture from someone who incarnates the scriptural message. One who abandons this process and simply tries to satisfy his curiosity is sure to be bewildered.

The Supreme Lord is one without a second. He is not subject to the law of duality. He is the master of the illusory power that reigns within the creation. He is not limited by time and space or by our subjective individual perceptions. He appears within this world in a manner that is controlled by His own incomprehensible, ineffable, divine powers. This is what it means to say that He is the Supreme Lord.

*etad īśanam īśasya*  
*prakṛti-stho’pi tad-guṇaiḥ*  
*na yujyate sadātma-sthair*  
*yathā buddhis tad-āśrayā*

**The characteristic of the Supreme Person is that He is never under the influence of the material qualities that govern the universe. When the individual places his intelligence under the shelter of the Supreme Lord, then even though he remains in contact with the material energy, he is never affected by its qualities.\[18\]**

The Supreme Lord is also known by the name *adhokṣaja*, meaning that He cannot be perceived by the material senses. And just as the materially conditioned soul can never expect to comprehend the transcendental lord through the material senses, he cannot expect to understand the spiritual nature of the Lord’s form or abode. To think it is within his capacity is a manifestation of arrogance. To material eyes, the Lord’s transcendental form appears material.

*ataḥ śrī-kṛṣṇa nāmādi*  
*na bhaved grāhyam indriyaiḥ*  
*sevonmukhe hi jihvādau*  
*svayam eva sphuraty adaḥ*

**Sri Krishna’s holy name, form, qualities and pastimes are divine and transcendental. They cannot be experienced by material senses. The Lord manifests himself spontaneously on the tongue and other sense of a devotee who is eager to serve Him. (BRS** [**1.2.109**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/rupa-brs1/1.2.109)**)**

The Supreme Lord can only be influenced through devotion, and never through works, knowledge or yoga. The Lord himself states this many times throughout the scriptures: *bhaktyā tv ananyayā śakyaḥ* (“I can only be known through exclusive devotion” – Gītā [11.54](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/11.54)), *bhaktyā mām abhijānāti* (“One can perfectly knows me through devotion” – Gītā [18.55](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/18.55)); *bhaktyāham ekayā grāhyaḥ* (“I can only be grasped through devotion” – SB [11.14.22](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-11/14.22)).

The *Māṭhara-śruti* also makes it abundantly clear:

*bhaktir evainaṁ nayati*  
*bhaktir evainaṁ darśayati*  
*bhakti-vaśaḥ puruṣaḥ*  
*bhaktir eva bhūyasī*

**Devotion attracts the Lord, devotion reveals Him; He is influenced by devotion. Nothing is more powerful than bhakti.**

As stated in the Upanishads, Lord Jagannath, the Supreme Lord and the creator of the entire world, grants boons to all creatures – *eko bahūnāṁ yo vidadhāti kāmān*. He appears to everyone according to their spiritual vision and desire. As the Lord Himself states in the Bhagavad-Gita,

*ye yathā māṁ prapadyante*  
*tāṁs tathaiva bhajāmy aham*

**As everyone surrenders to Me, so do I reveal Myself to them. (Gita** [**4.11**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/4.11)**)**

As a result, it is often remarked that the worshipers of all branches of Hinduism have seen their *iṣṭa-devatā* in Lord Jagannath, and this can even be seen reflected in certain aspects of His worship, such as the elephant dress Jagannath wears on Snana Purnima. Historically, it is also true that Jains and Buddhists have also shown faith in Lord Jagannath at different times, and on occasion, even some individual Muslimsand Christians have done the same.\[19\]

Thus, the Purushottam Lord Jagannath is sometimes said to be “all things to all people.” The Vaishnavas in the line of Chaitanya Mahaprabhusee Him as Vrajendranandan KrishnaHimself.

*bhuje savye veṇuṁ śirasi śikhi-picchaṁ kaṭi-taṭe*  
*dukūlaṁ netrānte sahacara-kaṭākṣaṁ vidadhate*  
*sadā śrīmad-vṛndāvana-vasati līlā-paricayo*  
*jagannātha-svāmī nayana-patha-gāmī bhavatu me*

**In His left hand, Lord Jagannath sports a flute. On His head He wears peacock feathers and on His hips, fine yellow silken garment. Out of the corners of His eyes, He casts sidelong glances upon His loving devotees and He always reveals Himself through His pastimes in the divine abode of Vrindavan. May the Supreme Lord, Jagannath Swami, please become visible to me.**

This does not mean that historically, all people have always seen Lord Jagannath in this way.

## Lord Balaram

Krishna’s alter ego is Balaram.\[20\] Balaram is the original Sankarshan(*mūla-saṅkarṣaṇa*) who then appears in the first group of four expansions in Dvaraka, also known as Sankarshan. Expanded from this form is Maha Sankarshan, who is situated in Maha Vaikuntha, whence he initiates the act of creation by first expanding in a partial expansion as the first Purushavatarwho lies down in the causal ocean and is thus named Karanodakashayi Maha Vishnu. He further expands as Garbhodakashayi Maha Vishnu and then as Kshirodakashayi Maha Vishnu, who lies down in the milk ocean.

A portion of Kshirodakashayi Vishnumanifests as the snake with unlimited hoods, Ananta Sesha. Each of Ananta’s hoods is billions of miles across and carries all the solar systems on them. The planet earth is nothing more than a mustard seed to him. More importantly, as his supreme devotee, Sesha constantly glorifies the Lord with all of his unlimited numbers of tongues. The four Kumaras and other great sages come to him to hear the Bhagavatam.

Not only that, but just as Ananta Seshaglorifies the Lord, he also serves him by manifesting in an infinite number of forms, such as his parasol, shoes, bed, pillows, clothing, home, sacred thread and throne. In his commentary to Chaitanya Charitamrita*Ādi* [5.125](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-adi/5.125), Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakur defines *śeṣatā* as “ultimate servitorship.” Lord Vishnu, through his manifestation as Lord Ananta Sesha, engages in the most extensive transcendental service to the Lord’s pastimes as his temple, his chariot, and even as the reins of his chariot. Thus even the Lord’s very own form is a manifestation of Ananta Sesha.

In his commentary on the second chapter of *Laghu-bhāgavatāmṛta*, discussing the Purushavatars, Baladeva Vidyabhushan writes:

*śārṅgiṇaḥ śayyā-rūpas*  
*tad-ādhāra-śaktiḥ śeṣaḥ*  
*īśvara-koṭiḥ bhū-dhārī*  
*yas tu tad-āviṣṭo jīvaḥ*

**The bed upon which the holder of the bow, Vishnu, lies is his support energy, Sesha. He belongs to the same ontological category of Vishnu. Though He holds up all the worlds, He enters into every single jiva.**

Baladeva is the master of all the living beings. When the jivas manifested (*prakaṭita*) by Him are freed from the bewilderment of the external energy and become eternally joyful in the Lord’s service, as His associates. The expansion of Baladeva’s partial expansion, Karanarnavashayi Maha Vishnu, glances over the material energy from a distance and impregnates it with the jivas. The jivas born of the material energy are bound by the three miseries, which cause them endless distress. The jiva suffers like this through a great number of births before having the good fortune, through knowingly or unknowingly having performed some good acts linked to devotion, to encounter a manifestation of Balaram in the shape of the pure devotee. From this contact, he becomes aware of his true identity and how to achieve it.

The Lord is supreme bliss personified. As long as we are ignorant of our relationship with Him, though He dwells in our very hearts, we are not able to understand what our true purpose is in life. It is this inability that leads us to flail helplessly in the depths of the material ocean. Even when our true friend, the spiritual master compassionately speaks to us the truths of spiritual life from the Bhagavad Gita and Srimad Bhagavatam, we do not want to hear.

Lord Balaram is the master of all the living entities within the creation. He is the alter-ego of Lord Jagannath. If he is content by the jiva’s service, he will induce the all-auspicious Lady Subhadra, the personification of pure devotional service, to cast a benevolent glance on him and give the opportunity to serve Lord Jagannath.

## Subhadra Devi

There is a bit of a mystery about Subhadra Devi’s identity. Sanatan Goswami calls Lord Jagannath *subhadrā-lālana-vyagra*, “He who is eager to shower Subhadra with affection.” According to *Hari-vaṁśa* (1.36.5), Subhadra Devi is the only daughter of Vasudevaand Rohini. She is thus the younger sister of Balaram. Sanatan Goswami, however, along with other Gaudiya acharyas like Vishwanath Chakravarti, says that she is the daughter of Vasudeva and Devaki (SB 10.1.56). Subhadra was married to Arjuna and had a famous son, Abhimanyu. The story of her marriage to Arjuna can be found in the Mahabharata (*Ādi-parva* 218-220).

In Jagannath Puri, however, Lady Subhadra is the Lord’s personified energy, in all her different forms. At various times of the year, she plays the roles of all of Krishna’s Shaktis, from Radhato Durga. The *Skanda-purāṇa* describes Subhadra’s form as follows:

*tayor madhya-sthitāṁ lakṣmīṁ subhadrāṁ bhadra-rupiṇīm*  
*sarva-devāraṇīṁ pāpa-sāgarottāra-kāriṇīm*  
*vikacāmbhoja-vadanāṁ varābjābhaya-kāriṇīm*  
*kuṅkumāruṇa-dehāṁ tāṁ sākṣāl-lakṣmīm ivāparām*

**Standing between Krishnaand Balaram, he saw LakshmiDevi, the embodiment of all auspiciousness named Subhadra. Subhadra is the source of all the demigods; she takes everyone across the ocean of sin. Her face like a blooming lotus, she holds a lotus in one hand and gives the boon of fearlessness with the other. Her body is the color of saffron. She is like another manifestation of Lakshmi Devi herself. (*****Utkala-khaṇḍa*****, 19.45-46)**

There is no distinction between Krishnaand Balaram. As the original supreme person, Krishna is primarily the possessor of the energy of consciousness (*saṁvit-śakti*); Balaram is his first expansion and the possessor of the energy of existence (*sandhinī śakti*), i.e., creation. Subhadra, who stands between them, is the personification of all auspiciousness (*hlādinī śakti*). This is the meaning of her name. She is thus a manifestation of LakshmiDevi, the Lord’s internal potency, who by her blessings bestows auspiciousness on all beings. She is the personification of pure devotional service. One thus proceeds through Balaram, the manifestation of the spiritual master, to the practice of pure devotional service, Subhadra, through which one can attain Krishna himself.

The following text is found in the *Utkala-khaṇḍa*(19.11-17):

*lakṣmīḥ prādurbabhūveyaṁ sarva-caitanya-rūpiṇī*  
*iyaṁ kṛṣṇāvatāre hi rohiṇī-garbha-sambhavā*  
*balabhadrākṛtir jātā bala-rūpasya cintanāt*  
*kṣaṇaṁ na sahate sā hi moktuṁ nīlāvatāriṇam*  
*na bhedas tv asti ko viprāḥ kṛṣṇasya tu balasya ca*  
*eka-garbha-prasūtatvād vyavahāro’tha laukikaḥ*  
*bhaginī baladevasya hy eṣā paurāṇikī katha*  
*puṁrūpeṇa strī-rūpeṇa laksmīḥ sarvatra tiṣṭhati*  
*puṁnāmnā bhagavān viṣṇuḥ strī-nāmnā kamalālayā*  
*deva-tiryaṅ-manuṣyādau vidyate naitayoḥ param*  
*ko hy anyaḥ puṇḍarīkākṣād bhuvanāni caturdaśa*  
*dhārayet tu phaṇāgreṇa so’nanto bala-saṁjñitaḥ*  
*tasya śakti-svarūpeyaṁ bhaginī śrī-pravartikā*

**Subhadra is Lakshmi, the form of all consciousness, in another body. During Krishna’s incarnation, she is born in the womb of Rohini. Her form resembles of Balaram because of having meditated on him. She cannot stand to be separated for even a moment from the blue source of all incarnations, Jagannath. O Brahmins! There is no difference between Krishna and Balaram. It is thus generally said that the two of them were born in the same womb. The Puranas say that Subhadra is Balaram’s sister. LakshmiDevi always appears both in male and female forms. As a male, she is Lord Vishnu; as a female, she is Lakshmi Devi. She is present within the gods, animals and humans as the indwelling Supersoul. Who else but the lotus-eyed Balaram, in his form as Ananta, can hold the fourteen worlds on his hoods? Subhadra is His sister and His energy; she gives Him His opulence. (*****Utkala-khaṇḍa*****19.11-17)**

What is unusual about Subhadra is that outside of Orissa, she is nowhere worshiped alongside Krishnaand Balaram in this kind of trinity. There are, however, many recorded and very ancient examples of Krishna’s sister Ekanamsa\[21\] being worshiped along with Balaram and Krishna. There is much historical or archaeological evidence of very ancient Krishna and Balaram or Vasudevaand Sankarshandeities being worshiped throughout India. In a panel founding the Lucknow museum, for example, Ekanamsa is depicted holding a lotus flower and flanked by Krishna and Balaram, who is holding a wine flask and ploughshare. Another such panel was found in Gaya and is preserved in the Patna museum.

The *Bṛhat-saṁhitā* (58.37) of VarahaMihira, a sixth century work, states that the image of Ekanamsa should be flanked on either side by the images of Balaram and Krishna.

*ekānaṁśâ kāryâ devī baladeva-kṛṣṇayor madhye*  
*kaṭi-saṁsthita-vāma-kara-sarojam itareṇa codvahantī*

**Ekanamsha is usually pictured as a black goddess with numerous arms and features more closely resembling Durga, whereas Subhadra, where described, is usually said to be of a golden color. She is always two-armed. In the Utkala-khaṇḍa, she is identified with Katyayani, Bhadrakali, Gauri, Lakshmi, and Vishnumaya. Nevertheless, it is clear that Subhadra and Ekanamsha are one and the same in the Jagannath temple, since her birthday is celebrated on the same day as KrishnaJanmashtami, as the sister of Krishna who was born in the womb of Mother Yashodaand who Kamsa unsuccessfully attempted to kill.**

As Lord Jagannath’s energy, Subhadra is the manifestation of His mercy on His devotees:

*bhaktānām avanāyaiva*  
*tathā bhadrāpi bhadradā*  
*adho-lambita-hastābjā*  
*kuṅkumābhā śubhānanā*

**The two arms of the beautiful, red-colored Subhadra hang down by her sides. The very embodiment of auspiciousness, she has come to save all the devotees and bestow auspiciousness on them. (*****Nīlādri-mahodaya*****)**

## Sudarshan

Though attention is usually paid to the trinity of Jagannath, Balaram and Subhadra, one should not neglect Sudarshan, who is often included with the them in the *caturdhā-murti* concept. Sudarshan is often equated with *jyoti-stambha* or the Sun god. He appears as a round stump six feet high with cross lines in a checked pattern.

## Bhaktivinoda Thakur’s siddhanta

In an article named “The Temple of Jagannath at Puri,” which appeared in the newspaper *Tajpore* on Sept. 17, 1872, Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakur gave the following explanation of Jagannath, Balaram, Subhadra and Sudarshan, the four deities that stand on the Ratnavedi:

In the middle room is an elevated seat on which stand four different forms, viz., Jagannath, Balaram, Subhadra and Sudarshan. According to the Vedanta, God is one without a second, but He has infinite energies and attributes which are not fully known to man. But then man perceives only three energies in God, because he has no other corresponding sides to understand the other powers. From one of the energies proceeds matter in all its different forms and properties and this energy is styled the *Maya Shakti* of God. From the second energy proceeds all spiritual creation, in all its relations and phases. This power is entitled the *Jiva Shakti* of God. The third energy perceivable by man is the energy of Will, which is called *Chit Shakti*. God moving in creation is what is meant by this infinite energy.

Jagannath is the emblem of God having no other form than the eyes and the hands. They mean to show that God sees and knows and creates. Balaram is *Jiva Shakti* of God; Subhadra is the *Maya Shakti* and Sudarshanis the energy of will. We cannot form any idea of God separated. We form all ideas of these energies and hence it is that the worship of Jagannath depends upon the collection of these four forms on the same platform. Here we see God analysed in the shape of forms for the sake of those who want to conceive of Him. It is the same thing to see Jagannath as to study the Vedanta in all its branches. The temple and its institution appear to me to be a book for those who can read it. To the foolish, the institution is certainly useless, except of reminding the Deity who created the world.

Another interpr etation of the three deities is that Jagannath is the Supreme Personality of Godhead himself; Balaram is the manifestation of the spiritual master, the Lord’s personal expansion; Subhadra is Krishna’s *svarūpa-śakti*, the incarnation of devotion itself. Everywhere in the Vaishnava world, the Lord’s three manifestations as the Supreme Lord himself, the spiritual master and the devotee are accepted. Kaviraj Goswami writes at the beginning of the Chaitanya Charitamritathat one makes an auspicious beginning by remembering these three manifestations of the Divine.

*guru vaiṣṇava bhagavān tinera smaraṇa*  
*tinera smaraṇe haya vighna vināśana*  
*anāyāse haya nija vāñchita pūraṇa*

**I meditate on the guru, the Vaishnavas and the Lord. By remembering them, all obstacles are destroyed and one quickly attains the fulfillment of all desires. (CC** [**1.1.20-21**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-adi/1.20)**)**

In Jagannath Puri, one most often hears that the trinity of Jagannath, Balaram and Subhadra represent Vishnu, Shiva and Durga. This is reflected by many of the rituals in the Jagannath temple – for example, Subhadra is worshiped with the same *bhuvaneśvarī-mantra* that is used for Bimala Devi. This is not unacceptable to Vaishnava siddhānta since Sada Shiva is an expansion of Balaram in His work of creation. There are also many other such speculations: Atibori Jagannath Dasconsidered Jagannath to be a symbol of the mind, Balabhadra of citta, Subhadra of Buddhi, while he took Sudarshanto symbolize the wheel of samsara.

## Refutation of the Buddhistorigins of Jagannath

Some of the first Europeans archaeologists and historians to study Orissa, like Sterling, Cunningham, Ferguson, and Hunter, as well as some Indian scholars such as Rajendra Lal Mitraand Akhay Kumar Datta, argue that Jagannath, Balaram, and Subhadra were originally Buddhistdeities. This opinion, which is unacceptable to Vaishnavas, has now also come to be rejected by most competent scholars, despite still being adhered to in some circles.

In the opinion of these historians, Lord Jagannath first made his appearance in the Hindu world during the life of YayatiKeshari, after Buddhismhad lost its dominance. The idea that Sri Kshetra, held by Hindus from the Himalayasto Cape Comorin to be the foremost holy spot in their religion and glorified as such in the Puranic literature, arose out of Buddhism is very recent. Indeed, it is quite an astonishing proposal. As L. S. S. O’Malley wrote in the *Puri Gazetteers* of 1929, “There are weighty reasons for rejecting the theory of a Buddhistorigin.” \[22\]

The idea that Jagannath was originally a Buddhistdeity has its beginnings in a number of different sources. Those who do not accept that the “*dāru-brahma* by the ocean” mentioned in the Rig Veda, the world’s oldest book, is a reference to Lord Jagannath and who reject the authority of the Puranic versions find no external evidence of Lord Jagannath’s existence prior to the construction of a temple by YayatiKeshariin the seventh or eighth centuries. They therefore look for His origins in the Buddhist or Jaintraditions, which were strong in Orissa at various times prior to the coming of King Yayati. Ashokapatronized Buddhism; later Kharavelapatronized Jainism.

Buddhismhad a strong presence in Orissa from the time of Ashokain the 3rdcentury B.C. right up until the rule of Prataparudra in the 16thcentury A.D. During this period, many Buddhists externally became Vaishnavas while continuing to harbor great affection for Lord Buddha. Since Lord Buddha was accepted as one of the ten incarnations, this was acceptable to both the Buddhists and the Vaishnavas, and the identification of Buddha with Lord Jagannath entered the Orissan literature of the period. On the temple grounds, there is a painting of the ten avatars in which Lord Buddha is depicted as Lord Jagannath. Some scholars even state that Jagannath is dressed as the Buddha at some time during the year, but this is without foundation. Though the *Nīlādri-mahodaya* gives a detailed description of Jagannath’s Sringara Vesh, which changes according to the different festivals celebrated throughout the year, it nowhere mentions His being dressed as the Buddha.

Though all these traditions lead some to conclude that Jagannath was originally Lord Buddha, there are reasons to doubt this conclusion. Under the rubric “*jagannātha*” in the *Viśva-koṣa* encyclopedia, however, the archaeologist Nagendranath Basuargues,

If some ignorant modern-day painter puts Lord Jagannath in the Buddha’s place in a picture of the ten avatars, this does not make Jagannath an incarnation of the Buddha. Wherever the Buddha’s image has been included in the series of ten incarnations found carved in Hindu temple walls, he is always conceived of in a meditating posture. Nowhere is he seen in a form without hands and feet like Jagannath.

Some archaeologists have identified a painting in the Buddhisttemple in Elloraas being that of Jagannath, while others point to a sculpture found at Sanchias an example of the three deities, here identified as the “three jewels” of Buddhism. In the Buddhist-Vaishnava culture found in post-Chaitanya Orissa, the three deities, Jagannath, Balaram, and Subhadra are also sometimes identified with the three Buddhist “ratnas” of Buddha, Sangha and Dharma. According to the Buddhist-origin theorists, this was their original identity. The Hindus imitated the Buddhists and continued to worship a set of three deities, simply changing the names. Nagendranath Basurejects this idea as baseless, saying that the Sanchi figures do not truly resemble Lord Jagannath, Baladeva and Subhadra. Furthermore, there is no real evidence that the Sanchi figures are in fact the three jewels. There is, indeed, little evidence to show that Buddhists ever worshiped the three jewels extensively in deity form. On the other hand, the tradition of worshiping Ekalavya, or Vishnu Shakti, between Krishnaand Balaram was both widespread and ancient.\[23\]

The Orissan historian Sadashib Mishraalso argues here,

According to the Vaishnava religion, Jagannath is the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Balaram is His expansion and Subhadra is His energy or Shakti. The Vaishnava religion everywhere stresses the trinity of Guru, Vaishnava and Bhagavan. Lord Jagannath is Bhagavan; Balaram, the expansion or *svayaṁ prakāśa* form of the Lord, is the manifestation of Guru tattva. Subhadra, as the embodiment of the Lord’s internal potency, is the manifestation of the Vaishnava. If the Buddhists created effigies of their trinity of Buddha, Dharma and Sangha, it may just as well have been done in imitation of the Vaishnavas.\[24\]

Some other scholars have remarked on the resemblance of the form of the three images and the Buddhistsymbol of an open Trishulaon a wheel. O’Malley remarks that this argument “though curious, is not convincing, for such symbols are common to Hinduism as they are to Buddhism, the Trishula being the well-known symbol of Shaivism and the wheel that of Vaishnavism.” Some Hindu scholars also attribute Jagannath’s appearance to the *praṇava* symbol (*om*), of which He is said to be the embodiment.\[25\] Most modern scholars, however, attribute Jagannath’s unusual appearance to His Shabaraorigins, as many similar such deity forms have been found by researchers in tribal Orissa.

Another source of the Buddhistorigins theory lies in the legend of Lord Buddha’s tooth. Lord Buddha’s tooth is currently said to be found in Sri Lanka, in the town of Kandy. Some people say that the custom of placing the Brahma-vastu inside Lord Jagannath’s body\[26\] stems from the placing of Buddha’s sacred tooth inside the Buddhist image. The fifth-century Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Fa-hsien (ca. 400 AD) described the yearly procession of this holy relic in a place called Dantapurin Kalinga. This was speculatively identified with Jagannath Puri. In 1929, however, O’Malley wrote in the *Orissa Gazetteer:*

The legend of Buddha’s tooth is, after all, only a legend, the historical basis of which has not been proved. And it is very doubtful whether Dantapur, “the city of the tooth,” can be identified with Puri. Modern scholars hold that this town, the Dantapur of the Mahabharata and the capital of Kalinga, should with greater probability be identified with Pliny’s Dandagulanear the Godavari River.

Similarly, the Buddhistcustom of taking the sacred tooth outside on a car ride (which still takes place every year on the Buddha’s appearance day in Kandy) is said to have been copied by the Hindus in Bhubaneswarand Puri.

Different scholars have pointed out the weakness in this argument. O’Malley writes --

As regards the Car Festival, it is noticeable that cars are used not only in Puri for the worship of Jagannath, but also in Bhubaneswarfor the worship of Shiva, in Jajpurfor the worship of the goddess Biraja, and also in many temples to the south. Moreover, the procession of cars of the gods is… mentioned in one of Ashoka’s edicts and is probably pre-Buddhistic.

Nagendranath Basualso argues,

…the idea that Jagannath’s Rathayatrais an imitation of the Buddha’s Rathayatra cannot be accepted. The use of such vehicles in religious ceremonies is very ancient. Such festivals are celebrated in many Hindu temples for various gods and goddesses. There is furthermore evidence that the practice was found amongst the Jains, even prior to the Buddha’s appearance, so clearly Rathayatra was a well-known practice since hoary times.

Sadashib Mishragoes even further:

The use of carts in religious ceremonies has been going on since Vedic times. Krishnauses a chariot in the Mahabharata. So it stands to reason that if there is a mention of Rathayatrafestivals in Buddhisttexts, the Buddhists undertook these ceremonies in imitation of the Hindus. Even if we look at the Buddhist texts that have been used to establish this argument, such as *Lalita-vistāra, Mahā-śambhu-purāṇa,* and *Aṣṭa-sāhasrikā*, it is clear that they have been written in imitation of the Hindu Puranas. It is a matter of establishing historical precedence.

Finally, it seems that this practice is universal. Even Roman Catholics in Europe took their religious symbols and icons out for a procession on certain holy days, sometimes using vehicles of various sorts. Thus Henrietta Caraciolo mentions a type of Rathayatrashe saw in Sicily–

A colossal car is dragged by a long team of buffaloes through the irregular and ill-paved streets. Upon this are erected a great variety of objects, such as the Sun, Moon, and principal planets, set in rotary motion and diminishing proportionately in size as they approach the summit of the structure. This erection is in itself really imposing, sumptuously decorated and put in movement in honour of her who gave birth to the God of Charity. But its functions recall to mind the famed car of Jagannath.\[27\]

Many chariot festivals are held throughout India in most of the different sects of Hinduism, but none is as famous as Jagannath’s Rathayatra.

It is also customarily pointed out that the weakness of caste barriers is a particularly well-known feature of Jagannath Puri, as people eat Jagannath’s prasad from the same plate, irregardless of their caste or race. This is said to be the result of the fact that Buddhismmakes no caste distinctions. But to find a connection between the two is artificial, as Sadashib Mishrademonstrates,

It will not take much effort to refute this argument, because it has already been shown that according to textual evidence, this place was established before the Buddha’s birth. Furthermore, a great number of \[Hindu\] scriptures say that Maha Prasad is never contaminated by the touch of someone from a low caste or from a non-Aryan race; furthermore, prasad is to be honored immediately even if it is old, leftover and transported from a distant place. Some of the texts in which such statements are found include *Padma-purāṇa, Skanda-purāṇa, Viṣṇu-purāṇa, Bhaviṣya-purāṇa, Brahma-vaivarta-purāṇa, Varāha-purāṇa, Garuḍa-purāṇa, Viṣṇu-yāmala-tantra, Tattva-yāmala, Ṛk-pariśiṣṭa, Rudra-yāmala, Caturvarga-yogīśvara, Vāyu-purāṇa, Brahma-purāṇa,* and the *Puruṣottama-māhātmya* of the *Skanda-purāṇa.*

Nagendranath Basufurther points out that the Hindu scriptures do not shy away from mentioning historical associations of holy places with Buddhism. For instance,

In the *Gayā-māhātmya* section of Hindu scriptures such as the *Vāyu-purāṇa*, it is recommended that Hindus pay their respects and make offerings to the Bodhi tree where the Buddhaexperienced his great realization. If Jagannath were truly a Buddhistdeity and Puri a Buddhist holy place, then surely mention of this would have been made somewhere in one of the Puranas or other Sanskrit scriptures. Instead, the *Utkala-khaṇḍa*of the *Skanda-purāṇa* says,

*ato daśāvatārāṇāṁ*  
*darśanādyais tu yat phalam*  
*tat phalaṁ labhate martyo*  
*dṛṣṭvā śrī-puruṣottamam*

**A human being can gain the same results that are had from seeing all the ten incarnations of Vishnu simply by looking upon Lord Purushottam. (55.13-14)**

The above verse clearly makes a distinction between Jagannath and the ten incarnations, indicating that He is not an avatarlike the Buddha, but the avatari, Purushottam.

Jagannath Puri site was associated with the Sanatan Dharma from the Vedic age. With the expansion of Buddhism, however, it was turned into a Buddhistplace of pilgrimage, like many other Aryan holy places. In some of these, all reminders of the Vedic religion were obliterated. Since the Buddhist influence was very strong in Orissa, the glories of Purushottam Kshetra were long hidden from the world of the Sanatan Dharma. Sadashib Mishrastates,

One gets the impression from reading the *Mādalā-pañjikā* that from Indradyumna’s time onward, the temple was always under the administration of prominent kings and emperors of India. Thus it is not surprising that the *Mādalā-pañjikā* says Lord Jagannath’s worship was conducted according to Buddhistpractice during the rule of King Ashokaor other Buddhist kings. If the Hindus were not eager to destroy Buddhism, the record would have made no mention of it. It is completely reasonable, thus, to accept the *Pañjikā*’s version as credible. It is said that from this time onward, Jagannath was accepted as an incarnation of the Buddha.

It is quite possible that when the Buddhists transformed Hindu sites into Buddhistones, they undertook to write new mythologies for them. With this intent, they may have renamed Sri Kshetra “*danta-pīṭha*” (“the place of Lord Buddha’s tooth”) and identified Jagannath, Balaram, and Subhadra with the three jewels (*tri-ratna*) of Buddhism: the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha. It is also possible that they imitated the Aryan practice of having a car festival for these deities like the Rathayatraof Lord Jagannath.

When Fa-hsien visited Purushottam in the fifth century, he noted with great pleasure that Buddhismwas being practiced freely, without any interference from the Brahmins. From this testimony it can be concluded that the then-powerful Buddhists had usurped the Brahmins’ holy place, but were still afraid of them trying to take it back. Something similar can be seen in our day, in the case of Madhavendra Puripada’s Gopal deity. Though this deity is beloved of the Gaudiya Vaishnavas, it was later claimed as another sect’s property. As a result, this sect was long afraid of reprisals from the Gaudiya Vaishnavas. So it is possible to conclude that the Sanatan Dharma of the Brahmins, i.e., Vaishnavism, existed prior to the expansion of Buddhism.

Current scholarship tends to accept the basic truth of the Indradyumnalegends – that at some time, Brahmins under the direction of a pious Aryan king took over the worship of the Madhava deity that was held holy by the indigenous people of Orissa, the Shabaras. This accounts for the unusual appearance of Lord Jagannath as well as for the Dayitapati or non-Brahmin priesthood at the temple. They usually maintain, however, that this took place during the reign of King Yayatiin around the 10thcentury.

## Chapter 5 - Lord Jagannath’s servants: the Kings of Puri

## Mādalā-pañjī

The history of Jagannath Puri has been kept in the records known as the *Mādalā-pāñjī*. There are different theories about where the name *mādalā* comes from. Some say that the book got the name because it was written on palm leaves and then bound in the form of a drum (*mādalā*). It is more likely, however, that it comes from an old Orissan word *madala,* which means “royal.” *Mādalā-pañjī* is thus the royal record of the dynasties that ruled over Orissa.

However, since Lord Jagannath is the true king of Orissa, the *Mādalā-pañjikā* was primarily created to give an account of the Jagannath temple. The names and biographies of the Orissan kings are given only inasmuch as these kings rendered service to Lord Jagannath and his temple.

According to the tradition, King Chodaganga established the *Mādalā-pañjī* tradition during his reign, which ended in the middle of the twelfth century. He created twenty-four families of Karans or scribes to keep the temple records. Of these, five were entrusted with the writing and preservation of the *Mādalā-pañjī*, each of which dealt with different aspects of the temple activities:

1\. The Raja Khanja or *Rāja-carita*: deals with the important events of the Rajas. It was kept by the Tadan Karan and was read annually on Paush Purnima (Pushyabhishek).  
2\. The Desh Khanja kept a record of all the major gifts of land and money made to Lord Jagannath, as well as recording when Lord Jagannath was plundered. It was kept by the Kotha Karan.  
3\. Karmangi. Summarized the daily rituals at the temple. Thus important events related to the rituals were recorded here. It was read daily at the Beherana.  
4\. Dina Panji. The daily almanac read by the temple astrologer at the time of the Avakash. The almanac was prepared annually and finalized on Vishuva Sankranti.  
5\. Chakadas. These were regional chronicles, giving accounts of the subordinate or Garjat kingdoms.

The *Mādalā-pañjī* was traditionally written on a year-by-year basis. Every year, on the Vijaya Dashami day, the Karans involved in keeping the chronicle would engage in certain rituals which included going to the Chudanga Sahi, where there is a shrine to Chodaganga.

There is much controversy about the authenticity of the extant version of the *Mādalā-pañjī*. It is likely that after Kala Pahar desecrated the temple in 1568, the original records were destroyed. The Gajapati Ramachandra I, who restored Jagannath’s service a few years afterward, also attempted to restore the historical record. As a result, it is possible that it was rewritten in a fashion that mixed legend with history. Some inaccuracies no doubt found there way into the record, as well as some deliberate misinformation. Most scholars, however, accept that there is much truth in the history of the temple as given therein.

It is said that if all the manuscripts of the *Mādalā-pañjī* were gathered together, they would easily fill an oxcart. Different manuscripts of *Mādalā-pañjī* have differing contents, both in major and minor points, leading to further confusion. *Mādalās* are scattered in the palace of the King, the houses of the Patajoshi, the Tadan Karan, and Deul Karan. The fact is that nobody has seen all the records and the published versions of *Mādalā-pañjī* do not necessarily contain the entire account.

Unfortunately, attempts by scholars to gather all the materials in one place have been thwarted, and the eccentric king of Puri, Ramachandra III, apparently destroyed a good part of the records in his keeping in the early part of the 20thcentury.

The Madala Panji has not been kept officially for more than fifty years now, though it is still said that some Karans continue to keep an unofficial record. Overall, there have been some published editions, but these have been based on a limited number of manuscripts. A real thorough study of the Madala Panji using all the different source materials has apparently not yet been done.

## Yayati Keshari

The *Mādalā-pañjikā* begins by telling how Lord Nila Madhava, holding a mace, discus, conch and lotus flower first appeared in Sri Kshetra. It goes on to recount the story of Indradyumna up to his departure for the eternal abode. Then the *Mādalā-pāñjī* tells of the many kings of Orissa who had the opportunity to serve Lord Jagannath in the Age of Kali. The greatest of these kings gave much land and riches as gifts to facilitate and expand Lord Jagannath’s service. The *Mādalā-pañjikā* gives a detailed account of the land grants each king made to Lord Jagannath, where, how, when and why.\[28\]

As we saw in the chapter on Nila Madhava, the temple built by Indradyumna was ruined in the course of time and was later rebuilt by a king of Puri. The king who is usually credited with performing this service was Yayati Keshari. Historians give his dates as 922-955 AD.

The Keshari kings, also known as Somavamshis, were Shaivas, but they did not neglect the Vaishnava deities of the region. Yayati Keshari was a great promoter of Brahminical culture and invited 10,000 pure Brahmins from Kanyakubja who were well versed in the Vedas and vastly learned in Brahminical rites and rituals. These Brahmins were settled permanently in the country with liberal donations of land and money.

In the *Mādalā-pañjī*, it is said that Yayati Kesari recovered the Jagannath image from Sonepur, where He had been concealed since the time of Raktabahu’s invasion during the reign of Shubhana Deva or Shubhakara Deva I (793-814). When Raktabahu approached Puri with his army from the sea, the king of Orissa fled from the city with his court and the images of Lord Jagannath lodged in a cart. They reached the kingdom’s western frontier and buried the images in Gopali village, about sixteen miles from Sonepur. This village still exists and has a Jagannath shrine. Yayati made new images after a lapse of 146 years, built a new temple at Puri and enshrined them there.

Yayati Keshari not only rebuilt the Jagannath temple, but he is also known for having built many Shiva temples, not only in Bhubaneswar, but also in Puri. His capital was in Jajpur, which is sometimes said to have taken its name from his (Yayatipur), or from the many sacrifices he performed (Yajnapur). But his greatest contribution was the construction of the Jagannath temple.

In the course of time, Yayati’s temple also became began to deteriorate. The construction of the temple we see today was the work of the kings of the Ganga dynasty, many of whom seem to have participated in the project. Tradition holds that Chodaganga Deva (1078-1147) the greatest of the Ganga kings, started construction of a new temple on the ruins of the old one. But other archaeological evidence also points to the kings Rajaraja II (1171-1190) and Ananga Bhima Deva (1190-1199) as the builders. Other evidence indicates that the main temple building was not finished until 1223, so it seems that none of these kings likely ever saw the full realization of their dream to see a beautiful temple for Lord Jagannath.

## Ananta Varma Chodaganga Deva

Chodaganga was the son of the Ganga king Devendra Varma Rajaraja I and his mother Rajasundari the daughter of the great Chola king Rajendra Chola. Prior to Chodaganga, the Gangas made their capital in Andhra Pradesh. Their dynasty ruled over Orissa for fifteen generations covering a period of 325 years. Choda is said to be a local pronunciation of Chola.

A copper plate inscription made by King Rajaraja III found on the Trimali Math near the north entrance states that the temple was built by Gangeshwar, i.e., Ananta Varma Chodaganga Deva:

*pādau yasya dharāntarīkṣam akhilaṁ nābhis tu ṣārvā diśaḥ*  
*śrotre netra-yugaṁ ravīndu-yugalaṁ mūrdhāpi ca dyaur asau*  
*prāsādaṁ puruṣottamasya nṛpatiḥ ko nāma kartuṁ kṣamas*  
*tasyetyādi nṛpair upekṣitam ayaṁ cakre’tha gaṅgeśvaraḥ*

**Previous kings thought themselves incapable of building an appropriate temple to Lord Purushottam, whose feet cover the three worlds, whose navel contains the entire sky, whose ears contain all the directions, whose eyes are the sun and moon, and whose head is the heaven above. The task they had thus neglected was finally completed by the Lord of the Ganga dynasty.**

*lakṣmī-janma-gṛhaṁ payonidhir asau sambhāvitasya sthitir*  
*nāmāsi śvaśurasya pūjyata iti kṣīrābdhi-vāsa-dhruvam*  
*nirviṇṇaḥ puruṣottamaḥ pramuditas tad-dhāma-lābhād ramāpy*  
*etad bhartṛ-gṛhaṁ varaṁ pitṛ-gṛhāt prāpya pramodānvitā*

**Lord Purushottam had been sad and ashamed while living in the ocean of milk, in the house where Lakshmi had taken birth even though he was well-treated by his father-in-law. He thus preferred to have a new home on the shore of the salt ocean, seeing which he became joyful. Lakshmi Devi also happily left the home of her father and came to her husband’s new mansion.\[29\]**

Some researchers hold that the Gangeshwar spoken of here was Rajaraja II (1171-1190), who preceded Ananga Bhima Deva.

## Nitei Dhobani and Chodaganga Deva

The *Mādalā-pañjī* tells many legends of Ananta Varma Chodaganga and records the events that led to Chodaganga’s conquest of Orissa from South India. At the time, Surya Keshari, the last king of the Keshari dynasty and a weak administrator, was reigning in Orissa. The king had a quarrel with a Brahmin named Vasudeva Rath Vahinipati over a land grant he had made to him. Vasudeva became angry and decided to overthrow Surya Keshari. He went to Bhubaneswar where he engaged in penances to get Lingaraj’s help. Lord Shiva appeared to him in a dream and told him to find Ananta Varma, then still a boy, who would become the conqueror of Orissa and found a new dynasty.
