In Mayurbhanj district there is a town named Pratapur or Pratapapur, about eleven miles south of the district capital, Baripada. The town was once called Ramachandrapur after the king Ramachandra Bhanj, but its name was changed when Prataparudra came to live there.

There is a temple in this town with Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, Jagannath and Balaram deities. The priests of this temple say that when Mahaprabhu left Puri for Vrindavan, Prataparudra had a wooden murti of the Lord made. When Mahaprabhu disappeared, the King decided to retire to Vrindavan. He left with this Chaitanya deity, but when he arrived at Ramachandrapur, he fell ill and could not proceed. Knowing that his death was nigh, he made land endowments and engaged 54 Brahmin priests for the deities’ continued service. From this time onward, the town was known as Pratapapur.

The king of Mayurbhanj built a temple in Pratapapur, but Kala Pahar destroyed it during his raids on Orissa not long thereafter (1568). During those troubled times, the Krishna Chaitanya deity was hidden in the Hariharpur fort, now in Bihar. A building reputed to be Maharaja Prataparudra’s samadhi stood near the Pratapapur Dak Bungalow, but it slipped into the river during a flood.

Every year, thousands of pilgrims are attracted to Pratapapur to worship the deity of Mahaprabhu on the Lord’s appearance day.

The *Mādalā-pañjī* says that he was succeeded by his son Kalua Deva, who rule for only one year, five months and three days. The young king was then assassinated by Govinda Vidyadhara, whose name has already been mentioned in connection with treachery during the war with Hussein Shah, and replaced by his brother Kakhadua Deva. This brother’s reign did not last a year before he too was assassinated by Govinda Vidyadhara, along with any other possible heirs.

## Writings attributed to Prataparudra

Many books have been attributed to Prataparudra, such as *Sarasvatī-vilāsa, Pratāpa-mārtaṇḍa, Kautuka-cintāmaṇi,* and *Nirṇaya-saṅgraha*. In fact, the first two of these books were written by two of his court scholars, Lolla Lakshmidhara and Ramakrishna, respectively.

In the description of Bengali manuscripts in the Banga Sahitya Parishad library in Calcutta, a notice is given of a song with Prataparudra’s signature. There is some doubt as to whether the song is indeed his or not. A portion of that song goes as follows:

**I will become an ornament on Your body, the ankle bells upon Your feet. I will become the chakora who gazes at the moons of Your fingernails, the bee who buzzes around Your lotus feet. I will become the mirror You look into, and the whisk that fans You. And I have yet another desire: Let me become a layer of fine dust on Your feet. If I cannot become the dust of Your feet, then be merciful and do with me as You please, this is Prataparudra’s prayer.**

## Chapter 7 - Temple history after Prataparudra

## The short-lived Bhoi dynasty

After assassinating King Prataparudra’s two successors, Govinda Vidyadhara sat on the throne himself in 1542 and founded the Bhoi Dynasty. According to the *Mādalā-pāñjī,* all the princes who survived Prataparudra were assassinated by Govinda Vidyadhara soon after his accession.\[49\]

Govinda Vidyadhara was a “Bhoi” or member of the writer class (Karan). His reign lasted only eight years and his dynasty was also short-lived.

Mukunda Deva Harichandan (1560-1568) overthrew the Bhois, but went down in history as the last independent king of Orissa. He made many efforts to fight off the attacks of the Muslims from the north, but was ultimately unsuccessful. In 1568, the Karabani Sultans of Bengal incorporated Orissa into their kingdom.

**BHOI DYNASTY**

Govinda Vidyadhar (1542-1549) Gopal caste  
Chakra Pratap Deva (1549-1557)  
Narasingha Deva (1557-1558)  
Raghu Ram Deva (1558-1560)

## Attempts to destroy Jagannath

Fabulous stories had spread far and wide about the vast riches in jewels and gold hidden in the temple’s inner sanctum and in the water pot (*kalaśa*) on the temple tower. These stories motivated many non-Hindu kings to come again and again to loot and desecrate the temple. A long list of such attacks is found in the historical records, starting with that of Bengal’s Hussein Shahin 1510. Over the subsequent years, Jagannath was hidden in Chilka Lake many times: during Purushottam Deva’s reign, four times; during Mukunda Deva’s reign (1607-1622), twice; during Dibyasingh Deva’s reign (1688-1716), once; the last time during the second Ramachandra Deva’s reign (1732-1743).

The most traumatic of these attacks was the one perpetrated by Kala Paharin 1568. Kala Pahar was born a Brahmin, but later converted to Islam and in the name of that religion became an enemy of Hinduism. Trying to satisfy the flame of envy burning in him, he was determined to destroy every temple and every deity image in the entire land. Ultimately he was destroyed by his pride for thinking that he could accomplish anything worthwhile by conquering and destroying another religion and culture.

It is said that Kala Pahar (“black mountain”) was originally a Brahmin known as Kala Chand who worked for the Bengali Sultan, Sulaiman Kararani. Kala Chand was robust in health and very handsome, so Sulaiman’s beloved daughter Dulari fell in love with him, even though he already had two wives. When she expressed her desire to marry him, Kala Chand objected that he was a Hindu and already married. However, the Sultan intervened on his daughter’s behalf and Kala Chand finally grudgingly agreed to marry the princess.

Kala Chand, however, was a staunch Hindu and not happy to spend his life as a Muslim. He thus came to Puri to see Lord Jagannath in order to wash out the sin of his conversion. He knew Jagannath to be Patita Pavan and therefore felt that he could be expiated of his sin by the darshan of the Lord. His two Hindu wives also accompanied him on his trip.

When Kala Chand explained his situation to the pandits in Puri and requested them to prescribe an atonement (*prāyaścitta*) for his sin, they became furious and not only refused to advise him, but insulted him with harsh and vulgar words. Because he had become a Muslim, they would not even let him enter the temple.

Kala Chand prostrated himself before them and requested them with folded hands to give him permission to have darshan of the Lord, but the priests became even more annoyed with him and even began to kick him. Kala Chand’s wives protested this rude action, only to be treated in the same way.

Kala Chand finally lost all patience. He stood up and took a vow in the presence of all the Brahmins: “Lord Jagannath cannot possibly be God. The attitude of His priests is false and idolatrous. They simply mislead the people. I swear that the day will come when I destroy both Jagannath and His temple forever.”

Humiliated, Kala Chand returned to Bengal and wholeheartedly embraced Islam. In due course he invaded Orissa with such ferocity that people were terrified at the mere mention of his name. His primary objective was to destroy all of Orissa’s temples and images. This story shows how even an orthodox Brahmin could become a dedicated iconoclast due to the intransigeant conservatism of other Brahmins.

In fear of Kala Pahar’s attacks, Lord Jagannath’s servants were forced to attempt to protect their worshipable Lord by hiding him on Parikuda Islandin Chilka Lake. Kala Paharmade inquiries, however, found out where the Deity was and captured Him.

According to the *Mādalā-pañjī*, Kala Pahar took Jagannath to the banks of the HooghlyRiver, where he threw the Deities into a fire, under the mistaken idea that he was dealing with a material object.\[50\] Whether or not Kala Pahar factually took Jagannath all the way to Bengal cannot be proved, but it is certain that he attempted to burn the Deities. Unknown to Kala Pahar, however, a devotee of Lord Jagannath named Bishara Mahanty had followed him. When Bishara Mahanty saw the Muslims burning the body of his Lord, he waited for an opportune moment and then jumped into the fire. The Muslims were taken aback by this apparent suicide, but there was nothing they could do to stop him. The pyre continued to burn for hours, and by the end of the day, as the fire began to die out, the devotee Bishara Mahanty suddenly emerged from the flames unharmed and walked off in front of the stunned guards.

In fact, Bishara Mahanty had jumped into the fire to save the Nabhi Brahma in the belly of Lord Jagannath. He had remained untouched by the flames due to his contact with the Nabhi Brahma and by the mercy of the Supreme Lord. He then returned to Orissa with the Nabhi Brahma and went to the town of Khurda where he began to worship it.

A few years later, when Man Singh restored the rights of the Hindu kings over Jagannath Puri, the King of Puri, Raja Ramachandra Deva, dreamt one night of Lord Jagannath. The Lord said to him, “Don't lament. I am still present. My dear devotee Bishara Mahanty has retrieved My Nabhi Brahma. He lives in Khurda, so find him and bring Me back here to My temple.”

Ramachandra Deva did as the Lord bade him, and, once he had found the Nabhi Brahma, he had a new deity of Jagannath made. Then with great fanfare, he brought the Lord back to Puri and reinstalled Him in the temple, much to the happiness of all the devotees. For his service, Bishara Mahanty was highly honored by the king, while the king himself became known as the second or new Indradyumna for his role in bringing Lord Jagannath back to His temple after an absence of more than twenty years.

Devotees with faith in Lord Jagannath say that Kala Pahar was never able to truly touch Lord Jagannath. He abused a mere shadow of the true Jagannath, much in the way that Ravanakidnapped an illusory Sita. Nevertheless, legend has it that Kala Pahar ultimately suffered the consequences of his offences when he died a horrible death.

## Did Mahaprabhu cause Orissa’s political decline?

Srila Prabhupada Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati once said one of the most destructive ideas about Lord Chaitanya to have arisen in Orissa after He and His associates disappeared from this world is that devotion to Lord Krishna caused the decline of Orissa’s imperial glory. Sundarananda argued strongly against such aspersions in *Sri Kshetra.* He presents the opposing argument by quoting R. N. Banerjee, who wrote as follows:

“Chaitanya was one of the principal causes of the political decline of the empire and the people of Orissa. Not only that -- the acceptance of Vaishnavism, or rather neo-Vaishnavism, was the real cause of the Mussulman conquest of Orissa twenty-eight years after the demise of Prataparudra. \[…\] Neo-Vaishnavism became fashionable and powerful officers of Prataparudra like Ramananda Raya, the governor of Rajahmundry before its final loss and Gopinath Barajena, that of the Majyatha Dandapat or Midnapore, were the most notable converts after the king himself. \[…\] The decline of the power and prestige of Orissa is solely due to the national adoption of the sublime Bhakti-marga of Chaitanya.”\[51\]

The basis of Banerjee’s argument is that Mahaprabhu’s religion gave people a too-optimistic view of human nature and made them reluctant to engage in the kind of military activity that was needed to maintain social discipline and a strong defence against invading armies.

“The religious equality and love preached by Chaitanya brought in its train a false faith in men and thereby destroyed the structure of society and government in Bengal and Orissa, because in reality, no two men are born equal and government depends upon brute force, specially in a country like India in the fourteenth, fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. A wave of religious fervor passed over the country and during this reformation, Orissa not only lost her empire, but also her political prestige.”\[52\]

More recently, the historian K. C. Panigrahi makes a similar argument. Though he absolves Chaitanya Mahaprabhu Himself, He argues that the culture of religion based on Radha and Krishna’s loving affairs as expressed in the *Gīta-govinda* sapped the Orissan nation’s moral strength. He overtly calls Jayadeva’s masterpiece a Sahajiya text and places the blame for the disintegration of the Orissan empire on it.

“The diversification of religious interest, the falsification of the Jagannath cult, and the general degradation of the moral conduct of the people were, more than other causes, responsible for the fall of Orissa. The fall was so great that her people have not recovered from it till now.”\[53\]

Like Banerjee, Panigrahi feels that the type of religion that became popular throughout Orissan society during the reign of King Prataparudra undermined the disciplined Kshatriya culture that was at the root of Orissan greatness.

The entire population participated in the military system built up by the successive Orissan kings. During the reign of Kapilendra Deva, this militarization reached its peak, and was based on a stern discipline, an unquestioning obedience to the king and above all, on the single-minded devotion to Lord Jagannath, who was conceived to be the only source of all powers and inspiration. The slackness in discipline and the diversification of religious interest which slackened the single-minded devotion to Lord Jagannath started in the reign of Parataparudra Deva and these factors undermined the military character of the Oriyas who sank into obscurity after the loss of their independence in AD 1568.\[54\]

Sundarananda writes forcefully in response to these arguments, and we quote him in full:

Nowadays, we measure our personal, community or national progress or decline purely in materialistic terms. This all-pervading materialism has introduced so many disease-carrying microbes into the body of human society, including the so-called educated circles. State nationalism is a symptom of this disease. If human society still cannot understand this after the experiences of the last century, then it is surely doomed to destruction. Do the last two world wars not give us sufficient warning about where this kind of so-called progress leads society and the nation?

Materialism is not fundamental to India, nor indeed is it inherent in any conscious entity. It is a foreign import that is an attack on our natural character that is leading to our destruction. India’s backbone is its spirituality; once that has been broken, everything else will go to ruin or be destroyed. Under the influence of foreign ideas, we take what is truly beneficial to be harmful. Thus we mistakenly think the culture of spiritual life -- the development of our affinity for service to God – to be the cause of both our individual and collective downfall. In other words, we mistake our search for the means to survival to be a cause of death. In fact, the real cause of our personal, communal or social downfall comes from the absence of interest in cultivating awareness of the Supreme Truth, and that alone.

Those who say that Lord Chaitanya damaged anyone’s attempts at personal fulfillment, or that he caused a particular nation’s ruin are themselves in the mouth of the beast of their own ruin. Illuminated by the blessings of Lord Chaitanya, the Bengali king Hussein Shah’s ministers Dabir Khas and Sakar Mallik gave up their high political posts, Ramananda Raya resigned his position as governor, and Raghunath Das abandoned wealth like that of Indra and a wife as beautiful as a goddess. If Maharaj Prataparudra became indifferent to military conquest, then it is more likely that his action resulted in genuine benefits to his subjects rather than the opposite. Today’s researchers and those of the future would do well to look into the ways that his rule led to social advances.

In their lust for power, worldly leaders are ready to pay illegal bribes, sacrifice the lives of others, or even go to prison to gain a name for themselves. They make numerous sacrifices at the altar of personal and collective power. Srila Sanatan Goswami’s ultimate goal was the liberation of all living beings from the beginningless source of their bondage. This was the example he set when he accepted imprisonment and paid a bribe of 7,000 pieces of gold in order to get out of his entanglement in Hussein Shah’s government. His indifference to worldly power was a source of amazement even to the Shah.

The worldly possessions, worldly independence, material sense gratification, and variegated consumer choice of western countries are now seen by the people of India as the ideal to follow. But are we incapable of clearly seeing the nefarious consequences of their nationalism and so-called independence? Our modern civilization and prosperity seem to lead either to constant state of alert as we ready to fight another world war or making non-proliferation treaties or hoping in some other way to make an imaginary peace. It is impossible to calculate the value of one human being’s life, and yet modern civilization seems intent on finding ways of destroying hundreds and thousands of such priceless lives in a single explosion. This kind of civilization, this kind of politics, this kind of science, and this kind of economics and society both directly and indirectly teach us that our modern civilization is turning us all into a kind of sophisticated savage. Does such civilization not result in complete ruin?

Mahaprabhu taught a doctrine of genuine non-violence. After coming into contact with Mahaprabhu, Prataparudra refused to continue ruling his country in a destructive, violent manner. He surrendered his kingdom to Lord Chaitanya as a way of serving Him, and by so doing, contributed to the genuine advancement of his people, his society and nation. The fact is that even today, the path shown by Chaitanya Mahaprabhu and His followers is the way to true auspiciousness, not only for Orissa, but for the entire world. All of Orissa’s civilization, education, culture, literature, arts, and sciences took a considerable leap forward as a result of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s influence. By casting aside the supreme truth or spiritual goal of life, no society or people can expect to attain true values.

The religious art and architecture of Orissa, such as the Lingaraj and Ananta Vasudeva temples in Bhubaneswar, the Jagannath temple in Puri and the Surya temple in Konark have impressed scholars from around the world. Raya Ramananda, Govinda Deva and other poets enriched Orissa’s cultural heritage with works inspired by Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. Impartial historians admit that even Jagannath Das, the Atibori whose poetic skill so inspired the people of Orissa, was in one way or another inspired by his contacts with Chaitanya Mahaprabhu and his associates. Madhavi Devi, \[55\] Ganga Mata and other women devotees showed the path of auspiciousness to all the people of the world. The intelligent observer can also see how the moral life of Orissa was purified by the influence of Chaitanya and his devotees. There is no room for narrow provincialism or nationalism in the liberated domain of spiritual truth.

The fact of the matter is that Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s blessings, the teachings that elucidate the highest realms of spiritual realization, have spread throughout the world from Orissa. Chaitanya Mahaprabhu revealed this hidden storehouse of the ultimate, supreme wealth, one that is still unknown to the world’s most civilized and advanced peoples.

Consider the following: If Maharaj Prataparudra had not taken shelter of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, or if Mahaprabhu had not come to Orissa or had not even appeared in the world, would its history have been any different, either before or after? Take the example of Krishna Deva Ray, the king of Vijaynagar who defeated Prataparudra in the south. Does his “golden empire” still stand? His kingdom was swallowed up during the reign of his successors Achyuta Raya and Rama Raja. During the battle of Talikot (1565 AD), the Muslims defeated the Hindus, killed Rama Raja, and destroyed the city of Vijaynagar. The Muslims leveled its proud marble buildings and palaces and the hopes for a Hindu empire and Hindu prominence foundered -- *sic transit gloria mundi.*

*yadu-pateḥ kva gatā mathurā purī*  
*raghu-pateḥ kva gatottara-kośalā*  
*iti vicintya kuruṣva manaḥ sthiraṁ*  
*na sad idaṁ jagad ity avadhāraya*

**Just ask yourself, “Where has the Mathura of the Lord of the Yadus gone? And where is the Uttara Koshala of Ramachandra?” Your mind will become steady when you are reminded that the world is impermanent.**

Great emperors like Prithu and Ambarish took shelter of the spiritual teachings of the Sanatan Dharma. Under the shelter of these teachings, the artistic masterpieces that adorn the temples of South India were produced. Under these teachings, great literary masterpieces like the Vedas, Upanishads, Ramayana, Mahabharata and Srimad Bhagavatam came into being. And later, with the appearance of Mahaprabhu, inspired by these same spiritual teachings, the entire corpus of Gaudiya Vaishnava literature was written, bringing into being an immense goldmine of material from which both the *rasa-śāstra* and popular songs could draw. If anyone says that this spiritual tradition could be the source of a society’s ruination, then he himself is no doubt a spiritual ruin himself. Nevertheless, we will admit that if one takes things meant for the enjoyment of the supreme to use as fuel for his own sense pleasure, it certainly can lead to his destruction.

Modern-day civilization, education, culture and so-called advancement or uplift, from the individual to the collectivity, dress the nation up as the supreme enjoyer, like a stool-eating crow dressed in the plumes of a peacock, and transforms it into an army for ever-new expeditions that lead to disaster. They provide it with fuel for its lusts, feeds it the bait of greed, and ultimately sacrifices its people into the fire of sense gratification. Is this kind of human sacrifice the religion of progress and civilization?

We have become incapable of assessing the truth because our heads have been filled with the notion that any religious path is as good as another. This, however, is a flawed concept of religion. People who follow the true concept of religious life are not spiteful toward humanity, but they do not approve of humanity’s disinterest in true spiritual life. If science produces dynamite that can be used to explode mountains that interfere with performing service to the Lord or preaching His message, then a genuine servant of the Lord has no difficulty in accepting it. If science produces an airplane that provides an opportunity to preach rather than serving as a way of killing thousands of people by dropping atom bombs, it helps them to achieve immortality; it helps the eternally unhappy jivas to become happy. Only the Bhagavata Dharma is capable of turning this untrammeled materialistic advancement and turning it toward the Lord, and as a consequence, to create auspiciousness for ever living being.

Some wise Orissans have observed that if King Prataparudra and his minister Ramananda Raya had not taken shelter of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu and brought spiritual strength to the people of Orissa, they would not have been able to spiritually resist the powerful Muslim kings in the age of conflict that followed their disappearance. The outcome would have been the conversion of the entire people to Islam and the ultimate inclusion of Orissa in Pakistan at the time of India’s division in 1947. Broad-minded historians believe that by preaching Lord Chaitanya’s message, Prataparudra and Ramananda Raya both directly and indirectly created great benefits for the Orissan people. In other words, they protected the Orissan people from the reckless fanaticism and wholesale oppression of the enemies of the cows and the Vedas. Thus, the misdeeds of Kala Pahar and other fanatics of his ilk were able to conquer the land and destroy many temples, but were never able to implant their violent religion in the populace, despite all their concerted efforts.

One historian has argued point by point against R. D. Banerjee’s proposition in the following way:

The real cause of the fall of the empire was not the acceptance of neo-Vaishnavism, but the weakness of \[Prataparudra’s\] successors. It is a law of nature that no family can produce an uninterrupted line of geniuses. The tottering empire, surrounded by powerful foes, was like the “bow of Ulysses” which only a strong man could handle.

Prataparudra died in 1540 AD and within twenty-eight years no less than seven kings belonging to three different dynasties occupied the throne. Taking advantage of the weakness of the centripetal force, the Samanta chiefs, specially the Bhanjas, grew turbulent. Thus, in a country where the administration is autocratic, the succession of ill-conditioned kinglings spelled disaster.

Assassination, rebellion and the struggle for power brought about internal anarchy. Govinda Vidyadhara Bhoi murdered the sons of his master. His grandson Narasingha Jena had to atone for his sin: Mukunda Harichandan, the commander-in-chief, murdered him to pave his own way to the throne.\[56\]

Along with these traitors, there were others who were ready to sell their mother country. Govinda Vidyadhara’s nephew Raghu Bhanja Chotaraya twice invaded Orissa with the help of Muhammad Khan Sur. Ramachandra Bhanja, the commander of Sarangarh betrayed the case of Mukunda Deva at the darkest hour of the country’s history.

It is difficult to link this sickening tale of moral turpitude with the Chaitanya Movement, which taught mankind to be faithful and honest. Similarly, centuries ago, senility crept into the spirit of the inhabitants of Nabadwip, long before Chaitanya was born there. The story of Bengal’s submission to Ikhtiyar-ud-din Khalji is a disgraceful one; and devotion to a religious movement serves as no more of an extenuating cause in that case.

Thus, Vaishnavism or no Vaishnavism, the succession of weaklings, the moral degeneration of high officials of the state and the decline in the military strength of the nation, would have brought about downfall, sooner or later. At this fateful hour of stupor appeared Kala Pahar, the Black Ogre, as the messenger of Nemesis. The treachery of the titled blackguards made any effective resistance impossible and Kala Pahar encountered no stiff opposition in his task of the conquest of Orissa.\[57\]

Those who are completely materialistic swallow everything that is fed them by empirical historians and researchers. Even the Orissan government has disseminated historical misinformation of this type in the past. Their basic message is that “whenever and wherever religion has had an influence on political life, it has spelt ruin for the country in question.”\[58\] When the above statement was made in an Orissan government publication, it caused a furor amongst straight-thinking people. Those who have experience in these matters can testify that wherever and whenever atheism and a purely this-worldly view of life has had an influence on a country’s political life, it has brought about its total ruin. This is a fact and will continue to be demonstrated in the future. This is the clear lesson of history. Cowardly fanaticism and the religion of devotion, the function of the Lord’s internal potency, stand in complete opposition to one another.

## The Mughal Period

**THE RAJAS OF KHURDA**

Ramachandra Deva I (1592-1607)  
Purushottam Deva II (1607-1622)  
Narasimha Deva (1622-1645)  
Gangadhara Deva (1645)  
Balabhadra (1645-1655)  
Mukunda Deva I (1655-1690)  
Divysingha Deva I (1690-1720)  
Harekrishna Deva (1720-1725)  
Gopinath Deva (1725-1732)  
Ramachandra Deva II (1732-1743)  
Birakishore Deva (1743-1780)  
Dibyasingh Deva II (1780-1795)  
Mukunda Deva II (1795-1817)

When Raja Man Singhconquered Orissa on behalf of the Emperor Akbar, the king of Khurdawas put in charge of the Puri temple. The first king of Khurda was the abovementioned Ramachandra Deva I (1592-1607), who was followed by his descendants. Ramachandra Deva was not only recognised as the successor of the former Gajapati line of kings but also as the controller of the Jagannath temple at Puri. The new Gajapati king made sincere efforts to popularise and glorify His rule.

Ramachandra Deva I had new images of the deities made and installed them in the sanctum of the Jagannath temple. For this service, he was reputed as the second Indradyumna. Sometime in 1596 he set the famous Blue-wheel (Nila Chakra) on the crest of the temple of Jagannath. He was furthermore a great patron of Brahmins. He set up many Brahmin villages in different parts of Puri district. These villages were known as shasans. Not less than sixteen shasans are ascribed to the time of Ramachandra Deva I. It was during his rule that the Mukti Mandap in Puri Temple was constructed by Gaura Rani, the wife of General Man Singh.

During the reign of Ramachandra Deva’s feeble successor Purushottam Deva II, however, the Gajapati king of Orissa lost the favor it had known in the Mughal court of Delhi during the reign of Akbar. Jahangir made Orissa a separate Subah and Quasim Khan was appointed as the first Subadar. With the connivance of its rulers, Lord Jagannath’s temple was repeatedly attacked during this time and Purushottam Deva was powerless against the acts of desecration carried out by the Mughals and their allies, many of whom were Hindus.

The first of these was a certain Kesho Das, who came to loot the temple with a large raiding party disguised as a pilgrims. Kesho Das and his men camped within the temple compound and were able to overwhelm the army sent by Purushottam Deva. Purushottam was forced to surrender to Kesho Das in the hope of seeing Lord’s Jagannath’s worship restored, for it had been completely stopped during the crisis. The terms of his capitulation called on him to send one of his daughters to the Mughal Badshah Jahangir’s harem along with a dowry of three lakhs of rupees. He also had to give his sister in marriage to Kesho Das.

A later Subadar, Kalyan Singh, also invaded Khurda to exploit money from Purushottam Deva. His successor, Muharram Khan, followed the newly established tradition, this time causing the Gajapati king to flee Khurda and take shelter in the fort of Manitri where he died in 1622. He took the images of Jagannath with him as a precaution against the ravages of the Muslims, hiding them in the town of Banpur.

## Aurangzeb

The following kings of Khurda were often troubled by the rapacity of the Mughal Subadars, but the Gajapatis managed to continue the worship of Jagannath, somehow or other. Mukunda Deva I ascended the throne in 1655 when still a boy. He is credited with the establishment of the shasan village Mukundapur. During his rule, Jagannath’s Rathayatra car was constructed of the wood brought from Daspalla forest (now under Nayagarh Forest Division) and the previous practice of bringing wood from Banpur for the purpose was discontinued.

The Mughal emperor Aurangzeb (1658-1707) was famous for his aggressive anti-Hinduism and his jealousy of Hindu achievements. In 1686, he installed Nasar Khan as the Subedar of Cuttack. This governor was especially anti-Hindu in sentiment and actively destroyed many temples, subsequently replacing them with the construction of mosques. Though many previous governors had been negatively disposed to Hindu worship, no one made as concerted an effort to destroy it as Nasar Khan.

In due course, Nasar Khan decided to set off to Puri with a party of soldiers, intending to raze the temple and replace it too with a big mosque. Halfway from Cuttack, on the road between Bhubaneswar and Puri, the party encamped at Pipili, not far from the residence of then Gajapati Mukunda Deva at Mukundapur Shasan. They planned to reach Puri the following day. However, during the night, a heavy rainstorm and lightning caused some damage to the camp, frightening the soldiers. Everyone in the Muslim army thought that it had been a sign of Jagannath’s supernatural power and so they refused to advance the next day. Nasar Khan was forced to retreat to Cuttack and the Jagannath temple was spared.

The emperor was not pleased by this failure, however, and in 1691 he sent his general, the Nawab Ikram Khan of Golconda, to attack and plunder the Jagannath temple and to put an end to the Rathayatra festival. This was during the reign of the first Dibyasingh Deva (1688-1716). The story of this attack is told both in a Mughal history named *Tabsirat-ul-Naizirin* as well as in the Orissan histories, *Mādalā-pañjī* and *Cakaḍā-poṅthī.*

When Dibyasingh learned of the attack, he provided Ikram Khan with the wooden horses and charioteers that are placed on the festival chariots, as well as with doubles of Lord Jagannath, Balaram and Subhadra, to give to Aurangzeb as proofs of Orissa’s defeat. Dibyasingh did not want to face them in battle and risk the unnecessary massacre of a huge number of innocent people. So he participated in destroying the temple entrance at the Simha Dvara, which was plastered and closed up. Nawab Ikram Khan’s brother Jamal Khan committed the blasphemy of climbing onto the altar and sitting on Jagannath’s throne.

The Muslim raiding party threw the image of Jagannath they had been given (believing it to be the real one) on the steps of a mosque so that every Muslim who passed on his way to prayer could kick it. Mir Sayyid Mahmud (who served under Ikram Khan) sent a sandalwood deity that stood over the temple entrance, as it had valuable jewels set as eyes, to Aurangzeb who was in Bijapur at the time. This deity was also thrown on the steps of the great mosque in Bijapur so that the Hindus would be humiliated by seeing their god being kicked by Muslims on their way to prayer.

However, by Dibyasingh’s foresight, the real images of Balaram and Subhadra had been transfered to Kokola Gar and the real image of Jagannath was hidden in a secret place behind the temple of the goddess Bimala where the priests continued to go to regularly worship Him through a secret passage from the temple’s southern gate.

Aurangzeb was not satisfied by these acts, for it was his wish to see the Rathayatra shut down forever. With this object in mind, he sent Mir Sayyid Muhmad to Orissa. Army camps were established on all the major routes to Puri in order to stop pilgrims from making their way there for the festival. Thus for twelve years, from 1691-1703, there was no Rathayatra and it was impossible for anyone to visit Jagannath Puri on pilgrimage. Indeed, none of Lord Jagannath’s festivals could be performed publicly during this time; the Snana Yatra took place on the Lord’s singhasan itself, while the Gundicha Yatra was celebrated in the Bhoga Mandap. Every rite and ritual had to be performed very secretly without the sound of bells.

The deities were subsequently transferred to Banpur, which was densely forested during that period. The place where Jagannath’s four images were secretly worshiped was known in the course of time as Niladri Prasad. It is said that Sri Kshetra looked like a cremation ground during this sad time, as pilgrims stopped visiting and the inhabitants of the town experienced great distress at their misfortune at losing Lord Jagannath.

Seeing the gravity of the situation, the abbot of one of Puri’s maths*,* Ram Dayita Goswami (also known as Dinanath), a devotee of Narasingha Deva, set off to Golconda to ask for permission to hold the Rathayatra festival. In the meantime, Aurangzeb had a dream in which he saw his God take the form of Jagannath and give the order to allow the Rathayatra to be held. Aurangzeb was flabbergasted by the vision and it put him to thought.

When Ram Dayita Goswami arrived the next day and made his submission to the Emperor for permission to hold the festival, Aurangzeb’s mind had been completely changed. The Lord’s pastimes are so wonderful; they make the impossible possible. The emperor’s heart had been completely softened as a result of Lord Jagannath’s entering his heart as his God. Aurangzeb thus turned over all the land of the Markandapur *tahsil*, or revenue area, to the Jagannath temple. This land is in the vicinity of present-day Khurda Road Junction. In this way, the Emperor became free of the sins that he had incurred by attacking the temple.

Murshid Quli Khan was made Subedar or governor of Orissa in 1703 and he lifted the ban on the performance of the Rathayatra festival. Dibyasingh Deva joyfully had new rathas constructed and magnificently celebrated the Rathayatra in full freedom after the long interruption in its performance. All the Vaishnavas from Puri’s fifty-nine maths participated, contributing ecstatic kirtans to accompany Lord Jagannath on his trip to Gundicha.

The land grant made by Aurangzeb to the Jagannath temple is preserved today in the Orissan Government Archives. There is also a copper plate with an inscription notifying the end of attacks on the temple signed by Murshid Quli Khan.

Even so, still more attacks were perpetrated by Muslims on the Jagannath temple after Aurangzeb’s death in 1707, and on several occasions Jagannath had to again be hidden in other Orissan villages such as Banpur and Athagarh. Finally, in 1735, when the Mughals realized that constantly interrupting the Rathayatra resulted in the substantial loss of pilgrim tax revenues, they stopped the persecution of the Jagannath temple once and for all. They thereafter exacted large amounts of taxes from pilgrims for passports and puja fees, annually extracting as much as 900,000 rupees.

The continual hiding of the deities ultimately had a positive effect on Lord Jagannath and His devotees. The persecutions truly made Jagannath the people’s deity and not simply a symbol of state power. Indeed, the troubles experienced by the kings of Khurda in the Muslim period created a closeness between the people, the king and their God.

## The Maratha Period

After the death of Aurangzeb, the Mughal hold over its empire slowly disintegrated. The Marathas became strong during this period and they eventually became dominant in Orissa. In 1760, Jagannath Narayan Deva, the ruler of Parla Kimedi, invaded the territory of Khurda and Birakishore Deva was forced to seek the help of Seo-Bhat Sathe, the Maratha governor. The Marathas came to the rescue of Khurda and drove away the invaders, but the Raja could not pay them the expenses of the campaign and was compelled to mortgage the best portion of his territory, including Purushottam Kshetra, to the Maratha Governor.

Birakishore Deva is said to have become mad towards the end of his rule, which caused him to murder four of his sons and commit various other excesses. He died in 1780 after a long rule and was succeeded by his grandson Dibyasingh Deva II. The Marathas acknowledged the accession on the condition that the Raja pay an annual tribute of Rs.10,000 to them. The large amounts of money paid in tribute made the Marathas unpopular, even though they, as Hindus, supported Jagannath’s worship.

**THE KINGS OF PURI**

Ramachandra Deva III (1817-56)  
Birakishore Deva II (1856-62)  
Dibyasingh Deva II (1862-77)  
Mukunda Deva III (1877-1926)  
Ramachandra Deva IV (1926-1960)  
Dibyasingh Deva III (1960 to present)

## The British Period

At the end of the 18th century, the East India Company was eager to take control of Orissa because they wished to join their south Indian territories with Bengal in the north. They were able to exploit the general disfavor in which the Marathas were held by the people of Orissa, in particular the priests in Puri and the King of Khurda. By winning them as allies, they were able to defeat the Marathas with a minimum of difficulty.

In 1803, a year after the consolidation of British domination, Lord Wellesleywrote the following letter to Lieutenant-Colonel Campbell, the chief of British forces in Orissa:

On your arrival at Jagannath, you will employ every possible precaution to preserve the respect due to the Pagoda and to the religious prejudices of the Brahmins and pilgrims. You will furnish the Brahmins with such guards as shall afford perfect security to their persons, rites and ceremonials, and to the sanctity of the religious edifices, and you will strictly enjoin those you command to observe your orders on this important subject with the utmost degree of accuracy and vigilance.

The Brahmins are supposed to derive considerable profits from the duties levied on pilgrims; it will not, therefore, be advisable at the present moment to interrupt the system which prevails for the collection of those duties.

You will assure the Brahmins at the Pagoda of Jagannath, that they will not be required to pay any other revenue or tribute to the British Government other than that which they have been in the habit of paying to the Maratha government, and that they will be protected in the exercise of their religious duties.

The British continued to collect the pilgrim tax, but at the same time made numerous improvements to the roadways and other amenities for the pilgrims. They also gave a substantial portion of these taxes to the temple in annual payments. However, they came under constant criticism for these payments from the Christian missionaries who felt that this constituted support for idol worship. Christians both in England and India put enormous pressure on the East India Company to stop the practice. Thus on April 20, 1840, Act No. X was passed, totally abolishing the pilgrim tax. All powers to control the priests and other temple servants and officers in regards to the internal temple administration were vested in the Raja of Khurda (Ramachandra Deva III), who was thenceforth to act as superintendent of the temple and became known as the King of Puri. In November, 1843, the British transferred the Satais Hazari Mahallands, which were the principal source of income for the temple, to the King of Puri. By turning over these lands tax-free to the temple administration in the name of the king, they were able to wash their hands of any direct involvement in “idol” worship.

After the death of the Khurda king Birkishore Deva in 1859, the rights and duties pertaining to the administration of the temple were handed over to his wife, in accordance with his last will and testament.

Dibyasingh was Bir Kishor Deva’s adopted son and heir, but he was still neglected by the queen. As a result, he became somewhat dissolute. He fell into bad association and took to drink. He was always quarrelling with the temple priests and pandits. So though he took charge of the temple duties when he came of age in 1874, he began to misuse the temple funds.

Bhaktivinoda Thakur was stationed in Puri at the time with the full powers of a magistrate and specific responsibility for the Jagannath temple. When Dibyasingh Deva misappropriated the large amount of Rs. 80,000 from the temple, Bhaktivinoda Thakur punished him by obliging him to offer *naivedya* to Lord Jagannath fifty-two times a day.

The costs to the king were great and he angrily decided to avenge himself by assassinating the Thakur. It was impossible to do this by ordinary means, as Bhaktivinoda was a very powerful and popular figure in the district. The king therefore decided to attempt to kill him by magical means. He organized a black magic ritual in his inner apartments that lasted thirty days, at the end of which period Bhaktivinoda Thakur was to have died. As it turned out, however, the king’s own son died, showing the impotence of such means to harm the pure devotee of the Lord.

In his autobiography, Thakur Bhaktivinoda wrote, “The king and other persons connected with the temple used to commit many illegal acts. I would go there to prevent all such things and thus made enemies of the king and his men. Because I was helped by Lord Jagannath, no one was able to harm me in any way.”\[59\]

As a result of such behavior, the dowager queen, Suryamani, thought that Dibyasingh was mad. She asked a sadhu with healing powers named Shiva Das to treat Dibyasingh in the hope that he could be calmed. But when Dibyasingh heard that Shiva Das had diagnosed him as a lunatic, he decided to have him killed. He and a group of friends tortured Shiva Das and left him for dead outside the palace compound, but the sadhu had not been killed and managed to communicate to his disciples what had happened before succumbing to his injuries in a hospital. In 1878, Dibyasingh was tried and convicted of murder and sentenced to be exiled to the Andaman Islands.\[60\]

Dibyasingh’s successor Mukunda DevaIII was a minor at the time and so the administration was once again placed in the hands of his grandmother, the dowager queen Suryamani Pattamahadei. The queen followed the custom of seclusion, or purdah, which led to many difficulties in doing this service. Because of the family tradition, the Rani could not come out of the palace to see to the management of the temple. She was completely dependent on intermediaries to issue orders. In fact, she only spoke to her maids, who communicated her desires in their own way to the royal family’s male servants, known as Bishoyis. The Bishoyis then communicated her orders to the temple officers for execution. Naturally this resulted in many difficulties, so that Armstrong, who was collector of Puri at the time, rightly remarked, “She is by no means incapable, but her position is such as to make it absolutely impossible for her to manage successfully.”\[61\] As a result many attempts were made to remove her from her position as custodian of the temple, but they were all unsuccessful.

In 1880, the British government appointed an Orissan as Deputy Superintendent to assist her in her custodianship. Various overseers, inspectors and superintendents worked under him. In 1902, the Orissan Rai Bahadur Raj Kishor Das, Deputy Magistrate, was made the first manager of the temple.

In 1926, King Mukunda Devadied and his adopted son took the name Ramachandra DevaIV and once again took direct responsibility for the temple management. As such, he eliminated the post of government-appointed manager.

## After Indian Independence

Many changes have taken place since India became an independent nation in 1947. The temple management taken over by the government in 1954. This has had a number of positive effects – better management of the Rathayatra, restoration and renovation of the temple buildings, naming it an officially protected monument. However, the control of the temple by the secular government has not always brought joy to the temple priests.

The king of Puri, currently Dibyasingh Deva III, continues to enjoy a great level of prestige in the province. Despite his primarily symbolic role, he plays an important role in many organizations dedicated to the service of Lord Jagannath.

## Chapter 8 - Temple parikrama: Circumambulating the sanctuary

*śrī-jagannāthāya namaḥ*  
*samudrasyottara-tīre saṅkha-cakrāṅkita-dhvajaḥ*  
*siṁhadvāram namaskṛtya praviśed dhari-mandiram*  
*patita-pāvanaṁ dṛṣṭvā kāśīśaṁ bhoga-maṇḍapam*  
*anādi-nāthaṁ vighneśaṁ baṭeśaṁ baṭa-maṅgalām*  
*baṭa-pradakṣiṇaṁ kṛtvāpy anantaṁ puruṣottamam*  
*kṣetra-patiṁ nṛsiṁhaṁ ca madhyasthaṁ mokṣa-maṇḍapam*  
*bimalākṣīṁ tato dṛṣṭvā daṇḍavat patito bhuvi*  
*sarasvatīṁ mahā-lakṣmīm arka-kṣetrādhipaṁ prabhum*  
*pātāla-nātham īśapam uttare cottarāyanīm*  
*pāda-padma-dvayaṁ dṛṣṭvā dhvajaṁ cakra-sudarśanam*  
*dehi me bhagavan viṣṇo jagan-mohana madiram*

**I salute Sri Jagannath. On the north of the sea is a temple with marks of conch and disc. Saluting at the Lion’s Gate one should enter into the temple of Hari. After seeing the Patita Pavan, one should then see Kashi Vishwanath and the Bhoga Mandap. Then see Anadinath (Satya Narayan), Bata Ganesh, Bateshwar Mahadeva and Bata Mangala.**

After circumambulating the banyan tree, see Ananta Purushottam. Then see Nrisingha, the protector of the holy Kshetra, Kshetrapala Shiva, and the Mukti Mandap in between them. Next, one should prostrate on seeing Bimala Devi. Then take darshan of Saraswati, Maha Lakshmi and Surya, the statue of the Sun God brought from Konark. Then pay obeisances to Pataleshwar, Ishaneswhar and Uttarayani. Then see the lotus feet of Lord Chaitanya and the flag and disc on top of the temple. Then pray for admittance into the temple.

Lord Jagannath’s temple is called the Boro Deul. In Orissan architectural terminology, a shrine with adjuncts is called *baṛa deula*. It consists of a main temple, or *vimāna,* along with three other buildings – the Mukha Shala, also known as Jagamohan, the Nat Mandir and Bhoga Mandap.

In Jagannath Puri, the Boro Deul is surrounded by two concentric walls: the Meghanad Prachir, which surrounds the entire complex, and the Kurma Berha around the inner enclosure. There are four points of entrance in the outer wall in each of the cardinal directions. Each of these entrances has an elaborate archway built over it. There are corresponding gateways in the inner wall also, and between the first and second gates there is a stairway going up, as the inner temple is on a higher level.

The main temple was originally built on a raised mound, known as “the blue hill” (Nilachala). The surrounding ground level was further raised in the construction of the main temple, as earth would be heaped up to form a gradient from the ground right up to the wall’s topmost layer. This was how the huge blocks of hewed stone were raised in layer after layer to construct the temple walls.

Within the enclosure inside the Kurma Berha are ninety-five smaller shrines and temples of Jagannath’s entourage, or *pārśva-devatā*. In the center of this paved enclosure stand the four buildings that make up the Boro Deul, built on an east-west axis. Lord Jagannath sits on an elevated throne facing the east in a chamber in the westernmost building that is commonly known as Mani Koṭha (“jewel-room”). The Lord’s altar is known as the Ratna Vedi (“jeweled altar”).

Normally, pilgrims enter the temple complex through the Singha Dwar in the east, go up the Twenty-two Steps, enter the Kurma Berha and then circumambulate the Boro Deul, keeping the temple to the right. The Sanskrit word for circumambulation, *pradakṣiṇa*, means keeping the sacred object to the right. In this chapter, we shall follow this procedure in describing the temple complex.

## The Meghanadwall and the Four Gates

The temple’s outer wall is called the Meghanad Prachir*.* It surrounds an area 665 by 640 feet. Its height is between 20 and 24 feet. It some places, it has been built higher to prevent people looking into the compound from certain vantage points. The present wall of laterite and sandstone blocks and capped with Saracenic battlements was built during the reign of Purushottam DevaII(1596-1621), as a protection against attacks from marauding Afghans and Mughals. The temple thus also served as a fort, allowing both civilians as well as soldiers to take shelter inside the compound

The inner surrounding wall, known as the Kurma Berha, 420 by 315 feet, is the older of the two. It also served a defensive purpose. Previously known as Hosan Berha, it was popularly renamed after the carvings of tortoises that decorate it. It was originally built as two rows of walls with a gap of eleven feet between them. This provided a gallery for defenders to move about and shoot at assailants without being exposed. This space has now been covered and converted into rooms used for various purposes.

To penetrate into the temple, one must pass through one of four main gates, each of which stands in one of the cardinal directions. The ornamental buildings at each of the entrances are known as *toraṇas*. The main entrance stands to the east and is known as “the Lion’s Gate” or Singha Dwar (#22). Two giant statues of crowned lions flank this entrance, giving it its name.

The southern (#72), western (#83), and northern (#85) gates are known, respectively, as the Ashwa Dwar(“Horse’s Gate”), the Hasti Dwar (“Elephant’s Gate”), and the Vyaghra Dwar (“Tiger’s Gate”). With the exception of the southern gate, each one is adorned with the animal by which it is named. Most of the gates have other elaborate carvings of deities such as the gods of the nine planets, the Navagraha.

The gates are said by some to represent the four goals of human life -- dharma, artha, kama, and moksha. Temple ritual, however, shows that they stand for four of the Supreme Lord’s opulences -- dharma, jnana, vairagya, and aishwarya, respectively. Each day, one of the temple priests makes a flower offering (*puṣpāñjali*) to each of the gates with a mantra corresponding to these four characteristics, e.g., *dharmāya svāhā.*

## The Aruna pillar and Singha Dwar

In the vast square outside the temple’s east gate or Singha Dwarstands a pillar of exquisite workmanship and elegant proportion dedicated to the dawn, Aruna (#21). In Indian temple architecture, such pillars known as the *dhvaja-stambha,* usually stand in front of the temples of major deities.

Aruna is Surya Deva’s charioteer. Out of ignorance, local Pandas sometimes mistakenly say that the image of Aruna is that of Hanuman or Garuda. According to the Puranas, Aruna was the son of the sage Kashyapaand Vinati(and is thus Garuda’s brother), but he took birth prior to being fully developed, so is said to be lame.

This pillar was originally placed in front of the KonarkSurya temple. During the reign of Dibyasingha DevaII(1779-1797), the influential Marathi sadhu Baba Brahmachari removed the pillar to its current site after the Surya temple started to collapse. This same Baba Brahmachari also collected money from pilgrims to Sri Kshetra to rebuild the Singha Dwar, as it was in a state of great disrepair at the time.

This pillar is a sixteen-sided polygonal column hewn from a chlorite monolith, 25 feet high. It stands on an artistic base in the form of a full-blown lotus, six feet high and nearly eight feet square. The base has various carvings on it, including a frieze of peacocks and lion rampant on an elephant in the four corners. These carvings are of the most sumptuous description, the like of which are to be seen nowhere else in India.

The cornice is formed of tow leads surmounted by a padma with a series of lotus petals and covered by two receding tiles holding the statue of Aruna, who poses with folded hands on the pericarp of a full-blown lotus, his left knee in the kneeling posture and the right knee bent and raised. The overall height of pedestal, column, cornice and statue comes to 34 feet.

As one enters the Singha Dwar, one can see the murti of Sri Jagannath known as Patita Pavan(#23) to the left. A more extensive description of this deity is found in the following chapter. A graceful sculpture of Jaya and Vijaya is also found on the Singha Dwar.

## The Twenty-two Steps

Since the temple itself is quite a bit above street level, all the entrances have a certain number of steps leading to the Kurma Berha. The longest staircase of these leads from the Singha Dwar and one has to traverse twenty-two steps (#24) to reach the inner compound. In Orissan, the word *pāhāca* means “steps,” and these twenty-two steps made of feldspar and khondalite are popularly known as the Baish Pahacha (*bāiśa pāhāca*)*.*

The Baish Pahacha are extremely venerated since Lord Jagannath treads on them every year while going in and out of the temple for the car festival, as He has done for centuries. They have thus acquired special sanctity from His sacred touch and it is said that they can heal the ailments of those who prostrate themselves there. One can frequently find a loving mother placing her tiny baby on the steps to invoke Lord Jagannath's mercy. Vaishnavas also roll in the foot dust of all the great devotees who have walked through up these steps for countless generations. This is also a favorite spot for pilgrims to offer Shraddha to their forefathers.

Human beings are said to have twenty-two bad habits that need to be controlled and subdued before they are eligible to have a vision of the Lord. With each step, the pilgrim prays to overcome another of these defects so that he or she can truly be worthy of the Lord’s darshan.Mahaprabhu used to wash His feet at the bottom of the Baish Pahacha as an act of ritual purification on entering the temple grounds.

*siṁha-dvārera uttara-dike kapāṭera āṛe*

*bāiśa pāhācatale āche eka nimna gāṛe*

*sei gāṛe karena prabhu pāda prakṣālane*

*tabe karibāre jāya īśvara-daraśane*

**Inside the Lion’s Gate entrance, behind the door on the north side and at the bottom of the Twenty-two Steps is a drain where Mahaprabhu would wash His feet before going into the temple for darshan of Lord Jagannath. (CC** [**3.16.41-2**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-antya/16.41)**)**

Along the way up the Baish Pahacha, there are a number of shrines. The most important of these are Kashi Vishwanath (#25) on the third step and a little above it, the shrine to NarasinghaDeva (#26). Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhuused to dance and sing before this Narasingha deity.\[62\] He would offer the Lord the following prayers from the *Nṛsiṁha-purāṇa:*

*namas te nara-siṁhāya*  
*prahlādāhlāda-dāyine*  
*hiraṇyakaśipor vakṣaḥ-*  
*śilā-ṭaṅka-nakhālaye*

**“I offer my respectful obeisances unto You, Lord NarasinghaDeva. You are the giver of pleasure to Prahlad, and Your nails cut the chest of Hiranyakashipulike a chisel cutting stone.”**

*ito nṛsiṁhaḥ parato nṛsiṁho*  
*yato yato yāmi tato nṛsiṁhaḥ*  
*bahir nṛsiṁho hṛdaye nṛsiṁho*  
*nṛsiṁham ādiṁ śaraṇaṁ prapadye*

**“Lord NarasinghaDeva is here, and He is also there on the opposite side. Wherever I go, there I see Lord Narasingha Deva. He is both outside of me and within me in my heart. Therefore I take shelter of the original Lord, Narasingha Deva.”**

This Nrisingha shrine is tiny, but beautifully decorated with cement frescoes. It is maintained by Mahasuar Niyog Committee, by which it was renovated in 1962.

At the highest step, one can either go straight ahead into the Kurma Berha, turn right into the Ananda Bazaar (#100) or left into the kitchen area (#71).

## Inside the Kurma Berha

Since there are nearly a hundred shrines to different deities in this area, it will be impossible to give a detailed description of them all. Only the most important will be named here.

In keeping with the pradakshina principle, pilgrims customarily turn left as they enter the Kurma Berha. The first shrine they encounter is that of Vrindavan Chandra (#28). Just after this Krishna deity, they come to the Shiva linga, Agnishwar (#29), who guards and supervises the kitchen. He stands at the opening to the covered pathway that leads from the kitchen to the Bhoga Mandap (#12). Agnishwar guards the cooking process and if anything is insufficiently cooked in the kitchen, it is said that he completes the process as it passes by him on the way to being offered.

Next is the Satya Narayan temple (#30). Satya Narayan was worshiped by both Hindus and Muslims, who called him Satya Pir. The temple here is of fairly recent build, but the deity, a four-armed Narayan form, belongs to the late Gajapati period. It resembles Alarnath at Brahmagiri and has been praised for its high artistic merit.

The southeastern portion of the compound is dominated by the Kalpa Bata (#32) banyan tree, under which lies a cluster of small shrines. This tree is very old and sacred. It trunk is said to be Brahma, the foliage Vishnu and top, Shiva. It is frequently mentioned in the Puranic accounts of Jagannath Puri. In particular, it is associated with the baby Krishna lying on a banyan leaf and sucking his toes, who was seen by Markandeya at the time of the universal flood. There are thus two shrines to Krishna’s baby form under this tree. One of these is Bala Mukunda (#34), who is in a sleeping pose lying on a banyan leaf, the other Bata Gopal (#35). Women often spread their saris under this tree waiting for a fruit to drop to assure fulfillment of their desire to have a child.

The following popular Sanskrit verse is sung to this form of the Lord –

*karāravindena padāravindaṁ*  
*mukhāravinde viniveṣayantam*  
*baṭasya patrasya pūṭe śayānam*  
*bālaṁ mukundaṁ śirasā namāmi*

**I bow down my head to the baby Mukunda, lying down on a banyan leaf and pushing His lotus foot into His lotus mouth with His lotus hand.**

The Pancha Pandava (#33) temple contains five shrines to the five Shivas of Puri: Markandeya, Lokanath, Kapala Mochan, Nilakantha and Yameshwar.

The temple of Bata Mangala or Sarvamangala (#36) is of modern origin, but the enshrined goddess, conforming to the iconographic features of Mangala, is old, dating to the 10thor 11thcenturies. Shweta Ganesh or Bata Ganesh (#37) is a beautiful sculpture in a temple of recent construction.

There are also shrines to Hari Sahadeva, a Shiva linga dedicated to the protection of livestock, a small Batavihari Jagannath deity, and an ashtadhatu metal image of Lord Jagannath called Nila Madhava who is housed in a small but dilapidated structure.

Directly adjoining the Nat Mandir is numerous shrines is LakshmiDevi’s Marjana Mandap (#13)*,* where Lakshmi Devi is given a bath every Thursday.

Higher up, on the southeastern side of the main temple building, one can see a deity of Lord Chaitanya in his six-armed form. There are in fact several paintings on the temple grounds of this form, which Mahaprabhu revealed to both King Prataparudra and his court pandit, Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya. The King had this form painted on the outside of the temple tower and on the ceiling of the Nat Mandir, as well as in a room near the southern gate.

## Mukti Mandap

After one passes the entrance in the Kurma Berha leading to the southern gate, there is a peculiar dog-shaped shrine called Kuttam Chandi (#39). There is a general belief that whenever there is an ill omen in the temple, Kuttam Chandi moves around the temple heralding the inauspicious happening. Other significant shrines in this area are Ananta Purushottam (#40) and Kshetrapal Shiva (#41).

Further to the west is the significant building known as the Mukti Mandap (#43). It was first built by Prataparudra Deva and then repaired by Man Singh in the 1590's. It covers a small area, 30 by 38 feet, with sixteen pillars on high plinth. It is flanked by a very old Nrisingha temple (#44) on the east and the Mukteshwar temple (#42) on the west. The Nrisingha deity is called Yajna Nrisingha as tradition holds that this is the deity to whom Chodaganga performed sacrifices before he started building the temple. An inscription inside the temple attests to this fact.

The Jagannath temple council is held in the Mukti Mandap, which is also known as Brahmasan, or the seat of the Brahmins. A literal translation of *mukti-mandapa* is “the temple or hall *(mandapa)* of release *(mukti*).” In the present context, *mukti* means “legal” rather than “spiritual” release; *sabhā* means “assembly or council.” The Mukti Mandap Sabha is composed of learned Hindus, both lay and ascetic, who meet twice a month to decide upon cases involving infractions of Hindu law.

The members of this council are known as the Brahmins of the sixteen Shasans (*ṣola śāsana*). A Shasan was a special Brahmin village in which only Brahmins were allowed to live. Nowadays, there are many more than sixteen such Shasans, but the original name has stuck. Some of them are still more prestigious than others, such as Bir Pratapapur, Bir Ramachandrapur, and Bir Narasinghapur. The names of these villages come mostly from the different kings of Orissa who established them and gave them large land grants on which to subsist. In return, these Brahmin villages were obliged to perform various auspicious religious ceremonies such as reading the Vedic literature or performing fire sacrifices for the benefit of the royal family.

The Brahmins from the sixteen Shasans consult the scriptures and advise on matters of temple and Hindu social policy. Their decisions in religious matters were formerly binding on the King and the people of the kingdom and are still given great importance. They decide, for example, when the Nava Kalevara ceremony should be held. Some people call the Mukti Mandap the Jagannath temple’s Supreme Court. The Brahmins who sit on Mukti Mandap have no actual temple duties, however.

The Mukti Mandap is a comparatively small area reserved for the use of the Sixteen Shasan Brahmins. The rest of the paved area in the Kurma Berha, however, which was used by the general public as they came and went in the hope of having the darshan of both the moving and non-moving forms of Brahman, was named after Lord Chaitanya, and is known popularly as the Chaitanya Mandap.

A little further on, one comes to the small but very significant holy tank known as Rohini Kund (#47). In the *Utkala-khaṇḍa*, it is said that the causal water flowed out from the Rohini Kund and spread over the world in the deluge at the end of the kalpa. According to the Nila Madhava legends, this is where the four-armed crow Bhushandi bore witness that Indradyumna had built the temple. The image of this crow is here preserved on a stone slab. Nearby is the Jalakrida Mandap (#45), where many festivals are held throughout the year. Nearby is a shrine to Natua Ganesh (#46), a beautifully worked figure with eight arms dancing on his mouse carrier.

On the southern side of the main temple buildings are a number of significant sites. The temple of Madana Mohan (#14), Lord Jagannath’s Vijaya Vigraha, who represents Lord Jagannath in festivals like Chandan Yatra. Just next to this temple is a raised platform that is set aside for the King of Puri to take prasad and take care of temple business, as well as grant audiences to the public.

In each of the three cardinal directions, the north, west and south of the main temple, three smaller temples have been built, directly attached to the outside of the building. These temples (*piḍha-mandira*) house Varaha Deva (#16),Nisha Narasingha (#17), and Bali Vamana Deva (#18), respectively. Next to the Bali Vamana shrine is a small pond where water from the temple, including Lord Jagannath’s charanamrita, collects. It is known as the Paduka Kund.

**Bimala Devi**

The temple dedicated to the mother goddess, Bimala Devi (#50), is one of the oldest and most significant temples in the Jagannath compound. The Tantras designate Jagannath Puri as one of the Shakti Piths, of which there are 108 in India. According to the Shaktas, Bimala is the presiding goddess of the Pith, and Jagannath is her Bhairava: *vimalā bhairavī yatra jagannāthas tu bhairavaḥ* (*Tantra-cuḍāmaṇi*).

Scholars of iconography assign the Bimala image to the 10thor 11thcentury. One of the unique features of this temple is that it is the only place in the Jagannath temple compound where animal sacrifices are carried out. Once a year, on the Ashwin Shuka Ashtami, during the Durga Puja celebrations, a goat is sacrificed amidst a great clamor of gongs and drums.

Pictures based on the *Devī-bhāgavata* have been carved on the ceiling of the Nata Mandir of Bimala’s temple. Ganesh and Karttik images have been carved into niches in the wall. Other images in the temple include an eight-armed dancing Ganesh and a six-headed, twelve-armed figure named Sadananda, who acts as the gatekeeper.

By the side of this temple is another room in which deities of Jagannath, Balaram and Subhadra have been placed. This Jagannath deity is called Venu Madhava (#51). Toward the western exit through the Kurma Berha are three other shrines: one called Jaya-pada-padma (#52), containing the footprints of Jayadeva, the author of the *Gīta-govinda*, Sakshi Gopal (#53) and Kanchi Ganesh (#54).

This latter deity has already been discussed in a previous chapter as one of the deities brought back from King Purushottam Deva’s memorable victory over the kingdom of Kanchi. Its iconography, which is recognizably South Indian, is rather unusual. Ganesh is seated in the *rāja-līlāsana* position; three of his four arms hold a broken tusk, a rosary and a battle-axe, while the fourth holds his own testicle. His trunk touches the genital organ of the goddess Siddha Devi who is seated on his left lap. This Ganesh deity is also called Bhanda Ganesh.

Next to this is another shrine dedicated to the emancipation of Ahalya, Gautama Muni's wife, who was cursed by her husband to turn to stone but later redeemed by Ramachandra’s touch.

## Lakshmi temple

To the north of the western entrance to the Kurma Berha, one comes to the temple of Bhuvaneshwari (#57), where the three devis, Satyabhama, Saraswati and Shashthi are worshiped. Nearby are shrines to Nila Madhava and Berha Kali (#58).

The most important temple in this part of the compound is dedicated to Lakshmi. It is a full temple with four buildings like the Boro Deul, though on a smaller scale. This temple was also built by Chodaganga Deva at the same time as the Sri Mandir.

Lakshmi is held in high esteem by the people and is closely connected with the cult of Jagannath. The elevation of Lakshmi Devi in the estimation of the Orissan people is said to be a contribution of Ramanujacharya. The *Lakṣmī-purāṇa* and other legends sing in eulogistic terms the praise of the goddess and her significance in the Vaishnava pantheon.

Besides being the consort of Lord Jagannath, Lakshmi Devi is also known as the giver of wealth, so this temple is one of the most frequented by pilgrims with fruitive desires. They sit for some time in the jaga mohan, which is known as *tripāda-vibhūti-vaikuṇṭha maṇi-maṇḍapa,* hoping to attain the goddess’ favour.

The lower portions of the biman and jaga mohan are exquisitely carved with images of sandstone. The important images in the niches are Lakshmi in the southern, western and northern niches with elephants pouring water over her head from water jugs, and surrounded by Nagas and Naginis, Dikpalas, Nrisingha, indolent nayikas and figures of elephants mounted by riders.

## Surya temple

The next significant temple is the one dedicated to Dharmaraj or Surya (#63). It is situated a little to the northeast of the Lakshmi temple. This temple consists of three parts contiguous to each other but of no extraordinary architectural value. The peculiarity of the temple is due to the nature of enshrined deity. The image of Sun is flanked by brass figures of the Sun and Moon. The main image of Surya is standing on the pedestal with a mutilated figure of the Buddha. Three small idols of Surya, Chandra and Indra are placed in this temple.

According to the *Mādalā-pañjī*, King NarasinghaDeva (1622-1646) had the murti of the Sun god (Maitraditya Virinchi Deva) removed from the Konark temple to Jagannath Puri, where it was placed in the Surya temple. This action was taken in 1628 for the safety of the deity during the governorship of Baqr Khan, who wished to attack the Konarktemple. Some people cast doubt on this account, saying that the colossal pedestal of Sun god seen in the biman of the Konark temple would require a much larger image than the one found here.

Next to the Surya temple are a number of smaller shrines dedicated to the nine planets, the Navagraha (#61), Indra (?), Krishna Kubja and Badrinath (#??). In the temple of Indra, the broken image of Indra is still there, but in front of it a small wall has been raised and the image of the Sun god placed there.

## The Northeastern corner of the Kurma Berha

On either side of the gate leading from the Kurma Berha to the Ashwa Dwar are the ancient Shiva temples dedicated to Pataleshwar and Ishaneshwar. The Pataleshwar temple (#66) may well have been one of the original buildings on the site.

It is 20' below the surface, on the same level as the town. A descending flight of stairs leads to the floor level or the sanctum, where the Shiva lingam has been enshrined. The entrance to the sanctum has epigraphs from the reign of Ananga Bhima III regarding the service pattern of the temple.

Ishaneshwar (#67) is a very old Shiva linga. He is called Mama, Lord Jagannath,s “maternal uncle.” It is believed that there is a tunnel underground from the Ishaneshwar temple to the Ratnavedi.

In front of this temple is a figure of Lord Shiva’s transport, Nandi the bull. It is said that inside its belly is a secret current of the Ganga and that a mere touch of the fingernails will cause water to spring forth.

Connected to the north side of the temple buildings are Bhandar Lokanath (#20), the Shiva who is said to be the keeper of Lord Jagannath’s storehouse. Also standing to the north of the main temple building is the Deul Karan’s office. Every day, the temple managers assemble here to consult the *Mādalā-pāñjī*to determine the type of worship that should be given on that particular lunar day (*tithi*).

## Mahaprabhu’s lotus feet

The Pada-padma (#68) or footprints of Sri Chaitanya are enshrined in the northeastern corner of the Kurma Berha after being moved from the Nat Mandir a little over a century ago. The Natya Mandir’s floor is made of stone slabs. It is said that once when Mahaprabhu was standing directly behind the Garuda pillar to gaze upon the form of the Lord, the stone melted on account of His ecstasies, leaving the outline of His feet imprinted on it. When Radha Raman Charan Das Babaji first came to Jagannath Puri in the 1880’s, he asked the king to have the footprints moved, because it pained him to see people walking all over them when the temple was crowded. The temple priests then moved Mahaprabhu’s footprints and enshrined them in this separate little temple. They are encased in a blooming lotus and preserved inside a tiny temple where they can be touched by all. Further, on the western gateway of the Bhoga Mandap there are fingerprints of Chaitanya.

In the northeastern corner of the Kurma Berha stands the shrine of Gupta Gauranga, “the hidden Gauranga” (#69). This is a wooden image of Lord Chaitanya in His sannyasi form; He is shaven-headed and seated. Tradition holds that King Prataparudra himself installed this image here. Over the course of time, service to this deity deteriorated to the point of almost being given up, but it was never moved. In the 1940’s, the abbots of the Radha Kanta Math arranged for the deity to be repainted, the building that houses Him to be repaired, and regular puja to be conducted.

## The temple complex: the Natya Mandir

One enters the temple complex from the north entrance to the Natya Mandir (#10) or dancing hall, after going up another short staircase of seven steps, the Sat Pahacha (#xx). The building measures 80 by 80 feet outside and 69 by 67 feet inside.

The Natya Mandir is the place where most programs of kirtan and dance are held for the entertainment of Lord Jagannath. It is also where most people come in order to gaze upon their Lordships’ beauty.

At the eastern edge of the Natya Mandirand in front of the Chatrabhoga Mandapstands the Garudapillaror Garuda stambha (#11). A statue of the Lord’s eternal associate Garuda stands atop this high pillar with hands folded, engaged in constant prayers of praise to Lord Jagannath, Balaram and Subhadra.

There is a custom of taking darshan of Lord Jagannath from behind this pillar. Many people believe that the Syamantaka Mani is hidden inside the Garuda pillar. They thus press their chest to the pillar in the hope that their diseases will be cured.

The Lord’s Devadasis formerly gave performances of the *Gīta-govinda* at noon and in the evening directly in front of the Garuda pillar, immediately before the Lord performed His pastime of taking rest.

*garuḍera sannidhāne rahi kare daraśane*  
*se ānandera ki kahiba āra*  
*garuḍa-stambhera tale ache eka nimna-khāle*  
*se khāla bharila aśru-jale*

**Mahaprabhu would stand beside the Garudapillarand gaze at Lord Jagannath. The ecstasy He felt was beyond description. There is a little drain that runs past the Garuda pillar, and this drain filled with the water of His tears. (CC** [**2.2.54**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/2.54)**)**

There are many paintings on the walls and ceiling of this building. King Prataparudra had Mahaprabhu’s six-armed form painted on the ceiling, but other significant paintings include the ten incarnations and Krishna and Balaram on horseback.

## Bhoga Mandap or Chatrabhoga Mandap

The Bhoga Mandap (#12) is where certain food offerings are made to Lord Jagannath. It is a *pañca-ratha* type structure like the main temple. It is made of yellowish sandstone, rendered red by ochre painting. Carvings of mythological scenes from Krishna's lila carved in the niches of the barandi or upper jangha. There are paintings of the king of Orissa participating the twelve principal festivals.

Other important sculptures on the wall mainly represent Krishna's lila, like Dola Yatra, Nauka Lila, Krishna playing the flute playing or herding the cows and various other poses.

Generally speaking, there are two kinds of food offerings, known as *koṭha-bhoga* and *chatra-bhoga.* Only *chatra-bhoga* offerings, which come from the gifts of the various maths of Puri and the personal contributions of pilgrims and other individuals, are made in this pavilion. *Koṭha-bhoga*, which is paid for from temple income and government funds (formerly by the King of Orissa himself), is made in the Mani Kotha itself. A portion of the *koṭha-bhoga* prasad is given to the king, the pujaris and the other temple servants, and what is left is sold in the Ananda Bazaar, the proceeds going into the king’s coffers.

## Mukha Shala or Jagamohan

Facing the main temple is the Mukha Shala (*mukha-śālā*) (#6). It is also sometimes called the Bahar Pokharia or the Jagamohan. This is the covered area between the door to the Garbha Mandir, also known as the Jaya Vijaya Dwar,and the sandalwood barrier (#3)(*candana-argala*) leading to the Natya Mandira. Visitors can gaze upon the lovely image of the Lord from the Mukha Shala.

A number of important rooms connect to the open area of the Mukha Shala, including the Shayan Thakur’s room, where the Lord’s representative deity takes rest at night. There are also store rooms where Lord Jagannath’s clothes and other paraphernalia are kept.

The Jagamohan is of the architectural type known as “pidha deul” (see diagram). That is, it is shaped roughly like a pyramid, though it also is crowned with the amla and kalasa like the rekha deul. The Jagamohan was built at the same time as the Biman, for the two buildings stand on same plinth or foundation. The outer surface of the Jagamohan is profusely decorated with erotic scenes.

Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, however, used to take Jagannath’s darshan from behind the pillar of Garuda in the Jagamohan or Natya Mandir. In keeping with that tradition, devotees in the Gaudiya Vaishnava line usually go to that spot, where Mahaprabhu’s footprints were preserved and look at Jagannath while remembering Mahaprabhu.

## The Biman

The main temple building or Biman is where Lords Jagannath, Balaram, Subhadra and Sudarshan are housed, facing the east. The deities are seated on the altar or throne called the Ratnavedi in the inner sanctum or *sanctum sanctorum* (“Holy of Holies”). This chamber is also known as the Mani Kotha*,* Garbha Mandir or Bhitara Pokharia.

Since their Lordships face the east, Jagannath sits on the northern side of the altar, Balaram is on the south and Subhadra sits between them. Since Jagannath is on the western side of the temple, the entire temple complex is built along an east-west axis.

It is commonly believed that a hundred thousand Shalagram Shilas were laid for the construction of the floor in the Mani Kotha.
