Orthodox Hindus thus refuse to tread on this floor lest their physical touch bring impurity to the holy cell. No sunlight comes into the Mani Kotha, which is illuminated only by ghee burning lamps.

Since their Lordships face the east, Lord Jagannath sits on the northern side of the altar, Balaram is on the south and Subhadra sits between them. Though one most often hears about three deities, one must not forget the other murtis who sit on the Ratna-vedi, the *saptadhā murti.* According to the *Nīlādri-mahodaya,* the Lord Himself is manifest on the altar in seven different forms (*saptadhā-mūrti*): Jagannath, Baladeva, Subhadra, Sudarshan, Vishwadhatri, Lakshmi and Madhava.

## The temple tower or shikara

The tower of the temple building is 217 feet high and 42 feet in diameter, on a base 80 feet square. It is built in the *pañca-ratha* style, meaning that its external wall is divided into five protruding segments, two *anurathas*, two *konakas*, and the central *rāhā.*

The chakrathat crowns the temple spire is called Nila Chakra. It is said to be made of the eight-metal alloy, *aṣṭa-dhātu.* In 1594, the first king of Khurda to take responsibility for the Jagannath temple, Ramachandra Deva I, replaced the old chakra when it was damaged in a typhoon.

At the very pinnacle of the temple, on a mast above the Nila Chakra, is a flag decorated with nada and bindu, representing pranava, that can be placed there by ordinary pilgrims with the help of the temple priests. The service of climbing on the temple tower and placing the flag on this mast or lighting lamps is the exclusive right of one particular group of temple servants, handed down from generation to generation. For a fee that may range anywhere from one to 700 rupees, they will scoot up the tower rapidly to tie another flag to the mast.

Every Ekadasinight, ghee lamps are placed below the Nila Chakra at the top of the shikara, as well as on the Bhoga and Natya Mandirs. These are called the “great lamps” (*mahā-dīpa*). As these lamps are being placed on the outside of these buildings, the assembled devotees give a great cheer or *jaya-dhvani.*

The temple shikara is also decorated with tilak. In the eleventh century, Ramanujacharya, the teacher of the *viśiṣṭādvaita* doctrine, came to visit Jagannath Puri. According to many, he converted Chodaganga Deva, a Shaiva, to Vaishnavism. As a result, the tilak of the Sri Vaishnava sampradaya was painted on the temple tower.

However, from the time of Prataparudra up until that of Mukunda Deva, the grandfather of the current Gajapati king of Puri, all the kings of Puri were initiated in the Gaudiya sampradaya. All were worshipers of Lord Chaitanya and Sri Sri Radha-Govinda. Throughout this period, the tilak of the Gaudiya Vaishnava sampradaya adorned the temple crown.

In the early 20thcentury, Ramachandra Deva IV, father of the current Gajapati, took initiation in the Ramanuja sampradaya from the abbot of the Emar Math. Now the tilak of the Ramanuja sampradaya is once again painted there. Despite this external change, however, Mahaprabhu’s image and lotus feet continue to be worshiped inside the main temple without controversy, and Gaudiya tilak is occasionally painted on Jagannath’s forehead during the Rathayatra. Many other signs of Mahaprabhu’s special position in Lord Jagannath’s temple continue to be evident.

In *Śrī-Kṣetra*, Sundarananda writes that not so long ago, the abbots of several rich and influential Ramanuja sampradaya monasteries offered a large amount of money to the temple in an effort to have a murti of Ramanujacharya placed on a platform near the Paduka Kund. However, all their money and influence did not move the king or temple management to approve their scheme. Apparently, the Gajapati said to them, “If you try to place a new image of your acharya within the Kurma Bera, then the tilak on the temple tower will disappear.”

## Entering through the other gates

The southern gate (#72) was originally guarded by two battle horses, hence its name of Ashwa Dwaror “Horse’s Gate.” Sometime back the horses were removed to the northeast doorway of the inner enclosure and have since been somehow lost (!)

As one enters the southern gate, one comes to a Narasinghatemple (#??). The Narasingha deity faces north. A great saint of the Ramanuja sampradaya, Vasudeva Ramanuja Das, installed this deity within recent memory.

Next to it is the 19th century Sadbhuja Gauranga Mandir (#73). The image is very old, but it falls within the part of the temple controlled by the temple cooks, so was long off limits to the general public. These Brahmins are Smartas rather than devotees and in the interests of purity, they blocked off entrance to this part of the grounds. This problem has now been resolved, since the time of Gauri Shyama, a former Deputy Magistrate who spent his retired life mostly in this temple.

It is a sign of the special favor accorded Mahaprabhu in the Jagannath temple that though no musical instruments such as gongs are permitted in the worship of any of the other innumerable gods who have shrines within the temple, an exception is made in the case of the six-armed form of Gauranga.\[63\]Kirtan accompanied with musical instruments is an accepted part of His daily worship.

Right next to it is the hut where Vasudeva Ramanuja Das did his bhajan. There is also a Hanuman shrine known as Baro Bhai (“twelve brothers”). An unusual colored sketch of the Jagannath deities has been painted on the wall of this temple. The deities are back-to-back amidst blazing fire, with Jagannath at the bottom, Subhadra, at his back on a higher level, and above her, Balabhadra.

Just before the gate that leads into the Kurma Berha, one can turn into Lord Jagannath’s kitchen to the right, while to the left lies the temple of Burhi Ma Thakurani, the goddess of small pox and cholera (#76). From there, one can turn left into a passage leading to the flower garden, known as Sri Jagannath Tota.

In the northeastern corner of this garden is a small building where Lord Jagannath’s garlands and flower decorations are made. There are three Shiva lingas in the garden, Siddheshwar (#82) and Chakra Narayan(#81) to the south and to the left as one enters the garden, Dhavaleshwar (no number). The upavana also has modern images of Navagunjara, Chakra Narayan, Kailasa Parvat, Ananta Narayan, Radha Krishna, Garuda, Panchamukhi Hanuman (#78), Rama, Vibhishan, etc.

Raj Panda Samanta Ramachandra Mahapatra of Bali Sahi constructed a Ramachandra temple. Rama Lakshman and Sita with devotees in two rows standing in two flanks (1) Bharata, Satrughna, Bibhishan, Susena, Hanuman, Angada, Nala, Sugriva, Nila, Gandharva, Madana, Jambavan and Susena. The shrine has marble flooring and an figure of Garuda with outstretched wings faces it.

At a distance of fifty yards from the stairway, there is a tiny temple dedicated to Pancha Mukha Hanuman (#78). The pathway leading to it is thorny. To the south of this temple is a cemented platform where nirmalya used to be dried out. From this point one gets a glorious view of the great temple, upon which the images of Jagannath, Subhadra and Balaram have been sculpted to a great height.

The surroundings covering south and west of the temple enclosure are not maintained at all. Scrubby jungle with overgrowth of thorny plants and creepers make a happy abode for reptiles, which need early clearance. Two business magnates of Calcutta, mainly the Birlas and Banguros promised to maintain the flower gardens for Jagannath and to construct Gita Bhavan therein.

## Lord Jagannath’s kitchen

The temple kitchen (#71) is on the southeast side of the temple grounds. It is accessible either from the south or east entrances, but entry is prohibited to anyone other than the authorized temple cooks.

The kitchen used to be attached to the east of the main temple building, but smoke would enter the temple to the great inconvenience of Lord Jagannath. The former structure was also felt to be too small. As a result, a much larger kitchen was constructed during the reign of Dibyasingha Deva (1690-1713). It was built from donations of Rajendra Raya under the auspices of the minister Govinda Mahapatra.

The cooks are named *sūpkārs* or *suārs*. The cooking is done in special clay pots on ovens with nine mouths placed according to the Vaishnavagni yantra. The fires are lit every day after a Vaishnava *agni-homa* is performed, invoking Lakshmi and Narayan. Over 200 ovens and 300 cooks participate in making Jagannath’s offerings every day.

The covered passage leading into the Chatrabhoga Mandap makes it impossible for outsiders to see the food before it is offered to Lord Jagannath. The cooks keep their mouths and noses covered with masks, which prevent them from smelling or tasting the foodstuffs before they are offered.

When the food is offered in the Chatrabhoga Mandap, then the doors to the temple doors are kept open so the deity can see it. Three pujaris stand facing the north to make the offering. At that time, visitors to the temple are allowed to be present; they must line up along the sides of the Natya Mandiror stand in the Jagamohan, but are not allowed to sit or stand in the middle of the Natya Mandir. *Koṭha-bhoga*, on the other hand, is offered with the doors of the Bhoga Mandir closed. Musical instruments are played during these offerings.

## Vyaghra Dwar (“Tiger’s Gate”)

The Western gate (#83) or Vyaghra Dwar (“Tiger’s Gate”) had no special sculpted guards. Apparently meant as a private entrance for the aristocratic ladies of thus named Khanja Dwar. The word *khañjā* refers to the materials that go into Jagannath’s offerings that are taken through this gate.

As one enters through the western gate, one comes across several images: those of Rameshwar Mahadeva, Jagannath, Dvarikanath, Badrinath, the lords of the four dhamas established by Shankara (#84-87).

One can turn right into the flower garden known as Jagannath Tota or Nilachala Upavan.

## Hasti Dwar (“Elephant’s Gate”)

The five-foot-high elephants with Mahouts that formerly graced Hasti Dwar (“Elephant’s Gate”) have since been shifted inside for safety as the narrow entrance way might have damaged them.

As one enters this entrance on the north side, there is a temple to Sitala Devi (#96). In the adjoining open space is a well known as Sona Kupa (#97). Water is drawn for the well for Lord Jagannath’s Snana Yatra, but otherwise is left unused. It is cleaned each year on the eve of the Snana Yatrafestival. Inside the second gate, if one goes through a door on the western side, one sees a huge banyan tree. Within this enclosed area, there is an elevated platform called Kaivalya (Koili) Vaikuntha (#93). According to the legend, this is the exact spot where Vishvavasuworshiped Nila Madhava..

Other shrines clustered near this entrance are Uttarayani, Hanuman, Somanath, Badri Narayan, Dhavaleshwar.

## Koili Vaikuntha

From the top of the steps leading from the northern entrance, one can enter the compound where the Koili Vaikuntha (#93) is found. This is a two-storied brick house, standing where Nila Madhava was worshiped. The actual name is derived from *kaivalya vaikuṇṭha*, meaning.

Those who desire to make a permanent grant to the temple undergo a ceremonial ritual here called atika bandhana to ratify the promise. Feeding of the poor at this place is considered especially meritorious. A small image of Gopinath (of recent make) is installed in the top story.

Attached to this is a Shiva linga, Vaikuntheshwar (#94). Ganesh, one of the Parshwa Devatas of this Shaivite temple, is seen in its southern niche.

There is a flower garden on the west and north of the compound that were laid during the time of Raj Sahib Gaura Shyam Mohanty as manager of the temple. This is the burial ground of the sacred figures called Madhavi Kunj or Koili Vaikuntha Upavan. Nowadays, it looks forlorn, as if abandoned. There is a well there (#91), now full of wild growth where after the Nava Kalevara the old images are consigned. There are two Shiva temples, one in the southwest corner (#89), the other in the northeast (#90), who serve as guards of the burial place. They are known as Smashanadhipati Shiva.

Two spacious platforms in this area are used to dry boiled rice prasad in the sun to be sold for pilgrims wishing to carry it back to their homes.

## Ananda Bazaar

The Ananda Bazaar (#100)*,* the site for sale of Maha Prasad occupies the entire northeastern corner of the temple complex. Lord Jagannath’s Snana Mandap (#101), where He is ceremonially bathed on the full-moon day in May-June, is also in this part of the temple grounds. From this elevated platform, the Deities can be seen from the Boro Danda. Close by is the Chahani Mandap (#102). On the occasion of Bahuda festival Lakshmi observes the return journey of Jagannath in the car (Ratha) from this platform and welcomes Him from the Singha Dwar.

The words *ānanda bājār* mean “marketplace of joy.” It refers to the portion of the temple grounds set aside for the sale of Jagannath’s Maha Prasad. This area is in the northeastern corner of the temple complex, near Lord Jagannath’s Snana Mandap.

Many scriptures have glorified food offered to Lord Vishnu, or Maha Prasad: it never becomes contaminated or transformed, it does not become affected even if touched by untouchable outcastes, it can be transported long distances without becoming polluted.

The gods headed by Lord Brahma all desire to obtain Lord Jagannath’s remnants and so they seek it out. If it is beneficial for them, how much more so it will be for humans.**

One who takes Jagannath’s prasad loses all his previously accumulated sins and starts on the road to devotion to Krishna. The same thing happens to one’s entangling pious credits. In the *Lakṣmī-purāṇa,* Balaram Das recounts a legend about the origins of the feature Lakshmi once visited the house of an untouchable woman. Jagannath and Balaram decided to punish her by driving her out of the temple. The trouble was that when Lakshmi was gone, Krishna and Balaram had no one to cook for them. Finally, they became so hungry that they went out on the street to beg for alms, but no one gave them anything. They wandered from door to door until they came to the very house of the untouchable whose friendship with Lakshmi they had condemned. There, they were surprised to discover Lakshmi Devi and they begged for her forgiveness, asking her to come back with them to the main temple. Lakshmi Devi accepted their apologies, but made certain stipulations before agreeing to come back to the temple. She insisted that Maha Prasad should always be free of caste distinctions and that even if an outcaste should touch the sacred food, no Brahmin should make any objection to taking it.

However, Svarupa Damodar stopped them and the shopkeepers returned to their shops and sat down with their baskets. In the Ananda Bazaar, Jagannath’s prasad is often spilled on the ground. Devotees must thus be very careful there, because it is considered offensive to touch with one’s feet anything that is sanctified by contact with Vishnu. A certain Seth Ram Kumar Rangorhad a covered, elevated concrete platform constructed to help solve the above problem, but other than during the rainy season, prasad is sold outside this covered area.

The open space is studded with mango and ashwattha trees giving cool shade. Now roofed platforms have been constructed for the protection of the buyers and sellers from the heat of the sun and inclemencies of the weather. Taps have been provided for washing. Some criticism is levelled at the disrespectful behavior of the prasad sellers.

One of the unique features of the Ananda Bazaaris that there is no consideration of contamination. People of different castes will eat from the same leaf plate without any fear of pollution. This is extraordinary behavior for caste Hindus, who are usually very careful about such things.

*ṭaṅkā nā thile bi purīre*  
*chāpan prakār bhog khāi hebā*

**“In Puri, even the pauper eats fifty-six items of Maha Prasad.” (An Orissan saying)**

## A Christian sailor gives a bell to Jagannath

To the south of the Boro Deul is the Niladri Bihar Museum where there are many historical artefacts related to the temple and town of Puri. One of the interesting exhibits is a large bell that was originally intended for a Catholic church in Pondicherry.

Even before the British had established their rule in India, the French were governing Pondicherry in South Indiaand had built a huge church there for their Catholic mission. A ship carrying an appropriately sized bell for this church set sail from France under the command of Captain Albaque Beatow. This ship docked in Calcutta, where a number of passengers set ashore and others were taken aboard, and then set sail southwards for Pondicherry along the eastern coast of India.

While the passengers were enjoying the voyage, Captain Beatow was reconnoitering with his telescope. He observed that a great storm was approaching from the south. Not only that, but a huge sea creature also seemed to be on a collision course with the ship. It was still two or three miles away, but the captain warned everyone on board of the imminent danger, telling them to take precautions in order to save their lives.

As the creature came closer, the captain saw that it was an immense whale with terrifying eyes, terrible teeth and a huge mouth that looked as though it could swallow the entire universe. The creature came closer and closer and the captain began to tremble with fear at what seemed to be imminent disaster. He saw that its mouth was big enough to swallow the entire ship.

Captain Beatow blew his whistle givingthe danger signal and told everyone to pray to Jesus Christ and prepare to give up their souls to him. Everyone fell to prayer, but the whale kept coming closer and a collision seemed inevitable. The captain began to lament, “Alas, it seems that I will be helplessly drowned today.”

At that time he noticed that one Bengali passenger was calmly chanting the Holy Names in front of a portrait of Lord Jagannath. The captain asked him what he was doing and the man answered, “I am praying to Lord Jagannath of Puri. If He is kind, then we will be delivered from all dangers.”

The captain said, “We have all been praying to no avail. So what harm is there in appealing to this deity as well?” So thinking, he fell to his knees and said, “O Lord, please deliver us from this terror.”

Amazingly, in a few moments, the storm died down and the whale changed course. The ship was saved! Captain Beatow was overjoyed and he embraced his Bengali passenger, saying, “My friend! Your deity has saved us from a great danger today. I thought we were doomed. What can I ever do to repay you?” After thinking for a moment, he said, “I know, I will give you the bell that was meant for the church in Pondicherry as an offering to your chosen deity.”

Afew hours later, the ship docked at Puri and the Captain had the bell unloaded and brought to the temple. He made a gift of the bell and also gave some money for Lord Jagannath’s service. The following words are inscribed on the bell:

‘IN LIBERALITE’ DE PEDRO MOUDELI  
COURT: DE LA COMP. DE FRANCE ME NOMME PIERRE  
JE PESE 900  
A PONDICHERRY, 1746  
BETPSALLAMINGEN  
CANTATIBUS.” \[64\]

When word of this event got out, it caused a furor in Christian circles. The Catholic Church appealed to the French government to arrange for the bell’s return. Through diplomatic channels, the French asked the British government and this request was conveyed to the temple authorities at Puri. However, the priests answered that it was not their policy to return gifts that had been given to Lord Jagannath.

For some time letters traveled back and forth between these various parties with no result. From time to time, the French government continues to request the return of the bell, even up to the present day. After Independence, while Jawaharlal Nehru was prime minister, the French ambassador again raised the issue. Nehru personally asked the temple authorities to return the bell but received the same answer that they had given for generations.

## Chapter 9 - Patita Pavan

Patita Pavan is a solitary deity of Jagannath who is visible to all pilgrims from the Singha Dwar entrance to the Sri Mandir. The name *patita-pāvana* means “savior of the most fallen.” Since everyone but those of legitimate Hindu birth are allowed inside the temple, the Lord mercifully manifests in this form at the gate where He can be seen by even those who are disqualified by sin or birth from entering.

## History

Some people say that the Lord took the form of Patita Pavan for the sake of Sal Beg, Jagannath’s celebrated Muslim devotee (see chapter 33), but the more accepted version is that this deity was consecrated during the reign of the second Ramachandra Deva (1732-1743).

Ramachandra Deva II was king of Khurda during a period of unrest. When the Muslim governor, Taqui Khan, decided to plunder the Jagannath temple, Jagannath’s priests saved the deities by concealing them on an island in the Chilka lake. The frustrated Taqui Khan proceeded to Khurda where he defeated and imprisoned Ramachandra Deva. He forcibly converted him to Islam, renaming him Hafiz Qadar Muhammad.

Taqui Khan died in 1734 and was replaced by Murshid Quli Khan II, who became the Naib Nazim or governor of Orissa. Murshid Quli Khan was a sympathetic ruler who allowed the images of Jagannath to be reinstalled and their worship to be restored. He also gave his daughter to Hafiz Qadar (Ramachandra Deva) in marriage in 1738. Ramachandra Deva, however, was ousted from Hindu society and even deserted by his own family because of his change of religion and marriage to a Muslim.

In his heart, however, Ramachandra Deva never truly converted to Islam and wished to be reinstated as a Hindu. He came to Puri to take darshan of Jagannath but was not allowed to do so. In sympathy for his genuine penitence, however, the priests of the temple came to a compromise and installed the Patita Pavan deity near the Singha Dwar entrance so that the king could take darshan of the Lord. Ramachandra is also credited as the author of the *Patita-pāvanāṣṭakam*, a Sanskrit prayer for the mercy of Lord Jagannath (see end of chapter).

## Temple Entry Prohibition

Traditionally, the following groups of people are not admitted into the Jagannath temple: fishers, leather workers, those who burn the dead, sweepers, distillers, brewers and wine sellers, potters, fallen women and prostitutes, members of non-Hindu tribes, foreigners and those belonging to other religions like Muslims or Christians. Besides these, other non-believers or atheists are not knowingly permitted to cross the temple threshold.

Some say that during British rule, a European tried to enter the temple disguised as a Hindu, but was detected before he could get as far as the Nat Mandir. Even so, because he had entered as far as he did, the priests considered the temple to have been desecrated and performed an elaborate bathing ritual (the Maha Snana) for Lord Jagannath to restore the temple’s purity. It was thus confirmed that faithless people of other religions are completely forbidden entry into the temple just to satisfy their curiosity.

In 1958, the Mukti Mandap Sabha handled a case that required an interpretation of the admissions policy for the Jagannath Temple. It involved four American women who had been converted to Hinduism at a Ramakrishna Vedanta Society in the United States and wished to enter the temple while visiting Puri. To gain permission they approached the Raja, who in turn placed the decision before the Mukti Mandap Sabha. The president of the Sabha, Saccidananda Saraswati, said that in order to decide the case he would have to interview the Americans. He was profoundly impressed by the American women, who wore Indian dress and who expressed a familiarity with Hindu manners and customs. Saccidananda's broad-minded “test of a true Hindu” is worth quoting:

“The American ladies had put on saris and veils and they bowed their heads before their superiors just as Indian ladies do. They were reserved and respected their husbands as embodiments of the deity. They were not short tempered. They did not eat fish, mutton, beef, or any other meat. They were fully knowledgeable of Hindu principles of life. They took a morning and evening bath and prayed for the welfare of humanity. They were honest and very sympathetic towards the poor and the sick... They had become truly Hindu.”\[65\]

Saccidananda Saraswati decided that the Americans should be allowed entrance into the temple and a majority of the other members of the Mukti Mandap Sabha accepted his verdict. This was the first time that the Mukti Mandap Sabha had ever granted foreign converts permission to enter the Jagannath Temple. This attempt at social reform, however, ended in 1964 when the Mukti Mandap Sabha reversed its earlier decision and denied temple entrance to several other American members of the Ramakrishna Vedanta Society.

Since then, a large number of Americans and Europeans have turned to Vaishnavism and have made several attempts to negotiate entry into the temple. The celebrated founder of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, visited Jagannath Puri on January 26, 1977 in order to request the Puri Brahmins to allow his Western disciples to enter the temple. A part of the speech he gave to them is as follows:

This stumbling block should be dissolved. You want to pack Jagannath Swami up inside your home, and do not want to expand His mercy. He is Jagannath, the lord of the universe, not only the lord of Puri, or the lord of Orissa. He is Jagannath. Krishna declares in the Bhagavad Gita, *bhoktāraṁ yajña-tapasāṁ sarva-loka-maheśvaram*. That is the definition of Jagannath, *sarva-loka-maheśvaram*. So why you should deny the inhabitants of all the world (*sarva-loka*) the darshan of Jagannath? Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu never approved such thing. Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu said,

*pṛthivīte āche jata nagarādi grāma*  
*sarvatra pracāra haibe mora nāma*

**“My name will be spread throughout every town and village in the world.”**

Now this is being done and people from all over the world are eager to come here, so why do you restrict them?

Of course, if you do not allow these foreigners to enter the temple, there is no loss for them, because Jagannath has already come to them and they are worshiping Him. But it is the proper etiquette to show respect to the Vaishnavas. They are strictly observing the four principles of pious life by negation: no illicit sex, no meat-eating, no fish-eating, no egg-eating, no intoxication, no gambling. They are thus purified.

Mahaprabhu has condemned Vaishnava aparadh. These European and American Vaishnavas are hankering after Jagannath’s darshan -- *jagannātha svāmī nayana-patha-gāmī bhavatu me*. Through your intervention they may be able to see Jagannath Swami. Since these Vaishnavas are so eager to come to Jagannath Puri and to see Jagannath, you should welcome them. You should receive them well, because Narottam Das Thakur says, *chāṛiyā vaiṣṇava sevā, nistāra pāyeche kebā* – ‘Who can be liberated without serving the Vaishnavas?” And the scripture also says,

*ārādhanānām sarveṣāṁ viṣṇor ārādhanaṁ param*  
*tasmāt parataraṁ devi tadīyānāṁ samarcanam*

**“Of all kinds of worship, that of Vishnu is supreme. However, superior to the worship of Vishnu is the worship of His devotees.” (*****Padma-purāṇa*** **6.253.176)**

I have thus come to specially request you to remove this restriction and be friendly to the foreign devotees.

The former chief minister of Orissa Hare Krushna Mahatab was very favorable to the Krishna consciousness movement and tried very hard for many years to help the western devotees gain entrance into the Jagannath temple but was unsuccessful, though other temples such as that of Ananta Vasudeva in Bhubaneswar did open their doors to foreign Vaishnavas.

The Mukti Mandap has remained intransigeant in its conservatism. As recently as June, 2000, the Shankaracharya of Govardhan Pith in Puri, who converted a number of Indian Christians and Muslims back to Hinduism asked that those whose ancestors had been forcibly converted to another religion be welcomed back into the Hindu fold and allowed to enter the temple. Organisations like the Vishwa Hindu Parishad also advocated that converts be treated like all other Hindus.

In response, however, Lingaraj Mishra, the secretary of the Mukti Mandap Pandit Sabha, affirmed the traditional position: “The lower caste people, mainly from the Pana community, who had been converted into Christianity are known as Mleccha (untouchables) and they eat the flesh of cows. We cannot allow Mleccha people to enter the lord Jagannath temple at Puri, whether they are Hindus or Christians. The temple is not open to people who eat beef because cows are worshipped in the Hindu religion.” He also added, “People who are returning to the Hindu fold may again go back to some other religion. Those whose entry in the temple is prohibited can have darshan of the Lord when He is taken out on procession during the Rathayatra.”

## Untouchability and devotional service

It is said in the scriptures that the Lord gives everyone the right to serve him. No one is deprived of this – *bhaktau nṛ-mātrasyādhikāritā.* And anyone who achieves devotional service is the best of humanity:

*nīca-jāti nahe kṛṣṇa-bhajane ayogya*  
*sat-kula vipra nahe bhajanera yogya*  
*jei bhaje sei baṛa abhakta hīna chāra*  
*kṛṣṇa-bhajane nāi jāti-kulādi vicāra*

**"A person born in a low family is not unfit for discharging devotional service to Krishna, nor is one fit for devotional service simply because he is born in an aristocratic family of Brahmins. Anyone who takes to devotional service is exalted, whereas a non devotee is always condemned and abominable. Therefore in the discharge of devotional service to the Lord, there is no consideration of one's family status." (CC** [**3.4.66-7**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-antya/4.66)**)**

*jāti kula saba nirarthaka bujhāite*  
*janmilena haridāsa adhama kulete*

**In order to prove to the world that one’s caste or family background have no relevance to one’s spiritual life, Hari Das took birth in a lowly family. (Cbh** [**1.16.237**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cb-adi/16.237)***)***

*je te kule vaiṣṇavera janma kene nahe*  
*tathāpiha sarva-vandya sarva-śāstra kahe*

**Wherever a Vaishnava takes birth, whether in a high or low caste, he is to be respected by all. This is the verdict of all the scriptures. (Cbh** [**2.10.100**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cb-madhya/10.100)**)**

Lord Krishna Himself states the same principle in the *Bhagavad-gītā:*

*māṁ hi pārtha vyapāśritya*  
*ye’pi syuḥ pāpa-yonayaḥ*  
*striyo vaiśyas tathā śūdrās*  
*te’pi yānti parāṁ gatim*

The translation of this verse, following in the footsteps of Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakur, is as follows:

**“O Partha! Outcastes and foreigners, fallen women like prostitutes, as well as those men who belong to the lower castes like merchants or common laborers, all quickly attain the supreme destination if they take refuge in Me by performing exclusive devotion. For those who have taken to the path of devotion, birth and race present no obstacle to attaining spiritual perfection.” (**[**9.32**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/9.32)**)**

Vishwanath Chakravarti comments on this verse in the *Sārārtha-varṣiṇī* (His commentary on the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam is called *Sārārtha-darśinī.*): “In the verse beginning *api cet sudurācāro*, the Lord says that devotion to Him does not take any consideration of sinful activities that arise accidentally. There is nothing extraordinary in that. Now in this verse, Krishna further expands the definition of sin to include congenital defects of sinful character and tells us that bhakti does not take any consideration of them, either.”

Vishwanath also elaborates on the word *pāpa-yonayaḥ* (“those born of sin or into sin”) to include even those born into the untouchable or non-Hindu castes (Mlecchas). The two following verses from the Srimad Bhagavatam are given as support for this idea:

*kirāta hūṇāndhra pulinda pulkaśā*  
*ābhīra śumbhā yavanāḥ khasādayaḥ*  
*ye 'nye ca pāpā yad apāśrayāśrayāḥ*  
*śudhyanti tasmai prabhaviṣṇave namaḥ*

**I beg to offer my respectful obeisances unto the Lord, the supreme power. By taking shelter of His devotees, Kiratas, Huns, Andhras, Pulindas, Pulkashas, Abhiras, Shumbhas, Muslims, members of the Khasa races and others addicted to sinful acts can be purified. (SB** [**2.4.18**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-2/4.18)**)**

The various castes, tribes and nations mentioned here are those who have a sinful defect arising from birth (*janma-gata*), while the words *anye ca pāpāḥ* refer to those who have fallen into sinful activity (*karma-gata*). All such sinful people can be purified by taking shelter of a pure devotee spiritual master.

The next verse tells that a devotee who chants the Holy Name, no matter what the nature of his birth, is superior to a Brahmin qualified to perform the Soma sacrifice:

*aho bata śva paco 'to garīyān*  
*yaj jihvāgre vartate nāma tubhyam*  
*tepus tapas te juhuvuḥ sasnur āryā*  
*brahmānūcur nāma gṛṇanti ye te*

**O my Lord, how much more can I glorify the person who chants Your holy name? Even though this name may only touch the tip of his tongue, and even though he may have been born of a low family like that of a dog eater, he becomes most worshipable. Such a person must be accepted as a functional Brahmin despite his low birth because he must have previously engaged in all the religious activities that give the Brahmin his qualifications, such as penances and sacrifices according to Vedic rituals, taking his bath in all the holy places of pilgrimage, studying the Vedic literatures and following strict regulations in one’s personal life. Only after thorough perfecting these activities would it be possible for him to chant the Holy Name in this lifetime. (SB** [**3.33.7**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/33.7)**)**

There are a vast number of other verses in the holy scriptures that indicate that bhakti is capable of destroying the character flaws that arise out of low birth and sinful behavior. The Lord himself stated this to the king of devotees, Uddhava:

*bhaktyāham ekayā grāhyaḥ*  
*śraddhayātmā priyaḥ satām*  
*bhaktiḥ punāti man niṣṭhā*  
*śva pākān api sambhavāt*

**I, who as the Supreme Soul am the ultimate object of affection and love, can be attained only through exclusive devotion born of faith. Such devotion performed with single-minded attention purifies even those who are outside the caste system. (SB** [**11.14.21**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-11/14.21)**)**

In his commentary to the above verse, Sridhar Swami glosses the word *sambhavāt* as *jāti-doṣād api*, “from even the faults arising with birth.”

So, though the natural state of the pure spirit soul is to serve Krishna, he falls down due to the influence of the illusory energy of the Lord. Nevertheless, there is a principle stated in the Chaitanya Charitamrita, that “Lord Chaitanya saved everyone who fell down before Him” (*je āge paṛaye tāre karaye nistāra –* CC [1.5.209](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-adi/5.209)). When a jiva remembers his true identity as Krishna’s servant and falls down before the Lord to beg forgiveness for all his previous sins, the Lord responds by giving His fearless lotus feet as an eternal shelter.

*keṅde kahe ohe kṛṣṇa āmi tava dāsa*  
*tomāra caraṇa chāṛi haila sarva-nāśa*  
*kṛṣṇa tāre dena cic-chaktira bala*  
*māyā ākarṣaṇa chāṛe haiyā durbala*

**When the jiva cries out, saying, “O Krishna! I am your servant. I have come to ruin because I rejected Your lotus feet,” then Krishna gives him strength from His spiritual energy. Maya weakens and the jiva can free himself from her hold over him. (Bhaktivinoda Thakur)**

Those jivas who are reluctant to serve the Supreme Lord are punished by His external energy. Once they turn to the Lord, however, they no longer have anything to fear. They simply have to take shelter of the Lord’s personal associate in the form of the spiritual master. The Lord is an ocean of unlimited beneficence to one who takes shelter of Him. If one who has taken shelter unknowingly commits some offence to the Lord, then He readily forgives him. He only admits of an inability to forgive offences made to His devotees -- unless that devotee first forgives the offender. The Lord is a devotee of His own devotees and thus He treats anyone blessed by His devotee as His very own, as the servant of His servant. Therefore it is said that God’s blessings follow the blessings of His devotees (*bhakta-kṛpānugāminī*). One who has never received the blessings of the Lord’s devotee should not expect to directly attain the blessings of the Lord.

## Dasia Bauri

In view of the Lord’s liberal attitude toward His devotees, it is something of a mystery as to why devotees born in lower castes or non-Hindu families are excluded from His temple in Jagannath Puri, especially when He has the reputation of being Patita Pavan, “the savior of the most fallen.” In fact, though there are many famous deities of Krishna in India such as Sri Nathji, Dwarakadhish, Balaji, Radha Raman, Udupi Krishna and all of them are certainly merciful according to their own particular mood, none of them is as famous as Lord Jagannath for being Patita Pavan. Nor are any of them generally addressed as Jagannath, Lord of the Universe. Yet although they are not known as Lord of the Universe, who should therefore be accessible to all, or “saviors of the most fallen,” still everyone can have entrance into their temples. So why is there so much restriction with the temple of Patita Pavan Jagannath here in Puri?

If we examine the exchanges that Jagannath has with His “fallen devotees” we see that He often shows them more favor than He does to His “high-class servitors” such as the Gajapati kings or Pandas. There is no other temple tradition in India where the prohibition against lower class persons entering has played such a dramatic role in the Lord's pastimes. There are many examples of devotees, such as Dasia Bauri, Balaram Das and Sal Beg, who though socially marginalized were the recipients of Lord Jagannath’s extraordinary blessings.

Dasia Bauri’s story is told in *Dāṛhyatā-bhakti*. Dasia Bauri lived in Baligaon, a village just a short distance north of Puri. He was a great devotee of Lord Jagannath but was not allowed in the temple because he came from the untouchable Bauri or sweeper caste. The Pandas would have to take a bath if they even saw someone from his caste, what to speak of touching him.

Eventually, Dasia Bauri became so surrendered to Lord Jagannath that he gave up his work as a laborer and passed his days exclusively in prayer and bhajan. This indifference to his normal duties not only caused great concern among his family members, but amongst the higher caste people of the village, who took it as a sign of rebelliousness.

One day, some of the upper caste villagers decided to go to Sri Kshetra to have darshan of Lord Jagannath. When Dasia heard this, he picked a green coconut from his garden and asked a young Brahmin to offer it to the Lord on his behalf. He made a special request: “Do not give the coconut to Jagannath unless He takes it directly from your hand. Just say, ‘Dasia Bauri from our village of Baligaon has sent You this coconut. Kindly accept it.’ If He does not take it, then bring it back and return it to me.”

The young Brahmin was surprised by the request, as it is customary to hand gifts to the temple priest, who then makes a ritual offering to the Lord. Furthermore, he was doubtful that the Lord would accept the offerings of an untouchable like Dasia Bauri. Nevertheless, he agreed to try.

When the group of pilgrims came to the temple, they took darshan of Jagannath from the Jaga Mohan. The young Brahmin silently stood behind the Garuda pillar and repeated the words of Dasia Bauri. While he murmured the prayer to Lord Jagannath to accept the offering, a gigantic hand that looked like the trunk of Indra’s elephant, Airavata, extended from the Ratna Vedi and disappeared with the coconut. All the devotees present were astonished by the supernatural event.

The amazing event convinced the villagers of Dasia’s great devotion to Lord Jagannath. They ceased to trouble him for neglecting his labors. Dasia Bauri, on the other hand, felt such intense joy at the blessings of the Lord that he forgot all the miseries of material existence.

## Lakshmi and Sriya Chandulani

(This story was told in abbreviated form in the previous chapter. I think that this version may be dropped completely.)

Another feature of the special nature of caste relations in Jagannath Puri is, as we have already seen, the mystique of Jagannath’s Maha Prasad. In Jagannath Puri, all caste distinctions are forgotten where Maha Prasad is concerned. The 16thcentury Orissan poet, Balaram Das, recounts the following story in his *Lakṣmī Purāṇa.*

Once, on a Thursday in the month of Margashira, Lakshmi left her temple to visit her devotees in the town of Puri. On Thursdays, Indian women worship the goddess in their homes by cleaning them and making designs with rice paint.

On this particular, occasion, however, Lakshmi found none of the houses to her liking until she reached the outskirts of the town where Sriya Chandulani lived in a thatched cottage in the sweeper neigborhood. To her surprise, she found the lady observing the Lakshmi Puja rituals with great devotion. She had plastered the floor with fresh cow dung and drawn lotus flowers in front of her door as a sign of welcome to the Goddess of Fortune. She had lit a lamp of ten wicks, had arranged the ten kinds of fruits and flowers preferred by Lakshmi and was prostrating herself on the ground with heartfelt devotion. Lakshmi was moved by Sriya Chandulani’s devotion and accepted her offerings. She bestowed many blessings on her and transformed her hut into a palace.

When Balaram heard that Lakshmi had eaten in the house of an untouchable, he decided to bar her entry back into the temple. Jagannath tried to pacify His brother, but to no avail. When Lakshmi was refused entry on the temple grounds, she became very angry. She threw off her jewelry at Lord Jagannath’s feet and cursed Him: “O Lord! Now that I have lost my caste and become untouchable, I am leaving You. But I curse You that until You accept food from my hand, You will have neither food nor clothing for as long as the sun and the moon continue to rise.”

She went to the seashore where she had Vishwakarma build her a beautiful golden palace. She sent the eight Vetalas to plunder the temple storehouse, after putting Lord Jagannath and Balaram under a spell of sleep. Lakshmi also instructed Saraswati Devi to see to it that everyone the Lord approached for food would refuse Him.

The next morning, the brothers awoke to find the temple deserted. Not a morsel of food or drop of water were anywhere to be had. They fasted the whole day. The next day, the two brothers decided to go begging for alms. Dressed as poor Brahmins, they wandered the streets, but under Saraswati’s spell, none of the town’s residents showed them any mercy. Wherever they went, Krishna and Balaram were rebuked and driven out.

At last, a mendicant advised them to go to Sriya Chandulani’s seashore palace where, unknown to them, Lakshmi had taken up residence. As they approached her residence, however, Lakshmi ordered the Sun God to heat up the sands on the beach to scorch their feet. They made it to the front door, but were at first turned away by the gatekeeper. Finally, Lord Jagannath was overcome with humility and begged to be given some food to eat.

The answer came that the owner of the house was an untouchable, so how could she give Them anything to eat? Balaram answered that They could cook themselves if given the necessary ingredients. Lakshmi had all the materials sent to them, but she had not yet finished making the brothers suffer. She asked Agni Deva to interfere with their cooking, and so the brothers were soon coughing and Their eyes watering from the smoke. Unable to cook anything, Balaram became angry and broke the earthen cooking pots.

Finally, Jagannath and Baladeva broke down and decided to ask for cooked food from the Chandala house. Lakshmi was pleased and gave Them a sumptuous feast that the brothers immediately recognized as her cooking. They realized the mistake They had made and begged Lakshmi for forgiveness. She agreed to come back to the temple on one condition: that thenceforth no distinctions should be made for Maha Prasad.

## Conclusions

There are many examples in Vaishnava literature where Krishna deprives His own devotees of His association in order to increas the intensity of their feelings for Him, such as when He left the Rasa lila. Similarly, Jagannath has created a very intense contrast in Puri that churns the ocean of feelings in the hearts of His devotees. On the one hand, He is very opulent and inaccessible -- so much so that He does not even allow many of His devotees entrance into the temple. This invariably increases the devotees’ feelings of separation, humility and longing for Him. Then the Lord comes out for His public festivals and gives His darshan to all in a way much more accessible than other deities in India. Having the Lord's darshan at that time melts His devotees’ hearts.

Moreover, it also melts the heart of the Lord. Sal Beg and Balaram Das were not granted admittance to the temple or on the Rathayatra cart, yet the same opulent and inaccessible Jagannath was so much under their control that He would not allow His rath to move until they were present.

In view of such examples, those who fall into the outcaste category but have firm faith in the Lord may gaze on His Patita Pavan form in all humility and beg Him for His mercy. Sincere humility is the principal proof of faith, whereastrying to enter the temple by force or making arrogant claims to have a right to enter the temple are sure signs of a desire for control and mastery, in short, of the absence of faith.

In order to teach the kind of humility characteristic of the pure devotee, Lord Brahma, the original spiritual master of the universe, appeared in Gauranga Mahaprabhu’s pastimes as the Muslim devotee Hari Das Thakur. He and the most worshipable Rupa and Sanatana Goswamis, who were born in a very high caste Brahmin family, considered themselves to be untouchable and consequently never tried to walk through the Singha Dwar. These devotees had attained the highest limits of divine love, yet never made an attempt to break the rules established by the temple tradition. Instead, they set the example of paying their obeisance to the Lord by prostrating themselves on seeing the temple spire, the Nila Chakra, and the flags fluttering on the pinnacle.

After some years of relationships with Western Vaishnavas and seeing their humility and sincerity, the current Gajapati Dibyasingh Deva has shown himself favorable to them going into the temple. It seems that this kind of humble approach will be more effective in producing change over the long term than aggressive attempts to force such change.

## Patita-pāvanāṣṭakam

*sa-cinta iva lakṣyase sapadi me caritraṁ smaran*  
*paraṁ kalita-sāhasaḥ patita-pāvana-tva-vratāt \|*  
*na mām agaṇayaḥ purā na hi vicāra-kālo’dhunā*  
*vrataṁ visṛja vāthavā varada pāvayainaṁ janam \|\|1\|\|*

**O Lord! Bestower of boons! I see You are concerned upon contemplating the record of my past activities; even so, I have dared come before You because of Your promise to purify the most fallen. Previously, You cared nothing for me, but now is no longer the time to make judgments: Either renege on Your promise or purify this most fallen soul.**

*na rāghava na vāyaso na khalu kṛṣṇa caidyo’smy aham*  
*na khalv aham ajāmilo naraka-nāśa nārāyaṇa \|*  
*pradhānam aparādhināṁ parivṛḍhaṁ ca māṁ pāpinaṁ*  
*kṣamājalanidhe vidan sapadi sāvadhāno bhava \|\|2\|\|*

**O Raghava! I am not Jatayu, the vulture king! O Krishna! I am not Sisupala, the king of Chedi! Nor, Narayan, destroyer of hell, am I the sinner Ajamila! O Ocean of Forgiveness! You should know that I am the leader of all the most sinful offenders, so be on Your guard against me.**

*yady udyad-agha-lekhanā-kalana-jāgrad-agrāṅguli-*  
*milat-prakhara-lekhanī-mukha-vighāta-vītodyamaḥ \|*  
*alaṁ kila lalajjire sapadi citraguptādayaḥ*  
*sa eṣa patitāgraṇī sadaya rakṣa dakṣo’si cet \|\|3\|\|*

**Chitragupta and the other scribes of Yamaraj, when trying to make a tally of my sins, write and write until the nibs of their pens break, causing them much embarrassment. O most merciful one, if You are expert enough, then save me, who am foremost amongst the fallen.**

*vidann api hṛd-antare pratipadaṁ yad aṁhaḥ-kṛte*  
*yate yadu-pate na te viphalatā vrate syād iti \|*  
*yato’si jagato guru smṛti-niṣedhatas te tato*  
*na nāma ca bhajāmi yady atha vṛthā krudhaṁ mā kṛthāḥ \|\|4\|\|*

**Within my sinful heart, I know full well at every moment that Your vow to save the fallen will never fail to bear fruit. O Lord of the Yadus, You are the spiritual master of the universe; the scriptures say I am unworthy to worship You because of my sinfulness; so if I do not chant Your name, please do not be angry with me.**

*ananta yad aghāvalī-manana-sāvadhānātmakair*  
*nije durita-maṇḍale nikhila-sākṣibhir nekṣite \|*  
*janā jagati nirbhayā jaya jayeti jalpanty amuṁ*  
*prabho khala-dhurandharaṁ patita-pāvanaś ced ava \|\|5\|\|*

**O unlimited one! All those who have witnessed my sins are so terrorized that they stop seeing their own flaws. and they fearlessly praise each other, O Lord. So if You are truly a purifier of the fallen, then save me, the worst of all miscreants.**

*aneka-patitādhipān avati cakravartī yathā*  
*nṛpān ayam asajjanaḥ patita-pāvanatvena nu \|*  
*iti pratidiśaṁ khalāḥ patita-pāvanaṁ māṁ vidur*  
*na pāvayasi cet phalaṁ nanu bhaved idaṁ kevalam \|\|6\|\|*

**The king of the circle can give protection to tributary kings, and I too have myself acted in this way as a deliverer of the fallen. All these rascals in every direction think of me as a deliverer of the fallen, but if You do not deliver me, O Lord, this reputation will be the only reward I get.**

*kadāpi hi padāmṛtaṁ tava mayāpi nāsvāditaṁ*  
*vṛthā bhavakathābharairapi ca nātha nītaṁ vayaḥ \|*  
*tvayā yadapi helayā mayi na cedvidheyā dayā*  
*tavaiva mahatī kṣatiḥ patitapāvanatvaṁ yataḥ \|\|7\|\|*

**Never once have I tasted the nectar of Your feet; my life has been wasted in mundane talk. If now You should capriciously discard me and refuse me Your mercy, then Your reputation as the savior of the fallen will be greatly damaged.**

*bhavān parama-dhārmikaḥ prakaṭitātikāruṇyakaḥ*  
*svatantra-carito yadi svayam ayaṁ ca kiṁ nedṛśaḥ \|*  
*alaṁ kim api cet svakaṁ patita-pāvanatvādikaṁ*  
*pradarśayatu nānyathā bhavatu te yaśaḥ sarvathā \|\|8\|\|*

**You are the most dutiful Lord; You have given ample evidence of Your compassion; You Yourself are completely independent, but if You are so, then am I not also? So now, if You are the deliverer of the most fallen, show it, or Your good name will everywhere be sullied.**

*vadanti yadi pāvitāḥ patita-pāvanatva-vrataṁ*  
*bhavantam adhikaṁ na tat parama-durvinīto’py aham \|*  
*punātu na punātu vā bhuvi yathā tathaiva bruve*  
*gṛhāṇa guṇam eva me kuru kṛpāṁ sadoṣā na ke \|\|9\|\|*

**If those who have been purified speak of Your promise to purify the fallen, I do not do so to any great extent, even though I am the most ill-mannered of all. Whether You purify me or not, whether I speak with propriety or not, please take me only for my virtues, for who in this world is without fault?**

## Chapter 10 - The Temple Structure and Renovations

In an article published in 1990 in *Chaitanya Vani*, Srila Bhakti Promode Puri Maharaj commented on an accident that took place in the Jagannath temple. At about noon on June 14, 1990, a piece of stone cemented to the amalaka, 175-foot above the ground on the biman, came loose and crashed to the ground. A heavy rain started at quarter to twelve in the morning and the large piece of stone, which weighed nearly six tons, tumbled down a few moments later. By Lord Jagannath’s limitless mercy, most people had taken shelter inside due to the rain, and thus no one was standing outside where they could have been hurt.

This event inspired Puri Maharaj to write: “Pilgrims pass through this particular gateway to visit the Nrisingha Deva shrine. Lord Jagannath is so kind that as the remover of obstacles to devotional service, He made sure that no one was present there when the stone fell. If the rain had been lighter, people would likely have continued walking back and forth through the entry way and some horrible tragedy would no doubt have taken place. This then was a sign that the all-merciful Lord takes care of His devotees. At the same time, it also shows that a complete renovation of the 800-year-old temple is needed.” To support this argument, he wrote the article “Krishna’s blessings come through the blessings of Balaram,” salient portions of which are given here:

## The piety of temple renovation

The temple building itself, as the abode of Supreme Lord in His *arcāvatāra* form, is sacred. The scriptures therefore repeatedly glorify the charitable act of restoring temples, often saying that such restoration is even better than building new ones. Many of these verses have been quoted in the *Hari-bhakti-vilāsa.* For example, the *Viṣṇu-dharmottara* states

*yasya rājñas tu viṣaya deva-veśma viśīryate*  
*tasya sīdati tad-rājyaṁ deva-veśma yathā tathā*

**The fortunes of a kingdom deteriorate in proportion to the deterioration of the houses of the gods within it. (*****Viṣṇu-dharmottara*** **2.31.45)**

*kṛtvā śīrṇasya saṁskāraṁ tathā deveśa-veśmani*  
*dvi-guṇaṁ phalam āpnoti nātra kāryasya vicāraṇā*

**Anyone who engages in the renovation of the Supreme Lord’s temple gains twice the merit, so no one should hesitate to perform such a good work. (HBV** [**20.333-4**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/hbv/20.333)**)**

In the *Viṣṇu-rahasya*, it is said

*patitasya ca yaḥ kartā patamānasya rakṣitā*  
*viṣṇor āyatanasyeha sa naro viṣṇu-loka-bhāk*

**One who rebuilds a temple of Vishnu that has fallen down or renovates one that is about to do so will definitely go to His abode. (HBV** [**20.335**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/hbv/20.335)**)**

In the *Agni-purāṇa*,

*patitaṁ patamānaṁ tu tathārdha-sphuṭitaṁ naraḥ*  
*samuddhṛtya harer dhāma dvi-guṇaṁ phalam āpnuyāt*

**A person who constructs or renovates a temple that has either fallen down, is in the process of falling down, or is as yet incomplete, attains twice the merit. (HBV** [**20.336**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/hbv/20.336)**)**

From the *Devī-purāṇa,*

*mūlāc chata-guṇaṁ puṇyaṁ prāpnuyāj jīrṇa-kārakaḥ*  
*tasmāt sarva-prayatnenajīrṇasyoddhāram ācaret*

**One gets a hundred times more merit by renovating an old and dilapidated temple than by constructing a new one. Therefore one should do possible to reconstruct old temples. (HBV** [**20.337**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/hbv/20.337)**)**

In the *Hayaśīrṣa-pañcarātra*,

*vāpī-kūpa-taḍāgānāṁ sura-dhāmnāṁ tathānagha*  
*pratimānāṁ sabhānāṁ ca saṁskartā yo naro bhuvi*  
*puṇyaṁ śata-guṇaṁ tasya bhaven mūlān na saṁśayaḥ*

**O sinless one! Those who refurbish tanks, wells, or lakes, the homes of gods, deity images and places where the religious can assemble, attain hundreds of times as much pious merit as those who build new ones. (HBV** [**20.338**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/hbv/20.338)**)**

The temple building itself is considered sacred because it is a manifestation of Krishna’s alter ego, Lord Balaram.

*śārṅgiṇaḥ śayyā-rūpas tad-ādhāra-śaktiḥ śeṣaḥ*  
*īśvara-koṭiḥ bhū-dhārī tu tad-āviṣṭo jīvaḥ*

**The bed upon which the holder of the bow, Vishnu, lies is His supporting energy, Sesha. Sesha belongs to the same ontological category as Vishnu. Though he holds up all the worlds, he also enters into every single jivas.**

Thus by serving the temple, we are engaged in direct service to the Supreme Lord Himself. And if even one single devotee can truly please Lord Jagannath by his service, then the Lord will certainly answer his prayers to bless the unfortunate, suffering conditioned souls of this world.

On the other hand, if we do not render service to the Lord’s temple, His chariot, His form and other external manifestations, then Baladeva is displeased. And if we are deprived of His blessings, Krishna’s blessings are impossible to get; all our bhajan thus becomes completely useless.

On this occasion, a piece of masonry fell from the Jagannath temple. But there have been other occasions when the wheel of Balaram’s car fell off and the car stopped advancing, putting devotees in danger. Such events have caused people to criticize and cast blame on others. Our response is to say that Lord Jagannath is the master and controller of the universe; He is the life of every living being’s life. If there is any defect in His service, it is incorrect to blame a handful of Lord Jagannath’s direct servants while making a great show of piety oneself. We all have a responsibility to serve the Lord.

*prīyatāṁ puṇḍarīkākṣaḥ sarva-yajñeśvaro hariḥ*  
*tasmiṁs tuṣṭe jagat tuṣṭaṁ prīṇite prīṇitaṁ jagat*

**May the Lord of all sacrifices, the lotus-eyed Krishna, be pleased with me. When He is satisfied, the whole world is happy; so if you can please Him, you please the world.**

## Temple renovations over the years

The Jagannath temple has, over the centuries, been rebuilt several times. Because of its great age, it has also often been in need of repairs and from time to time, the special efforts of individuals have resulted in renovations being made. In the 20thcentury, however, it became clear that there were real dangers to the structures as a result of their great age. In 1943, the Jagannath Temple Repairs Committeewas formed to publicize damaged parts of the temple and collect money for their repair and upgrade some aspects of the service to the Deities.

Up until 1974, the temples were looked after by the Committee appointed by the Government of Orissa under the Jagannath Temple Act of 1954. However, this committee was unable to deal with structural problems and profuse leakage throughout most of the temple, so they referred the matter to the Ministry of Culture at the central government. The Government of India directed the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) to examine the matter. An Expert Committee was formed in 1973, consisting of leading archaeologists and scholars. In order to facilitate the restoration and protection work, the ASI declared the Lord Jagannath temple complex a Centrally Protected Monument in 1975 and took up direct responsibility for the work in hand.

The first matter attended to by the Expert Committee was the plastering. The Jagannath temple and other buildings in the compound were covered with a thick layer of lime plaster that gave it a brilliant white color, with the result that it was given the epithet “White Pagoda” by European sailors, who also named the Konark Surya temple “the Black Pagoda.”

The smooth plaster covering made it seem that there were no sculptures whatsoever on the Jagannath temple and other buildings in the compound, and certainly not the exuberant artistry found in Konark. Archaeologists were puzzled by the general absence of sculptures on these structures, speculating that they had been built in a decadent period of Orissan craftsmanship when these arts had already died out.

Unfortunately, this 18” coat of plaster over the years had had an adverse effect on the structure. Lime plaster is very absorbent and holds twice its own weight in water, adding a great deal of weight to the building and leading to various problems for both the structure itself and the foundations. After the ASI had removed this thick coat of lime plaster and whitewash, they discovered that magnificent sculptures covered the edifice to an extent that has no peer anywhere in Orissa. The question remained -- why on earth would anyone have wanted to cover this magnificent artwork?

Many theories have been put forward. The most common is that the ocean breezes were having a negative effect on the building. As S. N. Sarangi remarks,

Nearly four hundred years after its completion, some damage to the fine carvings and idols and wearing out of the outer surface of the temple were noticed. This was supposed to have been due to saline south eastern wind from the sea, which is very near to the temple. Raja Mukunda Deva, the last Hindu King of Orissa in about 1560 AD, in order to protect the Jagannath temple and other small temples of Lakshmi,Nrusimha, Surya, Ganesh, Bimala, etc., got them plastered with lime to a depth of 45-50 cms. (18" to 20") and 25-30 cm (i.e., 10" to 12") respectively.\[66\]

After deplastering, this theory has fallen out of favor as the statues in question appear to be in remarkably good shape, showing little sign of any such damage. Another speculation is that the coats of plaster were applied as part of purification rituals following each defilement by the Muslim iconoclasts. This too seems unlikely, as historical records show that Mukunda ordered the plastering in 1560, more than fifty years after the previous such desecration – a long delay for a purification ritual by any account. On the other hand, it is quite possible that the plastering was done as a preventive measure against iconoclastic depradations, which were perhaps expected and did indeed come about a few short years later.

Another theory holds that the plastering was done as an attempt at making stop-gap repairs against leakage or to cover the ugly appearance caused by broken figures or fallen materials. It was observed, however, upon deplastering, that the lime coating was exacerbating rather than helping the leakage problem.

Some temple Pandas say that in the 1700's one of the queens of Puri, reputed to be a little mad, ordered the plastering because she thought it made the Mandir look nicer!

Qualified sculptors (Maharanas or Sthapatis) and restorers were put to work in cleaning the plaster away. By way of experiment, the first temple tackled for plaster removal was the Lakshmi mandir inside the Kurma Berha. After it was complete, the original beauty of the temple with its delicate carvings was brought to light.

Other conservation work was done by changing the missing or damaged architectural pieces. The iron dowels that kept the stone blocks in place had become rusted and expanded, with the result that stone chunks were often falling from the building. Experts recommended epoxy resin and grouting and this was done with great success.

When it came to working on the main temple building, however, the temple Pandas raised objections and the general public also showed reservations. Temporary court injunctions stopped the deplastering work in the early 1980’s, but Orissa High Court finally directed that a Technical Expert Committee be constituted in 1985. This resulted in the formation of the Bhubaneswar Circle under the leadership of superintending archaeologist, Dr. G. C. Chauley. These experts decided to work on simultaneously deplastering many of the other subsidiary shrines, like the Nrisingha temple, Surya temple, etc.

The deplastered surface of the Jagannath temple brought to light an array of sculptures and other decorative details. The minute designs and figurines were carved and cut in stone with such consummate skill that they create an illusion of being carved in wood or ivory. The lower portion of the platform contains friezes of elephants, horses, camels, and processions of warriors. Many of the classical motifs of Orissan temple sculpture are found on the structure, including *gaja-siṁha* (lion rampant over crouching elephant), horse and elephant processions, the gods of the directions, various socio-cultural scenes, as well as many erotic panels flanked by floral, geometric and animal motifs. It is thus clear that far from being from a decadent period of Kalinga art, the Jagannath temple was built at the height of this art’s flowering.

## Erotic sculptures on the temple

Life-size carved figures of men and women in various sexual postures (mithuna) as described in the *Kāma-sūtra* of Vatsyayana have long been visible on the outside of the temple building and inside the Jaya Vijaya gate. Even so, with the deplastering and restoration program of the Archaeological Survey of India, many more such carvings on the temple came to light after being hidden for centuries.

For a devotee, the erotic depictions that cover the temple present something of a problem. If God is transcendental to this world, and if sexuality is the aspect of the material creation that most strongly binds us to it, then how can it be so explicitly glorified on the house of the Lord? As one scholar, A. P. Singh, comments, these sculptures appear to be “an apparent contradiction to the spiritual and religious fervor noticeable in the sacred precincts of the temple." He goes on –

Could our sculptors, who were seemingly well-versed in Hindu mythology as well as the tenets of Hindu religion, stoop so low as to depict highly provocative mundane figures engaged in sex with the most vibrant erotic impulses side by side with the divine images of our gods and goddesses? Is this not a mockery of the sacred rites performed at the altar of the presiding deity of the temple?

When British Christians first came to Orissa and saw such explicit depictions of the *Kāma-sūtra* on the outside of religious buildings, they were shocked. It added fuel to their prejudices against Hindu society as decadent. They considered these sculptures to be pornographic representations mirroring the degeneration of moral standards in Orissa, reflecting the perverted tastes of the patrons of the temple. They even took them as proof that ritual activities of a fertility cult, so-called “sacred prostitution,” took place in the temple – even though there is no proof of the existence of any such lewd rituals.

Sundarananda Prabhu suggests that such opinions are the expression of an overactive imagination, misled by the presence of the six enemies of spiritual consciousness – lust, anger, greed, illusion, intoxication and envy. The fact is that such sculptures are a generalized feature of Hindu architecture and are found not only on the facade of the Puri temple, but on many other temples throughout India, and not just in Orissa. They are even present on one Roman Catholic church!

Ancient architectural texts ordained the carving of such figures on temples as a way of warding off lightning and other natural calamities. The reasoning given is that such figures protect the temple from lightning since Indra, the wielder of the lightning bolt, is himself a voluptuary and would not damage a replica of his own heaven and its sensual sports. Indra once blessed all women that they should never be disturbed when engaged in sexual union; his vajra would thus never strike a structure upon which the mithuna figures have been carved.

Indeed the *Utkala-khaṇḍa* contains the following verses:

*vajra-pātād-bhītādi-vāraṇārthaṁ yathoditam*  
*śilpa-śāstre'pi mapyādi(?)-vinyāsa-pauruṣākṛti*  
*adhaḥ-śākhā catuṣṭāṅgo pratihāro niveśayet*  
*mithunair atha vallībhiḥ śākhāśeṣaṁ vibhūṣayet*  
*mithunaiḥ patra-vallībhiḥ prādhaś copaśobhayet*

**These verses say that the mithunas are supposed to be carved all around the lower part of the temple structure, along with floral designs, in order to ward off the fear of thunderbolts.**

However, this is not the only explanation of these sculptures. After all, temple ritual does include a tradition of worshiping these sculptures on Ananga Trayodasi, when Kamadeva or Cupid is feted. On that day, the first mithuna worshiped is Anangatura, which is found on the outer northern wall of the Jagamohan. The Bhagavatam tells us that Kamadeva is a portion of Lord Vasudeva (*kāmas tu vāsudevāṁśaḥ,* BhP 10.55.1).

Does this mean that these sculptures are glorifications of Tantric sexuality, where sex seen as a spiritual path in its own right, in which man and woman in erotic embrace symbolize the ultimate union of the soul with the Divine? Some say that such erotic pictures are graphic equivalents of the mystical syllable om. There is little doubt that Tantric attitudes to sexuality form an undercurrent throughout Hindu society, but there is no evidence that such esoteric practices were ever promoted in the mainstream of that society or ever held in anything but suspicion by the orthodoxy.

For some, the sculptors who decorated the outside of Lord Jagannath’s temple were trying to depict life of in all its manifestations, both realistic and ideal. Many scenes reflect various aspects of life, from the ordinary life of a cultivator to that of kings and gods. The erotic carvings were thus simply a part of this realistic depiction. Some say the temple represents heaven on earth, and since heaven is the abode of apsaras, the place of sensual delight, erotic sculptures have also been placed on the temple.

Lord Jagannath is the national deity of Orissa as well as its king. As such, He is not only there to provide liberation to His progeny, but to assure them the possibility of experiencing the fullness of material life as well. In general, the agricultural society of Orissa relies on reproduction; economic development is based on “going forth and multiplying.” Its success is achieved in enjoying human life, the pinnacle of which is sexual enjoyment, which in turn leads to reproduction and the continuation of the cycle of life.

Dharma, artha, and kama are also goals of human life that are not to be discarded. This then is symbolized in the temple structure: it is there for all the people, regardless of their level of spiritual advancement, their desires or their objectives in life. Lord Jagannath is the God of all these beings as well as being the God of His exclusive devotees. He does not exclude anyone, but takes the desires of His devotees seriously.

*ye yathā māṁ prapadyante*  
*tāṁs tathaiva bhajāmy aham*  
*mama vartmānuvartante*  
*manuṣyāḥ pārtha sarvaśaḥ*

**As one surrenders to Me, so do I respond to him. All men follow my path in every way, O Partha. (Gita** [**4.11**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/4.11)**)**

The way of salvation passes through the material world with all its charms and attractions. Unless a devotee overpowers the captivating charms of the flesh, he cannot have access to the divine spirit. One must first come to realize the futility of the flesh and its charms in order to have a clear conception of the way that leads to the Divine. Thus some people hold that these erotic carvings serve as a reminder of the potential pleasures of the material world to the *sa-kāma* and also tests the sincerity of the *niṣkāma* sadhaka who seeks liberation from material desire.

*akāmaḥ sarva kāmo vā*  
*mokṣa kāma udāra dhīḥ*  
*tīvreṇa bhakti yogena*  
*yajeta puruṣaṁ param*

**All people of expansive intelligence should worship the Supreme Person by the process of intense** ***bhakti-yoga,*** **whether they are pure devotees without any personal desire, or whether they are filled with all kinds of desires, or seek liberation (SB** [**2.3.10**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-2/3.10)**).**

Thus, the temple represents the five koshas that one has to pass through to reach the stage of pure spirituality. One has to symbolically overcome Maya by circumambulating the temple before one can enter the innermost sanctum. They are meant to test the devotion of the pilgrims and the sincerity of their prayers. But whatever the case, a devotee who enters the temple to pray to Lord Jagannath receives the Lord’s mercy –

*satyaṁ diśaty arthitam arthito nṛṇāṁ*  
*naivārthado yat punar arthitā yataḥ*  
*svayaṁ vidhatte bhajatām anicchatām*  
*icchāpidhānaṁ nija-pāda-pallavam*

**It is true that Lord Krishna fulfills desires whenever someone petitions Him to do so. However, He does not award anything that, once having been received, will be asked for again and again. Even if such worshipers show no desire for His lotus feet, the Lord personally bestows the benediction on them whereby they will forget all their transitory material desires. (SB** [**5.19.28**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-5/19.28)**)**

Another way of looking at the temple structure is as a glorification of the Lord’s pastimes. Jagannath is the king, not only of Orissa, but of the entire universe. Every aspect of His life is to be glorified, including his conjugal pastimes with His divine energies and consorts, His Lakshmis.

The divine *śṛṅgāra-rasa* is the basis of Lord Krishna’s pastimes in Vrindavan. It is the basis of the concept of beauty. Lord Jagannath is Madan Mohan, the enchanter of the mind of even Cupid. He is the supreme emperor and exclusive enjoyer, the transcendental Cupid. Those whose eyes have been daubed with the salve of divine love will recognize these sculptures as depictions of that reality.
