*yajeta puruṣaṁ param*

**All people of expansive intelligence should worship the Supreme Person by the process of intense bhakti-yoga, whether they are pure devotees without any personal desire, or whether they are filled with all kinds of desires, or seek liberation (SB** [**2.3.10**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-2/3.10)**).**

Thus, the temple represents the five koshas that one has to pass through to reach spirituality. One has to surpass this Maya after circumambulating the temple in order to enter into the innermost sanctum. They are meant to test the devotion of the pilgrims and the sincerity of their prayers.

Yet others claim that these sculptures are glorifications of Tantric sexuality, where sex seen as a spiritual path in its own right, in which man and woman in erotic embrace symbolize the ultimate union of the soul with the Divine. Erotic pictures are graphic equivalents of the mystical syllable om. There is little doubt that Tantric attitudes to sexuality form an undercurrent throughout

The temple is a royal structure. Jagannath is the king. Every aspect of His life is being glorified, including the erotic. The temple is a representation of heaven on earth, and since heaven is the abode of apsaras, and a place of sensual delight, the erotic sculptures are placed on the temple.

Lord Jagannath is Madan Mohan, the enchanter of the mind of even Cupid. He is the supreme emperor and exclusive enjoyer, the transcendental Cupid.

Eroticism has a distinct role in the evolution of the concept of beauty. Creativity is also intrinsically connected to eroticism. This is just beautiful decoration as seen in a society without sexual hangups.

## Chapter 11 - The temple servants

Lord Jagannath’s service is divided up into hundreds of categories known as nijogs (or *niyogas*), each of which is the hereditary right and duty of a particular family or families and is handed down from generation to generation. Thirty-six of the nijogs are consider primary, because they are needed on a daily basis. They are called the Chatish (36) Nijog. Jagannath servants are designated by the Sanskrit word “sevak” or the Orissan “sevayat,” or by the general term “panda.” The thirty-six different kinds of servants include the priests who perform the worship or puja, those who dress the Deity, the cooks, etc. On an average, it takes about seventy-five Sevaks to perform the ritual services every day for Jagannath.

Besides these Nijogs directly connected to Jagannath’s service, there are other groups of sevaks who do the puja and care for all the deities in the smaller shrines in the temple compound, including Bimala, Lakshmi, Surya, Shiva, Krishna, Rama and Ganesh.. They are known as Bahar Deul Sevaks

According to some scholars, these thirty-six categories were introduced by King Ananga Bhimadeva in the 13th century. The *Mādalā-pañjī* states that Jagannath’s original servants were the Dayitapatis, but that number of sevak families was increased to six different families after Sankaracharya visited Puri in the 8th century. The number of sevaks and associations of sevaks known as Nijogs increased gradually and new ritual services were introduced. According to C. Grome, the British collector at Puri, the number of Nijogs had grown to 250 by the beginning of the 19th century.\[67\]

The Record of Rights of the Shri Jagannath Temple, prepared under the Puri Shri Jagannath Temple (Administration) Act of 1952, listed 119 categories of Sevak, but some of these, such as the Gita Govinda Seva, have since been discontinued, while others have been revived.

From earliest times, the Puri Raja has been called the Adya Sevak, the foremost sevak of Lord Jagannath. Grome noted that “during the period that the affairs of the Temple were under the immediate control and management of the Rajas of Khurda, any, even the slightest, deviation from the prescribed duties were severely punished either by fine or corporal chastisement.”

The Sevaks do not receive a monthly salary from the Temple Adminstration. Each of them is entitled to get a portion (known as *khei*) of the Raja Bhog or Kotha Bhog. In addition, most Sevaks receive a daily remuneration according to the scales prescribed by Temple’s managing committee. Some of them also receive cash awards at particular times of the year as a compensation for their service. However, many of the Sevaks depend on donations from pilgrims to make a livelihood.

A “hundi” (donation box) was placed in the Jagamohan in 1983. 90% of the money collected in the hundi is invested in a foundation, whose interest is divided between the temple (50%), the Sanskrit University (45%) and the Sevayats Welfare Fund (5%).

Amongst the temple servants, there is a bias against too much education because such learning tends to lead people away from their traditional service to lucrative jobs far away from the holy city. Jagannath’s service is no synecure: on service days, a pujari spends a minimum of eighteen hours in the temple. Cooks work over hot wood-burning stoves with no fans. To those who are not genuinely devoted to Jagannath, the work is hard and sometimes tedious. Sevaks are paid only a token wage and depend excessively on donations from pilgrims. Though it may be said that they are dependent on Lord Jagannath for everything, the need to elicit donations from pilgrims has resulted in their developing an unsavory reputation of rapaciousness over the centuries.

Even so, most of Lord Jagannath’s servants are so attached to the temple that they cannot conceive of life without Lord Jagannath. Many of them know only two places – their home and the temple. When a sevak dies, his funeral pyre is lit with the sacred fire from the temple kitchen.

One saying that is heard among the sevaks is that in the Satya Yuga they were born as sages or seers, (*tapī*); in the Treta Yuga, they were monkeys serving Lord Rama (*kapi*); in the Dvapara Yuga, they were gopis with Krirshna, and now in the Kali Yuga, they have become the servants of Lord Jagannath.

Sevayats generally marry only other Brahmin sevayats living within the Atharo Nala, the entry point of Puri. They cannot marry outside Puri and outcaste marriage is also prohibited. Anyone who does so is debarred from his paternal seva puja in the temple. For non-Brahmin sevayats these rules are not followed as strictly.

It is impossible to give a fully detailed description of the services performed by each of the Nijogs, but some of the most important are listed here.

## Management positions

The Chatish NijogMahapatra is the supreme authority of the temple and sees that all seva is carried out properly. He executes all the orders of the temple’s government administrator and the king of Puri. He is also called the Patjoshi Mahapatra.

The next level of management is the Paricha Nijog.These sevaks lead the procession of cooks carrying bhog from the temple kitchens to the main temple at offering times.

The Bhitarchon Mahapatrais the supervisor of the inner temple. He is temple’s head priest for daily rituals, opening the temple doors in the morning and overseeing the purity of the temple kitchens.

There are a number of sevaks whose business it is to make sure that others perform their service. The Charchiat Nijog sevak reminds worshipers of their temple duties the next days. The Pradhani calls the Puja Pandas when it is time to start puja and tells the kitchen when to bring in the food offerings. The Paiks and Lenkas also make sure that everyone is aware of his service and is on time to perform it.

## Pujaris

There are several groups of sevaks who are engaged in direct service to the Deities.

The Puja Pandas perform the puja at the time of all the Naivedyas or food offerings, especially where sixteen ingredients (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) are required. This is the most difficult seva to learn. There are many mantras that must be memorized for each ritual. It takes about two years to master the puja system.

Boro Pandas form part of the Puja Panda Nijog, but do no temple seva. They formerly served as directors of the service. Many of them now serve as Tirtha Gurus, or spiritual guides to pilgrims coming from all parts of India.

The Pashupalakas have the privilege of dressing and decorating the Deities. There is one Pashupalaka for each of the three deities. The Srimukh Singhari Sevaks wipe the Lord’s face and paint in the eyes during the Netrotsava every year. The Datta Mahapatras also decorate the Lord’s face at certain times.

The Mudiraths (Mudirasta or Mudra-hasta) are divided into two groups – one having the title Agnisharma and the other Vishnusharma. The former group serves Lord Balaram, the latter Lord Jagannath. Prior to the Lord’s bhog, the Mudirath offers the Deities sandalwood and a garland of damanaka (Artemisia Indica) flowers.

During festivals, the Mudirasta cleans the Deity, performs arati, and offers bhog. He bathes the Deities during the Snana Yatra, ritually prepares the water from the Golden Well (Sona Kupa), moves the Deities in the Pahandi Vijaya, offers prayers appropriate to the occasion and stands in for the king of Puri in his absence at certain ceremonies.

Traditionally, the Mudirasta Brahmins would take the sacred thread at the age of 12, after which they could take up the service to the Lord. However, only unmarried Brahmins could engage in this service. Once they married, they were replaced by someone else.

The Dayitas (sometimes written as Daita or Daitya) have a very special position among the temple servants. They are non-Brahmin descendants of the original worshipers of Nila Madhava (see chapter 3) and are thus highly respected. The word *dayita* itself refers to one who has received the mercy of the Lord.

They do all the service of Jagannath, except for puja and cooking, during Jagannath’s Anasar, i.e., between Snana Yatra and Rathayatra, when the Lord “catches a fever” and is not available for public darshan. They offer Him sweets and fruits and also give Him cold fruit drinks and medecine to help cure His fever.

At other times, only the Puja Pandas and Pashupalaks are allowed to touch Lord Jagannath’s body. The Dayitas also play a privileged role during the Nava Kalevara ceremonies (see chapter 19). The Dayitas notably perform the service of Pahandi Vijaya, pulling Lord Jagannath, Baladeva and Subhadra with silk ropes to carry them to the chariots at the beginning of the Rathayatra festival. Altogether, they number about two hundred families.

In the *Kṣetra-māhātmya,* the Dayitas are said to be descended from the Shabaras, a caste that keeps and sells pigs. However, there are also many among the Dayitas who are considered to be Brahmins and these are given the title Dayitapati, or “leader of the Dayitas.” Besides offering sweetmeats to Lord Jagannath during the Anasar, Dayitapatis also make the early morning ballabha bhog offering of sweetmeats on a regular basis.

Another important group of priests are the Purohits who perform the fire sacrifices every morning before cooking starts and during the festivals. They also perform fire sacrifices on other special occasions.

## Other direct services to the Deities

The Darpania Sevak holds the mirror up to the Deities after They have been dressed. The Dhwajadhara Sevak holds the standards before the respective deities during bhog: the Garuda flag for Jagannath, that with the Tal tree for Baladeva, and the lotus flower for Subhadra. The Chamar Sevak fans the Deities with yaktail whisks and the Chatra Nijog holds the Lord’s parasol. The Alat Sevak also fans the Deities with a different kind of fan.

The Khat Sejghar Mekaps place the Deities’ beds in front of the throne at night at Their bed time. They also decorate the various vehicles the Deities use, such as the ratha, palanquins and altars.

## Assistants to the Pujaris

The Sudha Suarputs all puja materials in the appropriate containers, for example, chandan in the chandan pot. During the Rathayatra they collect the offerings for the bhog that is offered the Deities on their cariots. They also gather the paraphernalia for arati and in the morning are the first to enter the temple to inspect it for impurities.

The Ghatuaris grind sandalwood paste and give it to the Pavitra Badu. They also grind the perfumed mixture containing chowa\[68\], camphor, musk, sandalwood, and saffron. This paste is given to the Palia Mekap. They also light the lamps in the tunnel from the kitchen to Jagannath’s altar.

The Hadap Nayak Nijogprepares daily betel for the Lord, offered after every meal and after the closing Pahuda.

The Suar Badu sevaks have a number of different services: they bring the flame from the kitchen fires to light the lamps for arati. They also wash the temple floor from the Deities’ throne to the Sandalwood Gate before food offerings.

The Gara Badu Nijogsevaks bring water from the temple well according to the needs of the Pashupalaks during the Deities’ bath and to wash the puja utensils. The Pania Apats bring water to clean the sandalwood barrier and the utensils used in making the Lord’s offerings. They also wash the floor where the bhog will be placed.

A number of different Nijogs are engaged in cleaning the puja utensils: the Jogar Maja Sevak. The Suar Gadus rewash all puja utensils three times before each puja. The Patri Gadus sevaks check to see that all puja utensils are ready throughout the day.

The Khadibinja Sevak prepares the Lord’s bed with clean sheets. The Patibadu Nijog sevaks bring incense and lamps for puja.

## Storekeepers

There are several subcategories of storekeepers, or Mekaps. The Bhandar Mekaps watch the temple storeroom or bhandar. The Changada Mekaps are in charge of the deities’ clothes, which are kept in a huge basket known as the changada. The Akhanda Mekap has the sole duty of keeping the *akhaṇḍa-dīpa* burning twenty-four hours a day. The Palia Mekaps carry Lord Jagannath’s jewels from the bhandar and bring them to the Pashupalaks who dress the Deity and return the previous day’s decorations to the storehouse. They also bring sandalwood and extinguish the lamps at either side of the Ratnavedi at night.

When the Bhandar Mekap leaves his work to return home, he must shake out his clothes to show that he has hidden nothing in them. If anything is ever stolen from the storeroom, then he has to pay three-quarters of the losses. The remainder is paid off by the others working in the bhandar.

## Suppliers

The Ratnakarja Bindhani makes the Deity’s jewelry. The Tulasi Nijogsupplies tulasi garlands to the temple daily. The Dayana Malisare gardeners who daily supply Lord Jagannath with scented flowers, both loose and in strung garlands. The Mahabhois supply all milk products from their shops outside the temple.

The Balita Sevaks supply balita, or lamp wicks for all the arati and dipa lamps. The Kumbhar Nijog supplies all the clay pots for Maha Prasad.

## Karans

The Karans belong to the writer caste, also known as Kayastha. They were in charge of keeping accounts as well as historical records. The main temple accountants are called Deul Karans. They also oversee the distribution of donations and Maha Prasad.

Several Karan families were formerly responsible for writing and preserving the *Mādalā-pañjī* – the Kotha Karan was the main compiler, the Tadan Karan would write it, the Panjia Karan preserved it, and the Baithi Karan was their assistant. The *Mādalā-pañjī* has not been kept officially for more than fifty years now, though it is still said that there are some Karans who keep an unofficial record.

The Talucchon Karan sevaks assist the accountants, keeping accounts of the storerooms. They also affix temple seals at night and posts dates of all important rituals.

## Temple Guards

A number of nijogs perform various kinds of guard duties. The Khuntias are the Deities’ bodyguards, preventing visitors to the temple from going where they should not. They also take offerings of flowers and cloth from the devotees to the Ratna Singhasan altar, giving them to the Pashupalaks for puja. They sprinkle water scented with sandalwood from the storehouse up to the Deity’s throne. At Pahuda time at night, they give the closing sloka, called Manima Dak, before everyone leaves the temple.

The Chamu Khuntias patrol the Deities’ throne. They also bring flowers and flower decorations from the gardeners to the storage room or bhandar. During the morning abakash, they call the Singhari and give him the flowers. They also bring camphor from the Bhandar Mekap. They also do a lot of calling “Manima” and guard the front gate during the Lord’s Anasar.

The Pratiharis (also called Pacharis or Parhiaris) enforce discipline on pilgrims and devotees inside the temple. Prior to the British rule, the Pratiharis or Pacharis were also responsible for collecting the Pilgrim Tax that was levied on all those who came to visit Puri. They turned over a portion of this to the Government, and kept the rest as a source of revenue for maintaining the temple and its servants.

There are three categories of Palia Parhiari. The first close the curtain at the sandalwood barrier. They call out the name of each preparation in the sequence that it is to be brought into the temple for offering. They also stand by with a stick to prevent anyone from coming close to the bhog offerings. The second group guards the southern inner door during offerings. They have the title Boro Dwar Parhiari. The third group guards the Jaya Vijaya Gate.

The Mudulis guard the store rooms and verify the number of puja utensils after every puja.

Gochhikarasguard the Lord’s kitchen. The Shuddha Paik also stands at the kitchen doors to insure that no impure foods enter.

## Cooks

The Suars, or Supakars, form the largest nijog, as there are more than 5,000 people involved with cooking for Lord Jagannath. There are five kinds of cooks: (1) The Maha Suars supervise the work of the other cooks and prepare the food for offering. (2) The Pitha Suars prepare cakes and sweetmeats. (3) Thali Suars cook the rice and vegetable preparations. (4) The Panti Badus arrange the offerings in rows (*panti*) in front of Lord Jagannath. (5) The Tola Badu light the way for the Suars who carry in Lord Jagannath’s Manikotha Bhog.

## Assistants to the Cooks

The Rosh Paik has the duty to arrange for making up any shortfall in ingredients in the kitchen during cooking times. They communicate with the Beharan Hakim, who directly seeks the ingredients. The Rosh Mekap makes sure that the spices and milk products supplied by the Mahabhoi are in order. The Rosh Mekap also provides the ghee for the cooking.

The Chaul Bacha sevaks clean the rice and prepare it for cooking. The Samarthas also clean and prepare the dal and rice, and also grind the dal for those preparations that need it. The Chunakutas make flour and paste from rice and dal to make the various cakes for Lord Jagannath.

The Lenkas make sure that the Suars start cooking on time. They are also responsible for performing the fire sacrifice and lighting the stoves in the kitchen.

The Maha Bhois supply the kitchen with milk products like milk, yogurt and curd. The Rosh Paik overlooks the cooking, while the Shuddha Paik stands at the door and inspects whatever foodstuffs are being sent inside the kitchen area. He makes sure that none of the prohibited foods – garlic, onion, refined sugar or salt, parboiled rice, machine milled flour, potatoes, ladyfingers, cabbage, chilis, bitter melon, different kinds of stemmed vegetables known as danta, certain kinds of gourds like lau (bottle gourd), and certain kinds of green leaf vegetables like pui. If even a little of these items is found present in a basket of other materials, the whole batch is considered wasted and new ones have to be bought. The wasted materials are buried.

## Special Services

The Biman Badu Nijogsevaks carry all palanquins going outside the temple. The Biman Badus and Hindola Badus carry the palanquins and pull the Lord’s chariot. They also clean the Lord’s kitchens. The Mandanis have the responsibility of decorating the Lord’s palanquins and other vehicles or modes of transport. They are also responsible for their safekeeping when not being used. The Ratha Dahukas direct the chariots from above the wooden horses during the Rathayatra.

The Chitrakars, as their name suggests, color and paint the faces of the deities and clean their eyes with camphor daily. The Vishwakarma Nijogsevaks make the new Deities at the time of the Nava Kalevar. The Maharanas are the craftsmen who build the chariots every year. There are many subdivisions of this Nijog, specializing in various aspects of the construction. The Maharana families are the descendants of Vishwakarma, the craftsman of the demigods, who is said to have carved the first Deities of Jagannath.

The Chuneras daily take the flags to the chakra at the top of the temple spire. No bhog can be offered until a new flag has been placed there. This is perhaps the most physically challenging seva, as there are more than three hundred uneven steps to climb before one reaches the Nila Chakra, 215 feet above ground level.

This is a dangerous task that must be done several times daily, rain or shine, even after dark. It is said that about a century ago, a young boy was performing this service when he fell. He cried out the name of mother Bimala and landed unhurt on a lion sculpture on the side of the temple. The Chuneras feel that Lord Jagannath will always protect them because they are engaged in doing His work. Apparently there are only two teenage boys from the Khuntia Mahapatra family who perform this duty today.

Chuneras also serve the Aruna and Garuda pillars and hang the canopies over the temple compound when needed.

## The Lord’s entertainers

The Purana Pandas are Brahmins who recite spiritual texts such as the Puranas, the Bhagavata and Gita in the temple every evening.

There are a number of Nijogs that specialize in playing various musical instruments. The Kahalias blow a bugle, called Bije (Vijaya) Kahalia, at all auspicious events. The Ghantuas play the big cymbals, called *ghaṇṭā*, during the bhog and pahandi, when the Deities are moved. Both the Kahalias and Ghantuas are also present to awaken the Lord at the end of night. The Madeli, who plays the madala, a long drum, and a sounder of the conch (Shankhua), as well as a Kahalias and others are present during the offerings of bhog, along with singers and dancers and a host of other servants who are occupied in various aspects of serving and preparing the foodstuffs.

A number of other musical services were offered Lord Jagannath at other times of the day, specifically related to the singing of *Gīta-govinda.* The Vinakarwould play the vina when the Deities were put to bed, often accompanying the Maharis or Devadasis who would sing *Gīta-govinda* and dance for the Lord at this time. The Devadasis would also perform for the Lord during the Chandan Yatra, while the Lord is on His boat.

## The Devadasis

Lord Jagannath is the supreme enjoyer and He takes pleasure in seeing His devotees dance, just as He loves to hear them sing. The *Hari-bhakti-vilāsa* states --

*nṛtyatāṁ śrīpater agre*  
*tālikā-vādanair bhṛśam*  
*uḍḍīyante śarīra-sthāḥ*  
*sarve pātaka-pakṣiṇaḥ*

**All the sins in the body fly away like birds when one dances before the Lord, accompanied by drums and musical instruments. (HBV** [**8.292**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/hbv/8.292)**, BRS** [**1.2.128**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/rupa-brs1/1.2.128)**)**

*bahudhotsāryate harṣād*  
*viṣṇu-bhaktasya nṛtyataḥ*  
*padbhyāṁ bhūmer diśo’kṣibhyāṁ*  
*dorbhyāṁ vāmaṅgalaṁ divaḥ*

**When a devotee of Vishnu dances in joy, his feet drive all inauspiciousness from the earth, his eyes drive inauspiciousness from the directions, and his arms from the heavens. (*****Hari-bhakti-sudhodaya*****, HBV** [**8.288**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/hbv/8.288)**)**

For Lord Jagannath’s pleasure, King Chodaganga Deva arranged that performances of song and dance should be held in the temple every day when the Lord took rest and during His midday meal. The women who performed this service were known as Devadasis or Maharis.

A legend is told in Jagannath Puri that there was once a flower gardener’s daughter who had learned *Gīta-govinda* and would sing it with great emotion while working. Lord Jagannath was attracted by her singing and would go in secret to listen to her, only returning to the temple after she had finished her songs.

One day, when the king came for the Jagannath’s darshan, he saw that the Lord’s body was all covered in dust and His clothes filled with thorns. He asked the pujaris the reason for the Lord’s disheveled condition, but no one could explain how it had come about. The servants of the deity were afraid with good reason that they would be punished, but that night Lord Jagannath appeared to the king in a dream and explained that no one was to blame for His clothes being soiled that day. He had gone to listen to the gardener’s daughter and had become covered with dust and thorns while hiding in the garden.

The king was struck with wonder by the dream and immediately sent for the gardener’s daughter to be brought to the royal court in a palanquin. After making inquiries from her, he decided that she should sing for Jagannath in the temple, rather than obliging the Lord to leave the temple and get all dirty. This was the beginning of the tradition of the temple engaging girls named Devadasis to sing *Gīta-govinda* for Jagannath’s pleasure.

Subsequent kings, particularly the Gajapatis, perpetuated this seva. In the fourth year of his reign, July 17, 1499, Maharaja Prataparudra placed an inscription at the Jaya Vijaya Dwar, containing ten lines of Orissan script, the text of which reads as follows:

“The heroic king of the Gajapati dynasty, lord of Gauda and Karnatak, Prataparudra Maharajah, in the fourth year of his reign, on Wednesday, the tenth day of the waxing moon in the month of Shravan, ordains that *Gīta-govinda* should be sung and danced for the Boro Thakur (Lord Jagannath) during his bhog. This performance will take place daily from the evening dhupa (Sandhya Dhupa) until Boro Sringar. The groups of performers associated with the Bana Thakur, Kapileshwar, the Puratan Sampradaya and the Tailangi Sampradaya will neither learn any other song nor perform any other song. No other song shall ever be sung in front of the Supreme Lord. Besides these singers, there are four other Vaishnavas who shall sing *Gīta-govinda.* Anyone who is not so instructed shall listen to them carefully and take their lessons in the *Gīta-govinda* from them. They should not learn any other song. Whatever Paricha or temple manager allows any other song to be sung for Lord Jagannath in full knowledge of this edict shall be considered an enemy of the Lord.” \[69\]

The Devadasis were recruited from respectable families when still young girls. The service was forbidden girls who came from disreputable or outcaste families. Once chosen and dedicated to the Lord by her parents, a girl would undergo strict training from until she reached puberty when she would be fully initiated or become Lord Jagannath’s wife, after which she could sing for Him.

There were two kinds of Devadasi – external (Bahar) and internal (Bhitar). Both Brahmin and non-Brahmin girls could become Bahar Devadasis and sing and dance by the Garuda Pillar. Only Brahmin girls, however, could become Bhitar Devadasis, who sang and danced for the Lord right by His bed next to the throne. Though they were Devadasis for life, those who passed a certain age became disqualified for this particular service.

A single Devadasi would sing for the Lord at his morning meal and at night before He went to sleep. She would stand in front of the Garuda Pillar where she would sing with an accompanist. The Devadasi who was to perform for the Lord would fast on that day. She had to sanctify herself with ritual bath and would then be bedecked like a bride, her eyes elongated with kohl and her hair coiled up high, her face radiant with the vermilion mark on her forehead. She would be decorated in rich garments and jewels. She would not only be beautiful to look at, but chaste in body and soul, for she was the Lord’s chosen servitor and privileged confidante for the day. After her evening performance, the Devadasi would return to her lodgings where she would dine on Lord Jagannath’s maha prasad. Then she would stay up the whole night glorifying the Lord’s qualities.

The Devadasis played an important role in the temple ritual throughout the year, but especially during the forty-two day Chandan Yatra festival. During this entire period, all the lamps around the Ratna Vedi would be extinguished at midnight. Three sevayats would stand before the deities and fan them in the darkness while a Devadasi sang a particular song and danced in front of the sandalwood barrier. One or two Devadasis would also join Madan Mohan on His boat while He enjoyed *naukā-vihāra* as a part of the Chandan Yatra festivities.

No promiscuous woman was ever allowed to serve as a Devadasi. The Maharis were exclusively committed to their one lord and husband, Jagannath. Because they had sold themselves to Lord Jagannath’s lotus feet, they were never to accept any man of flesh and blood as their husband or lover. Their only thought was for the pleasure of the Lord. The word *deva-dāsī* means servant of the Lord who engages in His eternal pastimes. The Devadasi was compelled to lead an extremely austere life. She was to neither look at nor converse with any man, especially while dancing. A temple guardian officer, the Deshandhi Paricha, was assigned to keep an eye on the Maharis' behavior and manner of life on behalf of the king and the deity.

Like the wives in a king’s harem, the Devadasis were styled *asūryampaśya,* meaning that they never saw the light of the sun. This meant that originally they never danced outside the temple in public gatherings. Though they may sometimes have sung for the pleasure of the devotees, they would not sing the same songs that they sang for Jagannath. In other words, they would usually sing devotional bhajans rather than the more intimate material that they sang for the Lord in the privacy of the temple.

At some time, however, the original ideals of the Devadasi institution appear to have been compromised. According to some accounts, Raya Ramananda was the first to bring the Maharis out of the temple to play in public roles in his play, *Jagannātha-vallabha-nāṭaka*. This was a disaster for the Maharis who once out of the temple were then preyed upon by the ruling class, who polluted them by making them drink alcohol and by using them for their own pleasure.

During the time of Dibyasingha Deva I, it was decreed that the Maharis could “marry” Pandas because it was felt that they, as women, would be unable to maintain the chaste dignity of their calling and concentrate their thoughts and sentiments exclusively on the service of the Lord. The children of such unions became automatically “baikesh” (drummers or instrumentalists), if sons, or dancers if daughters. The Maharis continued to dance even after this “marriage.”

Dhirendra Nath Patnaik, secretary of Orissa Academy of Music and Dance, described the situation as follows, “Due to the successive Muslim invasions and weak political authority there must have been moral degeneration on the part of the Devadasis. Because, it is from this period that the Devadasis, who were originally intended for the temples and gods alone, came to be employed in royal courts as well. From now on, the Devadasis ceased to be respected as dasis of the Lord and came to be associated with concubinage.”\[70\]

The stigma on the Devadasi name grew. They began to be referred to as prostitutes and their children defamed as illegitimate. They were so much discriminated against that even barbers would refuse to shave the son of a Mahari. “Those whose status was once so noble that people would take the dust from the front of their houses came to be branded as women of loose morals because of circumstances beyond their control. Their art also fell into disrepute and they were constrained to become Magunis, singing in the mansions of the rich for a fee on festive occasions.”\[71\]

In the nineteenth century when Christian missionaries in India focused their attacks on Hinduism at the Jagannath temple, a part of their energy was directed at the Devadasi, who were accused of prostitution. As one of them wrote, “Dancing girls who have retired form the service of god Jagannath are now making both ends meet by leading a life of prostitution in the streets of holy Puri. Their patrons are the worshippers who come in their thousands to the sacred city.” They were also used sexually by the king and the temple priests, who took the “responsibility” for deflowering them after their marriage to Lord Jagannath.

The result was that educated Hindu society became convinced of the need to reform or even eliminate the institution, which existed not only in Puri, but in many other temple towns, especially in southern India. The Theosophist Annie Besant wrote, “The ancient religion trained the Devadasis as chaste virgins, and their ancient religious functions were dependent on their virginity. Losing that, they have lost their ministry…”

Frederique Marglin, who spent many years interviewing the last Devadasis in Puri, argues that the above view is narrow and based principally on European moral values that have no “context sensitivity.” She writes:

“From my readings in the epics, classical plays, puranas, and other texts, I formed an image of the highly accomplished woman dancers, singers and artists which these texts call ganika, veshyas, heavenly and earthly apsaras, as well as Devadasi. These women were indeed indispensable members of a prosperous and well-ruled kingdom and their presence was required at all joyful public functions. They seemed indeed to be respectable members of the kingdom, even though they were not chaste wives or chaste virgins… When Rama and Sita return from their long exile to Ayodhya, Rama’s brother, who had kept his throne for Rama during the latter’s long absence, gives instructions to welcome the king and queen back:

…all masters of musical instruments, and the *gaṇikā* in full numbers, the king’s wives and ministers, the soldiery and the bands of army women, the Brahmins and the nobles, and the corporations… all these shall go out to behold the moonlilke countenance of Rama. When Rama and Sita have arrived, they watch a dance and music performance by the finest ganikas in Ayodhya. (Compare SB [9.10.35-38](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-9/10.35))

It is well known that the Bhagavata mentions veshyas in a similar context in Dvaraka ([1.11.9](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/11.9)). The special function of the Devadasis in the royal and temple society was thus eventually made illegal. R. K. Das defends the tradition, now extinct, with the following argument:

Sages like Vishwamitra and celestial dancers like Urvasi and Menaka failed to follow absolute morality, so how can such perfection be expected of every Devadasi, who are simple mortals like the rest of us? Nevertheless, the Maharis deserve credit for preserving the tradition of Orissan dance, that harmonious blend of eroticism and spiritual devotion, through the centuries. They were true devotees of their Lord. In any case, what right does a society that accepts cabarets and night clubs have to condemn the dancing of the glorious padams and slokas of Kshetrajna and Jayadeva before the temple deities by devoted girls? How can a society so morally imperfect condemn the Devadasis and deprive the Lord of His celestial dance?\[72\]

The last of the Devadasis has now died and there unfortunately no movement to see the institution reestablished. From time to time, certain families or individual women have tried to voluntarily take up the service again, but on each occasion, public opinion has impeded any progress in the matter. In 1995, four girls were even interviewed for the purpose of being inducted as Devadasis, but the hue and cry in the public and the press forced the temple administration to abstain from taking further action.

The temple authorities were nervous about accusations that they are trying to resume the Devadasi system. They thus claimed that the interviews were instigated by the girls themselves with the approval of their families. A similar event was reported in Orissan newspapers in February, 2001. Such incidents show that there is still a segment of Orissan society that considers the Devadasi institution a worthy one, one that should be revived, but that general public opinion in Orissa is still strongly against it.

The Devadasis were originally assigned residence in Chudanga Sahi, but they also lived in the neighborhoods of Bhandimal Sahi, Markandeshwar, and Narendra Patna.

## Kavi Jayadeva

The loss of the Devadasis’ leaves a gaping hole in Lord Jagannath’s service. Jayadeva Goswami, the author of the *Gīta-govinda*, lived in Jagannath Puri while the temple was being completed. This song about Krishna’s passionate love for Radha quickly became the focal point of Lord Jagannath’s worship. When Sri Chaitanya came to live in Puri, He was absorbed in Radha’s mood and during this time, He would constantly savor the songs of the *Gīta-govinda.*

Day and night, the Lord would speak as though He were Radha when meeting Uddhava. He would also relish the poems of Chandi Das, Jayadeva and Vidyapati. (CC Ādi 13.41-2)

Mahaprabhu was never pleased to hear books or verses opposed to *siddhānta,* nor did he like hearing *rasābhāsa,* an improper mixture of devotional sentiments. It was the practice of Svarupa Damodar Goswami to examine all works of literature to find out whether their conclusions were correct. Only then would he allow them to be heard by the Lord. Sri Svarupa Damodar used to make Mahaprabhu very happy by singing the songs of Vidyāpati, Chandi Das and *Gīta-govinda.* (CC Madhya 10.113-5)

Svarupa Damodar would sing songs that reflected the moods of the Lord whenever they arose, while Ramananda Raya selected verses from Vidyapati, Chandi Das and *Gīta-govinda.*

The Lord returned to external consciousness for a moment and told Svarupa to sing some sweet song. Svarupa sang one of Vidyapati’s songs and then songs from the *Gīta-govinda*, which were greatly appreciated by the Lord. (CC Antya [17.62](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-antya/17.62))

*caṇḍī dāsa vidyāpati rāyera nāṭaka gīti*  
*karṇāmṛta śrī gīta-govinda*  
*svarūpa rāmānanda sane mahāprabhu rātri-dine*  
*gāya, śune parama ānanda*

**Day and night, Mahaprabhu ecstatically relished the songs of Chandi Das, Vidyapati and Ramananda Raya’s plays, as well as** ***Kṛṣṇa-karṇāmṛta*** **and** ***Gīta-govinda*** **in the company of Svarupa and Ramananda. (CC Madhya** [**2.77**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/2.77)**)**

Many legends are told about Jayadeva, but not much is truly known about his life. We do know that he lived in the 12th century and that he spent part of his life in Bengal, at Nabadwip, and another part in Jagannath Puri. There is a difference of opinions about the place of his birth. Generally, Bengalis say that he hailed from the village of Kenduli, presently in the district of Birbhum, while Orissans claim that he came from a village named Kendubilva not far from Jagannath Puri. Yet another tradition claims that Jayadeva was a Maithili.

Wherever Jayadeva was born, it is certain that he was Lakshman Sen’s court poet when that king made his capital city in Nadia in the 12th century. He may have come to Orissa when Bengal was conquered by the Afghans in 1205. There too he was engaged as the court poet of the king of Orissa. He spent the remainder of his life in the abode of Lord Jagannath. This is where he wrote the transcendental poem based on the sentiments of divine separation and union known as *Gīta-govinda* or *Aṣṭapadī.* Most of the legends surrounding Jayadeva’s life are Orissan in origin.

It is said that Jayadeva was obliged to marry his wife Padmavati at Lord Jagannath’s order. There was a Brahmin who had no children. He worshiped Jagannath for many years in the hope of having a son. Finally, he and his wife had a daughter and they named her Padmavati. When she came of marriageable age, the Brahmin brought her to Jagannath to offer her to His lotus feet as a Devadasi. When Lord Jagannath saw them, He spoke to the Brahmin, “I have a servant whose name is Jayadeva. He has given up family life and has dedicated himself to chanting My names. Give your daughter to him in marriage.”

The Brahmin took his daughter to Jayadeva and asked him to marry his daughter. However, since Jayadeva had no desire to get married, he refused to agree to any arrangement. Then the Brahmin told him that it was Jagannath himself who had arranged this marriage and without another word, left, leaving his daughter behind. Jayadeva found himself totally unprepared for the situation and told the girl, “Tell me where you want to go and I will take you and leave you there. You cannot stay here, however.”

Padmavati started to cry and said, “My father brought me here to marry you on Jagannath Deva’s order. You are my husband, my all in all. If you do not accept me, then I will fall down at your feet and die right here. You are my only hope, my lord.” Jayadeva could not abandon her after such a heartfelt plea and so, at Jagannath’s instance, he became a householder. And “Padmavati served her husband and he shared her devotion to Jagannath. As Jayadeva composed, she danced...”\[73\]

## The Lord helps Jayadeva write Gīta-govinda

Jayadeva established the worship of a Narayan deity and in the waves of love which he felt for this deity, he began writing *Gīta-govinda*. It is said that though Jayadeva is responsible for all the moods and sentiments which appear in the *Gīta-govinda,* he had some reticence about writing that Krishna fell down at Radharani’s feet to beg her forgiveness when she was angry with Him for having deceived her.

On that day, when he left the house to take his bath in the ocean, Lord Jagannath Himself came in, disguised as Jayadeva, opened his manuscript and completed the verse he had started *smara-garala-khaṇḍanaṁ mama śirasi maṇḍanaṁ* with the words *dehi pada-pallavam udāram*: “O Radhe! Place your delicate and generous foot on My head, as the ornament that dispels the poisonous desire in My mind.” (GG [10.8](https://vedarama.com/en/books/gg-pd/10.8))

Padmavati was surprised to see her husband back so soon from his bath and asked, “What are you doing here? You just left a minute ago.” The disguised Jagannath answered, “I thought of something on my way. I was afraid I might forget, so I came back to write it down.”

Not long after Jagannath had left, the real Jayadeva returned. This time, Padmavati was really astonished to see him. She said, “You left to go and take your bath. Then you came back. and were writing in your manuscript. Then just a few moments ago you left again! How could you have finished your bath and come back so quickly? I am beginning to wonder who that was and who you are!”

Jayadeva was clever enough to guess what had happened and he went and looked at his unfinished text and saw the words that the Lord Himself had written. His entire body was covered with horripilation and tears came pouring from his eyes. He called Padmavati and said to her, “You are so fortunate. Your life has been made worthy. You have had the good fortune to see the Lord himself. I am so lowly that I did not have that opportunity!”

Many other amazing and miraculous events surrounded the life of Jayadeva. He used to serve his deities Radha and Madhava in a trance of divine love. It is said that just as the devotee dedicates himself to the Lord, the Lord also dedicates himself to His devotee. One day, Jayadeva was thatching his roof under the unforgiving midday sun. Jagannath saw the discomfort of his devotee and decided to help him finish the work quickly by handing him the rope needed to bale the straw and removing the finished bundles and placing them on the roof. Jayadeva thought that it was Padmavati who was helping him in this way. But when he came down from the roof after finishing much earlier than expected, he saw no one there. He asked his wife and she told him that she had been busy elsewhere at the time. He was curious about what had happened, but struck with wonder when he went into the deity room and saw that Madhava’s hands were black from handling the straw. He was thus able to understand that it was Madhava Himself who had come to help him thatch the roof. He fell down before his Lord and started to cry.

## Padmavati is tested

Jayadeva’s wife became a close friend of the queen. In those days, the custom of a wife dying with her husband was in vogue. After her brother’s death, the queen was mortified that her sister-in-law would have to die on the funeral pyre with him. Padmavati said to the queen, “From the moment that her husband dies, a faithful wife’s life airs leave her body.”

When the queen heard this, she decided to test Padmavati herself. One day she announced to Padmavati that her husband Jayadeva had suddenly died. As soon as this news entered her ears, Padmavati gave up her life. This shocked the queen and she began to cry out of a sense of guilt for being responsible for her death. The king also came to Jayadeva and begged him to return the life to his wife’s corpse. The great devotee Jayadeva whispered the name of Krishna into Padmavati’s ear and she opened her eyes as though she were just waking up. Having seen this manifestation of both Jayadeva and Padmavati’s glories, the king and queen as well as all their courtiers and servants paid their obeisances at their feet.

## Jayadeva goes to Vrindavan

Towards the end of his life, Jayadeva wanted to see Vrindavan. He took leave of the king and queen and then, taking his deities, Radha and Madhava with him, he set off on the long journey. Once in Vrindavan, he began to serve his deities in a spot near Keshi Ghat. When the residents of the dham heard Jayadeva sing the *Gīta-govinda* in his sweet voice, they were entranced. One merchant built a large temple for his deities on that spot.

There is a difference of opinions about where Jayadeva finished his life. One version says that Jayadeva lived in Vrindavan for many years before returning to his birthplace in Kendubilva. Each day, he would make the long walk to the Ganges to take his bath there. One day, for some reason or another, he was unable to make it. Ganga Devi was so kind to him that she came personally to the village of Kendubilva so that he could take his bath in her waters. It is said that he died there in Kendubilva, where every year on the first day of the month of Magh a large festival is held in his memory.

Jayadeva’s original Radha Madhava deities were taken by the king of Jaipur to a place named Ghati sometime after his death and they are still being served in the Jaipur area.

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati Goswami Thakur has stated that Jayadeva died in Jagannath Puri. His disappearance day is on the sixth day of the waning moon of the month of Paush.

## Chapter 12 - Lord Jagannath’s daily puja

Lord Jagannath is the true king of Orissa and is therefore served in royal fashion. His worship comprises many intricate and elaborate rituals, called nitis, which are principally described in texts like the *Nīlādri-mahodaya*and *Mādalā-pañjī.* The *Nīlādri-mahodaya* is the standard and most extensive text, with more than fifty chapters giving authentic and meticulously detailed information regarding the puja ceremony and the various sevas. A few other important shorter works like *Gopālārcana-vidhi*, ascribed to Gajapati Purushottam Deva, *Nīladrinātha-pūjā-vidhi* of Chodanga, and *Gopālārcana-paddhati* of Vasudeva give abridged versions of the puja. It is said that it takes at least two years for a Puja Panda to master the entire system.

Lord Jagannath’s puja takes place five times a day. The common expression for puja in temple terminology is “dhup,” which originally means incense. The doors of the Garbha Griha are closed during puja and nobody is allowed to watch the puja ceremony.

A summary of the daily routine of worship or niti is given here. Though prescribed times for these rituals are given, the truth is that most have a tendency to run late. Certain aspects of Jagannath’s worship are unique, for the most part the various *nyāsa, śuddhis*, etc., are done according to standard formulae that can be found in any manual on the subject. Some of the special features will be mentioned here, but for fear of excessively expanding the size of this volume, we refer the reader to the original texts or to B. L. Roy’s summary study of the *Nīlādri-mahodayam*.\[74\]

## Dwar Phita (dvāra-phiṭā)

In the morning, representatives of five different servant groups must be present to open the temple. According to the *Mādalā-pañjī*, the doors to the inner sanctum must be open by 5 a.m. every day.

The day begins with the ceremonial sounding of kettledrums, or dundubhi. The Bhitarcho Mahapatrathen examines the seals placed on the padlocks of the Jaya Vijaya gate the previous night by another sevak known as the Talicho Mahapatra. After it has been confirmed that no one has tampered with the locks, he opens the doors and enters with the Palia Mekap, Akhanda Mekap, Pratihari and Muduli. They then examine the passage up to the Chamu Dwar (the door of Jagannath’s inner sanctum) with the help of lamps. looking for any impurities that may have fallen there during the night. The Chamu Dwar is then unlocked and the sevaks enter calling the Lord’s name, “Maṇimā! Maṇimā!” The Akhanda Mekap lights the lamps around the altar while others remove the coconut, scented water and tambul that were given the Deities at His bedtime the previous night. While doing all this, Sanskrit stotras are recited.

On festival days, extra rituals are performed and the Deities are not put to rest. On such days, there is no need of ritually opening the temple doors on the following morning.

## Mangala arati

The early morning lamp ceremony is performed by the Bhitarcho Mahapatraand two other Pashupalaka sevaks. They stand below the altar or Ratnavedi, offering a ghee lamp of twenty-one wicks. This is followed by the *piṣṭakārati*, or the offering of a ghee lamp protruding from a lump of dough.

## Mailam Lagi

The first change of Jagannath’s dress is scheduled for 6 a.m., but usually takes place at 8 o’clock. The Pashupalakas remove the previous evening’s Boro Sringar, and replace it with a clean, fine white cloth and shawl. These cotton clothes, known as *taḍapa*, are special for the Lord’s bath. They are washed by the Dhoba sevaks, who perform this service despite being Brahmins by caste.

## Abakash (avakāśa)

Next, the paraphernalia for the Deities’ morning purificatory rites such as flowers, sandalwood, camphor, panchamrita, and twigs for cleaning the teeth is brought into the temple’s inner sanctum. This is called Abakash and includes the Deities’ cleaning of teeth and bathing. This activity is supposed to take place between 6 and 6:30.

The Lord is bathed by three Pashupalaks, who sit on the floor below the Ratnavedi. They sprinkle water mixed with camphor, curd, amlas and sandal paste on three brass mirrors, each about two feet high and placed on silver plates, which reflect the three deities.

## Mailam

After the bath is finished, the deity is dressed according to the season and decorated with various jewels and flower garlands. The sevak known as the Akhanda Mekaplights and maintains the Akhanda Baitha, a ghee lamp that burns throughout the day in the inner sanctum. It is not extinguished until *pahuḍa* when the Deities are put to bed.

The court astrologer comes and stands before the Lord and gives him the daily almanac: which lunar day it is, the asterisms, and other astrological information.

## Sahanamela

*Sahana-melā* means “general audience” (*sadharaṇa-darśana*). Sahanamela is not really a part of Lord Jagannath’s worship rituals, but is held only to give the general public an opportunity to go near the Deities. Devotees and pilgrims are allowed to go up to the Ratnavedi to have darshan of the Deities without paying any fees, thus getting a unique chance to see the Lord close up. Its prescribed time is 7 a.m. and it goes on for about an hour.

Though there is provision for Sahanamela to take place twice a day, in practice it usually only happens once, in the morning. On certain festive days, Sahanamela is held after Sandhya Dhup (evening puja). During the month of Karttik it is held in the evening after Sandhya Arati. Sometimes it is also held after morning dhup, but on other festive days, there is no provision for Sahanamela.

## Vesha lagi

Vesh lagi means the dressing of the deities. This is performed between 8 and 8:30 a.m. Jagannath wears silk clothes that are changed according to the lunar asterisms. His clothes are also changed at least five times a day. In the midst of shouts of “*Maṇimā, maṇimā*!” He is smeared with sandalwood paste.

## Fire sacrifice in the kitchen

In the meantime, after mangala arati, the temple kitchen is cleaned. Before cooking starts the Puja Panda Sevaks perform a fire sacrifice in the kitchen, with the participation of Dhopkalias and Mekaps. According to the *Nīlādri-mahodayam* mentions that the Homa ritual in the kitchen is instituted after the bath of the deities, at the same time that they are being dressed.

Twelve oblations or *āhūtis*are offered to the sacred fire of Homa in honor of the different significant events in Krishna’s life, or samskaras. The first oblation is given in commemoration of His being conceived in the womb of Devaki, and this is followed by other *āhūti*s for His birth ceremony (*jāta-karma*), the sacred thread ceremony (*upanayana*) and marriage (*vivaha*).

After Homa has been completed, cooking starts in Lord Jagannath’s kitchen. The cooks pray to Lakshmi Devi and Ganesh before beginning the task of cookng. The prayer to Lakshmi asks her to give the food a better taste while Ganesh is asked to remove obstacles in the cooking.

One of the Puja Pandas then worships the Sun god in the inner enclosure near the Mukti Mandap, after which he worship the divine gatekeepers (*dvāra-pālas*), Jaya and Vijaya.

## Gopal Ballabha Bhog

At around 9 a.m., the Deities receive their breakfast. This consists of khoi, puffed rice made from sun-parched rice, and *muṛkī*, which is khoi coated with brown sugar and is known as *ballabha* in the Orissan language. This offering is made from the Anasar Pindi, just outside the Kalahat door. This offering is made in a simple manner, with only five of the elements of worship (*pañcopacāra*).

When this ballabh bhog offering has been completed, the temple is cleansed from the inner sanctum to the Chandan Argal. When the cleaning is finished, a curtain (called *terā*) is drawn over the Chandan Argal and the Sakal Dhup, or morning food offering is made.

After breakfast, Lord Jagannath, sitting on His jeweled throne and dressed in royal garb, receives His devotees to grant them audience, listen to their prayers and panegyrics.\[75\]

## Sakal Dhup (sakāla dhūpa)

Three Puja Pandas (or Archakas) usually worship the deities Jagannath, Balabhadra, Subhadra, Sudarshan, Lakshmi, Vishwadhatri and Nila Madhava simultaneously. One Panda worships Sudarshan, Lakshmi, Vishwadhatri and Nila Madhava along with the main deity Lord Jagannath. Two other Puja Pandas are required to perform the puja of Balabhadra and Subhadra. The three Archakas sit on the Ratnavedi to the right of the images facing north (the deities face the east) to conduct their worship. In the winter, however, they sit on the ground below the Ratnavedi since no place is available for them there due to the dressing of the deities in their winter clothing.

The Sakal Dhup consists of a puja in sixteen aspects, or *ṣoḍaśa upacāra:*

1\. *āsana* (offering a seat)  
2\. *svāgata* (hymns of welcome)  
3\. *padya* (water for washing the feet)  
4\. *arghya* (offering of flower, sandal paste, etc.)  
5\. *ācamanīya* (water for sipping)  
6\. *madhu-parka* (honey, ghee, milk and curd offered in silver or brass vessel)  
7\. *ācamanīya* (mouth wash)  
8\. *snāna* (bath)  
9\. *vastra* (cloth)  
10\. *āvaraṇa* (cloth)  
11\. *gandha* (scent and sandal paste)  
12\. *puṣpa* (flowers)  
13\. *dhūpa* (incense)  
14\. *dīpa* (lamps)  
15\. *naivedya* (food offerings)  
16\. *vandana (*hymns of praise and prayers)

## The method of offering sixteen upacāras

As the Puja Panda offers each item or *upacāra,* he also shows the appropriate hand gestures (*mudrās*) and recites the relevant mantras.

The Archaka offers the Lord a seat (*āsana*) by giving five flowers and showing the lotus *mudrā*, the lotus symbolizing the Deity’s seat. The act of welcoming (*svāgata*) is also done with flowers, ten in number, and by showing a mudra with both hands in a gesture of welcome to a guest. *Padya* is kept in a metallic bowl out of which a few drops are sprinkled at the feet of the image. *Arghya* is sprinkled on the head as well as face. *Ācamaniya* too is offered in a metallic bowl and after offering it the worshiper presents a towel to the Deity to dry the mouth. *Madhuparka* is a mixture of honey, curd and milk, and was invariably offered to guests in ancient times when they came to the house of their hosts after a tiring journey. It is offered to the deity in a small bowl with appropriate mantras. After taking *madhuparka* the deity again requires *ācamaniya* to clean His mouth and to sip a few drops from it.

The Archaka then invites the Deity to the Snana Mandap to take His bath. He is given bath in a mirror fixed in a bowl in which His image is reflected. The Archaka then offers Him two garments (upper and lower) of yellow color; the lower one is placed on the waist of the image and the upper one on its shoulders. A sacred thread also forms part of the offering of *vastra*. *Ābharaṇa* mostly consists of one or two golden ornaments that are usually stuck on the Deity’s garment. Sandal paste is then applied on the Deity’s forehead, chest, and arms; this is the *gandha upacāra.* Then flowers mixed with Tulasi leaves are offered to the Deity and are placed on His head, heart and feet.

Before offering the rest of the *upacāras* like *dhūpa, dīpa, naivedya* and *vandana*, Lord Jagannath’s entourage is worshiped.This entourage consists of numerous divinities who surround the Lord in concentric circles known as *āvaraṇas.* In each one of these circles, there are a certain number of demigods of the pantheon. The worshiper ends the *āvarana-pūjā* by ringing a small bell held in his left hand. This bell is purified before its use.

After worshiping the *āvaraṇas*, the Archaka resumes the task of *upacāra-dāna*, beginning with the offering of incense. The incense consists of specially prepared mixture of many fragrant ingredients. The utensil in which the incense burns is held under the Deity’s nose.

The worshiper then shows a flame or *dīpa* made of seven cotton wicks soaked in clarified butter. It is moved slowly in a circle three times before the deity. The offering is accompanied with its mantra and mudra.

Now cornes the most important of all *upacāras*, the *naivedya*. The *naivedya* is is of six types of food, *bhakṣya, bhojya, coṣya, lehya, carvya* and *peya.* The sakal dhup offering traditionally consists of twenty courses of rice, kitcherie, dal, vegetable curries, spinach, cakes and other sweetmeats.

The *naivedya* has to undergo a long process of ritual purification before it can be offered to the Deity. The worshiper looks at it with a particular mudra, sprinkles and guards it with the *astra-mantra* (= *svāhā*), dries it up with the *bīja-mantra* of air (*yaṁ*), places his right hand over it while uttering the *bīja-mantra* of fire (*raṁ*) in order to burn out any remaining impurities. The pujari then recreates the same bhog, now devoid of all impurities, with the help of the *bīja-mantra* of water (*vaṁ*), turning it into *amṛta* (nectar or ambrosia), the only food that the gods take, with the help of the *dhenu-mudrā.* After offering the Deity *padya* and *ācamanīya* anew, the worshiper offers this *amṛta* to Krishna by uttering the basic mantra and the *naivedya* mantra.

During the performance of the rites of *naivedya*, the doors of the sanctum are closed. While Lord Jagannath is eating, the worshiper repeats the basic mantra fifty-four times, offering this japa to the Deity. At the end of the *naivedya,* he offers the Deity water to drink. Other formalities like the offering of the water for cleaning the mouth, towel and finally, a betel-leaf, are carried out in the prescribed manner.

After *naivedya* is over, the doors of the sanctum are opened and the *ārātrikā* (lights) is offered to the deity to the loud accompaniment of music played in the Natya Mandir. For *ārātrikā* camphor is burnt in a special metallic plate generating seven flames. The *Nīlādri-mahodaya* mentions that the Pujaka performs the Homa ritual before *āpoṣaṇa* (offering water to drink) and offers *piṣṭakārati* after completing the task of *āpoṣaṇa*. Then, the worshiper goes out of the temple and makes offerings to the deities in the temple’s inner compound.

Finally, the worshiper offers a heap of flowers to Lord Jagannath in the form of *puṣpāñjali* and bows to all the deities. He prays to the Deity and recites His virtues. This is called *vandanā*, the last *upacāra*. Here, the devotee submissively offers himself totally up to the Lord.

The puja of Lord Jagannath contains an additional element, namely the offering of the royal *upacāras*, i.e., articles that attest to His royal authority. The royal insignia offered Him include a *chātra* (umbrella), *cāmara* (chowrie), *vyajana* (fan), *darpaṇa* (mirror), *pādukā* (sandals), dance (*nṛtya*) and song (*gīta*) by the Devadasis accompanied by instrumental music, all of which are offered with corresponding mudras and the recitation of prescribed verses.

The worshiper concludes the puja ceremony by uttering the *brahmārpana-mantra* with which he dedicates his worship, the merit that arises from it as well as all his other actions to the Lord. Then, with the *saṁhāra-mudrā,* the puja comes to an end.

After completiing Jagannath’s puja, the pujari takes the the flowers and tulasi that were used in the ritual (*nirmālya*) and offers them in turn to deities like Bali, Vibhishana, Bhishma, Narada, Phalguna, Prahlada, and Kapila, who are situated in the temple’s inner compound. Then he himself takes *nirmālya* flowers and tulasi in his hands to take the Deity’s spiritual power (*tejas*) up into his heart.

After the offering, Lord Jagannath’s prasad is sent first to the goddess Bimala where it is offered to her. It only assumes the designation of “Maha Prasad” after it has been relished by Bimala Devi. After becoming Maha Prasad,it is distributed as *khei*among the day’s sevaks, including the GajapatiMaharaj.

The scheduled time for the morning (*sakāla*) food offering is 10 a.m. This bhog is also known as Kotha Bhog (because it is offered in the Mani Kotha), or Raja Bhog. Previously, the Raja Superintendent of the Temple bore the cost of materials for preparation of bhog, but now these costs are borne by the Temple administration, which supplies rice, wheat, ghee, sugar, fuel, earthen pots, and vegetables.

## Mailam and Chatra Bhog

The prescribed time of these rituals is 11 a.m. After morning dhup, the Deities change their clothes again and an abbreviated puja takes place in the Bhog Mandap, behind the Garuda pillar of the Jagamohan. The Puja Pandas worship with five *upacāras*, namely *gandha, puṣpa, dhūpa, dīpa* and *naivedya.* A large food offering is made, provided by the Maths and the general public, consisting of rice, dal, curries, cakes of different kinds, shak, etc.

On most days, Bhog Mandap is only performed after morning dhup, but sometimes it may also be offered in the afternoon, or even three times during the day, in order to meet the demand of pilgrims for Maha Prasad.

## Madhyahna or Dviprahar Dhup

The second dhup is offered between 12:30 and 1 o’clock in the afternoon. The bhog offered in the Pokharia near the Ratnavedi is offered by three Puja Pandas with the sixteen upachars. This is the biggest offering of the day. with all kinds of curries and soups offered with rice, sweets and cakes of different kinds. Generally, fifty-six kinds of bhogs are included in Madhyahna Bhog, but in fact the number of items in the offering often exceeds a hundred.

After they have eaten, the Deities’ clothes are changed again. Then three palanquins are brought before them. The Deities are given green coconut, pan and scented water; a camphor flame, and are then put to rest (pahuda) for their afternoon nap, if time permits. The Kalahat, Jaya Vijaya and Beherana gates are sealed. This ritual is to be completed between 1 and 1:30 p.m.

## Sandhya arati

In the evening, the Bhitarcho Mahapatra examines the seals as he did in the morning and the doors are opened again. This is followed by the 21-wick lamp sandhya arati or *sañjha-kāhāli* arati. This arati is performed from the Jaya Vijaya gate. If there is no afternoon pahuda, this lamp offering takes place after afternoon dhup and after the change of clothes. On Ekadasi days, the Deities change their clothes and wear another set after arati.

## Sandhya Dhup

This is the third puja of the day and is performed with sixteen ingredients. The bhog items are less in number and quantity, consistingly primarily of watered rice, cakes like *puli*, and *amalu, dadhi-pakhāla, śākara, sūāri, pārijātaka, māṇḍuā, māṭha puli, jhaṛāi nadā, baṛ piṭhā, komala puli, sān piṭhā.*

This is followed by another arati, called Jaya Mangala Arati. The curtains are again drawn in front of the deities.

On Ekadasis, the great flame (mahādīpa) on the temple spire is lit. During the sandhya arati, three flames in silver lamps are offered. The Chunera lights the Mahadip from these flames and then carries it to the top of the temple. At the same time, Sudarshan is offered a separate arati with a seven-wicked lamp.

Another feature of the Sandhya Dhup is that the king of Puri or one of his representatives is normally supposed to be present, carrying the silver staff.

## Mailam and Chandan Lagi

This is followed by another Sahanamela or public darshan of the Deities. If there is no Sahanamela due to lack of time, the Deities change their clothes and are anointed with sandal paste (chandan) mixed with camphor, saffron and musk. This task falls to the lot of the Pashupalaka Sevaits. Other sevaks required for this ritual are the Suar Badu, Ghatuari, Muduli, Palia Mekap, Palia Parhiari, and Gara Badu. The Hadap Nayak provides the tambul and the Palia Khuntias accompany all these offerings with calls of “Manima, Manima!”

This was to be followed by the performance of the *Gīta-govinda* with the accompaniment of musical instruments like the vina.

## Boro Singar Vesh

After Chandan Lagi, the Deities are dressed up again for Boro Singar Vesh. The Deities wear Baralagi Patta, or silken robes. Some verses of Jayadeva’s *Gīta-govinda* are woven into these robes. The Deities wear flowers, garlands and floral headgear, *nākuāsi* (a flower garland for the nose), tulasi garlands, garlands for the wrists, and earrings. This vesh is very attractive to look at.

## Boro Singar Dhup

After the gods and goddesses in the Kurma bera have been served their Maha prasad, the last bhog of Jagannath’s day takes place. The time for this dhup is 11.15 at night. The Puja Pandas worship the Deities with five upachars sitting on the floor below the Ratnavedi. This is a much smaller offering, including items like mishta pakhal, watered rice, deep fried plantains in sauce, kshiri, kanji, sweet rice, various kinds of cakes, etc.

## Khat-sej Lagi and Pahuda

The Lord is put to rest again some time around midnight. This ceremony is called *pahuṛibā huyantu* or just “pahuda.” The Deities’ bedsteads are arranged. The Pashupalaks carry the Sayan (or Pushpanjali) Thakur deity from his room, the Palanka Ghar, to the Ratnavedi and place Him near Lord Jagannath. The Sayan Thakur is a metal deity in the shape of Lord Vishnu and Lakshmi Devi, a conjoined figure of Purush and Prakriti.

As He is taken into the Garbha Griha, a parasol is held over Him. He is placed on a seat shaped like an hourglass where He receives flower offerings. After an offering of green coconuts, betels, flower and camphor arati is made to Sayan Thakur, He is placed in Lord Jagannath’s bedstead and then taken back to to the Bhandarghar.

The priest invites the Lord to rest with the following mantra:

*āgaccha śayana-sthānaṁ*  
*priyābhiḥ saha keśava*  
*divya-puṣpāḍhya-śayyāyāṁ*  
*sukhaṁ vihara mādhava*

**O Keshava! Come with your beloved wives to your sleeping chamber. There, Madhava, delight on a divine bed of flowers.**

Jagannath is the lord and life of the universe. His sleep is called *yoga-nidrā* and cannot be compared to the sleep of mortals. It is not touched by the material mode of ignorance.

During these rituals, a Devadasi of the Bhitar Gayani group, would stand at the Kalahat door and give a full performance of the the *Gīta-govinda* for the Lord’s pleasure, dancing to the sound of jangling ankle bells. The king’s chief priest, the Praharaj, would also chant hymns from the Veda.

The lights are put out. The Palia Khuntia shouts “Manima Manima” from the Manikotha door. Then locks on the Kalahat, Jaya Vijaya and Dakhin (Beharana) doors are sealed. The Jaya Vijaya gate is closed by tying the rings on each door with a stout rope. The Talicchon Mahapatra then puts clay on the rope and stamps it with Lord Jagannath’s seal (Madan Mohan Mudra). A lamp burns all night outside the Jaya Vijaya gate. The temple premises are vacated of all sevaks and visitors. Only a few temple police officials and sevaks from the Palia Muduli and Palia Mekap nijogs keep watch at night.

Altogether then, there are five bhogs or food offerings during the day. These are the Ballabh Bhog, Sakal Dhup, Dinardha Dhup, Sandhya Dhup and Boro Sringar Dhup. To this is added the Chatra Bhog offering which comes after the morning offering. The Ballabh Bhog, Boro Sringar Dhup and Chatra Bhog are offered with five upachars, while the other offerings are made with sixteen upachars.

## The nature of the Deities and the mantras for their worship

Lord Jagannath is worshiped as Krishna in different aspects, but primarily as the beloved of the cow-maids (Gopijana-vallabha). The *daśākṣarī* (ten-syllable) and *aṣṭādaśākṣarī* (eighteen-syllable) are the two main mantras used in His worship. The ten-syllable mantra is *gopī-jana-vallabhāya svāhā* and the eighteen-syllable mantra is *klīṁ kṛṣṇāya govindāya gopī-jana-vallabhāya svāhā.*

For Jagannath-Krishna there are four different dhyanas depending upon the time of worship. In the morning, He is meditated upon as a child playing in the courtyard of Nanda with a lump of butter in His hand. The midday meditation is called Vrindavan dhyana. It sees Krishna as the youthful god seated on a white lotus flower under the Kalpa Vriksha (wish-giving tree) in Vrindavan, playing on flute and surrounded by the gopas, gopis and cows. In the evening (*sandhyā*), Lord Jagannath is imagined in a four-armed form seated inside a mandapa in a garden of Dwaraka. The Deity is visualized sitting on a deerskin placed on a throne, teaching the mysteries of divine knowledge to Narada and others. At night, in the Rasamandala-dhyana, the pujaris meditate on Lord Jagannath as Krishna during the Rasa lila. In this dhyana, He is visualized dancing and sporting with the cowmaids in the forest bowers by the bank of the Yamuna.

Balabhadra is worshiped as the son of Vasudeva with the twelve-syllabled Vāsudeva mantra (*oṁ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya*). He is worshiped with the hymns of the *Puruṣa-sūkta* and treated as the embodiment of the universe, the Virata Purusha.

The puja rites of Balabhadra as performed in the Jagannath temple also contain some elements of Shiva worship. Because Balabhadra is Sankarshan, he is also Lord Shiva. The Pancharatra Agamas identify Sankarshan with Siva. According to the Pancharatra Chaturvyuha theory, the one, transcendent and highest God, termed Vasudeva, manifests in three expansions during the work of creation; they are known as Sankarshan, Pradyumna and Aniruddha. Of these, Sankarshan is endowed with the characteristics of *jñāna* and *bala*, Pradyumna with those of *aiśvarya* and *vīrya* and Aniruddha with *śakti* and *tejas.*

Subhadra is worshiped as the goddess Bhuvaneshwari with her monosyllabic (*ekākṣara*) mantra *hrīṁ*. The full mantra is *om hrīṁ bhuvaneśvaryai namaḥ*. The goddess Bimala who plays an important role in the Jagannath temple is also worshiped with the same mantra.

Sudarshan has a special mantra in which he is referred to as the “thousand-spoked one” (*sahasrāra*). The *saptākṣara* or seven-syllabled mantra is *oṁ sahasrāra hruṁ phaṭ.*

Sudarshan’s puja represents the violent aspect of the worship of Vishnu and contains many elements of the worship of Narasingha.

Lakshmi is is worshiped with the monosyllabic mantra *śrīṁ*. The Vaishnavas also take Saraswati to be a wife of Vishnu. They worship her as Bhudevi, the earth.

## About the jewels on Lord Jagannath's forehead

In olden days, Orissan merchants traveled across the sea to trade in the East Indies: sailing to Java, Bali, Borneo, Sumatra, and Malaysia. Once, it is said between 500 and 700 years ago, one of these merchants was returning from a successful voyage and had laid anchor one evening in an island port somewhere to rest. A few hours into the night, he noticed a bright light at some distance from the shore. Since he had been under the impression that the island was uninhabited, he became curious about the source of this light. He mentally estimated its distance and direction and the following morning, remembering Lord Jagannath’s lotus feet, he bravely set off to find it.

The merchant searched for some time and then finally found the source of the light underneath a thorn bush. He immediately recognized it as the jewel that decorated a snake’s hood. He picked it up, wrapped it in leaves, and started back to shore. He had only gone a few steps when he heard the jewel's owner, a great serpent, hissing behind him. He began to shake with fear and to call out to the merciful Lord Jagannath to save him. In his mind he promised the Lord that if he survived, he would make Him a gift of the jewel. He kept running with all his might until he came to his beached rowboat. He rowed to the ship and ordered the sailors to make haste and lift anchor.

The boat sailed with the speed of a flying arrow, but when the merchant looked to the aft, he saw that the great serpent was swimming behind the boat, giving chase. Indeed, the serpent was so large that it seemed as though it would be capable of swallowing the entire ship. Its eyes burned with a fiery gaze and its hood spread fearfully wide.

The merchant was so afraid that he could do nothing but take shelter of Lord Jagannath, the refuge of the helpless. The merciful Lord did not leave him to what seemed like an inevitable death. Before everyone's eyes, a huge sea monster rose out of the sea in the very next moment and cut the giant snake in two, and after churning up the sea for a few moments, disappeared into the water, leaving it red with blood.

The merchant devotee felt such relief and joy that he lost himself in gratitude to the Lord. He began to sing His glories again and again. When the ship docked at Puri, he had the diamond set in a lotus flower of gold at great expense and then offered it to the Lord. Lord Jagannath still wears this jewel, now known by the name Manichula, on his forehead all year long while He sits on his altar in the main temple. It is taken off only during the Rathayatra period, when it is carefully placed in the storehouse until He returns from the Gundicha.

## Special services on different days of the week

On Sundays, after mangal arati, the Deities clothes are changed. Then three Datta Sevaks come with camphor water in silver bowls and wipe the Deities’ faces. This is followed by the usual offering of the tooth twig and bath.

On Thursdays, the Madan Mohan, Lakshmi and Saraswati deities are taken from the main temple building to the Marjan Mandap. These deities are bathed and offered a mixture of scents called banak – aguru, sandalwood, gorochana, musk, and saffron.

After this ceremony, the three deities are returned to the inner sanctum. Then in the presence of the Khuntia Mekap servants, the three Datta Sevaks apply the banaka to Lord Jagannath, Baladeva and Subhadra.

Two extra flower garlands are given to Jagannath. They are then taken down from His neck and given to Madan Mohan and Lakshmi Devi as *ājñā-mālā* (“order garlands”). Madan Mohan and Lakshmi Devi then go to Saraswati’s temple. Madan Mohan then goes to Lakshmi’s temple where He gives her His garland as prasad.

After this, Madan Mohan is offered camphor and then again placed on his palanquin and take back to his usual place.

## Special events according to asterisms

In the Rohini Nakshatra, sun-dried rice and durba grass are offered to Jagannath, Subhadra and Balaram. This is called Akhata Lagi. They are then offered a camphor flame. On this day, only Lord Jagannath is given Mangala Arati and Sandhya Arati.

During the Shravan Nakshatra, Madan Mohan is placed on the throne after the midday offering. Then two of the deities (Baladeva and Jagannath?) are offered Akhata Lagi. Afterwards there is the offering of a camphor flame and then Jaya Mangala Arati and Sandhya Arati are offered to Balaram.

## Special rituals on particular lunar days and festivals

Vaishnavas follow the lunar calendar. They especially hold Ekadasi, the eleventh day of both fortnights – that of the waxing and the waning moon, to be a sacred time. On Ekadasis, a number of special rituals take place in the Jagannath temple.

The Madan Mohan deity is given Jagannath’s flower garland (*ajñā-mālā*) and is then placed on a palanquin and taken to the base of the Kalpa Bata tree. He is then carried around the temple and taken to the Jaya Vijaya gate. There He is offered chandan prasad, fresh fruit bhog (sitala bhog) and an arati before being returned to His own temple.

If Ekadasi falls on a Monday, Madan Mohan is taken to the Lokeshwar temple. Fruit is offered to Him there and He is then taken to the Jaya Vijaya gate with Lokeshwar. There He is again offered fruit, sandalwood and arati before returning to His own altar. The only exception to this rule is the period between Rukmini Haran Ekadasi and Bahura Ekadasi. During this time, the Dol Govinda deity takes Madan Mohan’s place in the temple for these and other rituals. The reason for this is that Madan Mohan is taken to the Vivaha Mandap with Rukmini during this period. On Bahura Ekadasi, Madan Mohan joins Jagannath Deva on his altar.

If Ekadasi falls on a Thursday, then Jagannath Deva is decorated with golden arms and is dressed according to the Boro Sringar with a silver cane, parasol, and all the other signs of kingship.
