On dark moon days (Amavasya), the Narayan deity is taken out to the seashore. On these days, the Lord kindly passes along the beach by the Purushottam Gaudiya Math and Tota Gopinath, giving the devotees the opportunity to see Him and pay their obeisances.

When there is a solar or lunar eclipse, then all that day’s ritual worship and food offerings must be completed twelve hours before the eclipse takes place. When the eclipse begins, the Deity is given a Maha Snana and an offering of Ballabh Bhog. The Maha Snana is repeated after the eclipse is completely finished and then the regular daily worship cycle recommences.

## Maha Snana

Maha Snana must be performed if anyone other than an authorized servant of the Lord touches Him. Other occasions for this purificatory ritual arise when any place between the Jaya Vijaya gate and the Ratnavedi is contaminated by the touch of stool, urine, blood, leather, bone, spit or some other impure substance. If a dog or some other unclean animal enters this sacred area, then whatever offerings are being made are considered impure and the Maha Snana must be performed. A special Maha Snanas called the Yatra Maha Snana is also performed during festivals.

The Maha Snana is performed in the same way that the Diety is bathed every day during the Abakash, except that the entire area from the Deity’s throne up to the Jaya Vijaya gate is thoroughly washed.

If any of the Deity’s bhog is ever rendered impure, it is thrown into a hole and buried in its entirety. The purificatory fire sacrifice is performed again, the fires relit and the cooking recommenced. The costs incurred at having to waste all the foodstuffs are borne by the person who is responsible for the impurity, who must pay the full amount as a fine.

## A detailed description of Lord Jagannath’s daily offerings.

The way that the people of Orissa devote themselves to their supreme lord and king is unequalled in the world. The expression *chāppānna-bhoga* is synonymous with the royal service give to Lord Jagannath. The term means either that He receives means fifty-six different kinds of preparations, or that the offerings weigh fifty-six mounds (*mon)*. One mound is equivalent to about forty kilograms. Since these amounts are usually exceeded in the major offerings, it is used to signify any large offering, especially of sweets. Sundarananda Vidyavinoda gives a list of eighty-five sweet preparations that are classified as part of the *chāppānna-bhoga*.\[76\]

Sundarananda has also given some summaries of the recipes of Lord Jagannath’s favorite foods, but it has not been possible to give details of every single preparation, nor indeed all of the lists of names of preparations, as most of them would be meaningless to the reader. The following is a *dig-darśana*, simply to give an idea of some of the principal foods that Lord Jagannath enjoys every day.

As has already been mntioned, there are many kinds of food that are not offered to Jagannath Deva. Included amongst the proscribed vegetables are potatoes, cabbage, chilis, tomatoes, cucumber, bitter melon, other kinds of melon, and gumbo (lady’s fingers). Parboiled rice is also considered unacceptable. However, there has been a loosening of standards in the use of vegetable ghee, rather than genuine clarified butter. This oil is used for lamps and is sold for that purpose on the temple grounds.

## Ballabh Bhog or Balya Bhog

In Orissan, puffed rice covered in unrefined sugar is known as *ballabh*. This is one of the main ingredients in Lord Jagannath’s breakfast and gives its name to this first offering given to the Lord. Ballabh consists of khoi, puffed rice made from sun-parched rice, and *muṛkī*, which is khoi coated with brown sugar. Other foodstuffs included in this offering are khua laddus, coonut sweets, kora, ripe bananas, curd and chipped coconuts, milk, butter and cream, yogurt, sor papri, seasonal fruits and coconut water.

Ballabh is made by melting gur with small pieces of coconut and then pouring the puffed rice (khoi) into it. There are two types of puffed rice used in eastern India: One is made from sun-parched rice and is known as khoi; the other is made from parboiled rice and is known as muri. The latter cannot be offered to Lord Jagannath. When the khoi and gur have been well mixed, powdered pepper, cloves, cardamom and camphor are added.

Sor papri is made from the skin that forms on boiled milk.

Khoa manda is made by mixing thickly condensed milk or khoa with rock sugar in roughly even quantities and adding raisins, pistachios, nuts, grond cardamom and camphor. These are rolled into balls.

Ballabh kora is made from cooking unrefined sugar with ground coconut and adding a mixture of ground pepper, cardamom, cloves and camphor.

Nariya Khudi is made from the meat of three half-ripe coconuts, which is cut into small pieces and served on six saucers.

Ghosha jol is water that has been mixed with ground nutmeg in a clay jar and to which a touch of camphor has been added.

## Raja bhog

The morning offering, which is also often called the Raja bhog consists of

Enduri -- This preparation is made as follows: one grinds soaked kalai dal into a paste, to which is added, asafoetida, ginger, and ground untoasted cumin seeds. This dough is then rolled out into pancake shapes and steamed. In Jagannath's kitchen, the enduri is steamed by placing it in a banana leaf on top of an iron plate (*jâl*) inside a clay pot filled with boiling water and covered by a hanri or wok. The enduri is served cold and sprinkled with ground rock sugar (*khaṇḍa*).

Khichuri (*kamrabāi khicuri*) – Khichuri is a well-known preparation made of boiled pulses mixed with rice. In Jagannath's kitchen, it is made as follows: Ten parts of rice mixed wth six parts husked moog dal. This is set to boil and salt, ginger and asafoetida are added. The khitcherie is removed from the flame before being fully cooked and finishes absorbing the water in its own heat.

Matha puli -- Kalai dal paste is mixed with ginger, salt, asafoetida, cumin powder and shaped into balls. These are then deep fried in ghee.

Hamsa jhili -- Is made like a jelebi. The same mixture as māṭha-puli is placed into a patissier's squeeze tube made into jelebi like shapes in boiling ghee. When the deep-frying is finished, the hamsa jhili is boiled in sugar syrup.

Chandrakanti. Ground coconut is added to the matha puli paste. These are rolled into round chapati-like shapes and fried. They are then made into rolls stuffed with a filling made of ginger, tamarind paste (*maṇḍa*) and sugar. This is also called bali-bhog.

Mitha kanika (*miṭhā-kaṇikā*). Into each pot of water, 1 1/2 powas of rock sugar is brought to a boil with bay leaves. To this 14 chataks of rice and half a powa of raw mug dal are added. When these ingredients are nearly cooked, salt is added. The pot is taken off the fire and four chataks of ghee, raisins, cardamom and cloves are mixed in. The preparation is then left to cook in its own heat.

Shak. It is said Jagannath does not accept this spinach preparation unless it is cooked by Lakshmi Devi herself. The kind of spinach used is known in Orissan as *neyutiya*, in Bengali as champa-notay (*cāṁpā-naṭe*). It is boiled with salt, ghee and water. To this are added fried cumin and asafoetida.

Others self evident -- fried plantain, tāṭ-khichuri, nukhurā khichuri, meṇḍā-muṇḍiyā, piṭhā-puli, bindiyā-khiri, mahā-deī, etc. Recipes not given for kakua-jhili, ādāpā-celi,

## Chatra bhog

The preparations offered for Chatra bhog are not made in Jagannath's kitchen, but brought from the various maths and donated by other individuals. The principal ingredient in this offering is rice.

Various kinds of dal. Jagannath does not accept split pea soup, but other than this accepts soups made of other pulses such as moog, biuli, khesari, chola (chick peas) and aharahar. Aharahar dal is Jagannath's particular favorite and has a unique taste not found in any other type of pulse. Jagannath's aharahar dal is flavored with toasted cumin powder, sugar and ginger.

Mahura. This preparation contains mixed vegetables indigenous to Orissa, including eggplant, various root vegetables, such as sweet potato, kachu, eddoes, deshi aloo, khamba aloo, and sweet pumpkin. These are boiled with a mixture of ground spices including cumin, black pepper, cinnamon, bay leaves, cardamom, cloves, and coriander. When the vegetables are cooked, the following spices are fried in ghee and added: mustard seed, cumin seed, fenugreek seed and mauri.

Besara. The same vegetables as above, but to which coconut kora and ground mustard seed and black pepper are added.

Ambal. This is a sour chutney-type preparation made with chalta cut into small pieces. Mustard paste, rice paste, gur, mauri bata, and coconut kora. Fried spices (sambara) added as in mahura.

Madhuruchi. Ripe tamarind paste, gur, rice flour, coconut kora, sweet pumpkin. cooked with salt and fried spices added as before.

Doi curry. Soaked chick peas cooked in a sauce of yogurt, chick pea flour and turmeric. To this fried spices are added as before.

Shakor (*śākara*). Chal kumra, a type of gourd, is cut into thin slices, then gur, taramarind and coconut are added and boiled again. Then sambara added as before.

Raita. Thin slices of Chal Kumra (Panikatharu in Orissan) are dry sauteed (amanna), then boiled, drained and rinsed. These are added to a mixture of yogurt, raw mustard paste, salt and fine cut cilantro. To this, fried cumin seeds are added.

Pita. This preparation has a slightly bitter taste. The following ingredients are used -- 5/8 banana flower and plantain tree marrow and 3/8 eggplant, kochu, plantain, kochu and the other kinds of root vegetables mentioned in mahura above. These are cooked together with coconut kora and a mixture of spices, the powder made from toasted fenugreek seed, black pepper, coriander seed and cumin seed. To this, fried spices as before.

Kakharu sambora. A sweet pumpkin is peeled and diced and sauteed. Water. gir. coconut, are added and a paste of cumin, black pepper, and coriander. Sambara is added at the end.

Gota-kochu marich pani. A vegetable preparation made with eggplant and a type of taro root, ghee and spices.

## Madhyahna Bhog

Subasa pakhal (fragrant rice). Water is left to stand for two hours with the petals of various flowers (rose, mallika, bel, and bui). Boiled rice is drained and washed with cold water. It is placed in a bowl with the above-mentioned scented water, after the petals themselves have been strained out. Salt is also added. This scented rice is eaten with the marich pani vegetables – plantain, eggplant, potal, ghee and spices.

Kancha arisha. Rice flour is mixed with liquid gur molasses and left to sit for four hours. The dough is flattened into pancake shapes on banana leaves and then deep fried in clarified butter.

Pag arisha. Liquid gur is brought to a boil until it becomes thick. It is then stirred into rice flour. When it has cooled, ghee is added and made into pancake shapes on banana leaves and then deep fried.

Tipuri. This is a type of puri made with the bark of the Garuda Govinda tree, found in Puri. The bark is sun-dried and then ground into a powder and sifted. This powder is mixed with water and rice flour and then rolled into pancake shapes. It is then deep fried in ghee and then soaked in sugar syrup.

Surpuli. A paste is made from soaked biuli dal, to which are added the following: salt, asafoetida, ground raw cumin seeds, ground fresh ginger, whole black pepper corns, ground fresh coconut, and cream. This mixture is made into pancake shapes on a pancake leaf and then deep fried in ghee. The finished fried cakes are sprinkled with sugar.

Other preparations offered at this bhog are: mog dal, cucumber, small cakes, large and small manohar, biri bora, laddu, jhili, pheni, sor pana, large and small nari, ghrita karambha, and many other kinds of sweet and savory preparations.

## Sandhya Dhup II

At this offering, jenamani (“prince’s jewel”) made of kalai dal, math puli, kaala puli made of kalai dal, sari, mandua, rasavali made of milk and curd, takua, dadhi pakhal (cooked rice soaked in yogurt), parijatak, amalu, shakar, marich naru, khoirachur, hamsa ballabh, malpoa (wholewheat flour and gur with whole peppercorns deep fried in clarified butter), churai nada (wheat flour and kalai dal), chulia pakhal, chupura pakhal and pani pakhal (water-soaked rice).

## Boro Sringar Dhup

Khiri khirisha, Tabha pakhal, kadali bora, suar pitha, mishta pakhal, dadhi kanji, keli and sorpuli are offered for Boro Sringar dhup.

## Pahuda

When the Deities are put to bed, they are given scented water, green coconut water and tambul.

The above are the daily offerings made in the temple kitchen and are given to Lord Jagannath on a regular basis. Besides these, there are many other preparations that are offered by the temples and the general public during festivals and other special occasions. Once again, the interested reader is referred to Sundarananda Vidyavinoda’s *Śrī Kṣetra* for more details.

## Chapter 13 - A city of festivals

Each year, the town of Jagannath Puri reverberates with hundreds of festivals, large and small. \[See calendar at end of book\]. The principal festivals are, of course, centred around the temple itself, where not only Jagannath, Baladeva and Subhadra have Their annual celebrations, but the various shrines in the Boro Deul also celebrate particular occasions of importance to thir respective deities.

The *Nīlādri-mahotsava* speaks of an annual cycle of twelve festivals, or *dvādaśa-yātrā-vidhi*. It names the following:

1\. Snana Utsava in the month of Jyeshtha (May-June)  
2\. Rathayatra in the month of Asharh (June-July)  
3\. Sayana-Yatra in Asharh  
4\. Ayana (Dakshinayan) Yatra in the month of Shravan (July-Aug.)  
5\. Parshwa Parivartan in the month of Bhadra (Aug.-Sept.)  
6\. Utthapana Utsava in the month of Karttika (Oct.-Nov.)  
7\. Pravarana in the month of Margashira (Nov.-Dec.)  
8\. Pushyabhishek in Paush (Dec.-Jan.)  
9\. Makara Samkranti in Magh (Jan.-Feb.)  
10\. Dola Yatra in Phalgun (Feb.-Mar.)  
11\. Damanaka Yatra in Chaitra (Mar.-Apr.)  
12\. Chandan Yatra in Vaishakh (Apr.-May)

The *Nīlādri-mahodayam* does, however, give a longer list of sixty festivals, a figure that probably could be made even greater. In this chapter, we will describe only the most most significant of these celebrations. At each of these occasions, Lord Jagannath dresses in a special way, and many of these festivals are made specially memorable by the specific costumes He wears.

The new year is observed at different times in different parts of India, according to the calendar that is used. For Bengalis, it is the beginning of Vaishakh; Orissans celebrate the Makara Sankranti; Northern Indians celebrate with Rama’s victory over Ravana in the fall. For some, the beginning of the rains marks the new year. The *Nīla-mahodaya* starts its list with the Snana Yatra, which is traditionally the day that Lord Jagannath first appeared to Indradyumna.

However, because the Rathayatra cycle of festivals is the most significant, we have decided to start this description with Chandan Yatra, for the first day of this festival, Akshaya Tritiya, is not only the day of auspicious beginnings, but because of its connection with the most important of Puri’s festivals, Rathayatra.

## Chandan Yatra

Vaishakh is the beginning of the hot season in Orissa. The Chandan Yatra festival centres on activities meant to cool the Deities, namely the application of cooling sandalwood paste and going out for an outing on the water. In the traditional agricultural society, the coming of rains after the hot season were an important annual event, and the rituals connected with this festival were in part meant to insure the fertility of the land and people in Lord Jagannath’s kingdom.

Chandan Yatra begins with Akshaya Tritiya, the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaishakh and ends 42 days later. It is divided into two periods of twenty-one days each, the “outer” or Bahar Chanda, and the “inner” or Bhitar Chandan. As its name indicates, the latter consists of various rites performed inside the temple, out of public view. The Bahar Chandan, on the other hand or Outer Chandan is marked by a procession in which the Deities are taken to Narendra Kund.

The origins of the Chandan Yatra, which is also known as Gandhalepan Yatra, are described in the *Utkala-khaṇḍa*, chapter 29, where Lord Jagannath tells His dear devotee, King Indradyumna:

*vaiśākhasya site pakṣe tṛtīyākṣaya-saṁjñakā \|*  
*tatra māṁ lepayed gandha-lepanair atiśobhanam \|\|*

**On Akshaya Tritiya, the third day of the waxing moon in the month of Vaishakh, you should smear Me with scented pastes and unguents.**

The word *gandha-lepana* is said to refer primarily to sandalwood in the *Viṣṇu-dharmottara-purāṇa* – *anulepana-mukhyaṁ tu candanaṁ parikīrtitam*. This is confirmed by the *Nārada-purāṇa*:

*yathā viṣṇoḥ samābhīṣṭaṁ naivedyaṁ śāli-sambhavam \|*  
*śukenoktaṁ purāṇe ca tathā tulasī-candanam \|\|*

**In all the Puranas, Shukadeva confirms that just as the Lord is particularly fond of offerings that include fine rice, He similarly loves sandalwood paste mixed with tulasi.**

On the day preceding Akshaya Tritiya, the preparatory rituals, or Adhivasa are performed to prepare and consecrate the fifteen seers\[77\] of sandalwood provided by the Raghava Das Math that will be used over the next month and a half. The door of the temple is then closed and a Lenka Paik stands guard to make sure no one makes off with the valuable sandalwood.

The next day the Chandan Yatra officially begins. After the Deities have been bathed and dressed, the sandal paste is taken in a procession thrice round the temple and then presented to Them. Then after Panchopachara worship, They are decorated with ornaments and finally painted with sandal paste. Not only Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra, but also the images of Lakshmi, Madhava and Saraswati are honored in this way. The giving of sandalwood paste is called chandan lagi.

After offering Chandan to Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra, the images of Ramakrishna, Madan Mohan, Lakshmi and Saraswati are brought to the Ratna Singhasan. The king of Puri prays to Lord Jagannath to give permission to take these vijaya vigrahas to Narendra. On Jagannath’s behalf, the priests give the *ājñā-mālās*, and the Deities are placed in their respective palanquins. The king’s elephant, decorated as Gaja Lakshmi, mother Lakshmi in elephant form, greets the Deities as They come out of the temple.

Every morning and afternoon through the twenty-one days of the Bahar Chandan, the Lord’s representative deity Madan Mohan, accompanied by Lakshmi and Saraswati, is taken on a biman or throne along the Granda Road and other streets of the town to Narendra Sarovar.

First in the procession comes Balaram’s representative deity, Ramakrishna, in a type of palanquin known as a palangi, which looks rather like a boat with one curved pole coming out each end, which allows the pandas to carry it on their shoulders and still be only about two and a half or three feet from the ground. Ramakrishna lies inside on His side, so it is easy to have darshan. The Pandas even allow pilgrims to touch the feet of Their Lordships. Like all of the palanquins the palangi is covered with an umbrella and various ornaments.

Madan Mohan covered in chandan follows with His consorts Laksmi and Saraswati. His palanquin is higher up as it is supported by two straight poles carried on the shoulders of four stout Pandas.

Prominent in the joyful procession from the temple are devotees from Haridas Thakur's samadhi who lead the way in front of Ramakrishna singing “Nitai Gaura Radhe Shyam” They are followed by a mixed group of devotees from Radha Kanta and other maths, singing the songs of the Gaudiya Mahajanas. After them comes a group of Pandas and Orissan devotees who accompany Madan Mohan, singing songs by Jayadeva and other kirtans.

Ramakrishna and Madan Mohan are followed by the five deities of Shiva, known as the Panch Pandavas, each in their separate palanquin. These five deities are the representative deities of the five main Shiva lingas in Puri – Markandeshwar, Lokanath, Kapala Mochan, Yameshwar, and Nilakantheshwar. The Panch Pandavas are said to be Lord Jagannath’s council of ministers.

The entire roadway from the Jagannath temple to the lake is colorfully decorated with flags, festoons, mango leaves and flowers. Dancing Durga Medhas and Nagas accompany the procession. One of the temple servants traditionally dresses as Nanda Maharaj, Krishna’s father, and leads the procession in the company of many other children dressed as cowherds and cowgirls. Other people are dressed in costumes, like that of Garuda. Widows wave fly whisks.

At several places along the way, there are canopies called chamundias, where the deities stop and are given offerings of food and dance performances are made and songs sung for Their pleasure. These temporary structures made from wooden or bamboo poles about twenty feet high that are covered with thatched roofs.

Once They arrive at Narendra Kund, the Deities sport in two beautifully decorated boats. The one meant for Madan Mohan and His wives is covered with white cloth, while another with red coverings is for Ramakrishna and the five Shivas.

Madan Mohan is accompanied in His boat by a priest and, formerly, by one or more Devadasis, who would perform for Them. The actual task of rowing is taken up by Shudra temple servants of the fisherman caste. The Devadasis would take turns singing and dancing with the accompaniment of a drum. The songs they would sing were “boat songs” in the mood of erotic love and their dances were a combination of pure and expressive dance (*abhinaya*). Like many of the other traditions connected with the Devadasis, the dance on the Chandan Sarovar was stopped in the mid-1970’s.

On Ramakrishna’s boat, a Goti pua, or young boy dancer, would perform, dressed as a girl. The Goti puas (meaning “only son”) are also known as “dancing boys” (natua pila) or “akhara boys” (akhara pila). This last name comes from their connection with the akharas (or Jagaharas), where they are trained. Some people trace this tradition of young boy dancers in Puri back to Ramananda Ray, or at least that it grew out of the *sakhī-bhāva* that was cultivated by followers of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. These boys still perform during certain festivals in the akharas, as well as in the maths, but they never performed inside the temple. Their dance in the boat has also been discontinued.

The Deities are taken around the sandalwood-scented lake three or four times. In the festive atmosphere, small boys swim alongside the Deities’ boats as they float to the island in the center of the lake, while wrestlers from the Jagaharas bathe and families picnic on the shores of the tank.

On the island are three temple structures. The largest of these houses Madan Mohan, Lakshmi and Saraswati, whereas the other deities are placed in the two other buildings. A well by the middle temple provides water to bathe the Deities who are worshiped and given food offerings. As night falls, these temples and the shores of the lake are lined with lamps.

When the festival is finished, the Deities are brought back to the mainland and placed on their seven travelling thrones to return to the Jagannath temple. It is usually midnight before they are back in Their customary places. On the twentieth day of the Bahar Chandan, the Deities are taken around the lake twenty-one times. This is called Bhauri. One of the Khuntia sevakas joins the boat party and throws flowers on the Deities throughout the two-hour voyage. On the last day, the boats are also sprinkled with turmeric water.

Beginning on Akshaya Tritiya, Madan Mohan wears something different for each of the twenty-one days of the festival. These different costumes are known as the Lord’s Chandan Vesh.

Tritiya Natabara (“the great dancer”) Vesh   Caturthi Krishna Janma (“Krishna’s birthday”) Vesh   Panchami Rajadhiraja (“king of kings”) Vesh   Shashthi Vanavihari (“walking in the woods”) Vesh   Saptami Vatsaharan (“when Brahma stole the calves”) Vesh   Ashtami Gomati Vesh   Navami Khatdoli (“riding on the swing”) Vesh   Dasami Chakra Narayan Vesh   Ekadasi Naukeli (“sailing”) Vesh   Dvadasi Natavara (“great dancer”) Vesh   Trayodasi Rasa Mandala (“the circle dance”) Vesh   Chaturdashi Kandarpa Ratha (“Cupid’s chariot”) Vesh   Purnima Aghasura-vadha (“killing the Agha demon”) Vesh   Krishna Pratipad Raghunath Vesh   Dvitiya Sri Chaitanya Vesh   Tritiya Giri Govardhan Vesh   Caturthi Giridhari Vesh   Panchami Vastra Haran (“stealing the gopis’ clothes”) Vesh   Shashthi Chintamani Krishna Vesh   Saptami Gajoddharana (“saving the elephant king”) Vesh   Ashtami There is no special dress on the festival’s last day.

During the second period of twenty-one days, the Bhitar Chandan, the images are not taken to the tank, but are placed in brass pots containing water scented with sandalwood. These are kept on the Jala-krida Mandap, the same platform where the wedding of Rukmini and Krishna is celebrated in the second week of Chandan Yatra.

## Mahaprabhu’s participation at Chandan Yatra

Krishna Das Kaviraj and Vrindavan Das have written about Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s celebration of the Chandan Yatra festival. Krishna Das gives the following abbreviated account:

*ei-mate vaiṣṇava saba nīlācale āilā*  
*daive jagannāthera se dina jala-līlā*  
*narendrera jale govinda naukāte caḍiyā*  
*jala-krīḍā kare saba bhakta-gaṇa lañā*  
*sei-kāle mahāprabhu bhakta-gaṇa-saṅge*  
*narendre āilā dekhite jala-keli-raṅge*  
*sei-kāle āilā saba gauḍera bhakta-gaṇa*  
*narendrete prabhu-saṅge ha-ila milana*  
*bhakta-gaṇa paḍe āsi prabhura caraṇe*  
*uṭhāñā prabhu sabāre kailā āliṅgane*

**When the Bengali Vaishnavas arrived in Jagannath Puri, it just happened to be a day when Lord Jagannath had His water pastimes. On this day, Govinda boards a boat on Narendra Sarovar with His devotees to enjoy the water.**  
**Mahaprabhu had just appeared there with His personal associates to watch these jubilant pastimes when all the devotees from Bengal came and saw Him. They immediately fell at His lotus feet and He lifted and embraced every one of them. (CC** [**3.10.41-45**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-antya/10.41)**)**

*gauḍīya-sampradāya saba karena kīrtana*  
*prabhura milane uṭhe premera krandana*  
*jala-krīḍā vādya gīta nartana kīrtana*  
*mahā-kolāhala tīre salile khelana*  
*gauḍīya-saṅkīrtane āra rodana miliyā*  
*mahā-kolāhala haila brahmāṇḍa bhariyā*  
*saba bhakta lañā prabhu nāmilena jale*  
*sabā lañā jala-krīḍā karena kutūhale*

**The Bengali devotees began to sing kirtans, shedding tears from the joy of meeting the Lord. In the meantime a great tumult of musical instruments, dancing and song arose on the banks of Narendra Sarovar where Govinda\[78\] was beginning His Jala Krida. The sound of the two groups mixed, creating a great clamor that filled the entire universe. The Lord then entered the water with His devotees and began jubilantly playing with them. (CC** [**3.10.46-49**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-antya/10.46)**)**

Vrindavan Das describes the Lord and His devotees’ Jala Krida in greater detail –

**“Soon after Mahaprabhu had come to Narendra Sarovar, the deities of Ramakrishna and Yatra Govinda, Lord Jagannath’s representative deity form, appeared there in order to enjoy Their water pastimes. A great tumult arose as people shouted the names of God, playing on mridangas and kettledrums, blowing bugles and conchshells. A crowd of thousands upon thousands of the Lord’s servants held parasols, flags and fans, creating a colorful scene. They cheered and called out the Lord’s names such that no other sound could be heard. Lord Jagannath and Balaram approached Narendra Sarovar and the crowd of Mahaprabhu’s devotees mixed in with the crowd of Jagannath bhaktas and all together they began to chant the Holy Names. What bliss when the two groups became one! It was as the though the joy of the spiritual world had descended and taken form. Everyone everywhere felt great jubilation and all was orchestrated by Lord Chaitanya Himself. Yatra Govinda were placed on the boat and devotees all around waved yak-tail whisks. Mahaprabhu was very happy to see the Lord on the boat. Then taking his devotees with Him, the Lord jumped into the water. (Cbh** [**3.8.101-112**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cb-antya/8.101)**)**

Vrindavan Das continues:

**“Listen, brothers and sisters, to how the Lord, incarnate as Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, played in the waters of the Narendra Lake! It was just as though Krishna Himself were playing in the Yamuna, splashing His cowherd boyfriends. At first, all the devotees made a circle, holding hands. In Bengal there is a water game called** ***Koya*****, and this was the first game that they started playing. They clapped hands in the water while shouting “*****Koyā! koyā!*****” All around devotees played instruments while standing in the water. Mahaprabhu’s associates all took on the nature of the children of Gokula and splashed each other unselfconsciously. Everyone splashed the Lord’s body, especially Advaita who completely forgot himself in a water fight with the Lord, splashing Him directly in the eyes. Sometimes he had the upper hand in the melee, and sometimes it was the Lord.**  
**Hundreds and thousands of people had gathered there for the Chandan Yatra festival and, whether householders, sannyasis or brahmacharis, they all splashed each other with the holy water, indifferent to their station in life. The Lord’s illusory energy is so powerful that no ordinary person could perceive these pastimes. The Yamuna and Ganges Rivers had enjoyed this blessing of the Lord in the past, and now the same good fortune befell the Narendra Lake. Any living entity who hears of these pastimes is liberated from repeated birth and death.” (Cbh** [**3.8.113-5**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cb-antya/8.113)**,** [**127-9**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cb-antya/8.127)**,** [**140-1**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cb-antya/8.140)**)**

**After He finished playing in the water, Lord Chaitanya took His entourage with Him to the Jagannath temple for the Lord’s darshan. On seeing the Lord’s form, they all shed tears of joy. After paying their obeisances to Lord Jagannath, all the devotees repaired to their quarters. The Lord fulfills His devotees’ desire to see Him in the form they love. Mahaprabhu treated His devotees like His own children, keeping them constantly near to Him. The Bengali and Orissa and devotees remained in each other’s company to discuss Krishna. (Cbh 3.8.142-3, 163-6)**

## The Devadasis’ gupta seva

The Devadasis had a particularly important role in the Chandan Yatra rituals. During the forty-two days of the festival, their daily routine increased from two performances to seven. Their regular dance during the main food offering was changed to the time of the chandan lagi. A Bhitar Devadasi would still sing the evening songs while the deities were being put to sleep as usual. Besides these two occasions, they would also perform twice daily on the boat and also twice during the time called alata lagi. This latter performance also took place by the Garuda stambha.

They also engaged in the “secret ritual” (*gupta-sevā*), which took place every evening during the entire Chandan Yatra period. This extraordinary ritual, the only one the Devadasis performed for Balabhadra and not Jagannath, has been described by Frederique Marglin in her book *Wives of the God-King.\[79\]* The following is an adaptation of her description:

Normally, the Devadasi proceeds into the dancing hall from the northern entrance. For the gupta seva, however, the gate leading from the dance hall into the Mukha Shala, the antechamber of the inner sanctum, is closed and she enters the side door on its southern side. Everyone except for three priests (Singharis) is kept out of this portion of the temple and the southern door is kept closed during the ritual. The eternal lamp that hangs on a chain in the inner sanctum is taken off its hook and placed on the floor behind the dais on which the deities stand. It is then covered with an upturned earthen pot, plunging the windowless rooms into complete darkness.

During the ritual, the three priests sit on the dais in the inner sanctum, one in front of each Deity, fanning them. The images are lightly dressed in a fine white cloth. Midway through the ritual, the astrologer who has been keeping track of the time for this purpose calls the three Singharis out and they are replaced by three Puja Pandas who continue the fanning.

The Devadasis would purify themselves much more rigorously during the forty-two days of Chandan Yatra. They dressed differently also: they did not wear the round red powder mark on the forehead indicative of marriage to Lord Jagannath, but a vertical line of vermilion; they did not wear red foot dye, scented hair oil or scented flowers. They did not wear ornaments that produced sound, like ankle-bracelets, even pushing their bangles up on their arms so they would not jingle.

The Devadasi would then start walking forward, snapping her fingers to frighten away the cobras she hears hissing in the dark. This was a time of great fear, but guided in the obscurity by the glow of the diamond on Jagannath’s forehead, she reached her station on the threshold of the door leading into the inner sanctum, facing Balabhadra. Once there, she undraped her sari to uncover the upper part of her body to perform the ritual half dressed. The ritual consists of singing a song by the Orissan poet Dina Krishna Das, *Snānotsava-catiśa –* “Thirty-four verses about the bathing festival.” This poem tells of the sorrow of the poet at not being able to see the splendor of the bathing festival with his own eyes.

## Rathanukula

Akshaya Tritiya, the first day of the Chandan Yatra, is held to be an auspicious time to take up new projects. Another important Puri tradition that begins on this day is the building of the Rathayatra chariots. A puja is performed to the wood that will be used to build the chariots in front of the King’s palace. Their construction is usually finished before the end of the 42-day Chandan Yatra period.

As Jagannath’s *vijaya vigraha*, Sri Madan Mohan, is taken in His jeweled palanquin from the temple through the north exit to Narendra Sarovar, He stops before the Gajapati’s palace, Sri Raja Nahar, where the wood gathered for building the raths has been deposited. He gives the king the order to build a chariot for Lord Jagannath.

The King appoints the three acharyas who are each to supervise the building of one of the raths and the craftsman who are to do the actual building by tying Lord Jagannath’s prasadi cloth around their heads. In this way, these people are given the Lord’s blessings through the King and invested with the power to do the work.

This is then followed by the performance of a fire sacrifice after which the three carpenters begin the actual work of building the chariot under the watchful eye of Madan Mohan. Once Madan Mohan is satisfied that the work has indeed begun, He returns to the temple via the Narendra Sarovar.

The service of building the chariots has been held by the same carpenter families for generations. As a result, the rights for the work have been divided into so many rights-holders that they are no longer able to do the work for nothing. They are paid the current concession rate. A great amount of money is set aside to pay the carpenters, the painters, tailors and other craftsmen who participate in the cars’ construction.

## Vanayaga Vidhi

According to *Nīlādri-mahodaya*, Akshaya Tritiya is also the day on which woodcutters set off to find trees to fell for the following year’s rath. Three Pandas or Brahmin servants of Lord Jagannath are given prasadi garlands or *ājñā-mālā,* tokens of their having been given a mission by the Lord. They then set off to Daspalla, the capital of the former princely state that is traditionally the source of the wood for the rath. This is called the Vanayaga Vidhi. It is said that if the chariots are constructed without the performance of Vanayaga Vidhi, then misfortune will strike the land.

Wood for the Rathayatra carts is brought from Daspalla, as it has been for many centuries. When Orissa was formed of many princely states, the kings of Banpur were responsible for providing the wood, not only for the raths, but also for cleaning Jagannath’s teeth (*danta-dhāvana*).\[80\] This service was subsequently taken over by the Daspalla kings, who were related to Banpur by marriage. Now after Independence, since these small principalities have been merged to form the Indian state of Orissa, the state government arranges for wood to be brought to Puri for the festival through the Daspalla Divisional Forest officer.

*Nīlādri-mahodaya* gives detailed descriptions of the process of collection. The preliminary ritual is performed on the previous day by worshiping the acharya, Varuna, the carpenters, and their tools with camphor, sandal paste, flowers and new cloth. After the Deities have been worshiped on the Tritiya, the temple servants, officials and carpenters proceed to the forest to collect wood.

Formerly, before cutting the first tree, a fire sacrifice would be performed in the area of the forest that had been protected for that purpose. The deities worshipped are Ganesh, Dikpala, Kshetrapala and Pashupati. After the last oblation was offered into the fire, a silver axe is sanctified with mantras. The acharyas then place three prasadi garlands on the designated trees. The Panda acharya would make the first stroke of the axe, but professional woodcutters completed chopping the tree down. Nowadays everything is done by government work order with professional woodcutters.

Until fairly recently, the wood for the raths would be floated down the Mahanadi, Kathjuri and Bhargavi rivers to a spot three miles outside Puri town. In 1983, a most interesting event took place in connection with the Rathayatra wood. In September of 1982, a terrible flood affected eight districts of Orissa, in particular those through which the Mahanadi flows. Many of Orissa’s largest cities and much of the surrounding countryside disappeared under water. The Mahanadi’s rising waters swept through the forested areas on its banks and carried elephants, snakes, huge trees, and all kinds of other things in its current, but the wood that had been cut and set aside for the rath was somehow left intact and did not move an inch. This astonishing bit of news was reported with large headlines on the front pages of all Orissan papers. The material nature affects all conditioned souls, but it can touch neither the transcendental and non-dual Supreme Lord Jagannath, nor those who have dedicated their lives to His pure service. The immobility of these stacks of wood destined to become Lord Jagannath’s rath is a testimony to this eternal truth.

Nowadays, of course, the wood is taken by lorry directly to the spot in front of the king’s palace where the work on the cars will be done. On its arrival, the Puri temple manager inspects the wood. In some years, as in 1983, the amount of timber coming from Daspalla was too small and it became necessary to buy more from local lumberyards in order to make up the difference.\[81\] Normally, asana and dhaura wood is used for the carts because it is tough and resilient and will serve its purpose even if it should crack. Gradual deterioration of the Daspalla forest has resulted in an insufficient number of trees of sufficient girth being available there. Thus, every year, it is necessary to go further and further afield to find the wood needed for the carts. It is thus important that steps be taken for the conservation of the state forest to ensure the supply of wood for Jagannath’s Rathayatra.

Indeed, in 1996 an American disciple of A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhaktarupa Das, started a 160-acre pilot program called the Jagannath Forest Project to grow trees, especially phasis, to be used in Jagannath’s service. Inspired by the success of that project, the Orissan Chief Minister Naveen Patnaik launched a Rs 6.5 crore project in June, 2000, called "Jagannath Bana Prakalpa" or to create a forest of phasi, asana and dhaura trees to meet the annual requirement of wood for construction of the raths. According to this plan, over the next eight years, a forest would be created on 2800 hectares of land along the Mahanadi River in the Puri, Khurda, Nayagarh, Phulbani, Cuttack and Dhenkanal districts. The Gajapati king of Puri, Divyasingh Deva, was put in charge of the project committee, whose members are the collectors of the six districts and divisional forest officers for the respective areas. Gajapati Maharaja, (the king of Puri) as well as C. Gourhari Misra (the retired head of the forest department) are both active participants.

## Rukmini Haran and Vivaha

In the Puranas, it is said that Krishna stole Rukmini after she had finished worshiping Durga just before she was to be married to Sisupala. This ceremony is observed in the temple of Lord Jagannath on the eleventh day of the bright part of the month of Vaishakh, eight days after the beginning of Chandan Yatra. After the completion of morning worship, the image of Madan Mohan is brought to the Ratna Singhasan where prayers are recited and other rituals performed.

The images of Hari and Rukmini are worshipped together on a beautiful altar situated in the east-side of temple, known as the Vivaha Mandap. The priests perform all the marriage karmas including Homa. On the same day, Krishna and Rukmini’s dice game and the Lord’s water sports (*māyā-jala-keli*) are dramatized in the temple. Madan Mohan is dressed in the Rukmini Haran Vesh, “the Krishna who kidnapped Rukmini.”

The *Nīlādri-mahodayam* also includes the descriptions of the fourth-night ceremony of the marriage of the deities. The rituals for the fourth-night (Chaturthi) are performed on the fourteenth day of the bright part of Jyeshtha. The image of Krishna is then taken to the bathing altar (Snana Mandap) where He is placed on the left-side of Lord Jagannath. Lakshmi and Lord Jagannath cast sights of each other. This continues until the Sukla Panchami of Asharh.

## Rukmini-Krishna Bhraman Lila

This function is held a month later, on the Jyeshtha Shukla Dvadasi. On this day the images of Krishna and Rukmini are brought to Lord Jagannath to take permission for going on a tour (*bhramaṇa*) of the town. After receiving the garland, they are taken to Yameshwar wbere fire sacrifices are performed and the deities are worshipped. They are then brought back to the temple and carefully put back in their places.

## Chapter 14 - Snana Yatra, Anavasar and Nava Yauvana

According to the *Nīlādri-mahodaya*, Lord Jagannath was born on the fulI moon-day of the month of Jyeshtha. As it is customary to give a king a ceremonial abhishek on his birthday, King Indradyumna invited all the demigods headed by Lord Brahma to perform this ceremonial bath for Lord Jagannath, Lady Subhadra, Lord Balabhadra and Sudarshan. This is the only time that the Deities are truly bathed. The rest of the year, water is poured on Their reflection in the silver mirrors.

Indradyumna built the original Snana Vedi, a permanent platform for the bathing ceremony located in the north-eastern corner of the outer compound wall. So that all the gods could watch in comfort, the King also put up a raised platform and had it covered with jewel-studded cloth against the sunshine. In the course of time, the original Snana Vedi disintegrated and Ananga Bhima Deva had another one built with the new temple in the 12th century.

In preparation for the bathing ceremony, the Snana Vedi is decorated with pictures of jewel-trees, flowers, flags and colorful archways. It is washed and purified by sprinkling water scented with sandalwood. The *Nīlādri-mahodaya* mentions other decorations that should be part of the scene: white and black parasols, chamara whisks, and parasols. The air is filled with a festive fragrance of incense and perfume to welcome the Deities.

Before being taken out of the temple, Jagannath, Balaram and Subhadra are offered Holi (red powder) and completely covered in a red silken cloth. They are then taken in a procession by the Pahandi Vijaya method, whereby they are carried, step by step, from one cotton cushion to the next.\[82\] The same method is used to take the Lords from the temple to the chariots for Rathayatra.

The *Nīlādri-mahodaya* gives the following description of the sounds that should accompany the Lord’s Pahandi Vijaya:

*kāhāḍa-yantra-vīṇādi sphurad-ghaṇṭāvalī-dhvanau*  
*mṛdaṅga-kāṁsya-tālānāṁ śaṅkhānāṁ ca mahat-svanam*  
*cālayed api yatnena cāru-cāmara-cālanam*  
*candra-maṇḍala-saṅkāśaṁ chatraṁ ca śyāmalaṁ tathā*  
*sūrya-candrānvitaṁ trāsaṁ meghāḍambaram uttamam*  
*etat sarvaṁ puro viṣṇor dhārayen nṛpa-sattamaḥ*  
*bhaktānāṁ jaya-śabdaiś karatālottama-svanaiḥ*  
*gītair nṛtyaiś ca vādyaiś ca viprāṇāṁ stuti-niḥsvanaiḥ*

**In the midst of a great tumult of sound made with kettle drums, lutes, bells, mridangas, gongs, conch bugles and the clapping of hands, devotees should carefully fan the Lord with beautiful yak-tail whisks and hold over him a blue-black parasol shaped like the moon as well as the** ***trāsa\[83\]*****, which is like the cloud with the sun and moon. The best of kings should hold all this before the Lord while the devotees continue to clap and cheer, making an auspicious sound. They should sing and dance and play instruments, while the Brahmins chant the Lord’s praises in Sanskrit.**

As the Lord is taken to the Snana Vedi in this way, a tumultous sound is made by musicians and drummers who play on various musical instruments such as conches, gongs, bugles and drums, making a great, joyful sound.A large number of devotees flow toward the Snana Mandap to witness the bathing of the deities, which is performed at dawn, and they glorify the deities with kirtan, cheers, calls of “Haribol!” and *ulu-dhvani.*

While being carried to the Snana Vedi, the Lord is turned face upwards. According to the Puranas, the gods think that He is looking upwards because He intends to join them in the heavens. In joy, they cheer and call His name, proclaiming His eternal victory over the forces of evil.

Once seated on the bathing platform, 108 pitchers of purified water are poured over the three Deities simultaneously to the accompaniment of Vedic hymns and mantras. The water is drawn the previous night from a well situated by the Sitala temple near the northern gate. This well is known as Suna Kua, “the golden well,” and its water is used only once each year, for this particular event.

In the *Utkala-khaṇḍa,* it is said that Lord Jagannath once ordered Indradyumna, “Near the ocean shores is the undying banyan tree – the Akshaya Bata. A little to the north of this tree is a well, in which the water of all the holy places has been reunited. In time, this well has filled with sand and become covered with grass. I originally appeared in this world in order to take bath in the water of this well, so it is very important that you find it and clean it for Me.

“Then on Chaturdasi, make the appropriate offerings to the protector-gods of this holy land and, in the midst of music, purify this well. Brahmins should then draw its water in golden pitchers so that Lord Brahma can bathe Subhadra, Balaram and Myself early in the morning on the full-moon day.” (*Skanda-purāṇa, Utkala-khaṇḍa*, chapter 29)

The sevaka who performs the ritual purifying the well and drawing its water is known as the Suna (Suvarna) Goswami. As the water is drawn, he chants the *pāvamānī* mantra. The 108 pitchers, made of gold, copper and brass, once filled with water, are kept overnight in the Adhivasa Griha.\[84\]

The sevakas who carry the waterpots from the Adhivasa Griha to the Snana Vedi tie a piece of cloth around their mouths and another over their heads. They are not allowed to talk while the pots are carried in case any spit or sweat should fall into them. Even so, the pots are purified a second time when they arrive at the Snana Vedi. The *Nīlādri-mahodaya* specifies that three jugs of the water must be mixed with sandalwood in proportions of 3:5.

The Snana itself is a veritable drenching, with some of the temple servants climbing the wall behind the Snana Vedi to throw water on the Deities from above, while others splash Them from below.

As the Deities are being bathed, some devotees sing the following kirtan:

*nāce re gaurāṅga-hari bhakt-gaṇa sātha*  
*sināna maṇḍape heri śrīla-jagannātha*  
*pūravera bhāve nāce śrī-śacīnandana*  
*jagannātha dekhe jena vrajendra-nandana*  
*vṛndāvana mājhe jena devī paurṇamāsī*  
*abhiṣeka karichen parama haraṣī*  
*svarūpere bale gorā hāsiyā hāsiyā*  
*hera go lalitā tomāra parāṇa baṅdhuā*  
*bhāvera taraṅge gorā adhīra haila*  
*mātiyā rādhāra bhāve nācite lāgila*  
*keha nāce eha gāya vibhora haiyā*  
*bhūme gaṛi jāya keha premāviṣṭa haiyā*

**See Gauranga dance in the company of His devotees, looking at Lord Jagannath on the Snana Mandap. As He dances, the Son of Sachi remembers His previous life and sees Jagannath as the Son of Nanda in Vrindavan, where Paurnamasi is joyfully giving Him the coronation bath.**

Gauranga turns to Svarupa Damodar, laughs and says, “Just look at your boyfriend, Lalita.” Then, overcome by waves of emotion and absorbed in Radharani’s feelings of love, He dances wildly. In this atmosphere of love, some of the devotees sing, some of them dance, and some fall to the ground in the throes of ecstasy.\[85\]

The water pours down the face of Lord Jagannath who becomes discolored as the paint runs. The water turns black, but the pujaris collect it to distribute as Paduka (*pādodaka –* “water that has touched the feet”). Devotees rush forward to eagerly drink even a little drop of the holy water. Once the bathing is complete, the devotees are granted permission to climb onto the Vedi to touch the Deities, and in an instant crowds of men and women swarm toward the Lord to achieve the ultimate purpose of their sense of touch.

Since the Snana Vedi is raised, the entire celebration is visible from the Grand Road. It generally draws a crowd of thousands of devotees, who take seats in the surrounding buildings where they can get a bird’s eye view of the ceremony.

## The Hathi Vesh or Ganesh Vesh

After the bathing platform has been cleared of people, either the King himself or the Mudiratha, his representative, sweep it with the golden-handled broom, or Chera Pahanra. Other sevakas sprinkle the platform with sandalwood powder. Then the Singhari sevakas carry in huge elephant-head masks that will completely cover the disfigured faces of Lords Balaram and Jagannath.

This is called the Hathi Vesh. The word *hāthi* or *hasti* means elephant, but in this case, it refers Lord Ganesh, the elephant-headed son of Lord Siva and Parvati. It is sometimes said that Lord Jagannath is the only deity who represents all the Hindu gods and goddesses in a single form. The Puranas say that these number thirty-three crores (330,000,000), though generally only five, including Ganesh, are considered to be most important.

An Orissan book, *Dārḍhyatā-bhakti*, tells the story of how this tradition began. Once there was a Brahmin named Ganapati Bhatta from the village of Kaniari in Karnatak who was devoted to Lord Ganesh. He once happened to be in Jagannath Puri on pilgrimage during the Snana Purnima. When taking darshan of the Lord, however, he was disappointed that he could not see Ganesh in Lord Jagannath. He thought, “Since I cannot see Ganesh in this deity, the Supreme Brahman is evidently not present in Him.”

For the followers of the Ganapatya cult, Lord Jagannath is Ganapati himself. Lord Jagannath was impressed by the sincere devotion of the Brahmin and so promised to appear as Ganesh every year after bathing on Snana Purnima “for as long as the sun and the moon rise in the sky.”

Another explanation given by some is that since Jagannath’s year begins with this festival, Lord Ganesh is being invoked for an auspicious beginning as is customary. Yet other devotees of Jagannath explain that Krishna sometimes dresses as an elephant to make the gopis laugh.

While both Balaram and Jagannath are dressed as Ganesh, Subhadra is dressed in the Padma Vesh, or “lotus garb,” in flowers that are shaped like a lotus around her face.

The costs for the Hathi Vesh were formerly borne in their entirety by the abbot of the Gopal Tirtha Math, but that monastery fell into poverty in the first half of the 20th century and so the king was obliged to turn the service over to the Raghava Das Math. Later when the Gopal Tirtha Math was back on more secure footing, its abbot asked the king to have the service restored to it, but the Raghava Das Math would not agree to give it up. Finally, the king arranged that the two maths should split the service with Raghava Das’s math providing the elephant dress for Jagannath, while Gopal Tirtha takes Baladeva’s elephant dress.

After They have been dressed, the Deities are given worship with the sixteen articles, including bhoga. This is the only occasion during the year when Lord Jagannath is given bhoga in public view. Though a thread is symbolically drawn in front of the Deities to symbolize the curtain that gives the Lord privacy while eating, on this day everyone can see the Suars as they carry the pots of food into the Snana Mandap area.

A Devadasi also used to dance for the Lord during this meal, at the bottom of the steps to the Snana Mandap and invisible to people outside the wall, but like all other services performed by the Devadasis, this tradition has died out.

According to *Nīlādri-mahodayam,* whoever sees Lord Jagannath during the Snana Yatra gets more merit than from performing the Ashvamedha Yajna. Not only will such a person achieve success in all endeavors, but will also go to Vaikuntha after death.

## Anavasar

*tataḥ pañca-daśāhāni snāpayitvā tu māṁ nṛpa*  
*acitraṁ vā virūpaṁ vā na paśyeta kadācana*

**“After I have been bathed, O King, no one is to look at Me for fifteen days. No one should ever see Me when My paint is runny and I am not pleasing to behold.” (*****Utkala-khaṇḍa*****, 29.29)**

It is said that as a part of Their human-like pastimes, the Deities catch cold or fever during Their bath and need to convalesce away from the public eye for a while. This period is called *anavasara* (meaning “quarantine”), which in the popular language has been contracted to *anasar*. Thus, the Snana Purnima day ends with a procession to the Anasar Pindi where Jagannath, Subhadra and Balaram will remain for a fortnight. The Anasar Pindi is in the Khatsej Griha, Nirodhan Griha, or Anavasar Griha.\[86\] While in quarantine, the Deities are treated with a specific medicine prescribed by the royal physician or Raja Vaidya, but administered by the Dayitas.

A portrait of the Deities is place on the wall of this chamber and all puja is done to this portrait. Inside, however, other than the Pati Mahapatra, no Brahmins are allowed and the Dayitapati sevakas perform special rituals for the Deities called Anasara Nitis. This is also called *gupta-pūjā* because the deities are served in private. The Dayitas only offer the Deities sweets, curds, fruit and water.

The Pati Mahapatra belongs to that class of Suars said to be descended from the Brahmin Vidyapati through Lalita, the daughter of Vishwavasu. Thus, though Brahmins, they are usually not allowed to make offerings to Lord Jagannath in the temple. Nevertheless, the Dayitapatis ask the Pati Mahapatra to serve the Lord during His quarantine.

Even so, the Dayitas serve Jagannath during this time with great informality and even intimacy. They peel the fruits in front of the Deity and even taste them to see if they are sweet before giving them to the Lord. They eat and sleep in the same room with the Lord. Their service is thus also called Shabari Puja because it is supposed to be done in the informal way that the original worshipers of Nila Madhava did.

During this time, any sort of pomp and ceremony, including singing, dancing, drumming and chanting the Puranas, is banned. All cooking in the main kitchen is stopped. Above all, the observance of silence is the main duty during the period of Anavasara. Even the making of auspicious sounds is forbidden. As prescribed by the different Sastras, there are fifteen rules to follow. These rules include the prohibition of talking with each other, singing, drumming, dancing, expressing words out of anger, producing sound, beating wood or stone, sexual contact, using cosmetics, using tilak dots, using garlands, reciting *Puruṣottama-māhātmya*, using a bell during worship and drawing picture of the deities. On he other hand, chanting the Nrisingha mantra is a specialty of the puja during this period.

## Alalanath

Krishna Das Kaviraj mentions that Lord Chaitanya used to go to Alalanath for the two week period of the anavasar.

*anavasare jagannāthera nā pāñā daraśana*  
*virahe ālālanātha karilā gamana*

**During the anavasar period, when Mahaprabhu could not go to see Jagannath in the temple, the Lord went to Alalanath to calm His feelings of separation. (CC** [**2.1.122**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/1.122)**)**

*gopī-bhāve virahe prabhu vyākula hañā*  
*ālālanāthe gelā prabhu sabāre chāṛiyā*

**In the mood of the gopis, the Lord felt greatly afflicted by separation from Lord Jagannath. Desiring to be alone, He left all His companions and went to stay in Alalanath. (CC** [**2.11.63**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/11.63)**)**

Very few people visit the Jagannath temple during the anavasar period, and it gives the impression of being very quiet and deserted. In fact there are scriptural injunctions forbidding going to the temple during this time and advising devotees to go to Alalanath.

*na paśyed gupta-pūjāyāṁ dāru brahma sanātanam*  
*tadā bhavet tu sampūjā sara-tīre yathā sukham*  
*śaṅkha-cakra-gadā-pāṇe āllabandara-saṁjñakam*  
*pītāmbara-dharaṁ devaṁ nārāyaṇaṁ vilokayet*

**Do not look on the eternal form of the Daru Brahma during the time of the secret worship of the Dayitas. Go rather to the seashore, when the Lord is absent, and worship the Lord Narayan there as you please. Look upon the Lord Narayan, known as Allabandara, who is dressed in a golden robe and holds the conch, discus and mace in His hands. (*****Utkala-khaṇḍa*****)**

Alalanath or Alabandarnath is the name of an ancient deity and temple in Brahmagiri, about twenty kilometers southwest of Puri, where Brahma is said to have worshiped the Lord in the Satya Yuga. Alabandar is a name of Yamunacharya, the spiritual master of Ramanuja. It is said that Alabandar once visited Puri in the month of to have darshan of Lord Jagannath in the month of Asharh, but because it was the Anavasara, he was unable to fulfill his desire. He was so disappointed that he decided to drown himself in the sea. Knowing tbe feelings of His devotee, the Lord appeared before him in this form to accept his service. This image of Lord Narayan thus became famous as the lord of Alabandar, or Alabandarnath, which in popular parlance became Alalanath or Alarnath.

Sundarananda holds that the word Alalanath derives from the word Alvar, the common name given to the twelve great Tamil bhakta saints, the ancient founders of the bhakti movement in South India. He suggests that the worship of this deity began with the Alvars who visited the area long before Yamunacharya’s time. Other people suggest that this deity was really worshiped by Ramanujacharya, who is only one of these saintly devotees of Lord Narayan known to have visited Jagannath Puri.

## Khadalagi Ekadasi

During the anavasar period, the Dayitas repair and repaint the Deities. The Deities in the Jagannath temple are not made of wood alone. In fact, the wood form is covered and wrapped with seven layers of other materials such as resin, sandalwood, cloth and paint. Some of these layers are opened and renewed, and then, beginning on the Ekadasi day, repainted. There is a ceremony in which the Dayitas bring prasad for the king and his family, and in which they are empowered to do this task. The first layer of paint or undercoat is called Khadi (*khāḍī*), a paste of chalk and gum, and kept in a silver pot. It is also offered to the king before the work is begun. The Datta Mukha Singhari performs this service, painting the entire body of the Deity with the exception of the pupils of the eyes.

## Nava Yauvana Vesh and Netrotsava

On the dawn of the fifteenth day, which is the new moon day (Amavasya), the Lord’s period of illness comes to an end. The gate to the dancing hall is opened and pilgrims flock to the temple to view the Deities’ Nava Yauvana, or “new youth.” This is done while the Deities are still reclining on the floor in front of the inner sanctum and before the pupils of Their eyes have been painted in.

After this preliminary Nava Yauvana darshan, the major purification ritual of Maha Snana is performed. Then it is time for the Netrotsava, “the festival of the eyes,” when three Puja Pandas come in to finish painting the Deities’ pupils. This “opening of the Deities’ eyes” is traditionally the time when They become alive. The Mudiratha, who represents the king, comes and performs the welcoming ritual (*bandāpanā*).

This is the signal to resume the Deities’ regular schedule worship. The kitchen sacrifice is performed and cooking for the offerings starts. Everything goes on in exactly the same fashion as usual, except that Lord Jagannath remains in the reclining position in the Anavasar Griha – i.e., between the inner sanctum and the Mukha Shala.

Again devotees throng into the temple for darshan. When devotees come to see the Lord, they sometimes sing verses like the following:

*bahu-dina pare āja dekhiyā śrī-mukha*  
*khaṇḍila hṛdaya vyathā parāṇera duḥkha*  
*dekha nā cāhiyā kibā rūpera mādhurī*  
*cāṅda mukha dekhe sabe āpanā pāsari*

**“After so many days, I am finally able to behold Your beautiful face. The suffering I have undergone, the pain in my heart, is gone. Just look at the divine beauty of the Lord’s moon-like face. Behold it and forget all the problems of life.”**

Krishna Das Kaviraj Goswami describes Mahaprabhu’s coming to the temple for the Netrotsava in the Chaitanya Charitamrita, Madhya [12 (205-221)](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/12.205):

The next day the great festival named the Netrotsava took place, the life and soul of the devotees. For a fortnight, everyone had been unhappy due to not seeing Lord Jagannath. Now that they could see Him, they all felt very happy. Mahaprabhu joyfully took the devotees with Him to see the Lord in the temple.

Kashishwar walked in front of Him, keeping the crowds of people back, while Govinda followed, carrying the Lord’s water pitcher. Paramananda Puri and Brahmananda Bharati also preceded the Lord, while Svarupa Damodar and Advaita Acharya walked on either side. The Lord’s other devotees followed them into the temple, anxious to have darshan of Lord Jagannath. So eager were they to see the Lord that they walked into the Bhoga Mandap to look at His face.

The Lord’s eyes were like bees that flew to Jagannath lotus-like face to drink its nectar. Lord Jagannath’s eyes were more beautiful than blossoming lotus flowers, and His cheeks as lustrous as a sapphire mirror. The Lord’s bright red lips conquered the beauty of the bandhuli flower and His delicate smile sent out waves of nectar.

The effulgence of the Lord’s beautiful face increased from moment to moment, and hundreds of thousands of devotees drank its honey like bumblebees. Even so, the more they drank, the more their thirst increased. Try as they might, could not turn their eyes away from Him.

Thus Mahaprabhu and His devotees continued looking upon the face of Jagannath until midday, all the symptoms of ecstasy appeared on the Lord’s body -- He perspired and trembled, and a constant flow of tears fell from His eyes. Even so, Mahaprabhu checked His tears so that His gazing on the Lord’s face would

not be interrupted. From time to time, food was offered to Lord Jagannath, interrupting Mahaprabhu’s enjoyment of His darshan. While food was offered, Mahaprabhu started chanting the Holy Names with the other devotees. The Lord forget everything in looking on Lord Jagannath, until finally devotees came and took him away for His noonday meal.\[87\]

## Chapter 15 - Cleaning the Gundicha Temple

The Gundicha temple lies about three kilometers northeast of the Jagannath temple, not far from the Indradyumna Sarovar. It is surrounded by a massive wall, about twenty feet high, and castellated at the top, like the fortresses of Northern India. This wall is 432 x 321 feet and more than five feet thick. Like the main temple, there are four buildings in the temple complex, the Biman, Jagamohan, Nat Mandir and Bhoga Mandap. The Biman is 75' in height, built on a raised platform four feet high.

There are two entrances into the Gundicha temple complex, the Singha Dwar (on the west side) and Vijaya Dwar (north side). The principal gateway is a handsome structure with a fine pointed roof adorned with lions that faces towards the main temple. W. W. Hunter described the temple’s appearance nearly a century and a half ago: “Inside one catches glimpses of long straight walks and groves of bright evergreen trees, with the ancient shrine at the end of the vista. A glory of tropical foliage, vocal with birds, overtops the lofty wall with every shade of green, from the slender-stemmed, feathery elegance of the coronetted palm, to the solid masses of the mango, and the hoary majesty of the banyan tree.”\[88\]

In the *Utkala-khaṇḍa* of the *Skanda-purāṇa*, it is said that the images of the three deities, Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra, were first made at the Mahavedi (“great altar”) or Yajna Mandap (“sacrificial altar”) after King Indradyumna performed a thousand horse sacrifices. This, then, is the birthplace of the Jagannath Trinity and so is also called, Janma Sthana, Janaka Puri and Gundicha Mandap.

According to the *Puruṣottama-māhātmyam*, King lndradyumna installed a Nrisingha deity before performing the thousand sacrifices. There is a temple of Nrisingha next to the Gundicha compound, so sometimes it is refered to as Nrisingha Kshetra.

The most popular name of the temple, however, is Gundicha Mandir or Gundicha Bari (“Gundicha’s house”). According to legend, it was named after King Indradyumna's principal queen who played the role of foster mother to Lord Jagannath, Indradyumna His father.

This is Lord Jagannath’s country house, and on the Rathayatra day, Lord Jagannath, Balaram and Subhadra ride their respective cars from His main temple to the Gundicha Bari. Just as the main temple is referred to as Nilachala, the Gundicha temple is also sometimes called Sundarachala. For devotees who follow the mood of Lord Chaitanya, the Gundicha temple symbolizes the land of Vrindavan.

After Krishna left Vrindavan for Dvaraka, He became so involved with city life that He apparently forgot the country folk who had so loved Him throughout His childhood. Many years later, He met them again at Kurukshetra. When Radha and the other residents of Vraja saw Krishna in the opulence that characterized His life in the Yadu royal family, they felt a strong desire to take Him back with them to His childhood home. Absorbed in the mood of Srimati Radharani, Mahaprabhu saw Nilachala – Lord Jagannath’s main temple – as the manifestation of Dwaraka, and when pulling the Lord’s chariot to Sundarachala (Gundicha), He believed He was taking Him back to Vrindavan, where He truly belonged.

However, before Lord Jagannath can be brought to the Gundicha temple, it must be cleansed – from the Jagamohan to the temple floor and the altar. In keeping with His mission to teach the world the path of devotion, Lord Chaitanya Himself would take His companions to Gundicha and clean it with them.

*śrī-guṇḍicā-mandiram ātma-vṛndaiḥ*  
*saṁmārjayan kṣālanataḥ sa gauraḥ \|*  
*sva-citta-vac chītalam ujjvalaṁ ca*  
*kṛṣṇopaveśaupayikaṁ cakāra \|\|*

**The golden Lord swept and washed the Gundicha temple with His personal companions, making it as fresh and bright as His own heart and a fitting place for Lord Krishna to sit. (CC** [**2.12.1**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/12.1)**)**

In the Chaitanya Charitamrita, it is said that as the Rathayatra festival approached, Mahaprabhu called for Kashi Mishra, the temple manager Tulasi Paricha and Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya, to ask them for permission to clean the Gundicha temple.

Upon hearing the Lord's request, the temple manager said, “My Lord, we are all Your servants. It is our duty to immediately fulfill Your every desire, for the King has ordered us to do so. Even so, my Lord, it is beneath You to engage in this kind of work. If You still wish to do it, however, we will accept it as another of Your inscrutable pastimes. You will need many waterpots and brooms to clean the temple, so if You order me to do so, I shall immediately arrange to have them brought to You.”

As soon as the Lord confirmed that this was indeed His desire, the Paricha arranged for the delivery of a hundred brooms for sweeping the temple and a hundred new waterpots for carrying water to wash it.

Early the next morning, the Lord gathered His personal associates and smeared sandalwood pulp on their bodies with His own hand as a way of preparing them for this holy service. After personally giving each of them a broom, they started off to the Gundicha temple. When they arrived, they immediately got down to work. They first swept the inner temple completely, including the walls and ceiling. They then removed the Deities’ throne from its platform, washed both platform and throne, and then replaced it. The Lord and His companions cleansed and swept all the buildings in the Gundicha compound, big and small, finishing with the Jagamohan.

*cāri-dike śata bhakta sammārjanī-kare*  
*āpani śodhena prabhu śikhāña sabāre*  
*premollāse śodhena layena kṛṣṇa-nāma*  
*bhakta-gaṇa kṛṣṇa kahe kare nija-kāma*

**All around Him were a hundred devotees with brooms in their hands. Mahaprabhu both swept Himself and telling the others what to do. As He lovingly cleaned the temple, the Lord joyfully sang Krishna’s holy names. Similarly, all the devotees also chanted as they carried out their own duties. (CC** [**2.12.84-5**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/12.84)**)**

Covered with dust and dirt, the Lord’s body became transcendentally beautiful. At times, He shed tears of love and even used these tears to clean the temple. They cleansed the Bhoga Mandira, where the Deity's food offerings are placed, then the yard and all the residential quarters.

After sweeping, the Lord used His own cloth to carry the straw, dust and grains of sand that had been piled up and threw them outside. All the devotees joyfully followed His example.

*prabhu kahe ke kata kariyācha sammārjana*  
*tṛṇa dhūli dekhilei jāniba pariśrama*

**The Lord told them, “We will be able to tell who has worked hardest at cleaning the temple by comparing everyone’s piles of dust and dirt.”**

Naturally, the Lord’s pile was the biggest!

The Lord’s intent here was to teach all of us that if anyone wants to invite Lord Sri Krishna to sit on the throne of his heart, he has to make sure that it is pure and suitable for devotional service. If the heart is full of weeds, dust and pebbles, then it is no place for the Lord. The things that contaminate the heart are desires for anything but pure devotional service – fruitive ritual, impersonal philosophy, and other kinds of yogic practice that lead one away from bhakti. This is explained in the fundamental definition of pure devotion given by Srila Rupa Goswami:

*anyābhilāṣitā śūnyaṁ*  
*jñāna karmādy anāvṛtam*  
*ānukūlyena kṛṣṇānu*  
*śīlanaṁ bhaktir uttamā*

**The highest category of devotion or bhakti is defined as the culture of a favorable attitude to Krishna, devoid of all material desires and without any adulteration by monistic philosophy or fruitive action. (BRS** [**1.1.11**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/rupa-brs1/1.1.11)**)**

“Other desires” (*anyābhilāṣa*) are like thorns that wound the delicate makeup of exclusive devotion. The wind of our material entanglements carries the dust of such fruitive desire into our hearts, making it impossible to see our true selves. Our entanglement in material life is such that cleaning our hearts is not easy. We are like the proverbial elephant that immediately rolls in the dirt after it has bathed. However we try to purify ourselves, selfish desires always seem to have a way of insinuating themselves into our hearts almost immediately afterwards. The only agent for cleaning the heart is loving devotion for the Lord. When the heart has been thus cleansed with love, the Lord eagerly takes up residence there.

Mahaprabhu taught us to gather up the dirt of other desires, the pebbles of dry, speculative philosophical thinking, and other litter and throw them all outside the confines of the temple of our hearts. Still, unless they are removed even further, a strong gust of wind may carry them all back inside. Not only that, but though we may be able to remove the visible dirt and litter when cleaning, we cannot always remove the fine dust that clings to the cracks. The fine dust that pollutes our hearts consists of things like the desire for prestige or an attachment to self-centred religious activities like going on pilgrimage or living the life of a hermit. When such activities take precedence over the demands of pure devotional service, they are just another contaminant – even though they may still be officially in the sattvic mode.

The heart becomes a fit place for the Lord to take His seat only when all desire for sense enjoyment, personal liberation or mystic powers is eliminated from it, when it has been cleansed of any desire for the satisfaction of one’s own senses and is completely dedicated exclusively to the satisfaction of His senses. When the heart of the devotee becomes like this, then it becomes an attractive place of repose for the Lord, a garden of delight for his pleasure. The gopis’ hearts are completely dedicated exclusively to the satisfaction of his senses and so they place Krishna there in the chariot of their hearts and take him off to Vrindavan. This is stated in the Chaitanya Charitamrita ([2.21.107](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/21.107)): *caṛi gopīra manorathe manmathera mana mathe* – “Krishna rides the chariot of the gopis’ minds and churns the mind of the mind-churner, Cupid.”

Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu had the entire temple cleansed of the dirt that had accumulated during the year and then washed it again. Even after cleaning the temple twice, He personally inspected its every corner, and if He saw a mark or a stain, He rubbed it with His own cloth until it was gone. The temple was thus a bright as a mirror or a jewel. In this way the Lord showed just how hard we must work to rid our hearts of even the slightest contamination in order to become worthy of pure devotional service. A pure devotee’s heart is like Vrindavan, where the majestic Lord of the Universe puts aside all His supremacy to rejoice in the intimacy of love.

As the devotees were cleaning, the Lord, the world teacher, would come to them and take them by the hand to show them exactly how He wanted the work done. He profusely praised those who were doing a good job, and lovingly chastised those whose work was not done in a spirit of total absorption in desire for the happiness of the Beloved. Such a show of compassionate affection won the hearts of the devotees, who become increasingly enthused to do an even better job for His sake. The merciful Lord thus showed that those who are most successful at cleaning their own hearts and who then show others how it can be done are the most dear to Him.

Finally, Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, also showed by this pastime that the best means to clean the heart is to loudly chant His holy names. His Holiness Bhakti Dayita Madhava Maharaj explained the cleaning of the Gundicha temple according to the first verse of the *Śikṣāṣṭaka*, *ceto-darpaṇa-mārjanam*:“One cannot rid gold of its inner impurities without placing it repeatedly in the fire, nor can the gold of the consciousness be purified without internalizing the spiritual fire of Krishna’s name and form. The Holy Name is eternal, pure, complete in itself and outside the clutches of the material energy. The Holy Name is in no way distinct from Krishna Himself and thus all of the Lord’s energies are present in the Name. The Lord is so merciful that He makes Himself available in His name, but the Holy Name itself is even more merciful than the Lord. For this reason, one can chant the Holy Name in any circumstances, whether clean or unclean, without consideration of time or place. This has made the Holy Name easily available to every living being.”\[89\]

The scripture says that even the indirect light of the sun-like Holy Name can erase the darkness of the worst kinds of sins: *hanta yan-nāma-bhānor ābhāso’pi kṣapayati mahā-pātaka-dhvānta-rāśim* (BRS [2.1.103](https://vedarama.com/en/books/rupa-brs1/2.1.103)). Bhaktivinoda Thakur said, “Just worship the Holy Name, meditate on the Holy Name and make the Holy Name the central thing in your life: *nāma bhaja nāma cinta nāma kara sāra*.”

The process of cleaning the Gundicha temple is thus done chiefly by chanting the Maha Mantra loudly. In the *ceto-darpaṇa-mārjanam* verse, Lord Chaitanya says that the Holy Name cleans the mirror of the mind, or the Gundicha temple of the heart. Therefore, everyone, man or woman, should engage in cleaning the Gundicha temple.

This custom of cleaning the Gundicha temple in the way Mahaprabhu had instituted it had unfortunately been practically discontinued until Charan Das Babaji incited all the Maths in Puri to join together to revive the tradition in the mid-1890’s. The Jhanj Pitha and Radha Kanta Maths continue to lead this festival up to the present day, cleaning the Gundicha temple to the accompaniment of appropriate kirtans based on the descriptions found in Chaitanya Charitamrita. The cleaning of Gundicha is traditionally followed by water sports in the Indradyumna Sarovar.

## Chapter 16 - Rathayatra

The most important festival held every year in Sri Kshetra is the Rathayatra. It has many other names, such as Nava Yatra, Gundicha Yatra, Nandighosh Yatra, Patita Pavan Yatra and Mahavedi Utsava. In the *Utkala-khaṇḍa*, Lord Jagannath tells Indradyumna,

**“On the Asharh Shukla Dvitiya, place Subhadra Devi, Balaram and Me on chariots and celebrate the Nava Yatra. Take Me to Gundicha, the house where I was born, and where you performed a thousand Ashwamedha sacrifices.” (*****Utkala-khaṇḍa*****, 29.32-34)**

The Rathayatrafestival is held every year on the second day of the waxing moon of the month of Asharh.

*āṣāḍhasya dvitīyāyāṁ rathaṁ kuryād viśeṣataḥ*  
*āṣāḍha-śuklaikādaśyāṁ japa-homa-mahotsavam*  
*ratha-sthitaṁ vrajantaṁ taṁ mahā-vedī-mahotsave*  
*ye paśyanti mudā bhaktyā vāsas teṣāṁ hareḥ pade*  
*satyaṁ satyaṁ punaḥ satyaṁ pratijñātaṁ dvijottamāḥ*  
*nātaḥ śreyaḥ-prado viṣṇor utsavaḥ śāstra-saṁmataḥ*
