**On the second day and eleventh days of the waxing moon in the month of Asharh, a great chariot festival should be held, with fire sacrifices and chanting of mantras. Anyone who sees Lord Jagannath travelling on His chariot during this festival and feels joy and devotion will surely attain the Lord’s abode. Truly, truly, I promise you, O best of the Brahmins, nowhere in the scriptures will you find a festival more beneficial than this one.\[90\]**

One legend says that Queen Gundicha requested the king to organize this festival in order to enable the sinners and the untouchables, who are ordinarily deprived of the opportunity to enter the temple, to have darshan of Lord Jagannath for their salvation. As a result, the festival also took her name.

The role that Lord Jagannath plays in the life of the state is made very clear by the many dignitaries who are present every year, usually including the Chief Minister of Orissa, members of his cabinet, several central government ministers, high court judges and other highly-place civil servants such as the Inspector-General of Police.

During the Rathayatra period, the Emergency Act is implemented and, according to its conditions, all departments of the Orissan government are assigned specific responsibilities related to the festival.

## Consecration of the chariots

On the day the Gundicha temple is cleansed, the three raths are still standing where they were constructed, on the Grand Road in front of the Gajapati king’s palace, Sri Raj Nahar. After Lord Jagannath, Balaram and Subhadra have been given their morning meal, their prasadi flower garlands are taken from the temple to the chariots, accompanied by the clamoring of conches, bells and trumpets. After the chariots have been garlanded, they are pulled one by one to the temple’s main entrance. The first to be placed there is Balaram’s chariot, Taladhvaja, then Subhadra’s Darpadalana, and finally Jagannath’s Nandighosh.

After the evening offerings and arati, or Sandhya Dhupa, three water jugs, which in olden days used to be made of gold but now are made of the eight-metal alloy known as *aṣṭa-dhātu*\[91\], are brought out through the Singha Dwar. They are used to crown the three chariots, after which flagpoles and flags made of prasadi cloth are assembled above them.

When the water jugs (kalasa) and flags have been assembled atop the raths, the Deities are dressed in their best clothes (Boro Sringar) and garlanded. After the bedtime arati, they are dressed again in special clothes for the next day when they will be placed on the rath in the Pahandi Vijaya ceremony. These clothes are known as the *senā-paṭā-lāgi* (“military dress”) and *śukla-sajja* (“white costume”).

Once the finishing touches on the chariots’ decoration have been made, the ritual inauguration (*ratha-pratiṣṭhā*) ceremony is held according to the traditions described in the *Mādala-pañjī.* This sequence of rituals is summarized in the following verse of *Nīlādri-mahodaya:*

*vandāpanāṁ tataḥ kuryād*  
*ājñā-mālyaṁ rathān prati*  
*dattvā rathān samānīya*  
*tat-pratiṣṭhāṁ samācaret*

**After welcoming the chariots, the Deities’** ***ājñā-mālā*** **must be placed on them. After so doing, the ritual consecration of the chariots must be performed.**

These Vedic rituals take place on the pavilion above the main entrance, called the Chahani Mandap. They consists of painting a beautiful mandala in the shape of a lotus flower with thirty-six petals. First, the god Varuna is worshipped. This is then followed by the Sankalpa Vidhi, or pronunciation of mantras indicating the firm intention to perform the Rathayatra festival. Next, the priests are customarily appointed in the *ācārya-brāhmaṇa-varaṇa*. A sacred water-pot is placed on the mandala, a piece of new cloth placed around its neck and mango-leaves and a coconut in its mouth. This water pot is consecrated and the god Narasingha worshipped there.This is followed by a fire sacrifice into which oblations of ghee are given, accompanied by one thousand and eight repetitions of the appropriate mantras. This goes on without much care being paid to it by the pilgrims, whose attention is fixed on the cars themselves.

## Rathayatra Day

Ideally, on Rathayatra day, mangal arati is held as usual at 4:30 AM. At 4:35, mailam takes place: the deities are undressed and changed into bathing clothes. The bathing ritual continued until 5:00 while the daily fire sacrifice is held in the kitchen area. At 5:30, the deities are dressed. Surya Puja, worship of the Sun-god, is held at 5:45, and at 6:00 the gatekeepers Jaya and Vijaya are worshiped.

In the meantime, the Pandas prepare the raths for the Lords’ arrival with ritual acts of purification like sprinkling *pañca-gavya* over them. After this has been done, the police form a cordon around them to prevent all those not involved in the Lord’s service to approach them.

The deities are served with their morning meal at 7:30, the Gajapati sends a golden plate containing a number of ingredients (coconut, betel nut, flowers, aguru, camphor, durva grass, unhusked rice) to their Lordships Jagannath, Balaram and Subhadra, inviting Them to mount the chariot.

Previously, the pahandi system was used, as will be described next. Sometime in the last fifty years, however, this has been discontinued. Nowadays, a big pole is fixed to the backs of Jagannath and Baladeva and used to manhandle them onto the carts. Subhadra and Sudarshan continue to be carried, as they always have.

The priests tie a silken rope (*paṭṭa-ḍori*) around Jagannath and Balaram’s waists. Then, after making flower offerings, they take the Deities down from the altar throne amidst cries of “*Maṇimā, maṇimā*!” Simultaneously, hundreds of other temple servants make a great noise with gongs, drums, and kettle drums. Some of the heads of Puri’s religious institutions or maths and temple priests hold the royal umbrella over Jagannath’s head while others fan with huge fans covered in silverwork (*ālaṭa*), fly whisks and *pānākṛti* or *trāsa.* And, in the midst the clamorous sound of the devotees’ cheering and hand cymbals crashing that filled the sky, Lord Jagannath’s pahandi begins.

With the sounds of the Pahandi Vijaya, the hundreds of thousands of devotees waiting outside the temple gates feel their hearts overflow with excitement. The entire scene is so filled with emotion and joy that it is beyond words.

Krishna Das Kaviraj describes the Pahandi Vijaya as experienced by Lord Chaitanya:

*advaita nitāi ādi saṅge bhakta gaṇa*  
*sukhe mahāprabhu dekhe īśvara gamana*  
*baliṣṭha dayitā-gaṇa jena matta hātī*  
*jagannātha-vijaya karāya kari hātāhāti*  
*kataka dayitā kare skandha ālambana*  
*kataka dayitā dhare śrī padma caraṇa*  
*kaṭi taṭe baddha dṛḍha sthūla paṭṭa ḍorī*  
*dui dike dayitā gaṇa uṭhāya tāhā dhari*  
*ucca dṛḍha tulī saba pāti sthāne sthāne*  
*eka tulī haite tvarāya āra tulīte āne*  
*prabhu padāghāte tulī haya khaṇḍa khaṇḍa*  
*tulā saba uṛi jāya śabda haya pracaṇḍa*  
*viśvambhara jagannāthe ke cālāite pāre*  
*āpana icchāya cale karite vihāre*  
*mahāprabhu maṇimā maṇimā kare dhvani*  
*nānā vādya kolāhale kichui nā śuni*

**Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu and his prominent devotees like Nityananda Prabhu and Advaita Acharya joyfully watched Lord Jagannath as he was being taken to his car.**  
**The powerful Dayitas, as strong as intoxicated elephants, carried Lord Jagannath manually from the throne to the car. Some of the Dayitas held the Lord’s shoulders and others took His lotus feet. Lord Jagannath was bound at the waist by the** ***paṭṭa-ḍorī*****, a strong, thick rope made of silk. A number of Dayitas stood on either side of the Lord and lifted Him with the help of this rope. Thick cotton pillows had been placed along the path from the throne to the car and they lifted Lord Jagannath from one of these to the next. Sometimes the pads broke when struck by the Lord’s heavy foot, making a heavy, cracking sound and sending the cotton contents floating in the air.**  
**Lord Jagannath is the maintainer of the whole universe, so who can make Him move? He only moves if He wishes to do so for the sake of His pastimes. Lord Chaitanya called out the words "*****Maṇimā Maṇimā*****," but could not be heard on account of the tumultuous sounds being made on various musical instruments. (CC** [**2.13.7-14**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/13.7)**)**

*sudarśanaṁ puraskṛtya balabhadraṁ tataḥ param*  
*subhadrā ca tato nītvā jagadīśaṁ sureśvaram*

**The Dayitas first carry Sudarshan, then Balaram and then Subhadra onto their respective chariots. Sudarshan is brought out in a rush as the Dayitas carry him out running and place him on Subhadra’s chariot. Lord Jagannath follows. Before leaving Maha Lakshmi Devi behind on the altar, Lord Jagannath gives her assurances, saying, “I would have been happy to bring you along, but because My big brother is with Me, I cannot. But don’t be sad, I will be coming back very soon.”**

It is said that Jagannath’s ratha Nandighosh does not move without the express wish of Jagannath Himself. Even at the time of Pahandi, it sometimes becomes impossible to lift Jagannath onto the chariot. For instance, in a story carried in many Orissan newspapers after the 1972 Rathayatra, it was reported that Jagannath started to become heavier and heavier as He was being carried to His chariot. It thus became impossible to lift Him onto the rath in the traditional way. This created a commotion amongst the crowds of people present there. Finally the Gajapati, Divyasimha Deva, approached the Lord with folded hands and requested Him, “O Supreme Lord! Excuse me, if it please You, would You come onto the chariot?” Then, magically, the Lord became weightless and it was no longer difficult to lift Him.\[92\]

Finally Lord Jagannath gives assurances to Maha Lakshmi Devi, his queen, saying, “I would have been happy to bring you along, but because my big brother is with me, I cannot. But don’t be sad, I will be coming back very soon.”

After the principal deities have been placed on their respective chariots, the Lord’s *vijaya-vigrahas*, Madan Mohan and Krishna-Balaram, are carried out on palanquins. Krishna and Balaram, two *aṣṭa-dhātu* deities, are placed on Balaram’s rath while Madana Mohan joins Jagannath on His.

With all the deities now established on Their raths, the city’s goldsmith community comes to present the three deities with special ornaments, called *citā*, to be placed on their foreheads. This is also done by the Lenkas and Paiks in the midst of gongs ringing and conch shells blowing. The rule is that every year at the time of the Snana Yatra, these ornaments as well as the Deities’ jeweled armlets and leaf-like earrings are removed and kept under lock and key until the day of the Rathayatra. Jagannath’s tilak jewel is embedded with diamonds, that of Subhadra with emeralds, and that of Balaram with lapis lazuli.

After this, the servants known as Kotha Suansias place two chests containing clothes, ornaments and materials required for the nine-day journey on Jagannath's chariot. Their Lordships are dressed in silken clothes (Patakhandua) and draped with flower garlands. The Brahmins of the Sixteen Shasans come out in a solemn procession carrying three tulasi crowns that are placed on the Deities’ heads. All these ceremonies are supposed to be completed by noon.

## Chera Pahara

Then begins the next important ritual phase of the Rathayatra festival, called Chera Pahara (*cherā paharā*). During this ceremony, the Gajapati king sweeps the cart all around the Deity. First a delegation of highly-placed members of the Orissan Government, representatives of the police department and temple priests go to the Raja Nahar royal palace where they announce to the king that Lord Jagannath has been placed in his rath.

The current king is name Divyasimha Deva. Because of his relation to Lord Jagannath, he is an object of reverence throughout the Hindu world. His full title includes reference to all the territories that were under Gajapati rule at the height of the Orissan empire under Purushottama Deva and Prataparudra Deva, when it included large parts of Bengal, Andhra Pradesh and even Karnataka. He is even considered to be a portion (*aṁśa*) of Lord Vishnu and is sometimes called “the walking Jagannath.”\[93\]

The king mounts a rich palanquin worked in silver and gold and embedded with jewels. He is accompanied by the royal guru, the royal priest and other Vedic Brahmins and his bodyguard corps. They carry parasols, fans, whisks, gongs, and drums, as well as the thirty-six kinds of royal paraphernalia (*raja-pariveśa*). Many thousands of pilgrims crowd around to catch sight of the King.

Then, as the king proceeds from his palace to the Lord’s chariot, the official panegyrists and eulogists recite Sanskrit verses of praise while crowds of people cheer with shouts of “*jaya, jaya.*” When he approaches the cars, the Dayitapatis welcome him and lead him to the chariot of Balabhadra. Other temple servants respectfully wait for him in the chariot with the paraphernalia needed for Chera Pahara. The Muduli stands ready to present him with the golden broom and the silver waterpot. The Mekap holds a golden perfume stick, vermilion paste, a yaktail whisk and camphor; the Gara Badu a water-pot, the Dayanamali white flowers, and the Ghatuari sandal-paste and a silver incense holder.

The king mounts Lord Baladeva’s chariot and pays his full, prostrated obeisances. He offers the Lord a handful of flowers and a camphor flame. Then he sweeps the platform all around the Deity with a gold-handled broom and sprinkles it with sandalwood water and powder. When he has finished sweeping, he once again prostrates himself before Balaram.

This ritual is repeated on Lord Jagannath’s car, and then finally on Lady Subhadra’s. In King Prataparudra’s time, the Gajapati would sweep and sprinkle sandalwood water on the entire path from the altar in the temple right up to the chariots, but now he only performs this service on the chariots themselves.

Mahaprabhu was greatly pleased with the King’s act of humbling himself in front of Lord Jagannath, as seen in Krishna Das Kaviraj’s description of the Chera Pahara:

*tabe pratāparudra kare āpane sevana*  
*suvarṇa mārjanī lañā kare patha sammārjana*  
*candana jalete kare patha niṣecane*  
*tuccha sevā kare basi rāja siṁhāsane*  
*uttama hañā rājā kare tuccha sevana*  
*ataeva jagannāthera kṛpāra bhājana*  
*mahāprabhu sukha pāila se sevā dekhite*  
*mahāprabhura kṛpā haila se sevā haite*

**While the Lord was being carried from the throne to the car, King Prataparudra personally engaged in the Lord's service by cleansing the road with a gold-handled broom. He also sprinkled the road with sandalwood scented water. Though he sat on the royal throne, the king engaged in such menial service for the sake of Lord Jagannath. Although the King was the most exalted person in the kingdom, still he consented to do this menial service for the Lord. He thus became the recipient of Lord Jagannath's blessings. Mahaprabhu became very happy on seeing the King engaged in this service and so the King also received Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s mercy as a result. (CC** [**2.13.15-18**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/13.15)**)**

## The Pulling of the Chariots

After the King has completed the Chera Pahara, the charioteers are placed on the raths. Matali first mounts Lord Baladeva’s rath, followed by Arjuna, who is Subhadra’s charioteer, and then Daruka, who drives Lord Jagannath’s chariot. The staircase (*cār māl*) made from tal trees is taken down and the horses are “hitched” to the chariots. Balaram’s horses are black; their names are Tivra, Ghora, Dirgha and Svarnanabha. Subhadra’s horses, Mochika, Rochika, Jita and Aparajita, are red. Lord Jagannath’s horses are white; their names are Shankha, Balahaka, Shveta and Haridashva.

Then the pulling ropes are attached. The rope that pulls Balaram’s chariot Taladhvaja is the great serpent Vasuki himself. Subhadra’s chariot Darpadalan is pulled by the serpent Svarnachura and Lord Jagannath’s chariot by the Shankhachura serpent. The first person to ceremoniously pull the rope is the king himself.

Finally, at around two o’clock, as hundreds of thousands of devotees, pilgrims, tourists and curiosity seekers look on, in the midst of a joyful noise made with drums, bugles, trumpets, conch shells and gongs and the loud singing of kirtan in numerous groups coming from the different maths of Puri, thousands of devotees lovingly pull the three great chariots slowly on their way to the Gundicha temple--first Balaram, followed by Subhadra and Lord Jagannath.

As the chariots started on their way, two helicopters belonging to the Orissan Government and the Indian Army fly over them and release baskets of flower petals, showering Lords Jagannath, Balaram and Subhadra with flowers like the gods did in the past. As one looks down on the scene, it seems as though three great ships are floating along in an ocean of people. The Boro Danda fills with hundreds of kirtan groups in front of each of the raths singing songs glorifying Lord Jagannath in ways suitable to their own understanding.

Nowadays, most of the pulling is done by pilgrims, and since the road has been improved, it generally takes only a single day for the three great cars to reach the Gundicha house. Until fairly recently, the Boro Danda was a sandy road, often made difficult to manage on account of rains. The wheels would sink deep into the sand and the journey would thus take several days. The pilgrims were often exhausted by the long trip to Jagannath Puri and though they would be able to muster up the energy to pull the chariots for the first few hours, after toiling for some time under the tropical July sun, their zeal inevitably flagged before the garden house was reached. The cars would then be deserted by the devotees and had to be dragged along by professional pullers engaged by the Temple.

The professional cart-pullers, known as Kalaberiyas, were needed to help the Lords reach Their destination. The Kalaberiyas numbered in the thousands – 1400 pulled Jagannath’s cart, 1200 pulled Balaram and another 1200 were assigned to Subhadra. Their numbers were made up of peasants from the neighboring villages who inherited this service from generation to generation, in return for which they were given free room and board in Puri during the festival.

The Kalaberiyas were even more necessary on the return journey. On the one hand, the Gaudiya Vaishnavas find the trip to Gundicha more attractive, in light of their understanding of it as the return of Krishna to Vrindavan. The return Rathayatra festival (Bahura), held nine days later, signifies Krishna’s voyage back to Dwaraka and thus is an occasion for sadness. Furthermore, pilgrims were often eager to return home after the Rathayatra and would not stay for Bahura. Though as many as 100,000 devotees would be present for the Rathayatra, very few would still be around nine days later. One British wit observed nearly two centuries ago that but for the professional car-pullers, Lord Jagannath would “infallibly stick” at His country-house.

## Balgandi

Halfway between the Sri Mandir and Gundicha is a place named Balgandi. Tradition holds that the Deities arrive here at noon, though this rarely happens as they do not usually start their journey until well after noon. The three Lords are fatigued from travelling in the hot sun and stop here for a short while before going on to complete their journey. To cool them down, they are bathed in the customary fashion, by pouring water over their reflections in a mirror, and are offered sandalwood paste and camphor. The priests make a breeze with peacock fans and offer them cooling drinks and seasonal fruit like dates, bananas, coconut, jackfruit and mangoes. Milk sweets are also offered and finally, the Lord is given spiced pan to round out the meal. This offering is called the Balgandi bhoga. A full list of the items offered at Balgandi is given in the Chaitanya Charitamrita:

*balagaṇḍi bhogera prasāda uttama ananta*  
*'ni-sakaḍi' prasāda āila jāra nāhi anta*  
*chānā pānā paiḍa āmra nārikela kāṅṭhāla*  
*nānā-vidha kadalaka āra bīja-tāla*  
*nāraṅga cholaṅga ṭābā kamalā bīja-pūra*  
*bādāma chohārā drākṣā piṇḍa-kharjura*  
*manoharā-lāḍu ādi śateka prakāra*  
*amṛta-guṭikā-ādi kṣīrasā apāra*  
*amṛta-maṇḍā sarabatī āra kumuḍā-kurī*  
*sarāmṛta sarabhājā āra sarapurī*  
*hari-vallabha seṅoti karpūra mālatī*  
*ḍālimā marica-lāḍu navāta amṛti*  
*padmacini candrakānti khājā khaṇḍasāra*  
*viyari kadmā tilākhājāra prakāra*  
*nāraṅga-cholaṅga-āmra-vṛkṣera ākāra*  
*phula-phala-patra-yukta khaṇḍera vikāra*  
*dadhi dugdha nanī takra rasālā śikhariṇī*  
*sa-lavaṇa mudgāṅkura ādā khāni khāni*  
*lembu-kula-ādi nānā-prakāra ācāra*  
*likhite nā pāri prasāda kateka prakāra*

**The King sent Mahaprabhu prasad from the Balagandi bhog, made up of uncooked food with milk sweets and fruits. It was all of the finest quality, and there was no end to the variety. There was curd, fruit juice, coconut, mango, dried coconut, jackfruit, various kinds of bananas and palm fruit seeds. There were also oranges, grapefruit, tangerines, almonds, dried fruit, raisins and dates.**  
**There were hundreds of different types of sweetmeats like m*****anoharā-lāḍu*****, sweets like** ***amṛta-guṭikā*** **and various condensed milk preparations. There were papayas and** ***sarabati*****, a type of sweet, juicy orange, and also crushed squash. There was also regular cream, fried cream and a type of fried bread made with cream.**  
**There were also sweets like** ***hari-vallabha*** **and sweets made of** ***senoti*** **flowers, camphor and malati flowers. There were pomegranates, sweets made with black pepper, others made with fused sugar, and fried sweets boiled in syrup. There was lotus flower sugar, a kind of bread made from urad dhal, crispy sweetmeats, sugar candy, fried rice sweets, sesame seed sweets and biscuits made from sesame seeds. There were sweetmeats made from sugarcane candy in the form of oranges, lemons and mangoes along with fruits, flowers and leaves.**  
**There was yogurt, milk, butter, buttermilk, fruit juice, a preparation made of fried yogurt and sugar candy, and salty mung dhal sprouts with shredded ginger. There were also various types of pickles lemon pickle, berry pickle and so on. It is quite impossible to describe everything that was offered to Lord Jagannath. (CC** [**2.14.25-34**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/14.25)**)**

As it cools off later in the afternoon, the chariots slowly set off again, reaching the Gundicha temple by evening. On arriving, they are offered arati and bhoga. They remain on the cart throughout the night and the next evening are moved in another Pahandi Vijaya down from the chariots and into the Gundicha temple, taking their places on their respective thrones. The three deities remain there seven days and finally on the Sayana or Bahura Ekadasi day return to the Nilachala temple.

While the Deities are on their cars, they do not take full meals with rice (*anna-bhoga*). They are made offerings of fruits and sweets, known as *nisakaṛi bhoga*. Over the entire Rathayatra period, Lord Jagannath is dressed in the different costumes of His ten incarnations, or Dashavatar Vesh.

## Hera Panchami

The fourth day of the Rathayatra festival, which is the fifth day of the waxing fortnight, is called Hera Panchami. Lakshmi Devi comes to visit Lord Jagannath at the Gundicha temple and engages in a festive destruction of the chariot (*ratha-bhaṅgotsava*).

Hera Panchami derives its name from the Orissan verb *herā*, “to see,” because on this day, Lakshmi Devi sets off to find her Lord, for whom she is feeling separation. There are other versions of the festival’s name, however. Some people call it Hara Panchami, from the verb *hārā*, which means “to lose.” This is also appropriate, as Lakshmi Devi in some sense loses Jagannath on that day. Another name is Hora Panchami. The verb *horā* means “to go.” Since Lakshmi Devi leaves her throne in the temple to go looking for Jagannath, it has been given this name. Indeed, Kavi Karnapur Goswami uses the term Hora Panchami in his *Caitanya-candrodaya-nāṭaka* (10.65). Krishna Das Kaviraj Goswami uses the terms Hera Panchami and *śrī-lakṣmī-vijayotsava* (“the festival of Sri Lakshmi Devi’s voyage”).

When Lord Jagannath leaves on his car festival with his brother and sister, poor Lakshmi is left at home alone. She becomes melancholic and retires to the store-room of the Jagannath temple. She refuses to eat the nice food she is offered, eating only ordinary rice and spinach. The anger builds up inside her for a few days. Then on the Panchami, Lakshmi is given a bath and dressed with nice ornaments. The Puja Pandas offer her Panti Bhoga.

On the Hera Panchami, Lakshmi Devi leaves the main temple with Yameshwar Shiva and the Devadasis. She comes to the Gundicha temple via the Narendra Sarovara tank. When she arrives at the Gundicha temple, Lord Jagannath’s servants refuse her entry into the bhoga mandira. She is received by a Pati Mahapatra who fans her from a position atop the wooden horses. Jagannath sends her His garland (*ājñā-mālā*), but Lakshmi returns it angrily. The Pujari comes with a message from Lord Jagannath,

*dina-traye jagannātho gamiṣyati punar gṛham*  
*nīlācale tvam adyaiva gaccha lakṣmi drutaṁ śubhe*

**“O Lakshmi! O auspicious one! The Lord of the Universe shall be returning home in three days, so please return quickly to Nilachala right now.” (*****Nīlādri-mahodayam*****, 16.95)**

Lakshmi becomes enraged and leaves the temple in a huff. On leaving the temple, she shows her displeasure by breaking a piece of wood from Lord Jagannath’s car. She then returns to the temple via Heragohiri Sahi, taking a meal on her way.

Krishna Das Kaviraj relished the Hera Panchami festival with the following extended description:

Aware that Hera Panchami festival was drawing near, King Prataparudra took care to speak to Kashi Mishra. “Tomorrow Lakshmi Devi will be leaving the temple, as it is Hera Panchami. Let us hold the festival this year in a way that has never been done before. Let us hold it in such a way that Chaitanya Mahaprabhu will be overjoyed to see it. Take all the printed cloths, bells, umbrellas and chamaras that are in both the temple and palace storehouses. Decorate Lakshmi’s palanquin with flags, festoons and little bells and organize the musicians and dancers to accompany it. Double the amount of prasad that is to be distributed. Let’s make the festival even more charming than Rathayatra itself. Make all arrangements for Mahaprabhu and the devotees to freely see the Deity.”

That morning, Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu went with His associates to see Lord Jagannath at the Gundicha temple. Then they enthusiastically returned to the main temple to see the Hera Panchami festival. Kashi Mishra received Chaitanya Mahaprabhu with great respect, and then gave them a privileged place to sit where they could watch everything.

Mahaprabhu wanted to hear about the spirit of the festival and so began to question Svarupa Damodar with a smile on His face.

*yadyapi jagannātha karena dvārakāya vihāra*  
*sahaja prakaṭa kare parama udāra*  
*tathāpi vatsara-madhye haya eka-bāra*  
*vṛndāvana dekhite tāṅra utkaṇṭhā apāra*

**“Although Lord Jagannath enjoys His pastimes at Dwaraka where He spontaneously manifests the greatest generosity to His devotees, once a year He still becomes very eager to see Vrindavan.” (**[**2.14.117-118**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/14.117)**)**

Pointing to the neighboring gardens, Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu said, “All these gardens remind Him of Vrindavan and so He becomes very eager to go there and see it again. In order to escape, He pretends to want to go for a ride on His chariot. He thus leaves Nilachala to go to Sundarachala. There He cavorts day and night in the flowering gardens, but why doesn’t He take Lakshmi Devi with Him?”

Svarupa Damodar replied, “My dear Lord, please let me explain. Lakshmi Devi, the goddess of fortune, is not qualified to participate in the Lord’s Vrindavan pastimes. Only the gopis assist in His enjoyment of the pastimes of Vrindavan, for no one but they can attract His mind.”

The Lord said, “On the pretext of going for a chariot drive, Krishna leaves for Vrindavan with Subhadra and Baladeva. The pastimes He has with the gopis in those gardens are secret, so no one else knows of them. So Krishna does not appear to have done anything wrong. Why then does Lakshmi Devi get so angry?”

*svarūpa kahe premavatīra ei ta svabhāva*  
*kāntera audāsya-leśe haya krodha-bhāva*

**Svarupa Damodar replied, “It is quite natural for a woman in love to get angry with her lover as soon as she thinks he is neglecting her in any way.”**

While Svarupa Damodar and the Lord were talking in this way, Lakshmi climbed into Her golden palanquin, which was bedecked with a variety of jewels. Being carried by four men, the palanquin was surrounded by servants carrying parasols, chamara whisks and flags, and was preceded by musicians and dancing Devidasis. Accompanying her were hundreds of attractively dressed and ornamented maidservants carrying water pitchers, chamara whisks and boxes for betel nuts.

In the midst of this opulent retinue, the angry goddess of fortune arrived at the lion gate of the Gundicha temple. There, her maidservants began to began to arrest all the principal servants of Lord Jagannath.\[94\] They tied them up and threw them down at Lakshmi Devi’s feet, punishing them like thieves and taking away all their wealth. The dasis angrily tear away at the unconscious car and swear and ridicule the Lord and His servants.

When Mahaprabhu and His companions saw the impudence of Lakshmi and all her maidservants, they covered their mouths and smiled. Svarupa Damodar said, “I have never seen or heard of a jilted woman being as angry as this anywhere. When a woman is angry with her husband or lover, she stops wearing fine clothes and jewelry. She sits on the floor, morosely marking lines on it with her fingernails. We have heard of this kind of pride in Satyabhama, and of course, such kinds of loving exchanges take place in Vrindavan, where they are most relishable. But Lakshmi Devi’s anger is expressed differently. She dresses herself in all her finery and shows her power by taking an army to go to war with her husband.” (CC [2.14.113-139](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/14.113))

After this, Svarupa Damodar explained the different kinds of *māna*, or loving anger spawned by jealousy, real or imagined. After hearing Svarupa Damodar’s discourse, in which Radharani and the gopis’ love was shown to be superior to that of Lakshmi, Srivas Pandit deliberately provoked him by taking Lakshmi Devi’s side. He laughed and said, “Listen, Damodar! Don’t you see just how glorious my goddess of fortune is? Compared to her opulence, what does Vrindavan have? A few flowers and twigs, some colored clays, a few peacock feathers and gunja berries. When Lakshmi heard that Jagannath had decided to go to Vrindavan, she felt disturbed and wondered, ‘What on earth has He gone to Vrindavan for, leaving behind all this wealth and comfort?’ So Lakshmi Devi prepared to have some fun at Lord Jagannath’s expense. Her servants say to Lord Jagannath’s servants,

*tomāra ṭhākura dekha eta sampatti chāṛi*  
*patra-phala-phula-lobhe gelā puṣpa-bāṛī*  
*ei karma kare kāhāṅ vidagdha-śiromaṇi*  
*lakṣmīra agrete nija prabhure deha āni*

**“Your Master gave up all this magnificence to go to the garden house so that He can enjoy some fruits and flowers. And for that, people call Him the cleverest epicurian? So go get your Lord and Master and bring Him here before Lakshmi Devi.”**

“So saying, Lakshmi’s maidservants bound the servants of Jagannath by the waist and brought them into the presence of the goddess of fortune. They make them bow down before her and then fine them. Then they make them beg for mercy. Having done so, they beat the Lord’s chariot with sticks and treat Jagannath’s servants almost like thieves.

**“Finally, Lord Jagannath’s servants give in and, folding their hands in supplication, promise Lakshmi Devi that they will bring Lord Jagannath to her the very next day. This pacifies Lakshmi and so she returns home. Her opulences are beyond description. Your gopis are engaged in boiling milk and churning it to turn it into yogurt, but my mistress, the goddess of fortune, sits on a throne made of jewels and gems.” (CC** [**2.14.203-214**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/14.203)**)**

Svarupa Damodar responded by saying, “Srivas! You mean to tell me that you don’t know anything about Vrindavan’s riches? Why, Dwaraka and Vaikuntha’s wealth are not even a drop in comparison next to the ocean of Vrindavan’s natural riches. Lord Krishna is the Supreme Person, Purushottam. He is full of all opulences, but these are not exhibited in their totality anywhere but in Vrindavan.

“Vrindavan is made of transcendental touchstone, which is used to make the people’s houses and decorate even the most ordinary servant girls who live there. The trees and creepers in the Vrindavan forest can fulfill all of one’s desires, so the residents of Vrindavan desire no wealth but the fruits and flowers of those trees. Countless wish-fulfilling cows wander from forest to forest in Vrindavan. Though they give nothing but milk, the people of Vrindavan desire no wealth but this.

**“The speech of Vrindavan’s residents sounds naturally like music, and their ordinary movements are naturally as beautiful as a dance. Everywhere, Vrindavan’s water is ambrosia. But most of all, the divine light has taken form there to be relished. The gopis are also goddesses of fortune, but their virtues surpass those of the goddess of fortune who lives in Vaikuntha. And in Vrindavan, Lord Krishna’s transcendental flute serves Him as His dearest companion.” (CC** [**2.14.218-226**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/14.218)**)**

## The return journey

On the seventh day of the Rathayatra festival, the *sandhyā-darśana* or “evening audience” festival is held. On the eighth day, the chariots are prepared for the return journey. This return journey, also known as Bahura, Punar Yatra or the Ulta Rath, takes place on the following day, that is, the Ekadasi.

Generally speaking, the return journey takes place on the Ekadasi, nine days after arriving at the Gundicha temple. However, under certain circumstances, the return trip takes place on the Dasami, i.e., one day early. This is because the Vaishnavas always take into consideration the overlapping of solar and lunar days\[95\] when determining fasts and feasts. This is stated in the Chaitanya Charitamrita in the Lord’s instructions to Sanatan Goswami:

*ekādaśī janmāṣṭamī vāmana-dvādaśī*  
*śrī-rāma-navamī āra nṛsiṁha-caturdaśī*  
*ei sabe biddhā-tyāga abiddhā-karaṇa*  
*akaraṇe doṣa kaile bhaktira lambhana*

**Vaishnavas observe Ekadasi, Janmastami, Vamana Dvadasi, Sri Rama Navami, and Nrisingha Chaturdasi. However, if these lunar days overlap with the solar day, they should be put off, for only then will their observance bring devotion. Not observing them at all is a serious fault. (CC** [**2.24.336-7**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/24.336)**)**

On the return journey, when the raths arrive at a place known as Shraddha Bali, they stop in front of the Ardhamshini (Ardhasani) Devi temple, which is also known as Jagannath’s maternal aunt’s (Mausi Ma) house. There Jagannath is fed offerings of *poṛā-piṭhā* or “burnt cakes.”

It is said that in the thirteenth century, the King Narasingha Deva had the bridge built at Atharonala or Shankhua River. A branch of this river known as the Malini River used to separate the Gundicha temple from the Grand Road or Boro Danda. This made it necessary to build six chariots for the Rathayatra, three on each side of this river. The Deities would be transferred across the stream by boat. Narasingha Deva’s queen Shraddha Devi had a bridge built across this river and made the sandy bed of the river suitable for the chariots. The sandy area thus took on the name Shraddha Bali (*bāli* means sand). The river has long since dried up.

From the Mausi Ma temple, the rath continues without stopping until it comes to the Marichika Devi temple, about 400 meters from the Singha Dwar and near the royal palace. Here, Lakshmi Devi comes out of the temple in a palanquin to greet Jagannath Deva.

Accompanied by the king, she first goes to the place on the temple wall called the Chahani Mandap (“observation post”). She then approaches the chariot and walks around it. Jagannath greets her with an *ājñā-mālā,* which is presented to her by the Dayitapatis, and she in turn offers Him the *bandāpanā*, i.e., rice, durba grass and a lamp, after which she goes back to the temple. This ritual is known as Lakshmi-Narayan’s *bheṭa* or meeting.

The chariots then continue on to the temple’s main entrance. Upon arriving, the Deities are offered the *adhara-paṇā bhoga,* a specially prepared sweet drink. In the midst of ecstatic chanting of the Holy Names, the Rathayatra festival comes to an end.

The Deities may remain on the chariots for one or two more days in the main gate area of the Temple. While here, they are dressed in their Suna Vesh. *Svarṇa* or *suvarṇa* is the Sanskrit word meaning gold. The Orissan form of the word is *suna*, so Suna or Svarna Vesh means the decoration of the deities with golden omaments. Their headdresses, or *kirīṭa*, are all gold. There are also special omaments made of gold for the hands and the feet. Lord Jagannath holds a silver conchshell in his left hand and a golden chakra or discus in his right. Similarly, Balabhadra holds a golden plough in his left hand and a gold mace in his right. Subhadra and Sudarshan are also decorated with golden omaments. This service has traditionally been sponsored by Royal Estate since the time of that Raj Kishor Babu was its manager.

In 1983, there was a great deal of rain on the day of the return Rathayatra and so the movement of chariots was very slow. Baladeva and Subhadra reached the Singha Dwar by the evening, but Lord Jagannath spent the night directly in front of the Chaitanya Gaudiya Math. Jagannath continued on His way the next morning and reached the Singha Dwar before noon. The three Deities remained there for three days, being served and worshiped by the public. Then, on the full moon day of Shravan, the Deities were brought into the temple and placed back on their usual altars.

## Niladri Utsava

The next day on the Dvadasi, Jagannath is moved back into the temple. This festival is called the Niladri Utsava. On this occasion, Lakshmi Devi has a fit of je alousy and refuses to allow Jagannath back into the temple. Lakshmi’s representatives, the Devadasis or Maharis, argue for some time with the Dayitas, who represent Jagannath. Lakshmi’s servants get the upper hand in the argument and when the Dayitas admit defeat, the Maharis open the gate and let Lord Jagannath pass and return to His throne.

The Gaudiya Vaishnavas desire the service of the gopis in Vrindavan. They therefore feel greater joy at Lord Jagannath’s journey to Gundicha, which they see as Krishna’s return from Dwaraka to Vrindavan. They feel less enthusiasm about his return to the main temple, which is like his leaving Vrindavan to go back to the city.

## Suicide at the Rathayatra

Uon their return home, early European travelers to India reported seeing or hearing of suicides at the Rathayatra, the very idea of which captured the imaginations of their European public. Stories of people throwing themselves under the wheels of Jagannath’s carts in a religious frenzy were rife and became a popular feature of Christian anti-Hindu propaganda, which made the name of Jagannath synonymous with organized self-slaughter. The word “juggernaut” entered the English language as meaning “an irresistable, destructive force.” Thus, even in Christian prohibitionist literature, the image of Lord Jagannath’s cart was used as the very symbol of evil –

“It is called the Gin Jagannath, and represents a hideous moving palace, with a reeking still at the roof, and vast gin barrels for wheels, under which unhappy millions are crushed to death*...* The vast cloud comes sweeping on in the wake of *the horrible body-crusher*.”\[96\]

In reality, however, most researchers agree that though there were undoubtedly cases of such suicide and of death by trampling, which came up from time to time even in the 19th and 20th centuries, not only at the Rathayatra but at other events like Nava Yauvana, they were comparatively rare.

In 1872, Hunter reported that he had made an index of all recorded incidences of suicides and attested that their number had always been insignificant. Furthermore, the few that did occur were for the most part “cases of diseased and miserable objects who took this means to put themselves out of pain.”\[97\]

Certainly, Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu disapproved of this practice, even in cases where one was suffering, such as that of Sanatan Goswami. Sanatan once came to see Mahaprabhu in Puri, taking the route through the jungle from Vrindavan. After drinking contaminated water, he came down with scabies. The running sores on his body depressed him terribly and he began to plan suicide in his despondency, thinking that due to his low birth and now disgusting physical condition he would not only be unable to go near the temple and see Jagannath, but would also be deprived of Mahaprabhu’s darshan. All in all, he thought it would be better to throw himself under the wheels of Jagannath’s chariot and be crushed to death while watching Mahaprabhu dance. In this way he would be assured of liberation, as the last thoughts and vision he had would be of his beloved Lord.

One day, the all-knowing Mahaprabhu came to see Sanatan at Siddha Bakul and suddenly confronted him with his intention to commit suicide in this way. He said,

“My dear Sanatan, if I could attain Krishna by committing suicide, then I would give up millions of bodies without a moment's hesitation. However, we cannot attain Krishna simply by giving up the body, but only through bhajan. Other than devotional service, there is no means by which to attain Krishna.” (CC 3.4.55-6)

Mahaprabhu taught the world through Sanatan that suicide is an act in the mode of ignorance that cannot be used to attain Krishna. It is only through the cultivation of pure devotion in practice that one can attain the Supreme Lord. The best forms of bhajan, or worship, are known as the nine kinds of devotional service, or *nava-vidhā bhakti.* The best of these is the congregational chanting of the Holy Names of Krishna, Harinam sankirtan*.*

Furthermore, Mahaprabhu taught that a devotee who has surrendered to Him gives up ownership of his own body to the Lord, who then acts through him to realize His own purposes in the world:

“You have already surrendered yourself to Me, so your body is now My personal property. Why do you want to destroy another’s property? Are you unable to distinguish right from wrong? Your body is an important instrument through which I shall accomplish many great things.” (Chaitanya Charitamrita 3.4.76-8)

Hunter argued that this vision had made inroads into the general Orissan culture, where even suttee, where widows immolated themselves on the funeral pyre of their dead husbands, was not widely practiced there as elsewhere in India. All in all, then, these reports of suicide may be considered to have been greatly exaggerated.

Even so, with today’s improved communications and the resulting increased numbers of pilgrims – more security measures are taken by the federal and state governments to insure that nothing of the sort happens, either by accident or intent. At the Rathayatra in 2000, sixty platoons of armed police and six of the Rapid Action Force were deployed for crowd control during the festival, which was attended by 800,000 people.

The great numbers of people can be dangerous and devotees should be careful not to fall on the ground in the midst of the great crowds. Still, everyone should try to at least touch the ropes, which are incarnations of Ananta Sesha himself, and pull the cars with devotion.

## Chapter 17 - The way Mahaprabhu’s devotees saw him at Rathayatra

His Divine Grace Srila Bhakti Promode Puri Goswami Maharaj had a deep affinity for Sri Kshetra. As a profoundly devout follower of Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, he considered Mahaprabhu’s inspired and ecstatic participation in the Rathayatra festival to contain the fullest expression of the confidential teachings of divine love He had descended to give. His Divine Grace recounted this in many speeches and articles, of which the following is one. It was first published in Bengali in May, 1985, in *Chaitanya Vani.*

Lord Chaitanya is the Supreme Person, the son of Maharaj Nanda, who has taken on the golden color and loving mood of his divine moiety, Srimati Radharani. After taking sannyas, He went to live by the Bay of Bengal, in the abode of Lord Jagannath, the Supreme Lord in a transcendental wooden form. There He gave the world the good fortune of being able to appreciate that divine sweet mood in His Rathayatra pastime when He took Jagannath from Nilachala, the main temple or Boro Deul that symbolizes Kurukshetra, and took Him to Sundarachala, the Gundicha temple that symbolizes Vrindavan. Who other than the Supreme Lord Himself could reveal the secrets of His own pastimes in His *arcā* incarnation, or deity form?

In so doing, Mahaprabhu also revealed the meaning of the name *sannyāsa-kṛt*, one of the thousand names of Lord Vishnu mentioned in the Mahabharata (13.135.75). In His life as a monk, Mahaprabhu was the object of devotion in a form and pastime imbued with the spirit of munificence. Given the name Sri Krishna Chaitanya, the supremely compassionate Lord quit His home in Nabadwip-Mayapur and established Himself in Nilachala, where His alter-ego Lord Jagannath engaged in one pastime that is significant above all others: that of going to the Gundicha temple. Mahaprabhu’s goal was to communicate the profound meaning of this lila by relishing its sweetness as the reservoir rather than the object of love.

In order to understand Mahaprabhu’s conception, we must recall the story of Lord Krishna’s meeting with the gopis in Kurukshetra as told in the 82ndchapter of the Srimad Bhagavatam, Tenth Canto: Once, while Krishna and Balaram were living in Dwaraka, sometime after Balaram’s visit to Vraja and before the five Pandavas performed the Rajasuya sacrifice, there was the rare occasion of a full solar eclipse, such as takes place at the end of every kalpa on the day of universal dissolution. When the astrologers had calculated the time of the eclipse and informed everyone, people of all social classes from all over India, from kings to field laborers, assembled at the holy place in Kurukshetra known as Samanta Panchaka.

Krishna wanted to relish the sweetness of the Vrajavasis’ love, for it makes a mockery of even the greatest majesty and divine power. In order to create a situation whereby their love could be seen and experienced in perspective, Krishna ordered Daruka, His charioteer, to cover His chariot with the most opulent decorations. He Himself was dressed in the fine raiment of a great emperor and, accompanied by all the Yadus and surrounded by a great army with all its four divisions\[98\], He went to Kurukshetra.

*vraja-vāsīra kṛṣṇe haya svābhāvikī prīti*  
*kṛṣṇera-o svābhāvikī prīti vraja-vāsī prati*

**The residents of Vrindavan have a natural and spontaneous affection for Him. Krishna similarly has a natural and spontaneous affection for the residents of Vraja.**

When Maharaja Nanda heard that all the members of the Yadu dynasty headed by Krishna would be attending the solar eclipse in Kurukshetra, had immediately loaded all their necessary paraphernalia on bullock carts, and had set off for Kurukshetra surrounded by all the cowherds. Now they were there, standing right next to them. Vasudeva and the members of the Yadu clan were overjoyed on seeing their dear friends, Nanda Maharaj and the residents of Vrindavan. They immediately stood up to welcome them as though the life had returned into their bodies and embraced them tightly in their joy.

## Krishna in regal garb at Kurukshetra

Thus Krishna went to Kurukshetra in the hope of meeting His beloved Vrajavasis; the solar eclipse was only an excuse for going there. The same was true for the Vrajavasis; their real purpose in going to Kurukshetra was to fulfill their profound desire to see Krishna, for they knew that He would be coming there from Dwaraka.

Amongst those who came were many members of the Yadu clan, including Akrura, Vasudeva and Ugrasena; Krishna’s sons Gada, Pradyumna, and Samba. Because almost all the members of the Yadu dynasty had gone to Kurukshetra, only Lord Aniruddha and Kritavarma, the commander-in-chief of the Yadu army, remained behind in Dvaraka along with Suchandra, Shuka and Sarana to protect the city.

After arriving in Kurukshetra, the members of the Yadu clan, who know only Krishna as their worshipable deity, performed all the usual ceremonial functions associated with visiting a place of pilgrimage, such as fasting. Before the eclipse, they took three kinds of bath in the Samanta Panchaka lake, praying for devotion to Krishna after each one of them. They then fed the Brahmins sumptuously and made them gifts of clothes and cows decorated with flower garlands and golden ornaments. Krishna then told them to sit down and eat, after which they rested in the pleasant shade of some trees.

They then prepared to receive visitors, among whom were relatives and friends, as well as many subordinate kings, including the rulers of Matsya, Ushinara, Koshala, Vidarbha, Kuru, Srinjaya, Kamboja, Kekaya, Madra, Kunti, Anartta, Kerala, and many other countries and provinces, some of who were inimical to Krishna and others who were friendly. Among all these pilgrims, however, the most significant were those from Vrindavan headed by Nanda Maharaj. Their number included not only Krishna and Balaram’s cowherd boyfriends, but also the gopis, who had been suffering for so long due to not seeing Krishna. They had taken advantage of the occasion of the eclipse to come and see Him after so many years of separation. Overjoyed at seeing each other, the residents of Vraja and Krishna immediately began inquiring after each others’ health and well-being.

It was also a family reunion for Kunti Devi and her sons, who met Krishna and Balaram’s father and mothers, their cousins, their children after their many years of exile. Of course, the main purpose of their trip to Kurukshetra had been to see Krishna – they had no interest in or need for any other religious ceremonies.

Kunti Devi, the mother of Arjuna and Yudhishthira, met her cousin Vasudeva, Krishna’s father. She expressed her regret that during their time of troubles, Vasudeva had not come to their aid even though he was her older brother. Vasudeva answered that he and his family had also faced many difficulties on account of Kamsa, who had imprisoned them and sent other members of the clan into exile. He stated philosophically that they were all pawns in the hands of fate and had to bear their troubles stoically. Now, their fortunes had changed and they were reinstated in their positions and had been reunited on this occasion, so there was no point in blaming each other for having been indifferent to their suffering.

After this conversation, Vasudeva and Ugrasena received the kings who came to see them, and they sufficiently welcomed them all. These visitors felt transcendental pleasure on seeing Lord Krishna present on the spot. Some of the prominent visitors were as follows: Bhishma Deva, Dronacharya, Dhritarashtra, Duryodhana, and Gandhari along with her sons, Sanjaya, Vidura, Kripacharya, Kuntibhoja, Virata, Bhishmaka, King Nagnajit, Purujit, Drupada, Shalya, Dhrishtaketu, the King of Kashi, Damaghosh, Vishalaksha, the King of Mithila, the King of Madras, the King of Kekaya, Yudhamanyu, Susharma, Bahlika along with his sons, and many other rulers subordinate to King Yudhishthira.

When they saw Lord Krishna with His thousands of queens, the kings were astonished at the sight of such beauty. Lord Balaram and Krishna properly welcomed them, giving each the appropriate respects according to the protocol. These kings began to glorify the members of the Yadu dynasty for their great good fortune in having taken shelter of Krishna and Balaram. They said, “You Yadus are the most fortunate people in the entire world, for you have achieved the goal of human activity. You are able to constantly behold Lord Krishna, who is sought for by mystic yogis undergoing severe austerities and penances for great numbers of years.

“Krishna’s holy fame is sung in the Vedic hymns; the water that has washed Krishna’s lotus feet delivers the world as the Ganges. The words that emanate from His tongue are the divinely inspired Vedic literatures that purify the entire universe. This world had almost lost its glory, but was reinvigorated by the touch of Krishna’s lotus feet. Now once again it fulfills the needs of all the people living here.

“You Yadus are related to Krishna both by marriage and blood relationship, so you are constantly in touch with Lord Krishna. You can see Him whenever you want. You touch Him, move with Him, talk with Him, lie with Him, and dine with Him. When Krishna gives His devotion, even to someone constantly engaged in worldly affairs, then that person becomes indifferent to the goals of heavenly sense pleasure or liberation. This Krishna is personally present in your homes, so there can be no doubt that your lives have been perfected.”

## Krishna is reunited with Nanda and Yashoda

After the princes had thus glorified the great good fortune of the Yadus, it was time for the Vrajavasis headed by Nanda Maharaj to meet with Krishna. When Lord Krishna met with the kings and princes in His role as a prince of Dwaraka, it had been a very public and formal occasion, with ostentatious displays of respect and honor. Now He met His most beloved Vrajavasis in a more intimate and private manner.

First, Krishna and Balaram embraced Nanda and Yashoda, greeting them lovingly. Indeed, the Divine Brothers were so overwhelmed by the emotion of being reunited with their foster parents that their throats choked up and their eyes overflowed with tears, such that they were unable to speak. Krishna and Balaram are the objects of parental love, the *viṣaya-vigrahas*; Nanda and Yashoda are the reservoirs of this kind of devotional feeling, the *āśraya-vigrahas.* In this moment of meeting, the condition of both the subject and the object of love was the same. There was so much that Nanda and Yashoda had wanted to say to their boys, but their voices were obstructed by the strength of their emotion and no sound came out. How they wanted to gaze upon them, but their eyes were so flooded with tears that they could not see. Indeed, these external manifestations of their feelings had to serve as the means of communication.

Krishna is the life of the Vrajavasis’ life. He is the only thing that gives their lives meaning. When He goes outside the range of their vision for even a moment, they felt as though the life force itself was seeping out of their bodies. When He left for Mathura, they were driven to the limits of sanity: they gave up food and drink, they even gave up sleep, and simply breathed hot sighs of distress and drenched themselves in the tears of separation. Sometimes they would become so completely delirious that they would fall to the ground, twitching from the pain that seemed to grow stronger with every passing moment. Mother Yashoda even swore that she would not even open her eyes again until her Gopal was standing before her. Now after all these years, He was standing before her and she wanted to drink His beauty in through her eyes, but they refused to cooperate. She lost all sense of where she was as she held Him tightly, and no words could find their way out of her mouth. She could not even manage to say, “Dearest Gopal, how are you?” This is the love of the residents of Vrindavan – Vraja prema.

When Krishna left for Mathura, Yashoda had been filled with the memory of Krishna’s childhood that would be no more: No more would He come early in the morning as she churned the butter, holding her churning rod so that she would stop her work. No more would she pick Him up and hold Him on her lap. No more would He break her churning pot in a tantrum in order to make Himself the center of her attention. No more would He follow her around waiting for an opportunity to steal the fresh butter and curds. No more would the other women of the cowherd community come to complain about her Gopal’s mischievous deeds in their homes. In his absence, the entire community descended into unbearable silence

Now that she held her heart’s treasure to her breast again, Yashoda drenched Him with a steady stream of tears as her gut wrenched in anticipation of yet another inevitable separation. Was it possible that Gopal could again leave the embrace of this incarnation of motherly love? Does Krishna ever leave the heart of His beloved devotees?

*bhaktera hṛdaye govindera satata viśrāma*  
*govinda kahena mama bhakta se parāṇa*

**Govinda always takes refuge in His devotee’s heart. He says, “My devotees are My life.” (Narottama Das’s** ***Prārthanā*****, 23)\[99\]**

Nanda Maharaj similarly held Krishna to his chest. His mind boiled and bubbled with memories of Krishna’s childhood: the way that Gopal used to crawl on the verandah; the way He used to follow him around and look at him and then, when He had his attention, begin calling out “catch me, catch me,” clapping His hands, then run away laughing. Nanda would run after Him, and when he caught Krishna, would hold Him to his chest and kiss Him repeatedly, even though the child was covered in dust and dirt.

If Nanda asked little Gopal to bring him his shoes, the child would find so many original ways of doing it – sometimes carrying them on His head, sometimes holding them to His chest. Nanda would be enchanted with his Gopal and would again hold and kiss Him, bringing laughter to Krishna’s beautiful moon-like face. Smitten by the recollection of all these childhood pastimes, Nanda Maharaj lost all sense of time and place and felt as though he were losing his mind altogether. He lifted Krishna off the ground in his arms and could not put Krishna back down.

Neither Nanda nor Yashoda saw any of the trappings of royalty that surrounded their boy Gopal. All they saw was the Krishna who had shared His childhood with them. How glorious is the son of Nanda! And how glorious are His pastimes in Vraja! And how glorious His parents, overflowing with affection for Him! In this way, Nanda and Yashoda hugged the two boys and found relief from the years of suffering in their separation.

After this, Krishna's mother, Devaki, and Balaram's mother, Rohini, both embraced mother Yashoda. They recalled her acts of friendship and in gratitude said, “Dear Queen Yashoda Devi, both you and Nanda Maharaj have proved your friendship to us by taking care of Krishna and Balaram and bringing them up when we were unable to do so. How could any mother forget that? They were entrusted to your care as soon as they were born, before they even saw their real father and mother. You protected them just as the eyelids protect the eyes, treating them just as though they were your own children and thus making it possible for them to grow up fearlessly amongst the cowherds.”\[100\]

## Krishna meets with his cowherd friends

While Devaki and Rohini were talking with Yashoda, Krishna met with His cowherd friends. These cowherds had also thought of so many things they wanted to say to their elder brother Dauji Balaram and to their brother Kanai. For so long they had been harboring feelings of hurt and resentment on account of their long absence. But as they hugged the two divine brothers, they could not find any words to express all the sentiments they had experienced. And just as they could only reveal what was in their hearts through the tears that filled their eyes, the same was true for Krishna and Balaram. The moisture in their eyes spoke the language of the overwhelmed heart.

Ever since Kanai had left Vraja for Mathura, His cowherd friends had been unable to eat, sleep or see to their bodily comfort. Of course, the same was true for every living creature in all of Vrindavan: the entire land had fallen silent with grief at Krishna’s absence: the birds had stopped their sweet singing, the bees their humming, the peacocks their distinctive cry of *kekā kekā,* the talking mynah birds and parrots had stopped their debates, the cows their lowing, what to speak of all the other creatures. The cowherd boys stopped going out to graze the cattle – and why should they have gone when the cattle no longer chewed on the grasses in the pasturing grounds? The cows simply stared at the sky and shed tears; the calves no longer skip and jump happily the way they used to. Even the flowers in the gardens stopped blossoming; it was as though the entire land was lifeless.

Krishna’s flute used to make the Yamuna’s waters overflow, but now the river was stagnant. The houses of the cowherds, where each morning the women would fill the sky with their songs and the sounds of churning butter, had also fallen silent. The pain of separation affected everyone in the entire land of Vraja: young or old, male or female, animal or plant – even the birds and insects. Now, here in Kurukshetra, Krishna tried to somehow alleviate the cowherds’ pain.

## Krishna meets with the gopis

Now the Lord turned His attention to the gopis, who were anxiously awaiting their chance to be with Him. After such a great length of time, the gopis were finally able to see Krishna again. But they cursed the creator for making their eyes so incapable of properly drinking in His beauty.

*koṭi-netra nāhi dilā dilā mātra dui*  
*tāhāte nimeṣa kṛṣṇa ki dekhiba muñi*

**“The creator did not give us a million eyes, he only gave us two. Not only that, but he has made it necessary to blink, so how can we possibly see Krishna properly?” (CC** [**1.4.151**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-adi/4.151)**)**

They took Krishna into their hearts with their eyes and there they embraced Him to their hearts content, achieving a state of concentration that the great yogis can only aspire to. Krishna took the gopis to a secluded place and there held them in His arms, inquiring after their well-being, and making them laugh with His affectionate words until they had forgotten the wounds left in their hearts by deprivation of His company. Then, in order to relish the depths of their love, He began to speak:

“My dear friends, you know that both Balaram and I left Vrindavan just to fulfill our obligations to our relatives and family members. We were long engaged in fighting our enemies and so were unable to see you. Did you forget us during our absence? Or perhaps you now dislike remembering Me, considering Me to have been ungrateful to you. You should know that it was never My intention to leave you. Our separation was ordained by Providence, which brings people together and then again disperses them. Sometimes we see that a strong wind brings clouds, grass, particles of dust or tiny pieces of cotton together, and then when it subsides, all the particles of dust and cotton are again separated, scattered in different places. However, you should know that in our case,

*mayi bhaktir hi bhūtānām*  
*amṛtatvāya kalpate*  
*diṣṭyā yad āsīn mat-sneho*  
*bhavatīnāṁ mad-āpanaḥ \|\|*

**“Whoever engages in My devotional service attains immortality, i.e., liberation or eternal felicity. You are especially blessed on account of the deep love you have for Me, by which you will surely attain Me. That is most auspicious. This love forcibly attracts Me and makes Me come quickly to your side.” (SB** [**10.82.41**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-10/82.41)**)**

Loving devotion to Krishna like that of the gopis has the power to attract Krishna. For this reason, Rupa Goswami gives bhakti the name *śrī-kṛṣṇākarṣiṇī.*

Krishna continued, “My dear women, whatever form there is in existence in the entire creation is nothing but a combination of the material elements: earth, water, air, fire and sky. The same physical composites make up all things, whether in their beginnings, during their existence or after their annihilation. In the same way, I am the cause of the birth and death of all living creatures, whether they are born of embryos, eggs, perspiration or from seeds in the earth. I am thus always present in them -- in their beginning, middle and end. Because of this, you can never be separated from Me and I can never be absent to you.

“In the same way, the five elements are present in the bodies of every living being. The living entity himself is all-pervading in the body as its enjoyer. But both the body and the living entity dwelling within it are contained within the supreme absolute, who is truly all-pervading. And I am that undivided supreme truth. This means that in both body and soul, you are always existing in Me, so your lamentation at being separated from Me must be attributed to ignorance. This false ego of the living entity is the cause of its imprisonment in material existence alone.”

After hearing these philosophical instructions from Krishna, the gopis felt as though there was still some hope of being united with Him and this kept them alive, for their constant meditation on Krishna during their separation had acted like the sun on the water-lily – it had made their life-force wilt to the point of being practically exhausting. Now that Krishna was in their presence, they revealed this hope aloud to Him directly:

*āhuś ca nalina-nābha padāravindaṁ*  
*yogeśvarair hṛdi vicintyam agādha-bodhaiḥ*  
*saṁsāra-kūpa-patitoddharaṇāvalambaṁ*  
*gehaṁ juṣām api manasy udiyāt sadā naḥ \|\|*

**“Oh lotus-naveled Krishna! Brahma and other great yogis like him who have unfathomable wisdom constantly meditate on Your lotus feet in their hearts, for such meditation is said to be the best means for conditioned souls to climb out of the dark well of material existence. May Your lotus feet always be manifest in our minds, for we poor women are only attached to our householder lives and families.” (SB** [**10.82.48**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-10/82.48)**)**

PART II

## Mahaprabhu in the mood of the gopis at Kurukshetra

Following the Srimad Bhagavatam, we have given the description of the various transcendental feelings that held sway over the minds of the gopis, and especially of the foremost of the gopis, Radharani, the daughter of king Vrishabhanu, while she was overpowered by feelings of separation from Krishna during their reunion at Kurukshetra. Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu was imbued with these very same transcendental feelings as He took on the mood and loving aspect of Radharani. His mood can especially be understood in the light of this last verse that ends the Bhagavata’s description of the gopis’ meeting with Krishna.

Those who are expert in tasting these same emotions have relished this pastime in their books, especially Krishna Das Kaviraj Goswami in the Chaitanya Charitamrita. If the Supreme Lord does not allow His heartfelt mood to be explained and revealed by His most intimate devotees, then how will people like us ever be fortunate enough to understand them? We should be careful not to discuss such matters amongst people who are completely unqualified to hear about them, but should we not take joy to hear and discuss the most elevated realms of pure devotion in the company of holy persons who are well-versed in its doctrines?

Gaudiya Vaishnavas continue to follow Lord Chaitanya’s mood during Lord Jagannath’s Rathayatra festival in Puri Dham. This festival is thus, to them, the occasion when Chaitanya Mahaprabhu most perfectly revealed not only Himself, but the true nature of the divine love between Radha and Krishna.

Whenever Mahaprabhu saw Lord Jagannath during the Rathayatra festival, He would think that He was looking upon Krishna in the holy field of Kurukshetra.

*je kāle karena jagannātha daraśana*  
*mane bhāve kurukṣetre pāñāchi milana*

**When He looked upon Lord Jagannath, He would think, “I am meeting Krishna in Kurukshetra.” (CC** [**2.1.53**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/1.53)**)**

The Lord danced like a madman in front of Lord Jagannath’s car with intimate associates like Svarupa Damodar, Ramananda Raya and Gadadhar Pandit Goswami, and relished all these flavors of divine love. And when dancing in front of Jagannath’s car, He would think that He was seeing Krishna after many, many years of separation:

*sei ta parāṇa-nātha pāinu*  
*jāṅhā lāgi madana-dahane jhuri genu*

**“Here is the Lord of my life. I have finally found Him for whom I have so long burned in the fire of desire.” (CC** [**2.1.55**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/1.55)**)**

Mahaprabhu thought that after meeting Krishna in His majestic glory at Kurukshetra, He was taking Him back to Vrindavan with Him*.* Three hours would go by before He stopped singing these two lines, and all the time He thought that He was taking Krishna to Vraja.

My worshipable spiritual master, Srila Prabhupada Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati has elaborated on this passage in his *Anubhāṣya* commentary to the Chaitanya Charitamrita. He writes: “As He had taken on Radharani’s mood of love toward Krishna, Mahaprabhu also accepted the transformations of that mood that took place during Krishna’s long absence after leaving Vraja for Mathura. Through His example, Mahaprabhu showed that cultivating the feeling of separation from Krishna is the single most effective practice leading to spiritual perfection, for it is said that the feelings of separation ultimately lead to union.

“The 82ndchapter of the Tenth Canto of the Srimad Bhagavatam gives an account of how the residents of Vrindavan who had been pining to see Krishna for so long were finally able to meet Him at the Syamanta Panchaka in Kurukshetra, where large numbers of pilgrims had gathered for a full solar eclipse. During the Rathayatra, Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu shared the mood of the cowherd girls of Gokula on that occasion as though the entire pastime was being reenacted. When the gopis in Kurukshetra saw Krishna’s royal splendor, they wanted to bring Him back to the more intimate atmosphere of Vraja. In the same way, Gaur Hari saw the main temple in Puri, or Nilachala, as representative of Kurukshetra. He wanted to take Krishna from there to the Gundicha temple, also known as Sundarachala and symbolic of Vraja. As He danced in front of Lord Jagannath’s car, it was this particular mood of Srimati Radharani that He became absorbed in. The Gundicha temple is also symbolic of the love in *parakīyā-rasa.*”

Factually speaking, the devotees of the Gaudiya Vaishnava school, who follow in the footsteps of Svarupa Damodar and Srila Rupa Goswami, have expert knowledge in divine loving relations, or *rasa.* They thus too reenact Radharani’s mood of wishing to take Lord Krishna, the son of the king of Vraja, in his form of Lord Jagannath, to Vrindavan in the form of the Gundicha temple.

Krishna appears in Kurukshetra in a majestic mode; He is dressed in the opulent costume of a great king and surrounded by chariots, elephants, horses, courtiers and ministers. Radharani finds it unbearable to see Him in this way. She pines to see Shyamasundar in His cowherd dress, His hair tied in a topknot with a peacock feather headdress, a flute touching His smiling lips, a garland of forest flowers around His neck, standing in His three-fold bending pose, with bells jingling on His ankles. This is the charming form that Radharani worships and she knows no peace for as long as she cannot see Krishna appear in exactly this way in some lonely wooded bower on the banks of the Yamuna.

## Rupa Goswami’s verse

While in front of Lord Jagannath’s car, Mahaprabhu kept repeating a classic Sanskrit verse from the *Kāvya-prakāśa*, as though in a deep trance.

*yaḥ kaumāra-haraḥ sa eva hi varas tā eva caitra-kṣapās*  
*te conmīlita-mālatī-surabhayaḥ prauḍhāḥ kadambānilāḥ*  
*sā caivāsmi tathāpi tatra surata-vyāpāra-līlā-vidhau*  
*revā-rodhasi vetasī-taru-tale cetaḥ samutkaṇṭhate*

**He who stole away my heart during my youth is here again as my bridegroom. And these are the same moonlit nights of the spring month of Chaitra. The same fragrance of malati flowers is there and the same sweet breezes blowing from the kadamba forest. I too am the same person with whom he made playful, ecstatic love. Yet my unsatisfied mind yearns for that place under the bull rushes on the bank of the Reva River. (CC** [**2.1.58**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/1.58)**)**

The mood described in this verse is mundane and not held in high esteem by transcendentalists, yet Mahaprabhu, a sannyasi, continued repeating it, much to the mystification of everyone except His close associate Svarupa Damodar. Another exception was Rupa Goswami, who wrote a verse of his own that brought out the Lord’s underlying understanding. He wrote His verse down on a palm leaf and tucked it into the thatch of Hari Das’s cottage at Siddha Bakul.

It was Mahaprabhu’s habit to came by to see Hari Das after Lord Jagannath’s *upala-bhoga* or *chatra-bhoga.*\[101\] He happened upon the palm leaf that was protruding from the bamboo cottage’s thatched roof and saw Rupa’s handwriting on it. Mahaprabhu read the verse several times, becoming increasingly ecstatic with each reading. When Rupa returned from bathing, he saw the Lord sitting down and reading his verse. He prostrated himself before the Lord, who gave him a playful slap on the cheek and then pulled him to His chest in an embrace.

With great affection, the Lord said, “No one understood the secret of my chanting that verse of mundane love poetry. Only Svarupa Damodar knew what I was getting at. How did you figure it out?”

Mahaprabhu showed the verse to Svarupa Damodar and asked him, “How did Rupa come to understand my innermost mood?” Svarupa immediately answered, “Rupa is the object of Your greatest blessings and thus Your most intimate thoughts have been revealed to him.” Mahaprabhu said, “I was so pleased with him that I embraced him and invested him with all of My powers. He is the most qualified person to discuss the intricacies of Radha and Krishna’s divine loving relations. You should also elucidate the mysteries of their loves to him.”

Rupa’s verse went as follows:

*priyaḥ so’yaṁ kṛṣṇaḥ sahacari kurukṣetra-militas*  
*tathāhaṁ sā rādhā tad idam ubhayoḥ saṅgama-sukham \|*  
*tathāpy antaḥ-khelan-madhura-muralī-pañcama-juṣe*  
*mano me kālindī-pulina-vipināya spṛhayati \|\|*

**O companion! This is the same beloved Krishna meeting me here in Kurukshetra and I am the same Radha; both of us are feeling the same joy of union. Even so, my mind yearns for the forest by the banks of the Yamuna where the fifth note of his flute reverberated so sweetly in my heart. (CC** [**2.1.76**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/1.76)**)**

It was not enough for Radha to be reunited with Krishna in Kurukshetra, for His attitude was all wrong. Her love needed the intimacy of the pleasure gardens by the Yamuna, where Krishna played the flute in the simple dress of a cowherd and the natural decorations gathered from the forest. His wealth, power and royal status in Dwaraka simply placed constraints on the natural and spontaneous affection they had known in Vrindavan.

Krishna Das Kaviraj is a member of Radharani’s entourage of intimate friends and is thus able to explain clearly how she felt:

*rāja veśa hātī ghoṛā manuṣya gahana*  
*kāhāṅ gopa veśa kāhāṅ nirjana vṛndāvana*  
*sei bhāva sei kṛṣṇa sei vṛndāvana*  
*jabe pāi tabe haya vāñchita pūraṇa*  
*tomāra caraṇe mora vraja-pura-ghare*  
*udaya karaye jadi tabe vāñchā pure*

**“Here in Kurukshetra, You are dressed like a prince and surrounded by elephants, horses and crowds of people. Where is that cowherd boy I used to know? And where is the privacy of the Vrindavan forest? If I could only have the same mood, the same Krishna and that same lonely Vrindavan trysting place, then my heart’s desire would be fulfilled. If You would make your appearance there, in my forest bower in Vrindavan, then I would want for nothing more.” (CC** [**2.1.78-80**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/1.78)**)**

Krishna Das again took up the same theme in the thirteenth chapter of the *Madhya-līlā*, describing it with even more sweetness --

*avaśeṣe rādhā kṛṣṇe kare nivedana*  
*sei tumi sei āmi sei nava saṅgama*  
*tathāpi āmāra mana hare vṛndāvana*  
*vṛndāvane udaya karāo āpana caraṇa*  
*ihāṅ lokāraṇya hātī ghoṛā ratha dhvani*  
*tāhāṅ puṣpāraṇya bhṛṅga pika nāda śuni*  
*ihāṅ rāja veśa saṅge saba kṣatriya gaṇa*  
*tāhāṅ gopa veśa saṅge muralī vādana*  
*vraje tomāra saṅge jei sukha āsvādana*  
*sei sukha samudrera ihāṅ nāhi eka kaṇa*  
*āmā lañā punaḥ līlā karaha vṛndāvane*  
*tabe āmāra mano vāñchā haya ta pūraṇe*

**In the mood of Radharani, Chaitanya Mahaprabhu spoke the following words to Lord Jagannath: “You are the same Krishna, and I am the same Radha. We are meeting again in the same way that we did when our love first began. Even so, my mind still yearns for Vrindavan. So please place your lotus feet there in Vrindavan once again. Here in Kurukshetra there is a forest of people making a great din with their elephants, horses, and chariots, whereas in Vrindavan there are forests of flowers and the sound of humming bees and the cuckoos’ song. Here you are dressed like a king and accompanied by great warriors, but in Vrindavan you dressed like an ordinary cowherd boy, accompanied only by your beautiful flute. Here there is not even a drop of the ocean of transcendental happiness that I enjoyed with you in Vrindavan. I therefore request you to come to Vrindavan and revel with me there. Only then will my heart’s desire be fulfilled.” (CC** [**2.13.126-131**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/13.126)**)**

In the mood of Radharani, Lord Gaurasundara spoke the following words to Lord Jagannath as he sat on his car: “O Krishna, even though you and I are the same people we have always been and we are meeting again just as we did before. Even so, My mind still yearns for Vrindavan, for it is completely taken by the mood particular to Vrindavan.

“I don’t like this great show of regal majesty here in Kurukshetra with all your elephants, horses, chariots, and crowds of people. If you really wish to give me your fullest blessings, then come with us back to Vrindavan where there are forests of flowers and the sound of humming bees and the cuckoos’ song. Here you are dressed like a king and accompanied by great warriors, but in Vrindavan you dressed like an ordinary cowherd boy, accompanied only by your beautiful flute. Have me stand on your left side if you sincerely want to do me a favor. Otherwise, I will understand that all your talk about loving us gopis is nothing but a deception.
