“Here there is not even a drop of the ocean of transcendental happiness that I enjoyed with you in Vrindavan. I therefore request you to come to Vrindavan and revel with us there in the natural way that you did before. Only then will my heart’s desire be fulfilled.”

Krishna Das Kaviraj then initiates an explanation of the *āhuś ca nalina-nābha padāravindaṁ* verse from the Bhagavatam that ended the story of Krishna’s meeting with the gopis at Kurukshetra. There Krishna had been trying to pacify the gopis with philosophical advice and instructions in the practice of yoga. Mahaprabhu chanted this verse while dancing in front of Lord Jagannath in the Rathayatra and Krishna Das’s poetic interpretation of its meaning is delectable and felicitous to an extent rarely found in any religious text.

*āhuś ca nalina-nābha padāravindaṁ*  
*yogeśvarair hṛdi vicintyam agādha-bodhaiḥ*  
*saṁsāra-kūpa-patitoddharaṇāvalambaṁ*  
*gehaṁ juṣām api manasy udiyāt sadā naḥ \|\|*

**“Oh lotus-naveled Krishna! Brahma and other great yogis like him who have unfathomable wisdom meditate constantly on your lotus feet in their hearts, for such meditation is said to be the best means for conditioned souls to climb out of the dark well of material existence. May these lotus feet always be manifest in our minds, for we poor women are only attached to our householder lives and families.” (SB** [**10.82.48**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-10/82.48)**)**

According to Kaviraj Goswami, Srimati Radharani is saying, “O Krishna! For the materialistic person, the mind that accepts and rejects sense objects is considered to be the heart. My mind, however, is free from all such desires for material sense objects and knows nothing but the desire for pleasing your senses. It is thus a place that is fitting for you to conduct your pastimes, for it is of the same nature as your eternal abode, Vrindavan itself.

“To give my heart instructions in philosophy and mystical practice is a waste of time. Previously you gave such instructions to us through Uddhava and now you are doing the same thing personally here in Kurukshetra. Our hearts are naturally full of love for you and so need no such advice. Yogis work hard to detach their minds from material sense objects and fix them on you in your form as the indwelling Supersoul. We, on the other hand, have to work hard to forget you for a moment so that we can fix our mind on our daily household duties. We try with great efforts to do so, but our minds are so imbued with thoughts of you that we cannot manage it. When you give us instructions to meditate on you, it makes us laugh.”

“We gopis have completely left bodily consciousness behind. This is our natural state. So how can the words ‘dark well of material existence’ apply to us? In fact, our suffering comes of having fallen into the ocean of separation from you, where the great whale of desire to serve you is swallowing us up. If you want to save us, then save us from that whale’s gaping mouth. In other words, save us from this state of separation.

“It is most surprising to us that in spite of being the pinnacle of virtue, you have forgotten Vrindavan, Govardhan, the banks of the Yamuna River and the forest bowers where we had our pastimes. Worse still, you seem to have forgotten all those who love you, including your own father and mother, your friends and the other people of Vraja.

“Perhaps you have no sympathy for us and our distress. We do not ask for it, but think for a minute about your mother, the queen of Vrindavan. When the people of the cowherd community see her suffering, their hearts break. Do you not feel the slightest twinge of remorse when you see her in this state?

“I don’t want to blame you for all this. We can only say that Providence has treated us unkindly and that is why You have become indifferent to us all. It is simply our destiny. We Vrajavasis find absolutely no pleasure in seeing you in your royal garb, living in a foreign land, and your attachment to new companions. Even so, we cannot leave Vrindavan to follow you. That is impossible, even if we have to come face to face with death itself as a result of not seeing you. Can you come up with any solution for our predicament?

“Sometimes you kill us with your separation and then sometimes, like today, you revive us by giving us the hope that we may be reunited again. Why do you do this? You are keeping us alive simply to kill us by again destroying our hopes.”

Having expressed her heartfelt distress in this way, Radharani becomes more and more overcome by the intensity of her emotions. She begins to cry and as her heart is torn in two, she stammers out the following verse:

*tumi vrajera jīvana vraja-rājera prāṇa-dhana*  
*tumi sakala vrajera sampad*  
*kṛpārdra tomāra mana āsi jīyāo vraja-jana*  
*vraje udaya karāo nija-pada*

**“You are the very life of Vrindavan. You are Nanda Maharaj’s life’s treasure. You are the only wealth the people of Vrindavan cling to. You are compassionate by nature, so please come and resuscitate the people of Vrindavan by placing your feet in this land again.” (CC** [**2.13.147**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/13.147)**)**

Krishna listened silently to Radharani’s effusive lamentations and could not help being touched. Indeed, the Vrajavasis’ declarations of love had left him feeling responsible and indebted to them. Trying somehow or other to console her, He said:

*prāṇa-priye śuna mora e-satya-vacana*  
*tomā-sabāra smaraṇe jhuroṅ muñi rātri-dine,*  
*mora duḥkha nā jāne kona jana*

**“My dearest Srimati Radharani, please listen to what I say, for it is the truth. I cry whenever I think of you inhabitants of Vrindavan and I think of you both day and night. No one here understands just how unhappy I am. (CC** [**2.13.149**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/13.149)**)**

*vraja-vāsī jata jana, mātā pitā sakhā-gaṇa,*  
*sabe haya mora prāṇa-sama*  
*tāṅra madhye gopi-gaṇa, sākṣāt mora jīvana,*  
*tumi mora jīvanera jīvana*

**“All the inhabitants of Vrindavan Dhama -- my mother, father, cowherd boy friends and everyone else -- are like my very life to me. Among all of them, however, the gopis are my life and soul. And you, Radharani, are the very life of my life. (CC** [**2.13.150**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/13.150)**)**

*tomā-sabāra prema-rase, āmāke karila vaśe,*  
*āmi tomāra adhīna kevala*  
*tomā-sabā chāṛāñā, āmā dūra-deśe lañā,*  
*rākhiyāche durdaiva prabala*

**“I am always subservient to the love of all you Vrajavasis. I am completely under your control alone, my dearest Radha. An unkind and powerful destiny has separated me from you and taken me to a distance place and obliged me to stay there. (CC** [**2.13.151**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/13.151)**)**

*rākhite tomāra jīvana, sevi āmi nārāyaṇa,*  
*tāṅra śaktye āsi niti-niti*  
*tomā-sane krīḍā kari, niti jāi yadu-purī,*  
*tāhā tumi mānaha mora sphūrti*

**“I worship Lord Narayan every day, praying for your health and well-being. By his blessings, I am able to come to visit you every single night. After we enjoy together, I return to the city of the Yadus. You remain here in Vraja, thinking that these visits are nothing but hallucinations, but it is not so.” (CC** [**2.13.152**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/13.152)**)**

*mora bhāgye mo viṣaye, tomāra je prema haye*  
*sei prema parama prabala*  
*lukāñā āmā āne, saṅga karāya tomā sane*

**“It is my good fortune that you have such great love for me. This love is very powerful and it thus brings me secretly to unite with you, and very shortly it will bring us together for real.”(CC** [**2.13.155**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/13.155)**)**

“Dear Radha, it is true that a woman who loves her man cannot live in his absence. If she goes on living it is only because she knows that he will not survive if she dies. You are my eternal beloved. I know very well that it is impossible for you to live if I stay away from you. That is why I worship Lord Narayan. He has given me the magic power to come to Vrindavan unbeknownst to anyone here. I come secretly to Vraja and make love to you; then I return to the city of the Yadus in the same way. You find yourself alone and still in Vraja, and so you think that you have only imagined my visit.

“It is my fortune that your love is so powerful that it forces me to come and visit you. It is so powerful that it brings me to you in secret and it will soon bring me back for real. Nearly all the enemies of the Yadu clan, the evil Kamsa’s allies, have been destroyed – only one or two are left. Once I have dealt with them, I will come to you, you can be sure of that. It may be only another two or three weeks, but then the rope of love that ties me to you will start to pull me to your side. When I am back in Vrindavan, I will once again be with you and we will enjoy our loving affairs day and night, just as we did before.”

Srimati Radharani’s eternal lover said all these things to bring her peace of mind, and to confirm his statements, he spoke a verse that convinced her that all her sufferings were not far off and she would soon be reunited with him forever. The verse is found in the Srimad Bhagavatam:

*mayi bhaktir hi bhūtānām*  
*amṛtatvāya kalpate*  
*diṣṭyā yad āsīn mat-sneho*  
*bhavatīnāṁ mad-āpanaḥ \|\|*

**“Whoever engages in my devotional service attains immortality, i.e., liberation or eternal felicity. You are especially blessed on account of the deep love you have for me, by which you will surely attain me. That is most auspicious. This love forcefully attracts me and makes me come quickly to your sides.” (SB** [**10.82.41**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-10/82.41)**)**

The meaning of this is that the strength of the gopis’ love for Krishna was the cause of their obtaining Krishna. The Lord is subject to the love of his devotees; devotion alone has the power to attract him. Devotion is glorified in all the scriptures – the Srutis, the Smritis and the Puranas and the Pancharatra. The *Māṭhara-śruti* says:

*bhaktir evainaṁ nayati*  
*bhaktir evainaṁ darśayati*  
*bhakti-vaśaḥ puruṣaḥ*  
*bhaktir eva bhūyasī*

**“Devotion attracts the Lord, devotion reveals him; the Lord is influenced by devotion. Nothing is more powerful than bhakti.” (*****Māṭhara-śruti*****)**

There are so many other glorifications of devotion in the scriptures: In the Gita, Krishna says, “By devotion alone can I be known in full.” In the Bhagavata, he says, “I can be captured by bhakti alone.” The Pancharatra says, “Devotion means serving the Lord of the senses with the senses.”

Krishna, who delights in loving relations, thinks as follows:

*aiśvarya jñānete saba jagat miśrita*  
*aiśvarya śithila preme nāhi mora prīta*  
*āmāre īśvara māne āpanāke hīna*  
*tāra preme vaśa āmi nā hai adhīna*

**“The whole world looks upon me with awe and veneration, but devotion which has been diluted by such consciousness of my majesty is not preferred by me. Someone who thinks of me as the supreme lord and controller and himself as being insignificant does not conquer me with his love and I never become subservient to him.” (CC** [**1.3.17-18**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-adi/3.17)**)**

Simply worshiping the Lord on the basis of scriptural injunctions according to the *vidhi-mārga* is a weaker form of devotion, because one is constantly aware of his supreme majesty. Krishna does no submit himself to the control of such weak devotion. On the other hand, those who worship Krishna in the *raga-mārga*, are able to make Krishna subordinate to their love. The intense and spontaneous absorption in the object of one=s adoration (*iṣṭa*) is called *rāga*. Devotion characterized by such *rāga* is called *rāgātmikā bhakti*. The devotion which follows in that spirit is called *rāgānugā bhakti*. Krishna appeared as Gauranga in order to preach this spontaneous, natural spirit of devotion.

Thakur Bhaktivinoda sang,

*vidhi-mārga-rata jane svādhīnatā ratna dāne*  
*rāga-mārge karān praveśa*  
*rāga-vaśavartī haiyā pārakīya bhāvāśraye*  
*labhe jīva kṛṣṇa-premāveśa*

**“To the person fixed in the regulative principles, The Holy Name gives the jewel of independence, placing him on the path of spontaneous devotion. That person, overcome by spontaneous attachment to the Lord, takes shelter of the** ***parakīyā*** **mood and goes on to become absorbed in love for Krishna.” (*****Śaraṇāgati*****)**

The Holy Name is a desire tree. Anyone who constantly chants the Holy Name receives the Name’s blessings. The greatest blessing of the Holy Name is the capacity to follow this path. The right to follow this path cannot be given by any artificially made-up process.

During the last part of his sojourn in this world, while living in the Gambhira, Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu constantly discussed the divine relations of Lord Krishna and His beloved gopis, hearing and chanting sacred texts in the company of His dearest companion, Svarupa Damodar. Today, while dancing in front of Lord Jagannath, He sang those same texts and relished those same feelings internally as Radharani’s *mahā-bhāva* washed over Him. Just like Radharani felt that she was taking Krishna back to Vraja with Her, so did Mahaprabhu, as He had perfectly adopted her nature.

All devotees who claim to follow in the footsteps of Svarupa Damodar and Rupa Goswami will be plunged into an ocean of joy on contemplating Lord Jagannath’s Rathayatra, for they will remember these pastimes of the Lord. Such devotees also dance in ecstasy as Krishna finally returns to Vrindavan to fulfill the deeply held desires of its residents.

## Chapter 18 - Other festivals and special clothes

## Sayanotsava

The *Nīlādri-mahodayam* mentions that the Sayanotsava or the sleeping ceremony of Lord Jagannath takes place on the Shukla Ekadasi of the month of Asharh, the same days as the return Rathayatra. Lord Vishnu sleeps for four months, which is the period known to devotees as the Chaturmasya, between the Sayana Ekadasi and the Shukla Ekadasi in month of Karttik.

After adhivasa rites, the representative images of Lakshmi Narayan, Ananta Vasudeva and Bhuvaneshwari representing Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra respectively are carried to the well-decorated sleeping chamber where they are placed with their heads towards east in baskets (*peri*) that have been decorated with beautiful flags, adorned with precious metals and ivory, and made fragrant with the grains of camphor. The Pujaris offer prayers to the deities and invite them to enjoy a peaceful sleep.

The following day, on Asharh Shukla Dvadasi, the image of Garuda is put to rest on over Lord Jagannath’s representative image where he will remain for the four month period.

## Dakshinayan Yatra

The Dakshinayana Yatra is observed in the Jagannath temple on Karkat Samkranti or the summer solstice, when the sun starts moving towards the south. After the morning rituals are performed, the images of the Deities are immersed in Panchamrita for Maha Snana. They are then smeared with perfumed substances such as aguru, sandalwood paste and kunkum and dressed in beautiful clothes. After arati and a fire sacrifice, the image of Lord Jagannath is taken from the Ratnavedi and carried towards the Jaya Vijaya door to the inner sanctum where appropriate rituals are performed. The Pujaris also worship the gatekeepers Jaya and Vijaya, and other deities like Kshetrapala, Ganesh and Kalaratri. After this service, Lord Jagannath returns to His throne.

Shravan

## Chitalagi Vesh

Chitalagi is an important celebration that takes place on the dark moon day of Shravan. The Orissan word *citā* literally means the decoration of the forehead with sandal paste, musk or gorachana, but is also used to refer to the jewelry or flowers that are sometimes used to adorn the forehead. In the case of Lord Jagannath, Balaram and Subhadra, it is used in this latter sense, for the deities have magnificient ornaments made of gold, diamond, sapphires and emeralds that are used in this way. Some call this Lord Jagannath’s “third eye.”

A goldsmith cleans the Chitas in the presence of temple officials and sevayats on the day before Amavasya. The next day, the Dayitas bring the Chitas to the Bhoga Mandap where they are offered to the Deities. Then after Maha Snana and Madhyahna Dhupa, the Pujaris place them on the foreheads of the four deities, Jagannath, Balabhadra, Subhadra and Sudarshan, who continue to wear them until the Snana Purnima when they are removed. Lord Balaram’s chita is made of emeralds, Subhadra’s of sapphires and Lord Purushottam’s chita is made of diamonds..

The *Nīlādri-mahodayam* tells Shravan Amavasya is the day that all the different kinds of jewels and precious metals came into existence, for it was on that day that the gods and demons churned the ocean. These precious metals and stones were immediately offered by the gods to Lord Vishnu who began to decorate Himself with them.

Two other books, *Śrī-tattva-nidhi* and *Ratna-tattvāvalī* tell another story about the beginnings of this custom. Once, the Lord in His Varaha incarnation was lifting the world, which had sunk down into the underworld, with his tusks. Because it was the dark moon day, everything was enveloped in darkness, so the goddess of the earth, Dharitri Devi, lit up the darkness with her diamonds, making it easier for the Lord to life up the earth. So, diamonds are offered to Lord Jagannath in memory of this occasion.

This day is widely celebrated in Orissa, where it is also known as Chitraka Parva. The Orissan people feed birds and insects with cakes known as chitraka (or *citau*). They draw a diamond figure with rice paint on the ground in their homes, worship it and then offer chitraka cakes to it as naivedya. Chitraka cakes are also offered to Lord Jagannath in the temple on this day.

A few days later, on the Shukla Panchami, the Lord is dressed in the Rahu Rekha Vesh, an ear decoration (*karṇa-patra*) that was also removed on the Snana Purnima.

## Jhulan Yatra

Shravan Shukla Dashami. Jhulan Yatra until Pratipad, a period of seven days.

Madan Mohan, Jagannath's representative deity, as well as Lakshmi and Vishwadhatri are placed on a decorative wooden swing in the Mukti Mandap (Jhulan Mandap).

## Baladeva Janmotsava

Balabhadra’s birthday ceremony is observed on the fuIl-moon day of Shravan, which is also Jhulan Purnima. After the morning puja and Maha Snana, Balabhadra is dressed in a special way with various kinds of ornaments, garlands and new clothes. Then a kalasa is installed in front of the deity and a special puja performed.

The priests request Lord Jagannath’s permission to allow His representative Sudarshan to leave the temple premises to perform a special ritual for Baladeva's appearance day. Sudarshan is taken to the ashrams of Narada, Angira, and Kanva. He is first taken around the Kalpa Bata tree on the temple grounds and then carried in a palanquin (*vimāna*) to the Markandeshwar temple.

At the Markandeya Sarovar, a special ceremony takes place. The sevayat known as the Vishayi supplies clay and one of the Sudha Suars models an image of Balabhadra from it. A Puja Panda then animates the figure with mantras and worships it with the five upacharas. After a full puja including a fire sacrifice, this image of Balabhadra is consecrated into the water while priests recite the Gayatri mantra. When the ceremony is completed, Sudarshan is carried back to the temple.

This day is also called Gahma Purnima. On this day, the deities Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra wear bracelets (*rakṣī*) made of gold and silk thread. There is some difference of opinion about the meaning of the word *gahmā.* Some say it signifies “ox,” and thus they worship the ox as the deity of agriculture on this day. Others say that there was a cow-killing demon named Gahma who was destroyed by Baladeva. In Orissan villages, Baladeva is worshiped with His plow and club as the deity who protects cows from the wicked Gahma and thus saves agriculture. People also worship cows, oxen, water-buffalo and other agricultural animals on this day.

Bhadra

## Svarnarekha Snana Utsava

This festival is performed on the Bhadra Krishna Panchami. The morning worship takes place as usual. Lord Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra are then given a special bath in Panchamrita and offered a ribbon of gold (*suvarṇa-rekhā*) three inches wide.

## Krishna Janmashtami

All the important events in Krishna’s life are celebrated in the Jagannath temple, so His birthday is observed on the Bhadra Krishna Ashtami, but celebrations start the day before and go on for several days. During this time Lord Jagannath is dressed in different ways related to Krishna’s Vrindavan pastimes and all the events surrounding Lord Krishna’s birth are dramatized in the temple courtyard.

The festival begins on the Saptami with Devaki Santvana Utsava, which means “the consolation of Devaki.” On this day, devotees commemorate the solace brought to Devaki by the gods led by Lord Brahma as she awaited the birth of her eighth child. Kamsa had killed her seven previous babies and Devaki fully expected him to kill her eighth also. In the second chapter of the Tenth Canto, one can read the prayers of the gods made to Krishna while he was still in Devaki’s womb. On this day, devotees remember Krishna’s mother Devaki, who gave birth to Krishna in Kamsa’s prison house.

In the evening of the Ashtami, the room where Devaki will give birth, called the Sutika Griha, is to be made ready for Krishna’s birth at midnight. The Puja Panda performs certain rituals before construction of a room made of bamboo and cloth is begun. Two armed door-keepers are placed at the doors of the Sutika Griha, or Krishna’s Janma Pith, to stand guard while a wooden image of the childbirth goddess Shashthi Devi is placed inside. A mandala twenty-seven inches across called the Janma Chakada is drawn. It has thirty-six sections, each painted a different color, with the center in the shape of a lotus flower. A waterpot representing Chakradhvaja is consecrated to the west side of the mandala. The *Nīlādri-mahodayam* designates all these preparations as a separate festival called the Sutika Griha Nirmanotsava

## Krishna Janmotsava

Temple servants of the Mahajan category enact the entire pastime of Krishna’s birth. One plays the role of Devaki and at midnight gives birth to Krishna in the form of the Madan Mohan deity. After the brass image of Madan Mohan “takes birth”, He is given a bath, His umbilical cord (which is made of chapati flour) is cut with a silver knife, honey is applied to the “wound” and the baby is given panchamrita as breast milk to drink. The newborn Madan Mohan is then placed in a cot for all to come and see.

After a little while, another Mahajan then takes the role of Krishna’s father Vasudeva and takes Madan Mohan to the house of Nanda in Vrindavan, which is set up near the Saraswati temple. Tradition holds that it rains every year on this day in Orissa in memory of Vasudeva’s walk through the rain to Vraja. Some members of the wrestling akhras in Puri take their little sons to the Bhargavi River, life them on their shoulders and carry them across, just like Vasudeva carried Krishna across the raging waters of the Yamuna.

The rituals (*jāta-karma*) following Krishna’s birth are also performed according to the scriptural regulations. The entire sequence of events relating to the birth of Lord Krishna is thus relived in Jagannath’s temple and elsewhere in the town of Puri.

It is well known that at the same time that Krishna took birth in Kaṁsa’s prison, Mahamaya appeared from the womb of Yashoda. Vasudeva then exchanged Krishna for Durga, as Krishna had ordered him. In the Jagannath temple, Mahamaya’s birth is also celebrated along with Krishna’s birth. Subhadra Devi represents Durga and hence is given special prayers and worshiped during the Durga Janmotsava.

The day following Krishna’s birth, the Krishna Navami of Bhadra, is called Nandotsava in commemoration of Nanda Maharaj’s celebrations at having a son. This event is also reenacted by Lord Jagannath’s sevaks. The Ramakrishna deities are laid on beautiful cots made of precious metals and then taken to Garuda where welcome ceremony (*bandāpanā*) is held. The Divine Brothers are rocked in a beautifully decorated. During this festival, Krishna’s parents and seniors like Devaki, Vasudeva, Nanda, Yashoda, Ugrasena, Rohini and Garga are worshiped.

## Avatar lila vidhi

For several days after Nandotsava, the events of Krishna’s life are dramatized by the temple sevaks and Jagannath, Balaram and Subhadra are dressed accordingly. During His time in Vraja, Lord Sri Krishna used to go to the forests with His companions and be dressed by them with colorful creepers, flowers and tender leaves. Two days after Janmashtami, that is, the tenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Bhadra, the Lord is dressed as a cowherd boy. This Vesh is marked by a series of performances meant to remind the devotees of Krishna’s childhood pastimes.

The following day, Lord Jagannath is dressed as the chastiser of Kaliya, the venomous viper. This is known as His Kaliya Daman Vesh. Madan Mohan, Jagannath’s representative deity, is taken in a procession to Markandeya Sarovar where this lila is reenacted.

On the Dvadasi, more attention is given to Balaram, who is dressed as the killer of the Pralamba demon. The special clothing used in these three days of festivity is sponsored by the Gajapati himself. On the Trayodasi, the Lords are dressed as Krishna and Balaram in Vraja.

## Saptapuri Amavasya

This festival, unique to Orissa, observed on the Bhadra Amavasya. Lord Vishnu’s weapons like Panchajanya, Sudarshan, Kaumudaki and Kidvalani are worshiped. In the temple, Lord Jagannath is offered seven kinds of cakes (*sapta puri*), shaped like these weapons.

## Lakshmi Vrata or Rishi Panchami Vrata

Lakshmi Vrata starts on the Bhadra Shukla Panchami and continues for sixteen days. Lakshmi Devi receives Lord Jagannath’s *ājñā-mālā* and given an offering of fruits. Then, wearing various types of precious ornaments, she is taken to the Markandeshwar temple where she herself observes the Rishi Panchami Vrata. Lakshmi there hears the account of Rishi Panchami Vrata according to *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa* and then welcomes the seven Rishis -- Kasyapa, Atri, Bharadvaja, Vishwamitra, Gautama, Jamadagni and Vasishtha. Elsewhere the seven sages are worshiped near other holy rivers or ponds. Lakshmi then returns to the Boro Deul accompanied by the women devotees who intend to take up the vrata. One of the special rituals performed on this day is a Shraddha ceremony to the Rishis held on the twenty-two steps inside Singha Dwar.

## Parshwa Parivartan Ekadasi

Lord Vishnu’s Parshwa Parivartan takes place on the Bhadra Shukla Ekadasi. Lord Jagannath goes to sleep in the month of Asharh, so the Chaturmasya is halfway complete. It is midnight for the Lord and so He turns over in His sleep..

On that day, regular puja is carried out. Then, in the evening, Madan Mohan is brought to Lord Jagannath to receive the *ājñā-mālā,* after which the Pandas place Him in a palanquin. He is first taken to the banyan tree and then circumambulates the temple. Bhoga is offered to Madan Mohan at the Jaya Vijaya door and then He is taken to his own shrine south of the main temple.

After the Sandhya Dhupa, the temple priest starts a Homa ritual in the Ananta-Purushottam temple. After Lord Jagannath’s Boro Sringar Vesh, a group of temple servants including the Mudirasta, Behera, Khuntia, Garabadu, Palia Mekap, Akhanda Mekap and Tadau enters His bedroom. According to the *Nīlādri-mahodaya*, a Mudirath of the Agnisharma branch opens the basket (*peri*) in which the images of the deities have been placed for the Chaturmasya period. He offers flowers to the Deities and then turns them over in their bed. The pujakas separate the deities and offer *puṣpāñjali* again before closing the basket again for another two months.

## Pavitraropan Utsava and Vamana Janmotsava

The Pavitraropan Utsava is held on the day following Parshwa Parivartan Ekadasi. This is also the appearance day of Lord Vamana, the fifth of the Lord’s ten incarnations. In this incarnation, the Lord appeared as a dwarf Brahmin. \[The word *vāmana* means dwarf.\]

In Orissa, this day also marked the beginning of the royal year of the kings of Puri. It is sometimes called the first day of the “human year” (*mānuṣa varṣa*). It is also called Sunia in Orissan. A thousand fire sacrifices are called for on this day to assure auspiciousness for the whole year. Traditionally, the Karans performed a special puja on this day and began a new volume of the *Mādalā-pañjī.*

The Deities are worshiped with more elaborate food and Maha Snana. The Varuna deity is also given special worship and cake offerings. After the Madhyahna Dhupa, the Pujaris ask Lord Jagannath for permission to observe Vamana’s appearance day. Lord Jagannath is dressed in His Bali Vamana Vesh and takes on the appearance of a sadhu. The golden image of Vamana is carried to the Garuda stambha and there dressed as a brahmachari, like Vamana Deva in his pastimes. From there, the image is taken to the shrine of Goddess Durga, who represents his mother Aditi, situated in northeastern corner of the compound. Vamana and His mother are worshiped together with the panchopacharas. At the end of the observances, Vamana image is taken back to His own shrine.

Naturally, the devotees remember the story of Vamana and how He deceived Bali Maharaj on this day as recounted in the eighth canto of the Srimad Bhagavatam. Besides this, another legend is told about Vamana in the *Nīlādri-mahodayam*. Trisanku was a great saintly king and devotee of the Lord who had achieved the ability to go to Swarga in his self-same body. As he approached the effulgent heavens, however, he began to feel proud and so immediately became disqualified to enter. The king was about to be punished by the wrath of the gods when Lord Vishnu in the form of Vamana helped him escape. This festival thus reminds the devotees that Lord Vamana protects His devotees from the dangers of pride.

The appearance day of Jayadeva Goswami is also celebrated on this day.

## Indra Govinda Utsava (Festival of Indra and Govinda)

This festival, which is unique to Orissa, is also called Shakradhvaja Utsava, Indra-Jagratotsava or Indu Purnima Utsava. It begins from Bhadra Shukla Dvadasi and continues for seven days. The Bhadra Purnima, however, is the main celebration day.

According to the *Nīlādri-mahodayarn,* this festival begins with the worship of Varuna and a fire sacrifice. Then a symbolic representation of Indra is prepared from twenty-five sticks of khadira, champa and sala wood. This representation, called “Shakradhvaja” (Indra’s flag), is worshiped with panchopachara. Then offerings are made to the gods of the eight directions.

During the period of this festival, the Jagannath temple is conceived of as Swarga and the outer part of the temple is taken to be Martya (earth). Indra, the king of the gods in heaven worships Govinda (Lord Jagannath), who has descended to the earth. On the full-moon day, the Dol Govinda murti representing Lord Jagannath is carried to the outer part of the temple, or Martya. In the meantime, Indra is brought there from the Hara Chandi Sahi on the back of his elephant, Airavata. The Shakradhvaja is worshiped alongside Dol Govinda and Sudarshan and, after seven days’ worship, is thrown into the water.

According to the *Nīlādri-mahodayam*, the purpose of this festival is to assure rains for the growing of crops. It commemorates the occasion when Devaraja Indra was placed on his heavenly throne and swore allegiance to the Supreme Lord Vishnu.

Ashwin

## Durga Puja

Durga Puja Utsava begins on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Ashwin. The golden image of Jayadurga presents herself to the goddess Subhadra and asks for permission to observe the festival. Durga is given abhishek with a thousand pots of water, after which she is installed on the altar. The image of the Goddess Durga is then taken to a beautifully decorated altar (mandapa) situated to the east of the temple. There, various rituals are performed. Then the image of Madhava comes to join Durga on her altar where they are worshiped together.

Other rites are performed on the Navami and Dasami. The Ashwin Shukla Dasami is particularly important, and is known as Vijaya Dasami or Aparajita Dasami. On this day, Durga and Madhava circumambulate the temple of Lord Jagannath and are then taken to the temple of Ardhasani or Mausi Ma, where they are again worshiped with Panchopachar before being returned to their shrines in the Sri Mandir..

In general, Subhadra is the representative of Shakti in the Jagannath temple. However, Durga Puja continues in the temple of Bimala situated there inside Sri Mandir. According to scholars, Bimala represents the Shakti of Jagannath and the Pitha is hence called Bimala Pitha.

Something about the sacrifice of a goat at the Bimala temple.

Lord Jagannath is dressed in royal garb (Raja Vesh) to celebrate Ramachandra’s victory over Ravana on Ashwin Shukla Dasami, also known as Dashahara or Vijaya Dasami.

Rajendrabhishek

On Jyeshtha Shukla Dasami, the swearing-in ceremony is performed as Krishna ascends the throne of Raja Rajendra. After completion of evening worships, the image of Madana Mohan (Krishna) is taken to Lord Jagannath. The *ājñā-mālā* of the deity is then given to Madan Mohan wbo also represents Krishna. Then, deity Madan Mohan mounting on the chariot, Nandighosa goes round the temple in order to exhibit the actions of a conqueror. Thinking that the Lord has won all the states, His swear-in-ceremony is instituted. Finally, the deity is worshiped and the *bandāpanā* ritual is performed.

Karttik

## Damodar Vrata and the Radha Damodar Vesh

The month of Karttik, measured from the beginning of the dark fortnight and ending with the full moon, is known to Vaishnavas as the month of Damodar and is celebrated with lights and special rituals. The Vaishnavas follow specific religious vows for the month; they bathe early in the morning throughout the month, without rubbing their bodies with oil. They abstain from oil, meat, and wine, and some even eat only an austere gruel known as Havishyanna.

Puri in partcular is filled with the sounds of puja for the entire month of Karttika, as many pilgrims come to follow the vrata in the holy town. It is especially favored by widows, who rise at four in the morning to bathe and begin their devotional observances. They eat no food cooked at home, but only maha-prasad from the temple, and that but once a day.

For the first twenty-five days of the month of Karttik, Lord Jagannath is dressed as Damodar and Subhadra as Radharani. Many dancing gopis made of sola (spongewood) and jari (gold thread) are placed on the altar in front of their Lordships.

The following legend is told about how the Radha Damodar Vesh first started. Once a Taluccha Mahapatra temple priest had an affair with a lady friend. It was his duty to bring Lord Jagannath’s prasadi flowers to the king, and one day the king found a woman's long black hair in these flowers. He became furious and went to the temple with the intention of punishing the priest for engaging in impure activities while serving the Deities.

In the meantime, however, the Talucchon Mahapatra was desperately looking for a way to save himself. He had an idea: he put a wig on Lord Jagannath in the hope that he could explain the black hair away. The king was no fool and saw what was going on. He pulled at the wig, hoping to rip it off and prove that it was fake. But miraculously, Lord Jagannath began to bleed from his head. The astonished king thought that the priest’s love affair must be very pure for the Lord Himself to intervene and so he forgave him. In celebration of the Lord’s own love for Radharani, this king inaugurated the Radha Damodar Vesh.

Balaram wears the Harihar Vesh throughout the month of Karttik. Hari refers to Vishnu and Hara to Lord Shiva, so Harihar is a combined form of Lord Vishnu and Shiva. There are temples to this combined form of Vishnu and Shiva in many places in South India, such as Tirupati and the Ayappa temple in Kerala. There is even an ancient Harihar deity in Nabadwip Dham. When Balaram is dressed as Harihar, then half of his body is blackened.

## Utthapanotsava

The Shukla Ekadasi of Karttik marks the end of the Chaturmasya period during which Lord Vishnu has been sleeping. It is thus called the “awakening festival”, as Utthapanotsava or Prabodhan Yatra.

The Puja Panda, Pati, Mudirasta, Tadau Pashupalaka are the temple sevaks who take part in this festival. The sleeping deities are awakened after the morning worship (Sakala Dhupa) and given a special worship with the full sixteen upacharas. On the same Shukla Ekadasi, “Lakshmi-Damodar” worship is performed with the special rituals of *bandāpanā* and Maha Snana.

The next day, on the Dvadasi, Garuda is also awakened, bathed with Panchamrita and offered worship.

## Panchuka

The last five days of Karttika month, from Ekadasi to Purnima, are known as Panchuka. Many devotees perform some austerities during this period, giving up some of their favorite foods. Starting with the Ekadasi, the Lord is dressed in different costumes on each of these days, ending with the very opulent Rajadhiraja Vesh.

On the Dvadasi, Lord Jagannath is dressed as Vamana. Many visitors to the temple are surprised to see that the Lord somehow looks smaller than usual when dressed as the dwarf incarnation..

On the Ekadasi, the Lord is dressed as Trivikram. The name Trivikram refers to the form that Vamana took, when he made His three steps to take possession of the entire universe. It also indicates that the Lord is master of the three spheres of heavens, earth and underworld. The Trivikram Vesh is a heroic dress, with the Lord holding weapons like the sword, conch, spinning chakra and club. The Lord wears this dress on Karttik Shukla Trayodasi.

Tradition holds that the Trivikram Vesh was started by the Pancha Sakhas, or “five friends.” Though these five Vaishnavas are not considered orthodox by the followers of Lord Chaitanya, they were very influential in spreading Vaishnava practices throughout Orissa, especially through their writing in the Orissan language. Atibori Jagannath Das, who translated the Bhagavatam into Orissan, is generally considered to be foremost of the five.

On the 14th day of the bright fortnight in the month of Karttik, the Lord is dressed as the half-man, half-lion incarnation. Nrisingha is the fourth of Lord Krishna’s ten important incarnations.

On the day of Karttik Purnima, which is also called Rasa Purnima, Lord Krishna’s circle dance with the gopis is celebrated. The Damodara vrata observed throughout the month of Karttik comes to an end. The Deities are dressed in their Rajadhiraja royal garb as on Vijaya Dasami, but this time Jagannath is Krishna Himself and holds a golden flute. This is the basically the same as their Suna Vesha, with gold ornaments, such as the palms made of gold that are fastened to their hands.

The temple-servants known as Mahajans reenact the dice games that Radha and Krishna play in Vrindavan. The vrata is concluded with a feast called Chadakhai.

The devotees bathe in the sea early in the morning of Karttik Purnima and then go around the temple of Lord Jagannath with the Ramakrishna deity. They then circumambulate Puri Dham, from Angirashram to Yameshwar.

In the evening of Karttik Purnima, the lamp-lighting ceremony known as Dipotsava is observed in the temple. After the Sandhya Dhupa, evening worship, the image of Narayan is taken to the Lakshmi temple where ghee lamps are lit. Devotees also go to offer worship to the great banyan tree (Kalpa Bata) and Ganesh, in front of whom twenty-one lamps (dipas) are lit and arranged in seven lines.

## Parashuram or Nagarjun Vesh

The lunar calendar is complex because the lunar and solar years do not correspond exactly. This means not only that every few years an extra month called Purushottam has to be added to the calendar, but also that extra days must from time to time be added to the months. Thus there are sometimes six rather than five lunar days between Ekadasi and Purnima at the end of Karttik month. When such an extra day is called for, the Lord wears the Parashuram or Nagarjun Vesh. The last time this happened, as of this writing, was in 1994.

Parashuram was the sixth incarnation of Lord Vishnu. It is not known why some people call it Nagarjuna Vesh. The only widely known Nagarjuna is the famous Buddhist philosopher who lived for some time in Orissa nearly two thousand years ago. How this Vesh is connected to him is unknown.

Agrahayan (Margashira)

## Shraddha Vesh

Throughout the month of Margashira, Lord Jagannath wears an austere dress known as Shraddha Vesh. Hindus perform an important religious duty called Shraddha annually on the anniversary of the father’s death. This usually includes some rites of purification, offering of food in the names of the departed souls and feeding one’s blood-relations, friends and the poor. During the Shraddha period of mourning, one is not supposed to wear fine or sewn cloth. When Lord Jagannath wears this dress, He looks grave and solemn. On three different days in the month of Margashira, Lord Jagannath performs the Shraddha of His fathers in the incarnations of Krishna and Ramachandra, namely Nanda, Vasudeva and Dasharath.

## Kshetra Bhraman Utsava

The *Nīlādri-mahodayarn* mentions that the Kshetra Bhraman Utsava is observed on the Krishna Panchami in the month of Margashira. More details of this festival are given in chapter 21 on other holy places in Sri Kshetra.

## Prathamashtami

This festival takes place on the Krishna Ashtami of Margashira, known in Orissa as Prathamashtami (“the first ashtami”). It is also celebrated with great pomp in the Lingaraj temple of Bhubaneswar. This festival is dedicated to the well-being of the oldest son in the family. Thus, Lord Balaram receives special treatment on this day. Shashthi or Jyeshtha Devi is considered to be the protector of the eldest son, so she is also worshiped in the temple on this day.

## Navanna

Each year, the temple astrologers specify the date of Navanna sometime in the month of Margashira. The term *navānna* means “new rice” and refers to the offering to the Deities of food prepared from the newly harvested rice. This function is observed in all Orissan homes, where a feast of cakes and sweet preparations is consumed.

## Dipotsava

Dipotsava means “festival of lamps.” It is celebrated in the temple on the Krishna Chaturdasi of Margashira. Twenty-eight ghee lamps are arranged in three lines. While they are being lit, the priests humbly entreat the Deities to accept the offering. Starting on the Ekadasi, Lord Jagannath’s Pujaris light lamps all around the temple, on the ground as well as on the roof. Lamps are also lit before the image of Lord Jagannath and placed in front of Him, while other priests sing Vedic hymns and offer the five ingredients of worship.

## Odhan Shashthi

With the onset of the cold weather, Jagannath is dressed in winter clothes known as Ghodalagi Vesh. The day that Jagannath is given a shawl, or *oḍhana*, is called the Odhan Shashthi or Pravaran Shashthi, the Agrahayan Shukla Shashthi. For one month, because of this shawl, only the Lord’s eyes and mouth can be seen. *Prāvaraṇa* means “covered.”

The ceremonies start on the previous day with an adhivasa ritual known as Vastradhivas, when Lord Jagannath’s winter garments are made ready. Twenty-one new clothes of white, black and blood-red colour are brought for the adhivasa rituals. The Pandas recite mantras to make the garments sacred. Finally, they worship Ganesh, the Dikpalas, Kshetrapalas and the Goddess Durga.

On the Shashthi, after Lord Jagannath has been bathed, the new winter garments are taken in a procession around the temple three times.The temple servants named Mudirasta decorate the deities with ornaments and the winter garments, after which hymns and prayers are offered to the Lord.

From the Pravaran Utsava day up to Vasanta Panchami, Lord Jagannath wears garments of a different color on different days of the week, according to the planet that governs that day. Every Monday, Lord Jagannath is clad in white clothes with black spots to show a connection to the moon. Likewise, on Tuesday, He wears red (the color of Mangala) and on Wednesday, blue (that of Budha).

The winter cloth is called *māṛuwā vastra*, because it has not been washed and still has *māṛa* (weaver’s starch) in it. The story is told in the Chaitanya Bhagavata that Mahaprabhu’s associate Pundarika Vidyanidhi was a pure *sad-ācārī,* attached to the proper etiquette of Vaishnavism. When he observed this custom, he did not feel happy about it as he felt such cloth was impure. He condemned Lord Jagannath’s servants for continuing this practice and was subsequently chastised by Lords Jagannath and Balaram themselves, who came to him in a dream and slapped him on each cheek. Lord Jagannath said,

“There is no end to your offensiveness. Just as there is no question of pure and impure in My case, the same holds true for My servants. You are staying here; you should know all this. If you thought that it was impure \[here in Puri\], then why did you stay at all? Go home then, if you want to maintain your purity.” (Chaitanya Bhagavata 3.10.131-2)

Since people tend to need more food in winter, for the month following Odhana Sasthi, Lord Jagannath is given an extra offering at dawn, called Pahili Bhoga. It consists of Pahanti Khichuri, which is made with rice and moog dal, ghee and salt, served with fried vegetables and sweet rice (*khiri*) made with raisins. It is said that the Pahili Bhoga is cooked by Yashoda, whereas all the other offerings are cooked by Lakshmi Devi.

In general, service to Lord Jagannath is more difficult during this month because all the morning rituals like Abakash have to be completed before sunrise.

Paush

## Chutankura Pradan Vidhi

Chutankura (*cutāṅkura*) refers to mango buds and shoots. In Orissa, mango trees start to sprout new shoots in the month of Paush, so on the day of Paush Amavashya, these are offered to Lord Jagannath after the Lord’s morning worship and bath. A special bhoga of beautiful cakes of circular shape called *gaiṅṭha* is also offered on this day. This day is also called Bakula Amavashya.

## Pushyabhishek Yatra

The Pushyabhishek festival takes place on the fulI-moon day of Paush. This event is also known as Ramabhishek as it commemorates the coronation of Lord Ramacandra. Dramatic performances of the Ramayan are also staged as a part of the festivities.

Adhivasa rites for Pushyabhishek are held on the eve of Paush Purnima. The Bhoga Mandap is cleaned and a decorative canopy is erected there. Under it, eighty-seven jugs fulI of water as well as twenty-one pots of cow ghee are placed. The temple priest performs the ritual and after which the Tadau closes the door of the Bhoga Mandap. After Boro Sringar Bhoga a mirror is placed on the Ratna Singhasan during the period of performance of adhivasa rites.

On the day of Abhiseka, normal puja takes place in the morning, including Mailam. The door of the Bhoga Mandap is opened and the ghee readied in the adhivasa is melted with holy fire fetched ftom Jagannath’s kitchen. It is mixed with water and taken to the Ratna Singhasan where it is poured from a copper bowl onto the mirror reflecting the image of Lord Jagannath.

After this special bath, the Deities are given new clothes to wear. Lakshmi is then made to take the role of Sita while one the Bhitarcho Mahapatra plays Lakshman and holds the royal umbrella. The Bhandar Mekap represents Hanuman and holds the umbrella stand.

## Uttarayan Yatra

Uttarayan Yatra takes place on the Makara Sankranti, or winter solstice, when the sun starts moving towards the north. The temple servants who take part in the function are Ghatuari, Talicha Mahapatra, Puja Panda, Patri Badu, Suar Badu, Gara Badu, Panti Badu, Hadap Nayak, Pati and Mudirasta.

The Makara Sankranti festivities are preceded by the Tandu1adhivas, in which new *śāli* rice is prepared and offered to the deities in a ceremonial style. After the evening dhupa, Madan Mohan is taken around the temple thrice to the accompaniment of music and dancing. This event is called Navanka Bhraman.

On the Makara Sankranti itself, the morning puja goes on as usual, with Maha Snana. After the midday rituals are complete, three plates fulI of the same *śāli* rice are taken around the temple three times and finally placed before the Deities. Ghee, curd, sugar, coconut, camphor, etc., are added to rice.

Magh

## Padma Vesh

During the winter, lotus flowers disappear from the tanks and reservoirs in Orissa. They start to reappear in the month of Magh, so Lord Jagannath is dressed in the Padma Vesh.

## Vasanta Panchami

This festival is observed on the Magha Shukla Panchami. On this day, puja to the temple Panji – the annual astrological calculations -- is performed in the Saraswati temple situated in the Kurma Berha. Vasanta Panchami is also Saraswati Puja, when the goddess of learning is worshiped.

Vasanta Panchami marks the unofficial beginning of spring. Lord Jagannath’s winter clothes, that He wore every day since the Odhan Shasthi are removed and He is dressed in the Chancheri Vesh. In the forenoon of Vasanta Panchami, rituals are performed for the Lord’s winter sringar. Then, the Vasantika Dolotsava or Vasanta Gundicha Utsava begins. The image of Lord Jagannath is placed on a beautiful chariot which is dragged upto Yajnavedi of the temple. Such a car festival held in the Spring season is called Vasanta Gundicha Yatra of Lord Jagannath.

This is also the beginning of the Dola Utsava or Holi, which lasts until the Phalguni Purnima. It is characterised by the throwing of colored powder over the heads of other people. to enjoy this pastime.

On the day of Phalgun Shukla Ekadasi, the routine rituals of morning Puja, Maha Snana and Madhyahna Puja are carried out in the temple. Garuda Dhvaja is also worshiped on that day. Starting on Vasanta Pancami, Lord Jagannath in His Dol Govinda form go with Saraswati and Lakshmi to enjoy his spring outing to the Jhulan Mandap in the Jagannath Vallabh Gardens. This Vasanta Bhraman Mahotsava may be observed for anywhere from three to seven days.

## Gajoddharan Vesh

The Lord’s lila of saving the elephant king is commemorated on the Maghi Purnima. In the eighth canto of Srimad Bhagavatam, it is told how Lord Vishnu saved a great elephant king from a dangerous crocodile. Trapped in the jaws of this gigantic beast, the elephant had no recourse other than to take shelter of the Lord of the universe. His prayers immediately moved the Lord to compassion and He hurled his discus at the crocodile and cut him to pieces. When dressed as the savior of the elephant, Lord Jagannath moves the Vaishnavas with a consciousness of his compassion.

*vātsalyād abhaya-pradāna-samayād ārtārti-nirvāpaṇād*  
*audāryād agha-śoṣaṇād agaṇita-śreyaḥ-pada-prāpaṇāt \|*  
*sevyaḥ śrī-patir eva sarva-jagatām ete yataḥ sākṣiṇaḥ*  
*prahlādaś ca vibhīṣaṇaś ca karirāṭ pāñcalya-halyā dhruvaḥ \|\|*

**There are so many reasons to love the Lord, and so many who have loved him for those reasons: Prahlada, because the Lord cared for him like a father, Vibhishan, because he promised him freedom from fear, The king of elephants, because the Lord saved him from distress, Draupadi, because of his magnanimity, Ahalya, because the Lord forgave her all her sins, and Dhruva, because the Lord gave him everything he desired. (Padyāvalī,** [**7**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/padyavali-rg/7)**)**

*vyādhasyācaraṇaṁ dhruvasya ca vayo vidyā gajendrasya kā*  
*kubjāyāḥ kim u nāma rūpam adhikaṁ kiṁ tat sudāmno dhanam \|*  
*vaṁśaḥ ko vidurasya yādavapater ugrasya kiṁ pauruṣaṁ*  
*bhaktyā tuṣyati kevalaṁ na ca guṇair bhakti-priyo mādhavaḥ \|\|*

**What was the strict pious life of the hunter? and where Dhruva’s seniority? What was the learning of the elephant king? and what beauty did Kubja possess? Did Sudama possess vast amounts of wealth? What was Vidura’s pedigree? and what great heroism did the Yadu king Ugrasena show? Ah, but Madhava is pleased only by a person’s devotion and not by their great qualities. Devotion is what is dear to Him. (Padyāvalī,** [**8**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/padyavali-rg/8)**)**

*atandrita-camū-pati-prahita-hastam asvīkṛta-*  
*praṇīta-maṇi-pādukaṁ kim iti vismṛtāntaḥ puram \|*  
*avāhana-pariṣkriyaṁ pataga-rājam ārohataḥ*  
*kari-pravara-bṛṁhite bhagavatas tvarāyai namaḥ \|\|*

**All glories to Lord Vishnu’s haste in coming to the aid of the great elephant king on hearing his roar of distress -- in such a hurry was He that He mounted the king of birds Garuda, ignoring the helping hand extended by the army chief, astonishing the women of His harem by not accepting the jewelled sandals they offered Him, and without even waiting for a seat to be placed on Garuda’s back. (Padyāvalī,** [**50**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/padyavali-rg/50)**)**

## Dola Yatra

The Dola Yatra lasts for five days from the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Phalgun to the fuIl-moon day of the month. It includes Phalgunotsava, Vahni Utsava and Dolakeli Utsava.

The first function observed during Dola is the Phalgunotsava which continues for three or five days beginning from Phalgun Shukla Dasami. On this day, mailam ceremony is performed and the deities are decorated with red clothes. During this period, Lord Jagannath is worshiped along with the image of Govinda. Each day, after completion of midday worships, the images of the two deities (Jagannath and Govinda) are brought together and worshiped with panchopachar. White, red and yellow coloured powders mixed with sandal paste and camphor are thrown upon the deities from head to foot.

On Chaturdasi, the image of Dola Govinda is taken in a procession to the Snana Mandap for a bath. After being given His bath, He is taken round the temple seven times before it is brought to the Dola Mandap. Here again, the image is moved seven times round the altar, seven times round the pillars and also seven times round the upper part of the altar. Once the deity has taken His position on the Dola Mandap, the Vahni Utsava or fire sacrifice is begun inside the Dola Mandap. The Homa ritual is performed by 108 oblations made with the *aṣṭākṣara-mantra.* After the final oblation or *pūrṇāhuti* is made, the fire is extinguished. Lord Govinda circumambulates the fire seven times before leaving the area to return to His shrine.

The Dola Mandap is a white-washed stone construction with sixteen pillars situated to the east of the Boro Deul.. For the occasion, it is decorated with fans and beautiful flags. Figures of spring-birds such as the cuckoo and parrot, are painted on it to create the atmosphere of spring. Two magnificent altars are prepared and decorated swings suspended so that the deities can enjoy swinging there on the next day.

On the full-moon day, the image of Govinda (Dolagovinda) is taken to Lord Jagannath. The Goddesses Vishwadhatri and Rama accompany Govinda to the Dola Mandap. The deities go around the temple of Lord Jagannath seven times. They are then seated on the Navel Cutting Mandap where they are bathed. They put on new clothes and are worshiped in the five Upacāras. This is followed by seven more circumambulations before these deities are brought to the Dola Mandap to enjoy swinging. This is a very festive occasion celebrated with dance and music.

After the deities are offered a good swing, three Dhupas (the morning, mid-day and evening) are performed. The deities go round the swing throne seven times and then they leave for the temple.

Before entering into the Jagannath temple, the deities make circuit of it seven times and wait for sometime at Saraswati's temple, where Sitala Manohi ritual is performed. After that the Vimana is brought to the store-room, some more rituals are performed and the deities finally are taken to their respective places. On this day, Lord Jagannath holds Raja Vesh. Offering of green mangoes to the Govinda and Vishwadhatri is one of the main features of Dola Yatra.

## Rama Janmotsava

The birth of Rama is enacted in the temple of Jagannath on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Chaitra. This day is popularly known as Rama Navami. Prearrangements are made on the previous day. After the Sandhya Dhupa, a special Bhoga called Jeuda is offered to the deities. The Sandhya Dhupa is followed by the Garbhodaka Vandapana ritual. The image of Rama is lodged beside that of Lord Jagannath.

Rama Navami begins with the regular morning worships, followed by Maha Snana and Madhyahna Puja. After taking bath, the deities wear beautiful garments and precious ornaments. The image of Rama is then taken to Lord Jagannath and prayers are offered there to beg orders for holding Rama Janmotsava. The purana mentions that the image of Rama is made of gold and is magnificent to look. After birth, this image is washed with Panchamrita. The temple servants called Mahajans reenact Ramachandra’s birth, playing the roles of Dasharath and Kaushalya. This is followed by the performance of birth rituals known as *jāta-karma.*

On each of the following days, Ramachandra’s different pastimes are enacted on the temple grounds. On Dasami, it is Ramachandra’s Yajna lila; on the Ekadasi, Sita's marriage with Rama; the Dvadasi, it is Ramachandra’s banishment to the forest; on Trayodasi Sita is stolen by Ravana after Lakshman has been deluded by the illusory deer; on the Chaturdasi, Hanuman burns Lanka, and on the full moon day, Rama defeats Ravana and brings Sita back to Ayodhya.

Throughout the town, there are also colorful festivals celebrating Lord Ramachandra’s appearance day in the various neighborhoods known as Sahis. These continue for nine days, with the performance of Rama lila held in different neighborhoods each evening. This is called Sahi Yatra.

## Damanaka Yatra

This is a spring festival with close connection to the Jagannath Vallabha gardens. It takes place in the month of Chaitra after Rama Janmotsava, when the Damanaka plant (*artemisia indica*), a type of fragrant sagebrush, is offered to the deities.

The *Nīlādri-mahodayam* explains the origins of this festival as follows. Once there was a demon named Damanaka, who threatened to destroy the three worlds. Lord Vishnu killed the demon on the Chaitra Shukla Chaturdasi. The Lord’s divine touch transformed the demon this fragrant plant, the flowers of which were made into a garland for His pleasure. The flower became one of His favorites and the occasion is remembered each year with this festival.

The festival also recalls Krishna’s stealing of the parijata tree from the heavenly abode of Indra on behalf of Satyabhama. The tree was then taken and transplanted in Satyabhama’s garden in Dwaraka, just as the damanaka bushes were transplanted in the Jagannath temple.

On the other hand, the *Bhaviṣya-purāṇa* states that Cupid is to be worshiped with the Damanaka flower. Indeed, another name for this festival is Madan (or Ananga) Chaturdasi or Madan Bhanji (“the breaking of Cupid”). The festival is significant as this worship of the divine Cupid is a way to control one’s passions.

The festival begins on the Chaitra Shukla Dvadasi with the Kandarpadhivasa at the Jagannath Vallabha Math. The representative deities of the Lord are worshiped along with Satyabhama.\[102\] Permission is requested to hold the festival and Lord Jagannath’s *ājñā-mālās* are given to the images of Ramakrishna and Kama Deva (Kandarpa).

The next day, Ramakrishna and a picture of Kandarpa are taken by palanquin in a procession to Jagannath Vallabha Math where a fire sacrifice is performed for the satisfaction of Kamadeva. Kamadeva is worshiped with the five *upacāras.*

According to the *Nīlādri-mahodayam,* the Damanaka Yatra would take place on a beautifully decorated mandap east of the Jagannath temple. After the completion of the evening worships, a bed of sand would be made and twenty-one damanaka plants, plucked earlier in the Jagannath Vallabha gardens, would be secretly replanted there. Krishna, Rama and Vishwadhatri are worshiped on the mandap and the plants offered to them.

The next day, on the Chaitra Shukla Chaturdasi, after Lord Jagannath’s morning worship and bathing rituals, the Archaka would go to the adhivasa-house and take the Damanaka plants covered with cloth, carry them around the temple three times and then place them on the three deities.

In actual practice, however, the festival is celebrated in a somewhat modified fashion. The damanaka plants are plucked earlier and replanted in the Jagannath Vallabba Gardens before the arrivaI of the image of Ramakrishna. Ramakrishna are taken to the Jhulan Mandap, where He is given Gandharva Puja and bhoga. Then, without any fanfare, the temple servants carry the two deities into the garden to silently steal the flower shrubs. In all, about twelve of these flower bushes are uprooted and given to the two deities who then return to the temple.\[103\]

Ramakrishna make the return journey to the temple by palanquin. Reaching the temple, the palanquin is placed under the great banyan tree from where He started. After the Boro Sringar Bhoga, the *ājñā-mālās* are offered to Lakshmi, Saraswati and Madan Mohan and then brougbt to Bhoga Mandap. There, the Pujaris fix three Damanaka plants on the arms of the three deities. The function goes with the Panchopachar worship of the deities.

Vaishakh

## Mahavishuva Sankranti

The *Nīlādri-mahodayam* includes the descriptions of the rituals performed on first day of the month of Vaishakh, the beginning of the Orissan new year, which is is popularly known as Mesha Sankranti or Mahavisuva Sankranti. It is also Hanuman’s appearance day.

The temple of Lord Jagannath observes this day with special offerings to the deities. The day begins with morning worships followed by the Deities’ Maha Snana. The deities are given new clothes and many precious ornaments to wear. Different types of cakes prepared from rice are offered to them.

There are many more Vesh but it is not possible to present an account of each and every Vesh here. It is the local experience that particular groups of pilgrims and devotees are fond of particular Veshs and on those days, they congregate in a state of profound devotional fervor to offer their prayers to the Lord

## Chapter 19 - Nava Kalevara - Lord Jagannath’s new body\[104\]

Every few years, a special festival named Nava Kalevara is held in Jagannath Puri. The words *nava-kalevara* mean “new body.” On this occasion, Lord Jagannath and the three other deities on the altar with wooden forms undergo a change of bodies.

The normal period between Nava Kalevara ceremonies is every twelve or eighteen years, but there are exceptions. Over the past 150 years, the period between Nava Kalevara celebrations have generally been longer: changes of Jagannath’s body recorded in the *Mādalā-pañjī* have taken place in 1853, 1877, 1904, 1931, 1950, 1969, 1977, and 1996.

Lord Jagannath performs the pastime of manifesting a new body through His Yogamaya potency in order to show mercy on the devotees by giving them a special opportunity to serve Him. In this way, He destroys their sins and increases their joy. Even so, Yogamaya’s protective curtain hangs over this pastime and makes it difficult for ordinary conditioned souls to understand. Those who try to understand it by the intellect alone, without following the path of the heart, will never be able to do so, no matter what their status as historian, archaeologist or empiricist of some other kind.

Most of the Nava Kalevara ceremony proceedings are held in strict secrecy. Many of them are accessible to only the Dayitas, who have descended from the original families that established Lord Jagannath’s worship. The *Mādalā-pañjī* gives a record going back several centuries of where the trees that supplied the holy Daru for Lord Jagannath’s body were found. It also gives a general outline of the temple servants’ duties on this occasion. The *N*ī*lādri-mahodayam* gives the most exhaustive description of the ceremony, but the *Yāmala* texts are also an important source of information.

Lord Jagannath’s principal servant is the Gajapati king of Puri. He is completely absorbed in devotion to the Lord in the mood of divine parenthood. As such he is always looking for ways to please the Lord, protecting Him and looking after Him. He thus keeps constantly informed about the state of Lord Jagannath’s body from the Bhitarchon Mahapatra, the supervisor of the inner temple.

Generally speaking, however, it is Lord Jagannath’s astrologer whose duty it is to determine the exact time that Lord Jagannath is to take a new body and to announce it to the king a few months ahead of time. This calculation is made according to a combination of factors. Every thirty-two months or so, an extra month has to be added to the lunar calendar to keep it even with the solar year. When this supplementary month is to be inserted between the Snana Yatra and the Rathayatra, or as stated in the *Nīlādri-mahodayam,* in years where there are two full moons in the same month of Asharh, it is time for Lord Jagannath to undergo a change of bodies.\[105\]

When the king learns about the desire of the Lord to appear in a new form, he summons the senior Pandas, the abbots of the major Maths of Puri, representatives of the Dayita clan and the descendants of Vidyapati (Pati Mahapatra), Maharanas (the craftsmen who carve the Deities) and prominent members of the other servant clans to a meeting where they discuss what needs to be done. Once the duties of each of these groups has been made clear, the king orders the Bhitarchon Mahapatra to wrap prasadi saris around the heads of the craftsmen and the Dayitas as a sign of their sacred commission.

Since the chief of the Dayitas has the responsibility for finding the Maha Daru (*mahā-dāru*) or “great tree” from which Lord Jagannath’s new body is to appear, he is also given Balaram’s flower garland or *ājñā-mālā.* The chief of the Dayitas traditionally also goes to the temple of the goddess Baseli Devi to ask for her blessings and help in finding the Nava Kalevara.

The *Nīlādri-mahodayam* states that descendants of Vidyapati and Vishwavasu strong in their faith should go into the sacred woodlands to seek the Maha Daru at an auspicious moment in the fortnight of the waxing moon during the month of Vaishakh. In actual practice, the tithi that the search begins varies from one Nava Kalevara to another, as does the makeup of the search party. This search is given the name *vana-yātrā*, or “trip to the woods.”

The *Nīlādri-mahodayam* ordains that when the preordained auspicious moment arrives, the Dayitas and Pati Mahapatras, accompanied by a representative of the king, four Brahmins knowledgeable in the Vedas, the king’s priest, and carpenters or sculptors should assemble in the Jagannath temple. The royal guru gave the members of the party the various auspicious objects they will need for the various rituals. The king gives his order and Lord Jagannath’s garland sanctifying their mission. The sevaks then prostrate themselves in front of the Deity and set off from the temple, chanting the holy names of the Lord. The party is accompanied by two ox-carts that hold all the articles of worship and other necessary items.

In 1950, the group that assembled in the Jagannath temple on the Krishna Saptami tithi consisted of nineteen Dayitapatis, four Maharanas or carpenters, a standard bearer Lenka (who carries the Sudarshan standard), the temple record-keeper (Deul Karan), five Brahmins, a sepoy (armed guard) and nineteen others, totaling fifty in all. In 1969, the group set out on the Chaitra Shukla Dasami. It was made up of forty-five people: twenty-eight Dayitas, the Pati Mahapatra, four Brahmin priests from the Jagannath temple, four sculptors, five temple guards, the Lenka, a Kahaliya or flute-player, and the Deul Karan. In 1996, the party had become much larger. It included members of the Pati Mahapatra family, twenty Dayitapatis, sixteen Brahmins, thirty police officers, three inspectors of police, a Lenka, and nine Maharanas.

## Mangala Devi

The party usually spends its first night in the Jagannath Vallabha Gardens in Jagannath Puri. The next morning, it sets off, meditating on the friend of the universe, Lord Jagannath, and singing His names. The Lenka leads the procession, holding the Sudarshan standard. They head in the direction of the Mangala Devitemple in Kakatpur, a town twenty miles away in the direction of Konark. Chaitanya Mahaprabhu is said to have visited this ancient deity on His way to Puri.

Mangala Devi is also known as Bimala. She is a manifestation of Yogamayaand her village of Kakatpuris also known as Yogamayapur. Some Pandas also say that Lord Jagannath considers her to be His mother. Mangala Devi participates in this inconceivable pastime of Lord Jagannath by directing the search party through dreams.

Upon its arrival in Kakatpur, the party spends the first two days cleaning the temple. Its members fast and chant their mantra, while the Puja Pandas perform a fire sacrifice. They all pray that Mangala Devi will guide them in their search. They are to stay there, taking shelter of her until they get some kind of sign indicating where they must go to look for trees for each of the four deities. During this time the eldest Dayitapati sleeps inside the inner sanctum, waiting for Goddess Mangala to appear to him in a dream and tell him where the trees will be found.

Once the chief Dayitapati has received such an order from Mangala Devi, he gathers up the chief priest, other temple priests (Deulkar) and other members of the Vana Yatra team to search for the neem trees according to the indications given. Of course, even before the Vana Yatra leaves Puri, suggestions come pouring in from all over Orissa about possible candidates for the blessed tree, so these are investigated.

In 1950, the head of the Dayitapatis, Govinda Das, spent several days fasting awaiting Mangala Devi’s directions. However, no sign came from her and so the party went on to the Deuli Math on the Prachi River. On the night of their arrival in the Deuli Math, Mangala Deviappeared to the Dayitapati and told him that he would not find any suitable trees on the banks of the Prachi River and that he should go to the Kushabhadra River.

## The characteristics of the Daru

When the party arrives at a site that has been revealed in either a dream or by some other method, they may find several trees growing there. They cannot select a tree on their own whim, but must examine all the trees according to specific characteristics that set them apart and make them recognizable as the specific tree in which Lord Jagannath will become incarnate. The auspicious signs that designate the trees are found in the *Sūta-saṁhitā* and are recognizable by all. The indications of the Maha Daru are many and rarely do they all appear at once in the same tree. Nevertheless, if a preponderance of such symptoms is found, the priests will judge it to be the one they are seeking.

The neem tree that will be used for Jagannath’s body can be compared to the Tulasi plant, which is an eternal resident of Vaikuntha even though it appears and disappears in this world like any other plant or animal. The Daru Brahma appears in this world by the Lord’s wish. Tulasi Devi, the Ganga, the Shalagram Shila, and the wooden form of the Lord, are all identical with Vishnu and should be seen as his different forms. Anyone who thinks otherwise of them is a mundane being commits an offence that makes him unable to recognize the Divine in any situation.

*arcye viṣṇau śilā dhīr guruṣu nara matir vaiṣṇave jāti buddhir*  
*viṣṇor vā vaiṣṇavānāṁ kali mala mathane pāda tīrthe 'mbu buddhiḥ \|*  
*śrī viṣṇor nāmni mantre sakala kaluṣa he śabda sāmānya buddhir*  
*viṣṇau sarveśvareśe tad itara sama dhīr yasya vā nārakī saḥ \|\|*

**One who thinks the Deity in the temple to be made of wood or stone, who thinks of the spiritual master in the disciplic succession as an ordinary man, who thinks a Vaishnava of the infallible Lord’s own clan to belong to a certain caste or creed or who thinks of charanamrita or Ganges water as ordinary water; who considers the mantra composed of the names of the Lord, which destroys all sins, to be an ordinary word; or who considers the Supreme Lord of all lords, Vishnu, to be equal to an ordinary human being, is taken to be a resident of hell. (Padyāvalī** [**114**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/padyavali-rg/114)**)**

Normally a tree can be selected for Jagannath’s new body even if it only has five of these signs. First of all, the site of the sacred daru itself must correspond to certain scriptural indications: it should stand near a place where three rivers, three mountains, or three paths come together. A temple of Lord Shiva and a crematorium, as well as an ashram of devotees or ascetics should be nearby. There should be a lake or a tank where the priests will be able to take their ceremonial bath.

An anthill should be found nearby, especially one in which a snake makes its home. Nevertheless, at least one snake should be residing close to the tree to guard it. If anyone tries to harm the tree in any way, the serpents bite them, causing their death.

They only leave the site after the search party has performed the fire sacrifice.

There is also a requirement for three trees of other auspicious varieties to be in the vicinity. The Bael or *bilva,*\[106\] Barun,\[107\] and Sahada\[108\] trees are the usual varieties named, but the Sal tree is also included.

The trees for Jagannath, Balaram and Subhadra each have slightly different characteristics. Nevertheless, whatever tree they are looking at must ideally have a thick trunk, stand straight The distance from the ground to the first branches should be at least 12 feet. The upper branches should all be intact, free from disease and any visible effects of lightning damage. The tree should be free from infestation by termites or other insects. Furthermore there should be no creepers or vines growing on the tree and no birds living there. If any birds have made their nested in the tree, it is considered impure and will not be used.

Its wood used for making the Jagannath Deity must be darker than ordinary. It should have four branches stemming from the main trunk. The wood should have the customary bitter taste of neem, but with an underlying sweetness. Furthermore, the four symbols of Lord Vishnu, namely the conch, club, chakra and lotus flower must be clearly visible on the bark of the tree. All these elements must be present for the tree to be acknowledged as the sacred daru.

The Baladeva daru must be white in color and have seven branches stemming from the main trunk. The signs of a club and plough must be clearly visible on the bark. Once again, the tree must be guarded by a snake.

Subhadra’s daru must be yellow in color and have five main branches. Its bark will bear the sign of a yoni and five lotus flowers. The Sudarshan daru is recognized by its reddish color, have three main branches and be marked with the sign of a disk.

## The Vana Yatras in past years

In 1950, the party searched along the banks of the Kushabhadra River, traveling a distance of roughly six miles until they came to a Vishnu temple named after Nila Madhava, where they spent the night. A party of fifteen men was sent out from there to look for the tree, and after a search of six days, they found Sudarshan’s tree near a Shiva temple in Jalalpur, about two miles south of the Kushabhadra. The signs that this was Sudarshan’s neem tree were the following:

• it was surrounded by Palash, Barun, Sal and Bael trees;  
• there was a anthill in the near vicinity, in which a snake had made its home;  
• there was a well near the tree and a water tank about 15 yards away;  
• the sign of the discus was clearly imprinted on the tree ;  
• the wood was white in color and  
• the tree had three principal branches;  
• the tree had no birds living in it and  
• there were no blemishes on it anywhere.

After ascertaining this to be Sudarshan’s tree, the advance group immediately sent news to the Nila Madhava temple where the others were waiting. The entire party then regrouped around the Sudarshan tree and set up camp there.

Happy with their success, a party of fifteen or sixteen devotees once again set out to find the “great tree.” After two days of searching, by Yogamaya’s blessings, they were able to find Jagannath’s tree in the village of Khorihar Kanpurin the Jagatsinghpurprecinct of Cuttack district,where it had been worshiped for almost twenty-five years by a deeply religious Orissan devotee of Lord Jagannath. It had five large branches, was marked with the signs of the conch and chakra, was black in color. The tree was in the middle of a wooded area between the Kushabhadra and Devi rivers. A Barun tree stood nearby, as did an anthill with a serpent living in it. The cobra that was living in the anthill had a sign of Krishna’s footprint on his hood. Although all the other characteristics sought in Jagannath’s tree were not found, the Vidyapatiplaced a flower garland they had brought with them from Puri on it, indicating that this was the tree they had been searching for. From there they returned to Jalalpurwhere they had discovered Sudarshan’s tree.

On the following day, a party of ten to twelve persons set out and after searching another three days, they found Balaram’s tree by the grace of the *sandhinī śakti*. The tree was found in a cremation ground near the Kushabhadra River in the village of BanamalipurNoapatnain Balipatnaprecinct of Puri district. The tree was white, had seven great branches, and had the signs of the plough and club. An anthill was found about thirty feet from the tree and a snake entwined around one of its branches. Local fishermen had been worshiping the tree for the previous seventy or eighty years. Once again, the members of the party placed a prasadi garland in the tree and returned to Jalalpur.

An interesting story about this tree is that its owner was a Muslim who at first refused to part with it. However, his wife not only agreed to give it to Lord Jagannath, but paid for workers to help cut it down. These pious Muslims also took charge of feeding and housing all the members of the search party for as long as they stayed in Jalalpur.

It took another two days to find the fourth tree, that of Subhadra, in the village of Baharana, Nimapara precinct, Puri district. This tree had five principal branches, was red in color and marked with the conch and discus. A snake, Barun tree and a few small anthills were found in the immediate vicinity of the tree. The villagers told the search party the following story: A local potter had long been ill with a disease that could not be cured by any means. Then one night he had a dream in which he was told that the nearby red neem tree that was under the protection of a snake was the incarnation of Subhadra Devi. He should make offerings of cow’s milk by pouring it on the roots of the tree and take this prasad. By so doing, he would be cured of his illness.
