The next day, the potter followed these directives and thereafter enjoyed a long life of good health. The search party heard the potter personally confirm this story.

## The 1969 and 1996 Darus

In 1969, the company found an ancient neem tree in Champajhara village, its branches intertwined with an equally aged tamarind tree. If this tree did not pass this test, it would have been necessary to continue the search elsewhere. The search party was overjoyed, however, to find that by the Lord’s blessings, the Champajhara tree had eight of the crucial signs.

It was a magnificent old tree that had a trunk eleven feet in circumference. It had three majestic branches that spread out from the trunk 12 feet above the ground. It stood near a cremation ground. A large anthill stood near the base of the tree and three cobras were found making their residence in this anthill. There were no nests in the trees branches, nor were there any vines twined around the trunk. Finally, there were clear imprints of a conch and discus on the bark of the trunk. It was also considered auspicious that the tree was found on land belonging to Lord Jagannath’s own holdings, on plot 128 of the Ekharazat Mahal, that was under the jurisdiction of one Govardhan Brahma.

Eventually, other trees were found for the other deities. Balaram’s tree came from the Bhakarshi hamlet in the Balipatna precinct of Puri district. This was on land under the jurisdiction of Keshav Chandra Patra. The wood for Subhadra’s image was found on commonly held grazing land in Kanhupur village in the Govindapur precinct of Cuttack district. Sudarshan’s wood also came from Balipatna precinct, from the village of Balara near Banamalipur.

In 1996 the Jagannath daru was found in a small village outside the town of Khurda, near Bhubaneswar. A disciple of Gaur Govinda Swami Maharaj visited the site and gave the following account:

“As we approached the site, we were encouraged to see three mountains surrounding the area and a lake nearby, all in accordance with the shastric description. Driving up a sandy track, we found ourselves in a desolate area whose inhabitants were oblivious to the onset of the twentieth century. The simple locals looked on with wide eyes at a makeshift village of entrepreneurs that had sprung up to cater to the hundreds of pilgrims. Devotees from all over Orissa had descended upon their home to see Jagannath in His form as a tree.

“One enthusiastic Jagannath bhakta began pointing out all the symbols out to us. Although a materialist might protest that they were just unusual knots in the bark, or a casual observer might not notice them at all, when they were pointed out to us, we could clearly identify the symbols of the lotus, chakra, conch and disk. Indeed, the tree had all the distinguishing features that we had heard about. Our guide also showed us the three other trees next to the Jagannath daru and the snake holes at the base of the tree. There were no snakes visib1e at that time, but he cheerily assured us that they would come out at night. We didn't stay to find out.”

## The cutting of the tree

Once the search party has established whether a tree has the necessary qualifications to be used for Jagannath’s body, they first worship it according to the scriptural rites and then cut it down, first using a golden axe, then one made of silver and then of iron.

Once a tree has been selected, it is customary to choose an astrologically propitious moment for felling it. From the time of selection to the felling, the Brahmin members of the Vana Yatra daily perform fire sacrifices and puja at the base of the tree. These rituals may go on for several days. Naturally, a large crowd of people gathers for the occasion and it is necessary for local government officials and police to see to crowd control, law and order, as well as to arrange for sanitation.

In the *Śaṅkha-purāṇa* it is said that no one should look at the tree during this period. Of course, most people have no knowledge of this injunction and it is practically speaking impossible to enforce. Therefore the crowds continued to grow because of the religious significance of the occasion. The people did not content themselves with simply looking at the tree, however. Considering it to be holy, many even start stripping pieces of bark from the trunk despite the attempts of the priests to stop them.

The priests first wash the base of the trunk with liquid cow dung after which they sprinkle sandalwood water over it. Then they meditate on the Lord riding on the back of Garuda and perform a puja. They will remain fasting for either one or three days, until one of them has a dream in which an appropriate sign. The Brahmins will recite the Vedas uninterruptedly and chant the Lord’s holy names. Some sadhus will engage in a vrata wherein they will chant one of the approved mantras a specific number of times. On the following day, after bathing and performing the regular religious activities and puja, the Brahmins and devotees will eat havishyanna.

The worship takes the following form: First, they perform the puja of the preliminary deities, or *āvaraṇa-devatā*, beginning with Ganesh, followed by Durga, Shiva, and Surya. Then they perform Jagannath’s puja. This is followed by the worship of Varuna. The priests conclude the puja with the appropriate mantras, *svasti-vacana* and prayers of surrender. Then, after nominating an acharya and priests, they perform a fire sacrifice, using the appropriate mantra (*mantra-rāja*). The first of these is the “*pātāla-narasiṁha*” mantra, which is repeated 2,000 times, each time accompanied by an oblation. Fuel is added to the fire 10,000 times. The sacrifice is completed with the *pūrṇa-āhuti*, and gifts are given to the acharya and the priests.

The acharya approaches the tree and chanting the japa of the mantra, the axe is offered puja with sandalwood and flowers. Then while the four Brahmins are chanting the four Vedas in each of the cardinal directions, the acharya himself makes the first cut in the tree.\[109\] Then, accompanied by a festive chanting of sankirtan, the designated carpenters cut down the tree.

At the end of the sacrifice, the Pati Mahapatra -- the descendant of the Brahmin Vidyapati – who has been fasting, makes the first cut on the tree with a golden axe, remembering the name of Jagannath while all around him the other devotees are engaged in making a joyful noise of *nāma-saṅkīrtana.* He in fact does nothing more than symbolically touch the tree with a golden axe the size of a tiny lapel pin.

The next person to “cut” the tree is the Dayitapati -- the descendant of Vishwavasu – who touches it with a small silver axe. Finally, the head Maharana -- the descendant of Vishwakarma -- touches the tree with an iron axe. During these ceremonies the priests hold a curtain around the tree so that outsiders cannot see the procedure.

After this ritual, the Maharanas on the party start chopping the tree down. Other carpenters and craftsmen also assist in chopping the tree down, but many others, including Brahmins and sometimes local villagers, also take turns at chopping until the tree has been felled. As the tree is being cut down, the one hundred and eight names of Lord Nrisngha Deva are chanted to invoke auspiciousness.

## Taking the Daru back to Puri

At each location where a tree is found, special four-wheeled oxcarts are made from other trees in the vicinity. The wood for the Deities is trimmed into square blocks of timber and then loaded onto the carts where they are given puja. The wood is then tied down with silk ropes and covered with silk cloth. The leaves, branches, bark and other unused portions of the tree are buried in a large hole.

The priests and other devotees pull the cart manually using rope made from rattan and set out on the long trek back to Puri, which in 1996 was a distance of eighty kilometers. The rest of the party sings the names of the Lord and plays various auspicious instruments in an amazing procession. While the cart is pulled, devotees with yak tail whisks fan and others hold parasols overhead to ward off the sun. In the evening, when the traveling stops, Brahmins perform puja to the Lord in the wood, offering fruits and other uncooked foods as bhoga. This worship is continued on a daily basis.

As the road to Puri is highly traveled during the daytime, the party mostly travels at night. In 1996, a fire truck washed preceded the oxcart to wash and purify the road all the way from Khurda to Puri. When villagers along the way heard that the Daru was approaching, they came out of their houses with kerosene lamps and lined the road in the hope of catching a glimpse of the holy wood. They would hear the cart approaching from the sound of cymbals and cries of Jaya Jagannath! The village folk would join the kirtan and volunteer to pull the cart a little way further along the road toward its destination.

Villagers also come out with fruits and sweets, and other materials for puja, all of which is offered by the Dayitapatis. People with musical instruments like mridangas and other drums, hand cymbals, bells and gongs, came and join the kirtan party, sometimes growing until two or three thousand people have joined the crowd. In this way the wood for the Deity is treated royally all along the path leading to the Jagannath temple.

They enter the town in the following order: first Sudarshan’s wood, then Balaram’s, then Subhadra’s and finally that of Jagannath. When they have arrived at the Narasingha templenear Gundicha, word is sent to the king advising him of their arrival. The king then comes to Gundichawith a retinue of elephants, fans, whisks and hundreds of devotees carrying instruments. After greeting the successful Vana Yatra party, the king escorts the four oxcarts with the holy lumber into the temple grounds, entering through the north gate.

There, another large crowd of jubilant devotees is ready to greet the Daru with kirtan and the chanting of Vedic mantras. The Daru is led through the northern gate into the area known as Koili (Kaivalya) Vaikuntha, where some say the original Nila Madhava deity was worshiped. A temporary structure called the Daru Mandap or Vishwakarma Mandap is built on the Koili Vaikuntha platform, where for the next thirty-one days the Lord Jagannath’s carpenters will give the Daru its new shape as Jagannath.

## Actual work on the sculpture

Astrologers select an auspicious moment on the day following Snana Purnima, at which time the king engages 108 Brahmins to perform a great sacrifice that will last twelve days until the Trayodasi. He gives turbans to the chief sculptors who, in the midst of a great fanfare, begin work on carving the Deities.

The three eldest wood-carvers are chosen for carving Jagannath. Three others will carve Subhadra and three more Baladeva. In addition to this there are more than forty assisting sculptors. The wood-carvers work according to the rules laid out in the *Sūta-saṁhitā.* They stay alone in the Koili Vaikuntha area for the duration of the twelve-day period. During this period they do not leave the temple, and no one, not even the head panda, is allowed to see their work. While they are in the Koili Vaikuntha area, the sculptors are allowed to neither eat nor sleep. These functions are performed in other parts of the temple compound at the end of the day. Throughout the time of carving, twenty-four hour bhajans are performed and priests chant Vedic mantras outside the enclosed area.

## Ghat parivartan

Upon completion of the carving, the descendants of Vidyapati and Vishwavasu greet the new Deities with gifts of cloth, ornaments, garlands and scents. The sculptors are also rewarded with similar gifts. The Deities are then wrapped in lacquer and cloth and prepared for being painted, or *aṅga-rāga*. Before they are painted, however, the ceremony known as Ghat parivartan, or the changing of the Deities, must take place.

On the Krishna Chaturdasi of the month of Asharh, all four gates to the temple are closed at about 8 p.m. and remain closed until noon the next day. The four newly carved deities are taken from the Vishwakarma Mandapto the main temple building and placed in front of the old ones on the altar. The ritual known as Brahma sthapan is then carried out in great secrecy, with the doors to the Garbha Mandir locked room and only a few servants present.

There is an aperture in Jagannath’s belly that is known as the Brahma sthaliwhere the sacred items called “Brahma”or “Nabhi Brahma” are kept, wrapped in tulasi and sandalwood paste. The word *nābhi* means navel.

Four Dayitapatis (Pati Mahapatras?) are carefully blindfolded and their hands and feet bound with cloth. In this condition, they remove the Nabhi Brahma from the old murtis and place them in the new. People who have participated in this ceremony say that though the tulasi leaves have been inside the Lord’s body for more than twelve years, they do not fade.

While the ritual is going on, the temple priests engage in singing Vedic hymns and chanting prayers and performing puja. Various heavenly signs are usually observed. These signs are normally considered inauspicious and portents of death or disaster. This is because no one should see the Brahmawith the naked eye. Thus the Dayita who performs the ritual has his eyes and hands bound in such a way that he can neither see nor feel what it is that he is handling. As no one is allowed to see or touch the Nabhi Brahma, no one knows what it looks or even feels like.

A legend is told of a rich landlord who wanted to observe this ceremony. He bribed the chief priest with a great amount of money to be allowed into the temple at the proper time. However, he died the instant he laid eyes on the Brahma*.*

The four Dayitas are chosen after long discussions amongst the chief members of the twenty-eight Dayita families. The actual person who performs the task of transferring the sacred materials from Lord Jagannath Himself is usually the seniormost member of the Dayita community. There is a saying that whoever does this task does not remain in this world much longer afterwards, so this is one of the reasons that the oldest person is chosen.

In 1950, a rumor went around that the Dayitapatis who placed the Brahma Maṇiin the new Jagannath deities died. Sundarananda Prabhu investigated this rumor and was told by the Dayitapatis themselves that it was not true. However, Krishna Charan Mahapatra, the Bhitarchon Mahapatrawho as the representative of Lord Jagannath gave the *ājñā-mālā* or garlands that signal the appointment of the members of the search party, apparently died not long after the Ghat Parivartan, but this is not a regular occurrence.

The Nabhi Brahma, also known as Brahma padartha, is sometimes called Lord Jagannath’s “life force.” Its history and nature are shrouded in mystery and legend. It seems that every scholar and devotee in Orissa has some opinion about what the Nabhi Brahma is. Some popular beliefs are that the Nabhi Brahma is a special blue sapphire with a Vishnu yantra engraved on it, that it is a piece of the original Deity of Lord Jagannath, that it is a Shalagram Shila that was donated by the King of Nepal, that it is Lord Buddha’s tooth, or even that it is a piece of Lord Krishna's navel from 5,000 years ago. This last account seems to be the most popular one in Orissa. However, this conception seems to have originated in the 15th century with the Shakta poet Sarala Das in his Oriya rendition of the Mahabharata. We have dealt with this story in the chapter describing Nila Madhava (chapter 3).

## Burying the old deities

Once the Brahma has been transfered, Lord Jagannath’s new form is worshiped with the sixteen ingredients. The old deities are place on wagons and pulled out of the temple building through the south door and taken by the Dayitapatis to the Koili Vaikunthaarea. The Dayitas then bury the deities in the Madhavi Kunj along with the things that He used, like His chariot, charioteer, and horses, etc.

The exact location where the Deities are buried is unmarked and unknown to any but select Dayitapati members, but it is the same place all the previous Deities have been placed, one on top of another. Some sources say that they are buried in a well in the Madhavi Kunj area (#91).

On this night the government orders a complete blackout of all electricity in the town so that no one can possibly see the burial ceremony, even from a distant rooftop, for it is said that if someone were to see it, he would die.

The transfer of the Deities is also considered to be a sad occasion, as the old Deity will no longer be seen. Lord Jagannath is the head of the family for the Dayitapatis, so at the time of Nava Kalevara they behave as if they have lost a loved one and follow the Hindu last rites. Their caste tradition dictates that when someone dies, the male family members must not shave for ten days. In fact, the Dayitapatis stop shaving from the first day of the search party's departure. They also whitewash their houses and for a period of ten days, from the Chaturdasi to the Shukla Navamitithi, the Dayitas eat only havishyanna\[110\] as a sign of mourning. On the eleventh day, they leave the temple compound and go to Markandeya Sarovar where they rub their bodies with oil and shave their heads. They then take a bath in the tank to complete the state of mourning. They dress in new clothes given them by the king and return to the temple where they drink the water of peace (*śānti-udaka*).

On the twelfth day, on the Dashami tithi, the king distributes Maha Prasad to the Brahmins of the Sixteen Shasans, the Brahmins from the seven Sahis of Jagannath Puri, and the Sevayats of the Chatis niyog. The king is not the only one to fund this event; the abbots of the various maths, the Dayitapatis, and other sevayats also share in some of the expenses. Sundarananda writes that in 1950, between six and seven thousand people took prasad within the temple precincts on this day. On that occasion, more than 100 kilos of clarified butter was used in preparing the feast. The math abbots purchased 300 Baihandi Maha Prasad and 1500 kudua pots of dal and vegetables for distribution. The king also gave new cloth to all the Brahmins and Dayitas.

On the day following the Brahma Sthapan, with the new Deities sitting on the altar, the normal routine of worship is resumed after a break of fifty-eight days. The public is still not allowed to see the Lord until the eve of the Rathayatra festival, but events now follow the normal course up until the Rathayatra. The next day, on the dark moon day (Amavasya), Lord Jagannath’s Netrotsava and Nava-yauvana ceremonies take place as described in the previous chapter. This is the moment when Jagannath’s new form is revealed to the public for the first time.

Nava Kalevara is the best attended of all of Lord Jagannath’s festivals. Nowadays, the Rathayatra festival draws about seven hundred thousand people each year. However, after the 1996 Nava Kalevara, the crowds at the Rathayatra reached two and a half million souls, all of them anxious to have their first darshan of the new Deity of Jagannath.

Lord Jagannath is the only Deity who undergoes this periodic change of bodies. It is one of the many unique and wonderful pastimes the Supreme Personality of Godhead performs in Jagannath Puri where He pretends to be made of wood.

## Chapter 20 - Refuting the material understanding of Lord Jagannath’s new body

*His Divine Grace Srila Bhakti Promode Puri Maharaj wrote the following article subsequent to the Nava Kalevara festivities in 1969. \[111\]In it he discusses the mistaken conception that arises from thinking that Lord Jagannath changes material bodies in the way that an ordinary living being does.*

In July of 1969, the Home Department of the Orissan Government published an English language booklet named *Orissan Review* to mark the occasion of the Nava Kalevara celebrations. An article named *Nava Kalevara*, written by the Right Honorable Sri Harihar Patel, the Orissan Minister for Industries, Commerce and Public Relations, attracted our attention, as it contained a great deal of interesting information. Nevertheless, this writer’s mundane attitude to the Lord’s divine form also caused us a great deal of pain.

*As in many such articles about the Lord’s Nava Kalevara, Sri Patel quotes the following famous Bhagavad Gita verse:*

*vāsāṁsi jīrṇāni yathā vihāya*  
*navāni gṛhṇāti naro 'parāṇi*  
*tathā śarīrāṇi vihāya jīrṇāni*  
*anyāni saṁyāti navāni dehī*

**Just as a man discards old clothes to put on new ones, the embodied soul gives up his old body to take on a new one. (Gita** [**2.22**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/2.22)**)**

The writer goes on to call the Brahma mani, the articles that are transferred from the outgoing body of the Lord Jagannath to the new one, Lord Jagannath’s “soul.” He seems to think that Jagannath’s body is made of mundane neem wood and that life only enters that body when the Brahma mani is placed therein. This is a grave misconception.

*The Chaitanya Charitamrita describes how Mahaprabhu’s associate Svarupa Damodar once corrected exactly such a misconception in a Bengali Brahmin poet who once visited Jagannath Puri. This poet had written a play describing Mahaprabhu’s activities and had come to Puri with the express intention of showing it to the Lord. Since he knew Lord Chaitanya’s associate Bhagavan Acharya, he first read the play to him and several of the Lord’s other companions. These devotees did not subject the play to a very close examination, but were sufficiently impressed by its poetic qualities to think that Mahaprabhu would enjoy hearing it.*

*Lord Chaitanya himself did not like to hear poetry or theological discussions that went against either the orthodox understanding of scripture or were confused by erroneous aesthetic conceptions. For this reason, anyone who wished to entertain the Lord with his own compositions had to first go through His secretary, Svarupa Damodar Goswami who had to give his approval.*

*Svarupa Damodar was reluctant to hear Bhagavan Acharya’s friend’s play, despite his entreaties, because he suspected that he was not astute in his understanding of spiritual matters. He said to Bhagavan Acharya,*

*kṛṣṇa-līlā gaura-līlā se kare varṇana*  
*gaura-pāda-padma jāṅra haya prāṇa-dhana*  
*grāmya-kavira kavitva śunite haya duḥkha*  
*vidagdha-ātmīya-vākya śunite haya sukha*  
*rūpa jaiche dui nāṭaka kariyāche ārambhe*  
*śunite ānanda bāṛe yāra mukha-bandhe*

**“Who is qualified to narrate Krishna lila and Gaura lila? Only those who have enshrined Mahaprabhu's lotus feet within their hearts and made them their life and soul. Mundane love stories only make me sad, but the writings of expert devotees steeped in ecstatic love bring great joy. Srila Rupa Goswami has set the standard for writing spiritual dramas. One gets ever increasing joy just from hearing the introductory passages to his two plays,** ***Vidagdha-mādhava*** **and** ***Lalita-mādhava*****.” (CC** [**3.5.106-8**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-antya/5.106)**)**

*Bhagavan Acharya kept on insisting, however, and finally Svarupa Damodar relented. The poet thus began by reading the invocatory verse to his play.*

*vikaca-kamala-netre śrī-jagannātha-saṁjñe*  
*kanaka-rucir ihātmany ātmatāṁ yaḥ prapannaḥ*  
*prakṛti-jaḍam aśeṣaṁ cetayann āvirāsīt*  
*sa diśatu tava bhavyaṁ kṛṣṇa-caitanya-devaḥ*

**Lord Krishna Chaitanya Deva, has appeared here in this world with a golden effulgence, becoming the soul of the body named Sri Jagannath, whose blooming lotus eyes are widely expanded, and bringing consciousness to the limitless material nature of dull matter, May He bestow good fortune upon you all. (CC** [**3.5.112**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-antya/5.112)**)**

*Upon hearing this verse, Svarupa Damodar decided to test the poet and asked him to elaborate on its meaning. The poet answered,*

*kavi kahe jagannātha sundara-śarīra*  
*caitanya-gosāñi śarīrī mahā-dhīra*  
*sahaje jaḍa-jagatera cetana karāite*  
*nīlācale mahāprabhu hailā āvirbhute*

**“Lord Jagannath is a most beautiful body and the mighty Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu is that body’s owner. He has appeared here in Nilachala to bring consciousness to the unconscious world of matter. (CC** [**3.5.114-5**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-antya/5.114)**)**

Svarupa Damodar was particularly pained to hear the poet use the word *śarīrī* (“owner of the body”), which is a synonym for the individual soul or jiva, when speaking of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. He immediately began to condemn the poet’s explanation of his own verse!

*āre mūrkha āpanāra kaili sarva-nāśa*  
*dui tañ īśvare tora nāhika viśvāsa*  
*pūrṇānanda-cit-svarūpa jagannātha-rāya*  
*tāṅre kaili jaṛa-naśvara-prākṛta-kāya*  
*pūrṇa-ṣaḍ-aiśvarya caitanya svayaṁ bhagavān*  
*tāṅre kaili kṣudra jīva sphuliṅga-samāna*  
*dui-ṭhāñi aparādhe pāibi durgati*  
*atattva-jña tattva varṇe tāra ei rīti*

**"You fool! Are you trying to destroy yourself? Have you no faith in either of these forms of the Lord? Jagannath is the embodiment of transcendence and absolute spiritual bliss, yet you have described His body as material, dull and inert. And you have described Mahaprabhu, the Supreme Reality, as though He were an ordinary mortal. He is the Supreme Fire from whom everything emanates; yet you have portrayed Him as a mere spark. In this way you have offended both Jagannath and Mahaprabhu and are doomed. This is what happens when those ignorant of the principles of divine truth comment on them.” (CC 3.5.118-20)**

*āra eka kariyācha parama pramāda*  
*deha-dehi-bheda īśvare kaile aparādha*  
*īśvarera kabhu nahe deha-dehī-bheda*  
*svarūpa deha cid-ānanda nāhika vibheda*

**“You have also made another great error. You have discriminated between the Lord’s body and soul. This is a great offense. There is absolutely no distinction between the body and soul of the Supreme Lord. The Lord's essential being and His body are one and the same.” (CC** [**3.5.121-2**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-antya/5.121)**)**

Svarupa Damodar then quoted a sloka from the *Kūrma-purāṇa* that is also found in the *Laghu bhāgavatāmṛta* of Rupa Goswami:

*deha-dehi-vibhāgo’yaṁ*  
*neśvare vidyate kvacit*

**“For the Supreme Lord, there is never any distinction between soul and body.”**

Svarupa Damodar concluded by emphasizing the gulf that exists between the supreme consciousness and the individual jiva.

*kāhāṅ pūrṇānandaiśvarya kṛṣṇa māyeśvara*  
*kāhāṅ kṣudra jīva duḥkhī māyāra kiṅkara*

**What a great difference exists between Krishna and the jiva! One is the Absolute Truth, full of transcendental bliss and divine majesty, the master of the material energy, while the other is a tiny, insignificant creature, a slave to the material energy who is always unhappy. (CC** [**3.5.126**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-antya/5.126)**)**

Everyone was quite astonished to hear Svarupa Damodar speak in this way. The Brahmin poet himself hung his head in shame. When Svarupa saw the poet’s dismay, he mercifully instructed him for his benefit:

*jāha bhāgavata paṛa vaiṣṇavera sthāne*  
*ekānta āśraya kara caitanya-caraṇe*  
*caitanya bhakta-gaṇera nitya kara saṅga*  
*tabe ta jānibe siddhānta-samudra-taraṅga*  
*tabe pāṇḍitya tomāra haibe saphala*  
*kṛṣṇera svarūpa-līlā varṇibā nirmala*

**Go and study the Bhagavatam from a Vaishnava. Take exclusive shelter of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu's lotus feet. Always associate with Chaitanya Mahaprabhu=s devotees. If you do all this, you will be able to plunge into the ocean of His divine teachings. This will bring your scholarship to fruition and allow you to describe Krishna’s nature and pastimes purely. (CC** [**3.5.131-32**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-antya/5.131)**)**

There are many instructions in the scriptures about the spiritual nature of the Supreme Lord’s body. In the *Padma-purāṇa* Vyasa Deva says that anyone who thinks that Vishnu’s deity form is ordinary wood or stone has hellish intelligence. Mahaprabhu himself said:

*prākṛta kariyā māne viṣṇu kalevara*  
*viṣṇu-nindā nāhi ihāra upara*

**“There is no greater blasphemy of Vishnu than to think that His body is material.” (CC** [**1.7.115**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-adi/7.115)**)**

Of course, it is true that to the mundane eye, the Lord’s form appears to be material. This is why it is said that we should work at transforming our senses so that we can see Him as He is.

*atah śrī-kṛṣṇa nāmādi*  
*na bhaved grāhyam indriyaiḥ*  
*sevonmukhe hi jihvādau*  
*svayam eva sphuraty adaḥ*

**The holy name, form, qualities and pastimes of Sri Krishna are divine and transcendental. They cannot be experienced by the material senses. The Lord manifests Himself spontaneously on the tongue of a devotee who is eager to serve Him. (BRS** [**1.2.109**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/rupa-brs1/1.2.109)**)**

In the same vein, we find the following important verse in the *Brahma-saṁhitā:*

*premāñjana-cchurita-bhakti-vilocanena*  
*santaḥ sadaiva hṛdayeṣu vilokayanti*  
*yaṁ śyāmasundaram acintya-svarūpaṁ*  
*govindam ādi-puruṣaṁ tam ahaṁ bhajāmi*

**I worship Govinda, the primeval Lord, who is Shyamasundar, Krishna himself with inconceivable innumerable attributes, whom the pure devotees see in their heart of hearts with the eye of devotion tinged with the salve of love. (*****Brahma-saṁhitā*** [**5.38**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bs/38)**)**

There are innumerable other verses that clarify the nature of Krishna’s form. In the Bhagavatam, for instance, the Lord says that He appears in the lotus of the heart that has been imbued with pure devotion (*tvaṁ bhakti-yoga-paribhāvita-hṛt-saroja āsse* – [3.9.11](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/9.11)). In the Gita also, Krishna says that He can only be known through devotion. He further states unequivocally that His appearance and activities are transcendental.

*janma karma ca me divyam*  
*evaṁ yo vetti tattvataḥ*  
*tyaktvā dehaṁ punar janma*  
*naiti mām eti so’rjuna*

**O Arjuna, the person who knows in truth that My birth and activities are divine does not take another birth upon leaving this body, but comes to Me. (Gita** [**4.10**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/4.10)**)**

*avajānanti māṁ mūḍhāḥ*  
*mānu.sīṁ tanum āśritam*  
*paraṁ bhāvam ajānanto*  
*mama bhūta-maheśvaram*

**The foolish disparage Me, seeing My human form. They do not know My supreme nature nor that I am the controller of all creation. (Gita** [**9.11**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/9.11)**)**

These words should keep us on our guard against thinking that Jagannath’s changing of bodies is comparable to the jiva’s passing from one mortal frame to another, leaving one body and its karma in order to continue enjoying or suffering in another.

Jagannath’s energy Yogamaya appears in the form of the goddess Mangala, who resides in Kakatpur, creates this pastime in order to liberate the conditioned souls and to realize what is most beneficial to them. Numerous factors are involved in attaining understanding of this particular pastime of the Lord in wooden form: good luck, qualifications and capacity, purity, the degree of offences one has committed, and good will. Those who have committed offenses will never be able to attain a simple faith (*laukika-śraddhā*), what to speak of a learned faith in accordance with scripture (*śāstrīya-śraddhā*). Such persons come under the influence of the illusory energy personified in Mangala Devi and thus raise all kinds of doubts and false arguments denying the identity of the Supreme Brahman with the wooden forms of Jagannath and His companion deities.

As to those people who consider themselves to be servants of Lord Jagannath, but whose hearts lack devotion due to being contaminated by offences to the Holy Name and the Vaishnavas, they may make a show of serving the Lord, but are simply lifelessly engaged in external acts of service without any genuine feelings of devotion. Because of their lack of deep faith, they too come under the control of Mangala Devi and commit offences to Lord Jagannath.

It is an unforgivable offence to think that Jagannath Deva is an ordinary lump of wood. People who write articles presenting ideas like this in contradiction to the scriptures are not doing anyone any good. Indeed, they are misleading them. The consequences of this disservice to humanity are inestimable. The Lord in wooden form is not affected by all these attacks on Him. He remains who He is. It is only those who are limited by their mundane sense perception who accumulate offences.

Since Lord Jagannath has a form of eternity, knowledge and bliss, not even the great demigods like Brahma and Shiva can hope to understand His pastime of taking a new body. One who thinks of this pastime in the same terms as the Gita speaks of the ordinary jiva, who takes on and discards bodies like suits of clothes in keeping with the machinations of karma, equates the Lord with the jiva.

The Nava Kalevara ceremony has been held many times over the last 150 years. Each time, an account of the event is preserved in the *Mādalā-pañjī*. The purpose of this pastime, which is carried out by the Lord’s internal potency, is to bring pleasure to the devotees and nothing else. Nevertheless, the Lord accomplishes many purposes through His every action. This transcendental pastime is beyond the perception of the empiricists and the comprehension of the logicians. It is foolish for any insignificant creature to think he can understand it completely. The closest we can come to understanding it is by accepting the wisdom received in disciplic succession. This is the purport of Svarupa Damodar’s instruction to the East Bengali Brahmin poet.

## Chapter 21 - Other holy places in the town of Puri

The *Nīlādri-mahodaya* describes the sacred geography of Sri Kshetra at some length. It is envisioned as a series of concentric layers or *āvaraṇas* spreading out from the Lord Jagannath temple, each of which are governed and inhabited by different gods. Different scriptures differ on the number of such layers – some describe three, others seven. The seven layers are briefly described here:

1\. First layer (*prathamāvaraṇa*) – begins with the Nabhi, i.e., Lord’s Jagannath’s Nabhi Brahma, the Ratnavedi and the Deities on the jeweled altar.  
2\. Second layer (*dvitīyāvaraṇa*) – includes the following deities within the Kurma Berha -- the four Shaktis (Bimala, Kamala, Mangala and Uttarayi), two tirthas (Rohini Kund and Suna Kua), two trees (Kalpa Bata and Shyamali), Garuda and the Nila Parvata.  
3\. Third layer (*tṛtīyāvaraṇa*) – includes the eight Shiva lingas and eight corresponding Shaktis, still within the Kurma Berha.\[112\]

Shambhus Shaktis   Agnishwar Dvaravasini   Bateshwar Mahavrajeshwari Indrani   Kshetrapaleshwar Svarna Bhairavi Kutama Chandi   Chakreshwar Bhadrakali   Vaikuntheshwar Bhuvaneshwari   Pataleshvara Mahakali Aghora   Lokeshwar Yajneshwari Jhara   Ishaneshwar Sitala

4\. Fourth layer (*caturthāvaraṇa*) – consists of the space between the Kurma Berha and the Meghanad Prachir.  
5\. Fifth layer (*pañcamāvaraṇa*) - consists again of eight Shiva lingas and their corresponding Shaktis.

Shambhus Shaktis   Vishweshwar Vishweshwari   Markandeshwar Saptamatrika   Mahakaleshwar Dakshina Kali   Karnameshwar Charchika   Mukteshwar Alameshwari   Ugreshwar Varahi   Kapalamochaneshwar Vanadurgeshwari (Hara Chandika)   Aghoreshwar Basulikeshwari

6\. Sixth layer (*ṣaṣṭhāvaraṇa*) - consists of the five Tirthas and four Ashrams.

*mārkaṇḍeyāvaṭe’kṛṣṇe rauhiṇeye mahodadhau \|*  
*indradyumne naraḥ snātvā punar janma na vidyate \|\|*

**“Anyone who bathes in the five tirthas -- Markandeya Sarovar, Shweta Ganga, Rohini Kund, the ocean and Indradyumna Sarovar -- will never take birth again.”**

7\. Seventh layer (*saptāvaraṇa*) – includes the deities on the boundary line of the conch, such as the Kshetrapalas Nilakantheshwar and Lokanath.

## Kshetra Bhraman Utsava

Devotees who come to Jagannath Puri visit not only the temple of Lord Jagannath and the numerous shrines on the temple grounds, but also bathe in the various holy tanks or Tirthas and visit the many other temples in the town, in particular the five Mahadevas: Lokanath, Markandeshwar, Nilakantheshwar, Yameshwar and Kapala Mochan. They sometimes attempt to do this in a single day, especially when observing the Kshetra Bhraman Utsava on the Krishna Panchami of the Margashira.\[113\]

The usual procedure followed by devotees is to first take bath in Markandeya Sarovar and to pay obeisances to the the image of Markandeya Muni installed there. They then go to Lord Jagannath’s temple and visit the various shrines and temples in the Kurma Berha. The *Nīlādri-mahodayarn* advises the devotees to go circumambulate Lord Jagannath’s temple while chanting the *Puruṣa-sūktas* with the hands folded tightly against the chest.

After visiting Lord Jagannath, devotees go to Shweta Ganga where they pray to Shweta Madhava and pay obeisances to the Ugrasena and Hanuman deities.

The next place to visit is the seashore at Swarga Dwar. The *Nīlādri-mahodayarn* recommends forming an image of Lord Jagannath in the sand and to worship Him there with sixteen upachars, or in the impossibility of doing full worship, to at least use the five upachars.. After this puja, the devotees take their bath in the sea, the king of tirthas, making offerings to the sea and to Sri Kshetra.

Thereafter, the devotees visit Yameshwar, Lokanath, Mangala Devi, Bilveshwar, Nilakantha, Jambheshwar, Chakra Tirtha, Chamunda Devi and Kapala Mochan in Manikarnika Sahi. The circuit ends at the lndradyumna Sarovara where the devotees pay their respects to King Indradyumna, performing tarpan after taking bath there. After thus having circumambulated the whole of Sri Kshetra, the devotees come to the temple of Lord Jagannath and offer prayers to Lord once again.

## Sri Markandeya Sarovar

At the time of the partial destruction of the universe, the sage Markandeya was floating in the flood waters. As he passed Purushottam Kshetra, he saw a great banyan tree. In the tree was a boy who called out, telling him to come to him. Markandeya did not see the boy at first and wondered where the voice was coming from. As he was wondering, he suddenly had a vision of Narayan accompanied by Lakshmi Devi. Markandeya immediately began to pray to the Lord, who said to him, “Look in this banyan tree and you will see a baby boy lying on one of its leaves. You will be able to take shelter in his immense mouth and he will protect you from the flood.”

Markandeya followed Narayan’s order and entered the child’s mouth. He was surprised to see that the entire universe created by Brahma present there. When he came out, he had a vision of Lord Jagannath who told him, “This holy land is eternal. It is never destroyed at the time of dissolution.” He then commanded the sage to make his home in Purushottam Kshetra.

Inspired by the Lord’s command, Markandeya excavated a vast tank to the north of the immortal banyan tree and began worshiping his beloved Shiva. This deity is appropriately named Markandeshwar, but there is also another Shiva deity in this temple, known as Nilakantheshwar Mahadeva.

There is also a banyan tree known as Markandeya Bata is on the south side of the tank, but the tree spoken of in the legend is in fact the Akshaya (“imperishable”) Bata on the Jagannath temple grounds.

Many of the Jagannath temple rites involve going to Markandeya Sarovar. On Balaram’s appearance day (Shravan Purnima), Sudarshan is taken from the Ratnavedi of the Boro Deul and brought here for various rituals. On the Bhadra Krishna Ekadasi, known as Ashoka Ashtami, Krishna’s defeat of the Kaliya serpent is celebrated here. A few days later, Lakshmi Devi is brought here from the temple for the Rishi Panchami festival.

## Shweta Ganga

The holy tank known as Shweta Ganga is a short way to the west of the main road leading from Lord Jagannath’s temple to the Swarga Dwar. The tank is surrounded by marble steps, and the famous Ganga Mata Math stands on its southern side.

According to the *Utkala-khaṇḍa*, there was a descendant of King Indradyumna named Shweta who lived in the Treta Yuga. He was a great devotee of Jagannath. and so followed the custom of arranging for Jagannath’s bhoga, just as his forefather had done. One morning, he came to the temple and had a vision of the demigods descending from the heavens to make offerings to Lord Jagannath. They were coming and making the Lord thousands and thousands of wonderful gifts that were beyond the power of any mortal to give. King Shweta became disturbed at the insignificance of his own offerings and stood at the temple door, his head hung in shame.

As he was meditating on his own insignificance and praying to Lord Jagannath, he had a second vision in which he saw Lakshmi Devi herself taking his food offerings and feeding them to both sets of Jagannath deities who were eating them with great enthusiasm. This sight made the King immediately feel that his life was indeed worthwhile and so his enthusiasm to serve Jagannath increased greatly.

Lord Jagannath eventually granted him the boon of being liberated in a spot that faces Matsya Madhava, midway between the Akshaya Bata and the ocean, and was subsequently named Shweta Madhava in his honor. The tank excavated here was also named Shweta Ganga (“the white Ganges”). On the banks of this tank, deities of Shweta Madhava, Matsya Madhava and the nine planets (Nava Graha) are still worshiped.

In the Dvapara Yuga, when Agni ate the Khandava forest he got indigestion. At that time Lord Shivaji appeared as Shweta Raja and performed a yajna to pacify his stomach. Shweta Ganga is the place where he performed this yajna. There are four wells in the four corners of the tank, which according to the priests of the Shweta Madhava deity were filled with ghee at the time of this great sacrifice. This explains the presence of the Shweta Raja deity of Lord Shiva that stands to the right of the Shweta Madhava deity.

The Shweta Ganga was last thoroughly cleaned and repaired in 1895 by the Dowager Rani Suryamani Pattamahadei.

## The great Tirtha, the ocean

Jagannath Puri is situated to the north of the Bay of Bengal, which Orissans know as the “blue ocean” (*nīla-mahodadhi*). Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu and all His associates used to bathe in the ocean daily. Mahaprabhu particularly glorified the ocean on the day that Hari Das Thakur disappeared. Mahaprabhu washed Hari Das’s body in the ocean before burying him in the sand. After he did so, He proclaimed the ocean as “the great tirtha” (CC 2.11.64).

After bathing in the ocean, the Lord would take darshan of the spire on top of the Jagannath temple. He also instructed His followers to do the same –

*mahāprabhu kahe śuno sarva vaiṣṇava-gaṇ*  
*samudra-snāna kori koro cūṛā daraśan*

**Mahaprabhu said, “Listen, all you Vaishnavas! Take your baths in the ocean and then respectfully gaze on the pinnacle of the temple.” (CC** [**2.11.182**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/11.182)**)**

*samudra-snāna kari prabhu āilā nija-sthāne*  
*advaitādi gelā sindhu karibāre snāne*  
*āsi jagannāthera kailā cūṛā daraśan*  
*prabhura āvāse āilā karite bhojan*

**After the Lord had taken His bath in the ocean and returned to His cottage, Advaita and the other devotees went to bathe in the sea. On their return, they paid their obeisances to the pinnacle of the temple and then went to the Lord’s cottage to take prasad. (CC** [**2.11.197-8**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/11.197)**)**

Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu was often overcome with ecstatic feelings of love for Krishna, thinking Himself to be the maidservant of the chief gopi, Srimati Radharani. When in this mood, He saw the ocean as the Yamuna River and the wooded shorelands as Vrindavan. One autumn night, on the Rasa Purnima, as the Lord was walking on the beach after leaving the Ai Tota and had a vision of Krishna and the gopis engaged in water sports in the Yamuna, just as they did after the Rasa dance. When He saw them playing in the water like this, He jumped in after them and was carried away by the ocean currents and was lost for some time before being caught in a fisherman’s net and brought back to shore (CC 3.18).

Rupa Goswami described this pastime in his *Caitanyāṣṭakam –*

*payorāśes tīre sphurad-upavanālī-kalanayā*  
*muhur vṛndāraṇya-smaraṇa-janita-prema-vivaśaḥ \|*  
*kvacit kṛṣṇāvṛtti-pracala-rasano bhakti-rasikaḥ*  
*sa caitanyaḥ kiṁ me punar api dṛśor yāsyati padam \|\|*

**When will I again see Sri Chaitanya, taking pleasure in devotion while His tongue constantly relishes the names of Krishna, overcome with love and thoughts of Vrindavan after seeing the beautiful vegetation on the shores of the ocean.**

*kāhāṅ mora prāṇa nātha muralī vadana*  
*kāhāṅ karoṅ kāhāṅ pāṅ vrajendra nandana*  
*kāhāre kahiba kebā jāne mora duḥkha*  
*vrajendra nandana binu phāṭe mora buka*

**“Where is the Lord of my life, Krishna, the flute player? What can I do to find him? Where is the son of Nanda Maharaj? To whom can I talk of my distress? Who would understand me? Without the son of Nanda, my heart is splitting in two.” (CC** [**2.2.15-16**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/2.15)**)**

The following prayers from the *Skanda-purāṇa* are to be recited when bathing in the ocean --

*namas te jagatām īśa*  
*śaṅkha-cakra-gadādhara*  
*dehi deva mamānujñāṁ*  
*tava tīrtha-niṣevaṇe*

**O Lord of the universe! You who holds the conch, disk and club! O Lord, please give me permission to serve Your tirtha.**

*tato maunī vrajed viṣṇuṁ*  
*cintayan saritāṁ patim*  
*ugrasenaṁ sthitaṁ parśve*  
*anujñāpya samāhitaḥ*

**One should then approach the sea silently thinking about the Supreme Personality of Godhead. With concentration and purity of mind he should request permission from Ugrasena:**

*ugrasena mahābaho*  
*balabānugravikrama*  
*labdhā varaṁ suprasannāt*  
*samudra-taṭa-māstitaḥ*  
*tirtharāja-kṛta-snāna-*  
*susampūrṇa phala-prada*  
*sindhusnānaṁ kariṣyāmi*  
*anujñāṁ dātumarhasi*

**O mighty armed Ugrasena, O powerful one of fierce exploits, after pleasing the Lord He granted you a benediction to stay by the seashore. You grant the benefit of taking a sacred bath in the ocean. I wish to take bath there now. Please give me permission. (*****Skanda-purāṇa*** **2.2.30.65-69)**

One should then pray to Sudarshan:

*sudarśana namas te ‘stu*  
*koṭī surya-sama-prabha*  
*ajñāna-timirāndhasya*  
*viṣṇor mārgaṁ pradarśaya*

**I offer my obeisances unto you, Sudarshan! You are as effulgent as millions of suns. I am blinded by the darkness of ignorance. Please illuminate the path to Lord Vishnu for me. (2.2.30.89)**

One should then offer obeisances to the ocean and pray:

*tīrtha-rāja namas tubhyaṁ*  
*jala-rupāya viṣṇave*  
*jīvanāya ca jantūnāṁ*  
*parinirvāṇa-hetave*  
*agniś ca te yonir ilā ca deho*  
*retodha viṣṇor mṛanya nābhiḥ*  
*upaimi te rupam apaska-hetum*  
*ānanda-saṇghātam anupraviśya*

**I offer my obeisances to the ocean who is the Lord of all tirthas. You are Vishnu in the form of water. You are the life of all creatures and are the greatest cause of liberation. Fire and earth are your source of origin. Lord Vishnu is situated in you. \[When the demons and demigods churned you\] nectar came from your womb. With no ulterior motive I happily approach you to take bath in your waters.** ***(Skanda-purāṇa*** **2.2.30.91-92)**

## Swarga Dwar

The word *svarga-dvāra* means “the gate to heaven.” Brahma and the demigods appeared at Swarga Dwar in response to Indradyumna’s prayer. A stone marks the exact spot where they descended from the heavens. Some call this stone *svarga-dvāra-sākṣī*, “the witness to the heavenly door”; others call it the “step to heaven.”

Not only human beings make a pilgrimage to Puri to have darshan of Lord Jagannath – the gods also come. For this reason, the northern gate of the temple is closed every evening. Every day, a minimum of a hundred, and up to four or five hundred quintals of rice are cooked for offering to Jagannath. All this maha prasad is given for sale in the Ananda Bazaar, which is within the temple compound. A certain amount of this prasad, which is hard for even the gods like Shiva or Brahma to find, falls to the ground all around the temple compound. Amazingly, however, when the gates to the temple open the next morning, not a grain can be found anywhere. Where does all this prasadam go? It is said that the gods who come at night to see Lord Jagannath eat all these remnants. Many perfected souls, yogis, sages, gods and goddesses come in disguise to see Lord Jagannath. These secret visitors are sometimes caught. Here is the story of one such eye witness.

Once upon a time, Lord Indra, the king of the gods, came to see Jagannath Deva.

After taking darshan of Lord Jagannath, he became hungry to taste some of the Lord’s maha prasad. He went into the Ananda Bazaar hoping to get some. There he saw one of the cooks joyfully eating a copious meal of rice, dal, vegetables, cakes and sweets. The cook thought that Indra was a member of the nobility and served him prasad. After taking his meal, Lord Indra got up and slowly started walking away without having paid the price for the prasad.

The Supakar thought that since he must be a member of the royal court and so assumed that he would pay one of the people stationed at the exit. However, he did not but started walking off in the direction of the seashore. The temple cook became angry and he started running after the demigod, hurling insults and swearing at him. But as he got closer, he saw that the nobleman he was following cast no shadow on the ground. Not only that, but his feet did not seem to be touching the ground. This made him suspect that this was no ordinary human being, but some kind of divine personality. Even so, he continued to follow Indra and hurle abuses at him.

When Indra got as far as the sea shore, he stopped, turned to the Supakar and said, “Listen, brother. You gave me Jagannath’s maha prasad to eat and so I am forever in your debt. I will do whatever you ask of me, but unfortunately I have no money to pay you.”

The Supakar answered, “You are dressed like a member of the king’s court and you expect me to believe that you have no money at all? I can’t accept that. Tell me who you really are.”

Indra replied, “I am the king of the gods, Indra.”

Naturally, the cook was doubtful and he asked for some proof of Indra’s identity. The king of the gods immediately showed his powers by making it rain. He told the cook to ask for a boon. The cook said, “Whenever I want it to rain, you must make it happen.” Indra said “so be it” and left.

The next day, the Supakar was at work in the Ananda Bazaar and conversing with his fellow cooks. He recounted all these events to them. They said, “If that is so, let us test you right away.” The Supakar immediately began to pray, “O Indra, please make it rain right here in the middle of the Ananda Bazaar.” Though it was not raining anywhere else, a downpour immediately started right there in the Ananda Bazaar.

News of these happenings soon reached the king who summoned the Supakar to the court. The Supakar once again told his story and to prove the truth of it, called on Indra to make it rain right there in the king’s court. The king was amazed and overjoyed to hear and see all these things. He decided to reward the Supakar for his great fortune. He said, “From now on, you will be known as Meghamaliya Suar. \[(*Megha-mālā* means ‘storm clouds.’\] Not only you, but all your descendents will be known by this name. For your benefit, a new kind of sweet cake made of ghee, karai dal, coconut and sugar will be offered to Lord Jagannath. This cake will be as big as a plate and four inches thick. It will satisfy the hunger of at least ten people. You and all your descendents will receive these cakes that are offered to Lord Jagannath.” This cake is known as the *sūār piṭhā.* The place where the cook confronted Indra has been known as “the door to Indra’s abode, or heaven” (Swarga Dwar) every since that time.

In 1983, Puri Maharaj wrote that the cost to the government for making the *sūār piṭhā* was Rs 25 and that they sold for Rs. 10 each. People from all over India buy these cakes and took them home to offer to the gods and goddesses of their locality, to whom they are very dear. They soak one cake in two litres of milk and add curd, bananas and sugar to make a delicious preparation to offer to their gods.

## The cremation ghat

Most pilgrims who come with fruitive desires bathe in the ocean here. The town crematorium used to be situated here, but with the population growth, it has been moved several hundred metres east.

In the past, many pilgrims came to Jagannath Puri specifically to give up their bodies. W. W. Hunter gave a touching description of one such person he encountered in the 1860’s:

One little group came to bury their mother. They had journeyed with a pilgrim band from the far west, beyond the limits of British India, and had visited the great shrines at Allahabad, Benares, and Gaya upon the way. They had done as much of the distance as they could by railway; but they had walked about five hundred miles besides. The journey had taken three months. One-sixth of them had already died; and several had been so disabled as to require they finish their pilgrimage in a bullock cart.

But the oldest woman in the party--a brave up-country matron--had never flinched. She had constantly urged them forward, in order, she said, that she might reach the holy city before she died.

The same day she arrived, she prevailed upon the priests to conduct her to the temple, where she gazed in silent rapture on \[Lord Jagannath\]. The next morning she fell ill.

The other pilgrims began to recover their strength, but she gradually declined; and now her sons had come to burn her body on the sands. She had reached the Gate of Heaven at last.

They laid down the bier at the edge of the sea, till the ripples wetted the vermilion-sprinkled yellow shroud. A green leaf had been placed in her girdle, and another on her breast. Then, with all her ornaments around her arms and ankles, they laid her on the pile, and in a few minutes the forked flames flashed up into the skies.

## Chakra Tirtha

Chakra Tirtha stands on the place where the Balgandi (Balukhanda) Nala empties into the sea, or Banki Muhana. This is about three kilometers from the main temple, and east of the Puri Railway Station. The place is remembered primarily because it was here that Lord Jagannath, the Daru Brahma, first floated ashore. A stone representation of the Lord’s Sudarshan Chakra is worshiped here in the middle of an enclosure. Chakra Tirtha is maintained by the same trust that runs the Jagannath Vallabha Math. Not far from the Sudarshan Chakra is a tank known as Piligram that is frequented by pilgrims who perform Shraddha rituals for their deceased forefathers.

On the beach nearby is the Chakra Narayan temple, which was built in the 1930’s. There are three Vishnu deities in the temple, Chakra Narayan in the middle, Lakshmi Narayan to his west and Ananta Narayan to his east. Each deity is embraced by Lakshmi Devi. There is also a small temple dedicated to Lakshmi Devi's father, the ocean. Though these temples are old, they are in fair condition.

Not far from this temple is another, dedicated to Hanuman. The deity here is named Beri Hanuman and is peculiar in that he is bound by chains from his hip to  
the wall! The story is that Lord Jagannath asked Hanuman to stand guard here in case the ocean should overflow. When Lord Ramachandra appeared on earth, however, Hanuman could not resist his desire to join Him in His pastimes and so he left for Ayodhya. It is sometimes said that it was the desire to eat sweets that he could not resist! Eventually, it was necessary for Lord Jagannath to kidnap Hanuman and bring him back. This explains why Hanuman is kept prisoner in this temple. He is also known as Dariya Hanuman, because he is by the ocean (*dariyā*). This temple is also under the care of abovementioned trust.

This temple is associated with the Jagannath Temple's Pana sankranti ritual.

Between the Beri Hanuman temple and the road is the Sonar Gauranga temple. This temple is quite opulent and attracts many pilgrims because of its striking asthadhatu image of Gauranga is striking. The deity also has many golden ornaments. It is clean and well maintained, but unfortunately barred to foreign visitors.

This temple is maintained by a Bengali trust of sixteen members. This trust has four branches: Jagannath Math in Bhubaneswar near Lingaraj, the Sadhu Maizi Math in Belur north of Calcutta, the Vrindavan Sadhu Maizi Math and Govardhan Sadhu Maizi Math. The siddhanta of this math appears to be at some difference with pure Rupanuga Vaishnavism.

## Indradyumna Sarovar

A hundred meters to the north of the Gundicha temple is a large tank surrounded by marble staircases. This tank has also been mentioned in the *Araṇya-parva* of the Mahabharata (3.191.9, critical edition). In the *Utkala-khaṇḍa*, it is said that this tank came into existence when Indradyumna performed an Ashwamedha sacrifice. As a part of the sacrifice, Indradyumna gave a large number of cows in charity to the Brahmins. Indeed, there were so many cows that they dug a huge hole with their hooves. The cows’ urine and the water that was offered as oblations during the giving of charity filled the hole to make the lake.

On the shores of this tank stands the temple of Nilakantheshwar Shiva, one of the five great Shiva lingas of Purushottam Kshetra. There are several small temples on the shores of the Indradyuman Sarovar – one is dedicated to King Indradyumna Deva with another by its side for his wife Gundicha Devi. There is also a small temple dedicated to Radha Krishna

Krishna Das Kaviraj describes Mahaprabhu’s water sports in Indradyumna Sarovar in his Chaitanya Charitamrita (Madhya 14.75-91). These events took place after Lord Jagannath had arrived at Gundicha during the Rathayatra festival:

There were many gardens near the Gundicha temple, and Chaitanya Mahaprabhu and His devotees used to reenact Krishna’s Vrindavan pastimes in them. They also engaged in water sports in Indradyumna Sarovar nearby. Mahaprabhu splashed all the devotees, and the devotees also surrounded the Lord and splashed Him. They sometimes formed a single circle in the water, sometimes many, clapping their hands and croaking like frogs. Then the devotees paired off to fight splashing duels in the water. The Lord watched the fun as one or the other would emerge victorious, defeating his opponent. Advaita Acharya and Nityananda Prabhu were the first to pair off in this way. In the waterfight that ensued, Advaita Prabhu was defeated and he began to call Nityananda all kinds of names. Others who paired off were Svarupa Damodar and Pundarika Vidyanidhi; Murari and Vasudeva Datta also splashed each other playfully. Another duel took place between Srivas Thakur and Gadadhar Pandit, and yet another between Raghava Pandit and Vakresvara Pandit.

Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya splashed Ramananda Raya, both of them lost their usual seriousness and became just like children. Seeing their childlike enthusiasm, Mahaprabhu smiled and said to Gopinath Acharya, “These two men are great scholars whose learning and gravity give them their authority. Now they are playing and laughing like little boys. You had better tell them to stop.”

Gopinath answered, “Your mercy is like a great ocean, even a drop of which can immerse great mountains like Sumeru and Mandara. These two are little hills by comparison, so is it any surprise that they should be completely submerged by it? Sarvabhauma has spent his entire life eating the dry remnants of mustard seed from which all the oil has been extracted. Now you are mercifully moistening him with the nectar of your pastimes. How great is your kindness!”

Mahaprabhu laughed and called Advaita Acharya. He made Advaita lie on the water like Shesha Naga, the great serpent who serves Lord Narayan as His bed floating on the ocean of milk. Mahaprabhu then climbed on top of him, playing the role of Lord Narayan in this pastime. Advaita Prabhu revealed his own divine power by floating about on the water, carrying Lord Chaitanya on his belly.

This is how the Lord and His companions sported in the water of the Indradyumna Sarovar. When they had finished, they returned to the Ai Tota gardens.

## Bathing at Indradyumna Sarovar

Before bathing in Indradyuman Sarovar, one should visit the Nrisingha temple by the Gunicha mandira and request Lord Nrisingha for permission with the following prayers:

*narasiṁha namas tubhyaṁ*  
*yasya te kṣetra uttame*  
*sahasraṁ vāji-medhasya*  
*kretoś cakre nṛpottamaḥ*  
*indradyumna prāsādāt tu*  
*tasya kratvaṅga-sambhave*  
*sarasi snātum āyāto*  
*mām anujñāpaya prabho*

**I offer my obeisances to You Lord Nṛsingha Deva, by Your mercy in Your excellent holy place, King Indradyumna performed a thousand horse sacrifices. I have come to take my bath in the sacred lake that originated as a part of that horse sacrifice. Please grant me permission to do so. (*****Skanda-Purāṇa*** **2.2.31.3-4)**

Then, while standing in the water, one should recite the following prayers:

*aśvamedhāṅga-go-koṭi*  
*kṣura-kṣuṇṇa-mahītala*  
*tan-mūtra-phena-dānābhaḥ*  
*pūritākhila-pāvana*  
*snātuṁ tavāgataḥ puṇye*  
*sarva-tīrtha-maye jale*  
*pūrva-janma-sahasrotthaṁ*  
*pāpaṁ snānād vimocaya*  
*The surface of the ground was*

**dug up by the hoofs of the millions of cows that formed part of the horse sacrifices. It was filled up with their froth and urine as well as the waters used in the rite of charitable gifts. You sanctify everything. I have come to take bath in your sacred waters that are filled with the waters from all of the tirthas. By this bath please remove all my sins that have arisen in my thousands of previous births.**  
***(Skanda-Purāṇa*** **2.2.31.6-7)**

While in the water one should remember Lord Hari in the form of Nrisingha Deva and utter Gayatri mantra.

## Narendra Sarovar

To the main temple’s northeast lies Narendra Sarovar or Chandan Pukur. It measures 873 feet by 743 feet (266m x 226.5m), making it the largest of Puri’s great tirthas. This tank greatly resembles the Bindu Sarovar in Bhubaneswar. It appears that it was named after Narendra Mahapatra, a minister of Kavi Narasimha, who had the lake dug in the 13th century.\[114\] Others say that Indradyumna himself excavated the tank for Lord Jagannath’s Chandan Yatra. The word *narendra* means “king.” The paving of the tank’s circumference and the building of its stone steps or ghats was undertaken in the 18th century by the Marathi guru, Baba Brahmachari.

It is said that Gadadhar Pandit gave lectures on the Srimad Bhagavatam on the banks of Narendra Sarovar, with Mahaprabhu, Nityananda, Advaita Prabhu, Svarupa Damodar and King Prataparudra in his audience.

## Chudanga Sahi

It is learnt nowadays that the karanas write the *pañjī* in their own homes. Some forty years back when the recording was still being made with due ceremony, offerings of Lord Jagannath’s prasad used to be made to two images of stone installed in Chudanga Sahi in Puri town on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Ashwin (*Vijaya-daśamī*). The offering was known as *kartā kheya*, or the offering to the master or the head. The custom was to take Balabhadra’s prasad to be offered to Bimala Devi, the oldest Shakti deity inside the temple premises. A portion of this offering was then taken and offered to the stone images in Chudanga Sahi by the Badu Mahapatra, an important temple servant. Some was also given to the Hanuman deity and to the image of a female deity called Garedi Suni. All these images are installed inside a small temple.

The two stone images, one of a male and another of a female, are of much significance. The beautiful male figure is seated on a throne and armed with a bow and arrow. On both his sides are the figures of two attendants, one holding the royal umbrella and the other a chamara. On the pedestal are the images of a man with an elephant and another with a horse. The figure so represented is clearly a royal image, and people widely believe that it represents Ananta Varman Chodaganga Deva, the builder of the great Jagannath temple.

By the side of this male figure is that of a female, seated on a stool and apparently husking rice. This figure is popularly known in the locality as Garedi Suni, which means a lady practicing witchcraft. It thus appears to be a portrayal of the Nitei Dhobani story found in the *Mādalā-pañjī* and recounted in chapter 5 above.

## Atharo Nala

Previously, the only way to enter the town of Puri was by crossing the Matia or Madhupur River. The bridge that one uses to cross is called Atharo Nala. Atharo means “eighteen” and refers to the number of spans that make up the bridge. In the Chaitanya Charitamrita, Krishna Das describes the ecstasy of Mahaprabhu and the Gaudiya Vaishnavas as the crossed the bridge to enter Puri. The bridge is said to have been constructed in around the 13th century.

The Chaitanya Bhagavata describes Mahaprabhu’s first arrival in Jagannath Puri in the company of Nityananda Prabhu, Jagadananda, Gadadhar Pandit, Mukunda Datta, Govinda and Brahmananda.\[115\] The Lord saw the flag on the main temple from the village of Kamalpur and even had a vision of Lord Krishna standing in front of the temple, which drove Him into paroxysms of ecstasy. It took Him another hour to reach Atharo Nala.

As soon as the Lord arrived at Atharo Nala, He controlled His ecstatic mood. Calming Himself, He sat down with His companions and humbly said, “You have acted as true friends by bringing Me here so that I can take darshan of Lord Jagannath. Now you go on ahead to see the Lord, or I will go on ahead of you. Tell me what you want.” Mukunda said, “You go on ahead.” The Lord said “Very well” and continued on toward the temple.

It is also described that when the Lord returned from His pilgrimages, the devotees would come to Atharo Nala to meet Him. And when Mahaprabhu heard that the Bengal devotees had arrived there, Mahaprabhu would send Govinda with flower garlands to welcome them.

The bridge itself is a testimonial to ancient Indian engineering. Another, similar bridge with eleven spans is found near Jajpur. In all, the bridge is 290 feet long and is made of laterite and sandstone. It is fourteen feet wide and eighteen feet high in the middle.

There are many different opinions about when this bridge was built. It is most likely that it was built by Raja Kavi Narasimha Deva at the end of the 13th or beginning of the 14th century. However some historians say that it was built by the King Matsya Keshari as early as the 8th century. One legend has it that the bridge was first built by King Indradyumna himself. He met with repeated failure until Lord Jagannath ordered him to sacrifice his eighteen sons and throw their heads in the river. After he did this, he was able to complete the building of the bridge.

## Kapala Mochan Shiva

Kapala Mochan Shiva is one of the five Shiva lingas in land of Puri. These five Shivas are sometimes described as Lord Jagannath’s gatekeepers, sometimes as his ministers. They are known popularly as the five Pandavas. They are also known as Kshetrapalas, or protectors of Jagannath’s holy land.

The Kapala Mochan temple is situated near the southern gate of the Jagannath temple compound. It is said that Brahma formerly had five heads, but that Shiva chopped one of them off. The head (*kapāla* means “skull”) immediately stuck to his hand and, try as he might, Shiva could not shake it off. He travelled the three worlds, desparately seeking a way to rid himself of the skull, to no avail. He finally came to the Lord’s abode on Earth, Jagannath Puri, and took shelter of Lord Jagannath. By so doing, he was liberated of the sin of trying to kill a Brahmin. Ever since, he has resided next door to the Lord, serving as a guard to His temple and singing His glories.

## Yameshwar

Yameshwar’s temple is located in Gaurbat Sahi. Yameshwar Shiva has the appearance of being half-human, half-lion, like Nrisingha Deva. Local people say, however, that he is a Harihar deity, a combined form of Shiva and Vishnu.

There is a Garuda pillar in front of the temple, as well as a Vrisha Stambha (a pillar dedicated to the bull Nandi). Next to the Shiva temple is another dedicated to Parvati Devi.

Thirty Brahmin families take care of the temple puja and they form the core of the village that formed around the temple and became the Gaurbat Sahi neighborhood. They are Smartas who perform the *pañcopāsanā.*

The Yameshwar temple and deity participate in many of Lord Jagannath’s festivals. On numerous occasions, Harihar, Yameshwar’s representative deity form or *vijaya-vigraha*, goes to the Jagannath temple to see Lord Jagannath. Harihar is a four-armed figure made of brass. Starting from the upper right hand and ending with the upper left, Shiva deity holds a trident, a dumaru drum, a discus and a conch shell. Representations of Garuda and Nandi accompany this deity on his peregrinations.

Yameshwar is also known as Muktishwar, the lord of liberation. Because he is the master of liberation, Lord Shiva crushes the pride of Yamaraj, the lord of death. As in Kashi, anyone who dies in the vicinity of the Yameshwar temple is not subject to the usual rule of Yamaraj.

Lord Yameshwar is always dancing with ecstatic love for Jagannath. On the last day of the Rathayatra, on the Ekadasi, Jagannath does not accept offerings of rice. So, on that day, the kitchens of the Jagannath temple are put at Yameshwar’s disposition and a full offering is made to him. This bhoga is then treated by Jagannath’s devotees as maha prasad. Yameshwar is given rice and vegetable offerings every day in his own temple.

The Yameshwar temple is surrounded by a wall. One has to descend a stone staircase to come to the temple. There is a small tank there known as Yavanika Tirtha.

Yameshwar’s temple has two principal annual festivals, one in the month of Karttika, Yama Dvitiya or Bhratri Dvitiya. The other is in Jyaishtha on Sitala Shashthi. Sitala Shasthi is particularly important festival for the five Mahadevas in Puri, because the marriage of Lord Shiva to Parvati Devi is celebrated. In Jagannath Puri, the representative deities of the five Mahadevas are taken to the Jagannath temple with the images of Parvati for the Lord’s blessing. The word *śītala* means “cool,” because marriage to Parvati made it possible for Lord Shiva to cool down.

The king of Orissa donated large amounts of land to maintain the Yameshwar temple. It endowed lands are found in the village of Dandas Pura.

To the south of the temple was a garden known as Yameshwar Tota. Mahaprabhu ordered Gadadhar Pandit to live here, and in time, the Tota Gopinath temple was built here. Mahaprabhu would come to visit Gadadhar every day and would take darshan of Yameshwar on his way to or from his residence.

## Lokanath

About a mile and a half (two kilometers) west of the Jagannath temple, on the Puri city limits, stands the ancient Lokanath temple, surrounded by a wall made of white marble. The level of the ground around the temple is high, indicating that the ground level was much lower when it was built. This is the result of the continuous sand drifting that is evident elsewhere in Puri, as at Govardhan Math.

Legend has it that Lord Rama Himself installed this Shiva linga when on His way to exile in the Panchabati forest. The linga remains submerged in water the year round. He is accompanied by two golden cobras with their hoods spread. This is an indication that Lokanath takes shelter of his master, Lord Ananta Deva. Because Lokanath is entirely submerged, it is not possible to see him and so pilgrims and devotees must be satisfied by taking darshan of his representative deity. On the Pankoddhar Ekadasi before Shiva Ratri, the water is bailed out, enabling the thousands of devotees who gather to see and worship the Lord by sprinkling water on him.

A fair is held at the Lokanth temple every year on the last Monday of the lunar month of Vaishakh. This day is known as Saranti Sombar. The temple is managed by a trust board under the control of the State Endowment Commissioner.

Lokanath is said to cause miraculously cures, and this attracts many diseased and invalid people to the temple. As a result, a community of lepers lives near this temple. These lepers often gather on the Swarga Dwar Road to beg from pilgrims.

In one article, Srila Puri Maharaj wrote, “On the way to the seashore, many lepers cried out for alms. Their painful calls melted the hearts of many of the devotees who gave them coins in charity. As they helped them this way, they also poured the great medicine of the Holy Names into their ears.

“Sin is manifest in so many signs, according to the Smritis. To give an idea, Visvanath Chakravarti quotes the following verse in his commentary to the Srimad Bhagavatam ([7.5.27](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-7/5.27)):

*brahmahā kṣaya-rogī syāt surāpaḥ śyāva-dantakaḥ*  
*svarṇahārī tu kunakhī duścarmā guru-talpagaḥ*

**“Someone who kills a Brahmin catches consumptive tuberculosis; the drunk gets rotten teeth; the thief catches a disease of the fingernails, while the sinner who seduces his elder’s wife becomes a leper.”**

“Simply the reflection of the sunlight of the holy name of the Lord can eliminate the darkness of all such great sins. Ultimately, it is a rejection of Krishna himself and his service that is at the root of all sin and sickness: it is called the disease of material life – *bhava-vyādhi*. The only cure for this disease is follow the instructions of a doctor – the pure Vaishnava devotee – and take the medicine of the Holy Names and a diet of maha prasad. The primary blessing of the Holy Name is to give love for Krishna. It cures the disease of material life as a secondary effect.”\[116\]

## Puruna Nahar

It is said that the area known as Bata Sagara is the holiest part of Puri. The king's palace and many of the city's principle religious institutions were built in Bata Sagara. The Govardhan Math, Radha Kanta Math, Ganga Mata Math and many others are all within the periphery of the Bata Sagara.

The word *nahar* is Orissan for palace. Puruna is a corruption of the Sanskrit word *purāṇa*, meaning "old or ancient." The ruins of the ancient royal palace are spread throughout the Bali Sahi district of the old part of Puri town. These ruins, covering a 30-acre piece of land, bear witness to the ancient glories of the Orissan empire and its kings.

Temples to various Hindu deities worshiped by these kings are still standing amidst these ruins. Four temples to the goddess are place in the four directions -- Mangala Devi to the east, Ramayani Devi to the west, Varahi to the north and Sathi Dauni to the south. In the northwestern (Agni) part of the palace compound stood a water tank surrounded by marble stairs. At present, these steps are broken and the water is muddy, but even so, it is evident that the tank had been built at great cost.

There are many reminders of King Prataparudra, who was blessed by Sri Chaitanya, as well as of his father Purushottama Deva. Sundarananda Vidyavinoda visited this site in the company of Vishwanath Rajaguru, a particularly distinguished and educated member of the family that has provided spiritual guidance to the kings of Puri for generations. From him he learned that these temples were established prior to Purushottam Deva's coming to throne.

Significant amongst these temples are the “eight Shambhus” or Shiva lingas. At the time that Sundarananda wrote, these deities were all reunited in one small temple, despite their long history of being worshiped by the Orissan royal family. The middle linga is the largest and is made of a white stone. The other lingas are of different colors. The white linga has the mark of Ananta Deva on his head.

Besides these Shiva lingas, a number of other deities are worshiped in this temple. There is a Kali deity known as Shyama Kali, Radha Kanta, and a number of other deities that were carried off from Kanchi by the King Purushottam Deva. The Radha Kanta Math claims that they have the deity of Radha Kanta brought from Kanchi; they hold that this deity is a representative or substitute of this deity.

Another temple on the palace grounds holds deities that both predate and postdate King Prataparudra. The temple has two rooms. One has the stone images of Sri Sri Radha and Krishna and their representative deities, the brass figures of Sri Rasika Raya. The other room has wooden deities of Sri Sri Gaura Gadadhar and Sri Sri Gaura Nityananda. These murtis are clearly very old and are said to have been consecrated during the time of King Prataparudra. They stand on an elevated altar where they are accompanied by a large number of other, smaller dei ties. The deities of Gaura Nitai are life-sized, while those of Gaura Gadadhara are somewhat smaller. All four figures are in dancing posture. The Gauranga deity resembles the Mahaprabhu deity from the Chaitanya Math in Sri Mayapur, standing with his right arm upraised.

The other deities in this temple include a four-armed Nila Madhava murti, stone figures of Ramachandra, Lakshman and Sita, a four-armed Vishnu figure known as Sri Dhyana Narayan, a Patita Pavan form of Lord Jagannath, Balaram-Krishna, another Radha-Krishna figure, and a four-armed Krishna-Narayan figure that holds a flute in its lower hands and the conch and discus in its upper hands and stands in the three-fold bending form. There are also Saraswati and Lakshmi murtis and a number of Shalagram Shilas that are placed in a circular formation like the eight Shambhus. To this must be added eight other smaller Shiva lingas that are called “the eight witnesses” (*aṣṭa-sākṣī-mahādeva*).

The financing of the worship of all the deities in these two temples comes from the royal family, but it has lost a lot of its former glory and is conducted in a routine manner. A professional pujari conducts the worship in a peremptory fashion. The Gaura-Nitai and Gaura-Gadadhar deities that were worshiped by King Prataparudra have no ornaments or finery and are housed in a dark building. They are given food offerings of kakra, a preparation made from flour, ghee and gur.

There were many other valuable stone inscriptions and sculptures in the ancient palace, but these were removed to the new palace or Bali Nahar on the Bara Danda when it was built. The new palace was built by Ramachandra Deva III between 1840 and 1842.

## The four ashrams

Connected with the Jagannath temple rituals are four ancient ashrams, Angira Ashram (Dol Mandap Sahi), Pandu Ashram, Markandeya Ashram and Parasara or Ugrasena Ashram. There is also a Bhrigu Ashram in Gaurbat Sahi.

On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Shravan, the Nrisingha deity of the Jagannath temple pays a visit to these four ashrams. This is called Badi Nrisingha Vijaya. Sital bhoga is offered to the deity in each ashram. On the full moon day of Shravan, Lord Sudarshan visits all these ashrams. They are managed by local committees.

## Baseli temple

Gives name to a road and neighborhood. Baseli or Basuli is a goddess who is unique to eastern India, and particularly to Orissa. She is worshiped by the Keutas or Kaibartas, i.e., the fishermen caste. She is depicted as having a horse’s head.
