She is propitiated every Tuesday and Saturday, particularly during the month of Vaishakh, from the Chaitra Purnima to the Vaishakh Purnima. Many legends surround her and the Orissan Achyutananda Das, one of the Pancha Sakhas, wrote about her in his book *Kaibarta Gupta-gīta.*

In Puri the dummy-horses are profusely decorated with flowers and the Tahia presents a magnificent show during dance. When the festival ends the horse-head is taken out ceremonially from the frame and is preserved in a temple. Next year during the festival it is again brought out and repainted for worship and use during the dance.

Baseli also get *khei* every day from Lord Jagannath’s Kotha Bhoga.

## Other temples within Puri

## Nrisingha Temple

Situated near the Gundicha ghar, it has a role in the Naba Kalevara ceremony.

## Mausi Ma Temple or Ardhasini Temple

This small temple to the Goddess Ardhasini is located on the Grand Road, midway between Jagannath Temple and Gundicha ghar. She is also known as Mausi Ma (the mother's sister), describing Her relationship to Lord Jagannath. The deity resembles that of Subhadra in the temple.

On the day the Return Ratha Yatra, Poda pitha bhoga is offered to Lord Jagannath on behalf of this temple. The temple is managed by a committee. Foreign devotees apparently have no difficulty entering here.

## Alam Chandani Temple

It is involved with the Saptapuri, Makar Sankranti and Nava Kalevara rituals.

## Dakshin Kali Temple

Goddess Dakshin Kali plays an important part in the *niti* of Saptapuri amavasya.

## Narayani Temple

The Deities of Durga and Madhava from the Sri Mandir visit this temple for eight days during the annual sixteen-day Durga Puja in the month of Ashwin.

## Charchika Temple

This temple of Goddess Charchika is on the Grand Road, near the Jagannath Temple office. The carpenters and Bhoi sevaks worship Charchika immediately prior to building the Ratha Yatra chariots, which are constructed anew each year.

## Kanak Durga Temple

Located in front of the Sri Jagannath temple office, on the grounds of the current Palace (Sri Nahar) of the Gajapati Maharaja. The deities housed within this temple are the personal deities of the king. The administration of the Sri Jagannath temple also supplies some of the ingredients for the bhoga for their worship.

## Siddha Hanuman Temple

This temple is behind the Gundicha temple. It is said that Tulasi Das, the great poet-saint, stayed here while he was visiting Puri.

## Jayadurga Temple (Bharati Kotha)

The administration of the Jagannath temple pays for the daily bhoga for the Goddess Durga at this temple near Narendra kunda.

## Other Temples of the Goddess

There are a number of other temples dedicated to the Goddess around Puri: Barahi, Gachha Kali, Bana Durga, Rama Chandi, Hara Chandi Temple, Smashana Chandi, Saptamatrika, Jadurani, Jhareshwari, Uttara Kali and Mangala. Besides the aforementioned Baseli, Barahi and Hara Chandi also get *khei* every day from Lord Jagannath’s Kotha bhoga.

## Chapter 22 - The Maths of Puri

Since Hindus of all sampradayas accept the sanctity of Sri Kshetra, they have nearly all established themselves here, honoring it by building temples and monasteries, or maths. Maths are monastic houses originally founded with the object of giving religious instruction to chelas or disciples, and generally of encouraging a religious life.

Bhakti Promode Puri Maharaj explains the meaning of “math” as follows: “The Sanskrit verb root *maṭh* means ‘to dwell, to reside.’ The word *maṭha* is thus derived in the following way: *maṭhanti vasanti yatra paramārtha-śikṣārthinaḥ* – ‘A math is a place where those desiring to learn about the ultimate spiritual truth live.’ In usage, however, the word *maṭha* is expanded to include the ideas of a student hostel, an educational establishment, and a temple or place of worship. Though the presence of a deity and temple are also implied in the term, a math’s primary purpose is the dissemination of knowledge to those who serve that deity, in the categories of sambandha, abhidheya and prayojana. There is furthermore an implied obligation to distribute this knowledge to those living outside the math’s confines, for their welfare.” \[117\]

The first major preacher to establish such a math in Sri Kshetra was Shankaracharya in the 9th century, who sent his four principal disciples to the four corners of India to establish outposts for preaching his doctrines. Thus Sureshwar Acharya established Sharada Math in Dvaraka in the west, Totaka Acharya established Jyotir Math in Badarikashram in the Himalayas, and Hastamalaka Acharya established Sringeri Math in Rameshwar, in India’s south. Finally, Padmapada Acharya founded Govardhan Math, also known as Bhogavardhan Math, in Puri.

Subsequently, even Shaivas and the sampradayas following Kabir and Nanak, who strictly speaking do not accept the Lord’s eternal form, have acknowledged the fundamental sanctity of Sri Kshetra by establishing maths there. On the whole, however, since Sri Kshetra is the eternal abode of Lord Vishnu or Purushottam, it exerts a natural attraction on the different schools of Vaishnavism.

King Indradyumna and all his descendants were worshipers of Lord Vishnu. After receiving Lord Chaitanya’s mercy, King Prataparudra supported many maths, establishing places where worshipers of the Lord could reside to pursue their cultivation of devotional service and preach the glories of the Lord’s holy name. Ramananda Raya thus established a math in the Jagannath Vallabha gardens, Paramananda Puri another to the west of the Temple, and Gadadhar Pandit in the Yameshwar gardens. Other associates of Mahaprabhu established maths near the Swarga Dwar: Svarupa Damodar -- Boro Asan Math, Jagadananada Pandit – Giridhari Asan Math, Raghunath Das Goswami – Madan Mohan Deva Asan Math, Bhagavan Acharya – Balaram Asan Math. Gopal Guru Goswami established the Radha Kanta Math, Narahari Sarkar the Vishakha Math, and Abhiram Thakur Sri Bali Math.

Second generation followers of Mahaprabhu continued to establish residences and maths in Puri. Shyamananda Prabhu and his disciple Rasikananda founded Sri Kunja Math; Jiva Goswami’s disciple Prema Das or Krishna Das founded the Radha Damodar Math; Seva Das, a disciple of Narottam Das Thakur, founded the Jhanj Pitha Math; Nandini, in the line of Advaita Acharya, started the Sri Nandini Math; Madhavi Devi, Sikhi Mahiti’s sister, established the Bentpur Gopinath Math; Sachi Devi, who was initiated by Hari Das Goswami and was later known as Ganga Mata Goswamini, established the Ganga Mata Math.

All these followers of Mahaprabhu, their disciples and descendants transformed the face of Puri Dham. Mahaprabhu’s devotees continue to come and establish maths and temples in Puri Dham. In the 19th century, Svarupa Das Babaji founded the Kadali Patka Asan Math and Bhaktivinoda Thakur established his own place of worship near Hari Das Thakur’s samadhi and named it Bhajan Kuti. Subsequently Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati Thakur established the Purushottam Math in the sand dunes of Gaurbat Sahi and his disciples and grand-disciples have followed his example by establishing many other beautiful maths and temples in Sri Kshetra.

Of course, other than the followers of Sri Chaitanya, the Vaishnavas of other sampradayas have also established branches in Puri, increasing the spiritual opulence of Lord Jagannath’s abode.

The largest number of Vaishnava maths belong to the Gaudiya Vaishnava sampradaya, especially with the large number of new maths that have been built in the last half-century by the disciples and grand-disciples of Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati Thakur. The next largest number belong to the Ramanandis, then Ramanuja, Nimbarka, and Vishnuswami. The Madhvacharya Sampradaya does not have any temples or maths in Puri. In all, the total number of maths in Puri is given by some to be as high as 752, but O’Malley gave the number as “about seventy” in the Puri District Gazetteer of 1929. A recent work by Surendranath Pradhan (1996) counts 116 working Maths and ashrams belonging to 20 different sects. He gives the following count, according to sampradaya –

Gaudiya – 20  
Ramanuja – 19  
Ramanandi –17  
Gaudiya Math –12  
Utkaliya and Atibori – 7  
Pancha Ramanandi – 6  
Angira – 7  
Nimbarka sect – 3  
Vallabhi – 3  
Others - 12

Many of the Puri maths are integrated into the life of the Dham through participation in both the regular rituals of the Jagannath temple as well as special festivals. Some of the maths that play a large role in the temple rituals are the Emar Math, Boro Oriya Math, Boro Chata Math and Sana Chata Math. In the past, the kings of Puri allotted wood-burning stoves in Jagannath’s kitchens to certain maths. Though the regular temple Suars cook on these fires, the bhoga that is prepared on them is stored in the Saraghara storeroom after offering. Devotees then from the maths come to collect this prasad and distribute it to the poor on the Boro Danda.

The heads of maths in Orissa are called mahants or mathdharis, which is often translated as “abbot.” They are chosen from among the disciples of the previous Mahant and are assisted in the management of their properties by adhikaris, who act as their business managers. In most maths the mahants are celibates, but some of them were founded by householders and in these the position of mahanta is passed on from father to son.

To ward off succession difficulties, the British government passed a law obliging mahants to name their successors in a written will. If for some reason the abbot of a particular math dies without having done so, or if the successor he names is unable to carry out his duties or behaves in a way unbecoming to his station, the mahants and monks of the four main Vaishnava sampradayas gather together in council and decide who is suitable for the position. They consecrate the person they thus select as Mahant on the thirteenth day of deliberations by tying a piece of Lord Jagannath’s prasadi cloth around his head. The successor is then formally recognized by the king of Puri in the ceremony known as Khandua Lagi, in which he ties a piece of cloth (or *khaṇḍuā*) with verses of *Śrī Gīta-govinda* written on it around their heads. On several occasions, the written testament of a dying mahant has been overturned by the council of the four sampradayas, showing the power of the established community in Puri.

The king or the temple administration would acknowledge the importance of a temple or math by giving it some duties to perform in the temple, attaching to it land endowments. O’Malley explains the system of endowments that supported the maths for hundreds of years:

Mahants are the gurus or spiritual guides of many people, who present the maths with presents of money and endowments in land. Thus, Sri Ram Das of Dakshin Parshwa Math received rich endowments from the Marathas, the abbot having been the guru of the Maratha governor; while the mahant of the Emar Math in the eighteenth century, who had the reputation of being a very holy ascetic, similarly got large offerings from his followers and was possessed of large estates.

The lands of the latter are known as *amṛta-manohi* (literally, “nectar food”) because they were given with the intention that the proceeds thereof should be spent in offering bhoga before Jagannath and that the Maha Prasad thus obtained should be distributed among pilgrims, beggars and ascetics. They are distinct from the amṛta-manohi lands of the temple itself, which are under the superintendence of the Raja.

In 1848, Babu Braj Kishore Ghose roughly estimated the annual income of twenty-nine maths from land alone at Rs. 1,454,000, and this income has increased largely in the last 80 years.\[cxviii\]

W. W. Hunter commented in his 1872 work, “In every country, monastic licentiousness has followed hard upon monastic wealth.” From the beginning of their rule, the British felt that the misuse of funds intended for use by the maths for religious functions had reached such a height as to require a legislative remedy. They passed the Board of Revenue Act in 1810,\[cxix\] only six years after their accession, placing the monasteries under government regulation. This act was repealed a few years later as the British, under pressure from Christian missionaries, tried to extricate themselves as far as possible from involvement in Indian religious life.

In 1860, Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakur wrote *Maths of Orissa* in English, in which he gave a brief description of many of Puri’s maths. Though this book is now impossible to find, we can get an interesting insight into the Thakur’s attitude to the maths he saw from the quotations from this booklet given by Hunter. Hunter noted that public indignation from native Hindu circles had grown louder every year in the face of monastic corruption. It was in support of this argument that he cited “a native gentleman who had visited all the larger monasteries of Orissa and who was himself a landholder in that province.” This is the passage he cites:

Licentiousnes, inhospitality, and petty robbery are the daily vices that have crept into \[the maths\]. When the abbots go out of their monasteries, they pass with a retinue composed of elephants, horses and sometimes camels. Tom-tom players and performers on the horn go actively along with them. They never think of doing their duty. The monasteries hold half the lands occupied by the landholders, but they are of very little use to the public... They have given up their ancient hospitality. Pilgrims and sick men never approach them for fear of being rudely expelled from their portals. The abbots have yielded to degrading carnal pleasures and their disciples emulate their vices.”

Bhaktivinoda Thakur further spoke of a math that stood on his own landholdings in Choti, his ancestral home:

I have a small village in the country of Cuttack, of which I am the proprietor. In that village is a religious house, to which was granted, by my predecessors, a holding of rent-free land. The head of the institution gave up entirely entertaining such men as chanced to seek shelter on a rainy night. This came to my notice and I administered a severe threat to the head of the house, warning him that his lands would be cruelly resumed if in future complaints of inhospitality were brought to my knowledge.\[cxx\]

The tradition of government interference in financially mismanaged monasteries goes back to 1810, as mentioned above. This was followed by a succession of regulatory acts during the Raj, culminating in the establishment of the Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Commission in 1936. The OHREC remained primarily concerned with finances, leaving other aspects of math administration to the discretion of the head ascetics. However, the Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act of 1951 broadened the powers of the OHREC, which can take full control over a math if it detects misappropriation or mismanagement of its funds. Although the government often has no alternative in trying to correct mismanagement at a particular establishment, in many cases its actions quicken the process of spiritual deterioration, for a mahant tends to lose any respect he might have had in the community if such intervention takes place. The math thus becomes estranged from the laity and tends to lose both moral and financial support.

Another important development in math financing after Indian Independence is the loss of royal patronage. For centuries, the support of the independent rajas was the most important source of math wealth and prestige. This was especially true in Orissa, where many of the rajas followed the tradition of being initiated by specific math abbots, from one generation to the next. When the princely states were abolished after Indian Independence, this important source of revenue dried up. Now only those maths that have a wide basis of popular support can afford to maintain nice establishments. In general, this has worked to the benefit of newer institutions and to the detriment of older ones that failed to adapt to the changing circumstances and where traditions had become lax.

The Orissan government now also supports most of the temple rituals directly. When it took over the math’s duties in this respect, it also expropriated the property endowments that donors had in the past made to the maths to support them. The burden of service at the Sri Mandir has thus been greatly reduced.

The maths still continue their seva, but on a smaller scale. Thus, though the ancient maths are not as rich and powerful as they once were, they still play a huge spiritual role in keeping the atmosphere around the temple holy and sanctified. The influx of other, newer maths, has further contributed to renewing the spiritual life of Sri Purushottam Kshetra.

## Chapter 23 - Radha Kanta Math

The Radha Kanta Math is situated in the Bali Sahi neighborhood just a few hundred metres from the Jagannath temple along the Swarga Dwar road.

For Gaudiya Vaishnavas, the Radha Kanta Math is the most significant holy place in Jagannath Puri, for it stands on the site of Kashi Mishra’s house where Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu made His residence for the last twenty-two years of His pastimes on this earth. The authorities at the Radha Kanta Math claim to still have Kashi Mishra’s original title deed to the land in their possession.

Vrindavan Das names Kashi Mishra as one of Mahaprabhu’s principal devotees in Jagannath Puri:

*kāśī-miśra parama-vihvala kṛṣṇa-rase*  
*āpane rahilā prabhu jāṅhāra āvāse*

**Kashi Mishra was always in a state of divine ecstasy, relishing the sublime nectar of Krishna prema, for the Lord stayed in his house. (Cbh** [**3.5.213**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cb-antya/5.213)**)**

King Prataparudra considered Kashi Mishra to be his spiritual master and treated him with great respect. Krishna Das Kaviraj has described the King’s attitude to Kashi Mishra in the following statement:

*pratāparudrera eka āchaye niyame*  
*jata dina rahe teṅha śrī-puruṣottame*  
*nitya āsi kare miśrera pāda-saṁvāhana*  
*jagannātha-sevāra kare bhiyāna śravaṇa*  
*rājā miśrera caraṇa jabe cāpite lāgilā*  
*tabe miśra tāṅre kichu bhaṅgīte kahilā*

**Whenever King Prataparudra stayed in Jagannath Puri, he had one duty that he performed without fail. Every day, he would come Kashi Mishra’s house to massage his feet and hear a report on Lord Jagannath’s service. As King pressed his feet, Kashi Mishra would indirectly tell him what he had on his mind. (CC** [**3.9.81-83**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-antya/9.81)**)**

Kaviraj Goswami also recounts how Mahaprabhu came to live in Kashi Mishra’s house. When Mahaprabhu left Puri to to preach love of God in South India, Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya, who had recently been converted by the Lord, spoke with King Prataparudra, explaining that Mahaprabhu was Krishna Himself. The King immediately believed everything that Sarvabhauma told him,

*rājā kahe bhaṭṭa tumi vijña-śiromaṇi*  
*tumi tāṅre kṛṣṇa kaha tāte satya māni*

**“Bhattacharya, you are the wisest person I know. Therefore, if you say that He is Krishna, I believe it is the truth. Should He ever return to Jagannath Puri, I hope that through your blessings I will be able to perfect my life by seeing Him.” (CC** [**2.10.17-18**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/10.17)**)**

In reply to this, Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya said,

*...teṅho āsibe alpa-kāle*  
*rahite tāṅre eka sthāna cāhiye virale*  
*ṭhākurera nikaṭa, āra ha-ibe nirjane*  
*e-mata nirṇaya kari deha eka sthāne*

**“The Lord will doubtless return very soon. When He does, He will need a place to stay -- one that is private and peaceful. It should be somewhere that is not only secluded, but near the Jagannath temple. Please make arrangements to find such a place for Him.” (CC** [**2.10.19-20**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/10.19)**)**

**The King replied, “Kashi Mishra's house is exactly what you require. It is near the temple, and yet very secluded.” On hearing this, Sarvabhauma went to Kashi Mishra to convey the King's desire. When Kashi Mishra heard the proposal, he said, “I am so fortunate, for the Lord of lords will be staying in my home.” (CC** [**2.10.23**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/10.23)**)**

Some time later, Mahaprabhu returned from his south Indian trip. The first thing He did on arriving was to take darshan of Lord Jagannath. As He did so, Sarvabhauma waited to take Him to His new quarters. Krishna Das writes:

After seeing Lord Jagannath, Mahaprabhu left the temple and Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya took Him to Kashi Mishra’s house. When Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu arrived there, Kashi Mishra immediately fell down at His lotus feet and surrendered himself and everything he owned to the Lord. Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu showed Kashi Mishra His four-armed form and then embraced him, thus accepting him as His personal servant.

Mahaprabhu sat down in the place Kashi Mishra gave Him, surrounded by all the devotees headed by Nityananda Prabhu. He was happy to see the residential quarters, which met all His needs. Sarvabhauma said, “This place is just right for You. Kashi Mishra hopes You will accept it.”

*prabhu kahe ei deha tomā-sabākāra*  
*jei tumi kaha sei sammata āmāra*

**The Lord said, “This body belongs to you. I will agree to whatever you tell me to do.” (CC** [**3.10.31-37**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-antya/10.31)**)**

Kashi Mishra’s house thus became Lord Chaitanya’s headquarters in Puri and thenceforth the Lord stayed there to distribute His mercy to the devotees and to relish His own pastimes in their company.

*hena mate śrī-gaurasundara nīlācale*  
*rahilena kāśī-miśra-gṛhe kutūhale*  
*nirantara nṛtya-gīta-ānanda-āveśa*  
*prakāśena gauracandra dekhe sarva-deśa*  
*kakhana nācena jagannāthera sammukhe*  
*tilārdheka bāhya nāhi premānanda sukhe*  
*kakhana nācena kāśī-miśrera mandire*  
*kakhana nācena mahāprabhu sindhu-tīre*

**In Nilachala, the Lord happily began to reside at Kashi Mishra's house. He spent all His time absorbed in the ecstasy of dancing and performing sweet, sublime kirtan and people from all over India could see these pastimes. Sometimes He would dance before Lord Jagannath, completely losing Himself in the joys of ecstatic love for Krishna; at other times, He would dance within the closed precincts of Kashi Mishra's residence, and occasionally He would run out to the ocean shores and dance there. (Cbh** [**3.5.130-3**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cb-antya/5.130)**)**

Mahaprabhu’s presence would attract crowds of devotees eager to get His darshan and His touch. Kavi Karnapur wrote the following description in his *Caitanya-candrodaya-nāṭaka* (8.35) *–*

*yugānte’ntaḥ kukṣer iva parisare pallava-laghor*  
*amī sarve brahmāṇḍaka-samudayā deva-vapuṣaḥ \|*  
*yathā-sthānaṁ labdhvāvasaram iha yānti sam śataśaḥ*  
*sahasraṁ lokānāṁ bata laghuni miśrāśrama-pade \|\|*

**Sarvabhauma said, “How amazing it is! At the time of the universal inundation, Krishna took the tiny form of a baby no larger than a banyan leaf, and yet all the universes entered His divine body. Now look, in the same way, hundreds and thousands of people are able to find a place to stand here inside Kashi Mishra’s house, small though it be!”**

## The Gambhira

In the Orissan language a small, windowless mud room situated on the grounds of a temple is given the name *gambhīrā*.\[cxxi\]Bhaktivinoda Thakur writes, “In traditional Orissan temple architecture, the deity room itself has a verandah (*alinda*) facing it. In front of the verandah is a paved and covered area known as the *dālān.* A small room within this area is given the name *gambhīrā*.”\[cxxii\]

In the Chaitanya Charitamrita, it is said that Mahaprabhu would rest in the doorway of the Gambhira after meals and Govinda would come to massage His feet (CC 3.10.82). At night, Mahaprabhu would sleep inside the Gambhira after Ramananda had parted for the night. Then Govinda and Svarupa Damodar would sleep in the doorway to prevent Him from going out in His ecstasies (CC 3.14.57-58). Often the Lord would not sleep but go on chanting the Holy Names while Govinda slept (CC 3.17.9-10). Indeed, sometimes He would get up in His ecstatic trance and go outside. For fear that He would hurt Himself, the devotees even locked the Gambhira’s doors, and He would rub His face on the mud walls, scratching it as He tried to get out.

Altogether, there were three walls between the street and Mahaprabhu’s room, three walls that had to be passed through for anyone to get in or out. This is made clear by Raghunath Das’ verse in the *Gaurāṅga-stava-kalpa-taru* (5)

*anudghāṭya dvāra-trayam uru ca bhitti-trayam aho*  
*vilaṅghyoccaiḥ kāliṅgika-surabhi-madhye nipatitaḥ \|*  
*tanūdyat-saṅkocāt kamaṭha iva kṛṣṇoru-virahād*  
*virājan gaurāṅgo hṛdaya udayan māṁ madayati \|\|*

**Without opening the three doors, Gauranga managed to get past the three walls and fell down amongst the Tailanga cows; His body shrunk and His limbs retracted into His body, making Him look like a tortoise. This is how Gauranga acted under the influence of intense separation from Krishna. This memory awakens in my heart and drives me mad with separation from Him.**

The clay cottage that was Mahaprabhu’s residence was replaced by a more permanent building in later times. Gopal Guru Goswami kept Mahaprabhu’s wooden shoes and a quilt, which was made either by Svarupa Damodar Goswami or Jagadananda Pandit, in the Gambhira where they are worshiped.\[cxxiii\] Many generations of devotees took small pieces of the sacred cloth over the years, leaving only a fragment of it. The waterpot from Vrindavan that Mahaprabhu used is also kept there, along with a wooden waterpot that was put there in later times.

## Gopal Guru Goswami

A line from Chaitanya Charitamrita was quoted above – “Kashi Mishra immediately fell down at the Lord’s feet and surrendered himself and everything he owned.” This indicates that Kashi Mishra morally gave his home over to Mahaprabhu. As he had no children, legal ownership of the property, including the adjoining gardens where Hari Das Thakur stayed, was transfered to Gopal Guru Goswami, who thus became the first mahant of the Radha Kanta Math after Mahaprabhu’s disappearance. His name is found in neither the Chaitanya Charitamrita nor the Chaitanya Bhagavata, but information about his life has been preserved by the Radha Kanta Math.

Gopal Guru was born in an Orissan Brahmin family. His father’s name was Murari Pandit, but his mother’s name is unknown. While still a child, he had the opportunity to serve Mahaprabhu under the guidance of Govinda, the Lord’s personal servant. His original name was Makaradhvaja Pandit, but Mahaprabhu used to affectionately call him Gopal.

Gopal Guru was the disciple of Vakreshwar Pandit, one of Mahaprabhu’s principal Bengali associates in Nilachala, who was espcecially known for his dancing in kirtan –

Vakreshwar Pandit, the Lord’s dear servant, once danced without rest for seventy-two hours. One day, while Mahaprabhu was Himself singing and Vakreshwar dancing, he fell down at the Lord’s feet and said, “O moon-faced Lord! Give me ten thousand Gandharvas so that I can dance to their singing! That will make me happy.” The Lord answered, “I have only one wing like you. If I had another, I would be able to fly in the sky!” (Chaitanya Charitamrita [1.10.17-20](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-adi/10.17))

In the book *Vakreśvara-carita,* it is said that there are five branches in the lineage descending from Vakreshwar -- those coming from Chandrasekhar, Shankararanya Acharya, Govindananda, Devananda and Gopal Guru, who is the most prominent of the five.

In his *Guru-praṇālī*, Adikanda Das states that Gopal Guru plays an eternal role in Krishna lila as Manjumedha Sakhi.

*vakreśvaraḥ samākhyāto rasa-rūpa-svabhāvataḥ*  
*siddhākhyā tasya kathitā tuṅgavidyābhidhā tu yā \|\|*  
*kṛṣṇa-priya-sakhī-madhye nāmnā tuṅgeti viśrutā \|*  
*paṇḍito bhakti-yogena nityaṁ vakreśvaraṁ bhajet \|\|*

**Vakreshwar was famous as a perfected soul because of his intense absorption in the relishing of devotional sentiments. He was Tungavidya Sakhi in his siddha form in Vrindavan, also known simply as Tunga to the other sakhis. The intelligent person should worship Vakreshwar according to the science of devotion.**

*asyā aṣṭa-sakhyo mañju-medhādayaḥ prasiddhāḥ \|*  
*tad yathā –*  
*mañju-medhā sumadhurā sumadhyā madhurekṣaṇā \|*  
*tanu-madhyā madhu-sudhā guṇa-cūḍā varāṅganā \|\|*  
*anugopī śrī-gopāla-gurur eva mahottamaḥ \|*  
*caitanya-kṛpayā tasyāḥ siddhākhyā mañju-medhikā \|\|*

**Tungavidya had eight sakhis, headed by Manjumedha. Manjumedha is a sweet thin-waisted girl with maddening eyes. Her words are sweet and she possesses all good qualities. She follows the chief gopis in incarnating during the pastimes of Lord Chaitanya as the great devotee, Gopal Guru Goswami. By Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s mercy, he is known to have the spiritual identity of Manjumedha.**

## How Gopal became known as Guru

There is a legend surrounding the addition of the word guru to Gopal’s name. There was once a devotee in Puri who was particularly attached to the chanting of the Holy Names. As a matter of fact, the chanting had become automatic for him, so that his tongue muttered the names incessantly. One day Gopal saw this devotee on his way to the toilet, holding his tongue between his fingers because he did not wish to chant the Holy Name while in an impure state.

Gopal was just a lad, but he was able to understand why the devotee was engaged in this strange behavior and said to him, “What are you doing? Don’t you know that there are no regulations governing the time and place for chanting the Holy Name? One should chant the Name in all times and circumstances, pure or impure. If you were not able to chant while defecating, how would your death be auspicious, should it suddenly come upon you at that time? Mahaprabhu’s teaching is *kīrtanīyaḥ sadā hariḥ,* ‘Always chant the names of Hari,’ and *niyamitaḥ smaraṇe na kālaḥ*, ‘There is no regulation governing the times when one may remember the Holy Name.’ This is the instruction of the world teacher, Sri Chaitanya. Anyone who disregards this teaching will surely fall down!”

Mahaprabhu overheard Gopal sharing this wisdom with the Vaishnava and was very impressed. He announced to all His devotees that Gopal was doing the work of a guru. So from that day on, the young Makaradhvaja Pandit was known to all the Vaishnavas as Gopal Guru. The name was appropriate, because he both preached and practiced and was thus factually acting as an acharya or guru.

It did not take long for Gopal Guru’s fame to spread through the Vaishnava world. Abhiram Thakur had the reputation of being able to verify whether a stone was a real Vishnu Shila or Shalagram Shila by paying his obeisances to it. If not real, it would crack or turn into dust. Only a pure Vaishnava would be able to resist his obeisances, which could prove fatal to a hypocritical devotee. When the Vaishnavas heard that Abhiram Thakur had come to Puri to test Gopal Guru, they were anxious for the boy, for whom they felt great affection. Mahaprabhu realized that everyone was troubled and so He placed His foot on Gopal’s forehead, thus creating the distinctive tilak marking that is used to this day by those in Gopal Guru’s spiritual lineage. Thus protected, Abhiram’s obeisances could do Gopal no harm. Some say that Mahaprabhu even took the boy in His lap for protection against Abhiram’s obeisances.

In *Jaiva Dharma,* Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakur describes the teachings of *bhakti-*rasa taking place at the Radha Kanta Math in Jagannath Puri, with Gopal Guru Goswami as their teacher. Before Vrajanath and Vijay head for Puri, their guru, Raghunath Das Babaji, glorifies Gopal Guru Goswami to them with the following words: “Vakreshwar Pandit’s disciple Gopal Guru Goswami is currently abbot of Mahaprabhu’s own math in the house of Kashi Mishra in Purushottam. Go there and take instruction from him, for he has completely memorized the teachings of Sri Svarupa Damodar Goswami.”\[cxxiv\]

Svarupa Damodar’s famous notebook, or korcha, gave two different methods of worshiping the Divine Couple in the *madhura-rasa*. These were passed on through two different lines. The first, considered to be the “internal” method, came through Raghunath Das Goswami and Krishna Das Kaviraj Goswami and is given shape in books like Chaitanya Charitamrita and *Govinda-līlāmṛta*; the other, “external” path, was taught to Vakreshwar Pandit and Gopal Guru Goswami and is described in the latter’s books, *Smaraṇa-krama-paddhati* (“A progressive guide to remembering Krishna”) or *Sevā-smaraṇa-paddhati* (“A guidebook to remembering and serving Krishna”) and *Gaura-govindārcana-paddhati* (“A guidebook to Gaura-Govinda’s deity worship”). In view of the high authority of the line of teaching coming from Svarupa Damodar through Gopal Guru, Bhaktivinoda Thakur also wrote: “Gopal Guru Goswami is the most important spiritual master of the Chaitanya sampradaya in Purushottam. He succeeds Svarupa Damodar on the world teacher’s throne.”\[cxxv\]

Gopal Guru’s successor, Dhyana Chandra Goswami, also wrote a *paddhati*, or instruction manual for worshiping according to the *rāgānugā bhakti* method. This book is also mentioned in *Jaiva Dharma.* Some people are of the opinion that the boy mentioned in the fifth chapter of the Antya-līlā of Chaitanya Charitamrita, who was so close to Mahaprabhu’s heart and caused Damodar Pandit to chastise the Lord, was either Gopal Guru or Dhyana Chandra.

## The service of Radha Kanta Deva

Kashi Mishra’s house became known as Radha Kanta Math from the time of Gopal Guru, because of the presence of the Radha Kanta deity. According to the Math’s tradition, Vakreshwar Pandit was never its official head or acharya, being always too absorbed in bhajan and kirtan in the Lord’s company. Mahaprabhu thus personally gave the responsibility for managing the Math and serving the Radha Kanta deities to Gopal Guru. The *tithi* marking this occasion is the Shukla Dvadasi of Magh. This tithi is observed as Acharyabhishek Mahotsava, and is even mentioned in the *Mādalā-pañjī.*

Maharaja Prataparudra’s father Purushottam Deva brought several deities back from Kanchi after defeating that city’s king. Among these deities was the murti of Radha Kanta. This deity was first placed in a small temple on the northwestern corner of Jagannath’s Chatrabhoga temple, but later, Prataparudra’s guru Kashi Mishra asked to be given the deity for his personal service. When Kashi Mishra bequeathed everything he possessed to Mahaprabhu, he also gave Him the service of Radha Kanta, which was later given to Gopal Guru.

During Kashi Mishra’s lifetime, the deity of Krishna was worshiped alone. While Gopal Guru was in charge of the temple, however, a deity of Radha was placed at Radha Kanta’s left side and a deity of Lalita on his right. Deities of Gauranga and Nityananda were also installed and the temple buildings repaired and enlarged during his time as mahant, that is, between 1538 and 1548 AD. Also worshiped in the temple are an oil painting of Advaita Prabhu, and on a separate throne, Lord Jagannath. This Lord Jagannath deity has separate land holdings for His service.

A few legends are told about Gopal Guru describing miraculous events. When Gopal Guru grew old, he turned the responsibility for the Radha Kanta Math over to his disciple, Dhyana Chandra. After he entered the eternal pastimes of the Lord, his successor took his guru’s body to the Swarga Dwar on the Puri seafront, where it was cremated and the ashes buried near Hari Das’ samadhi. The samadhi shrine that holds Gopal Guru Goswami’s ashes stands on the southeastern corner of Hari Das Thakur’s samadhi. Ever since, the ashes of all the mahants of the Radha Kanta Math are traditionally buried here.

Not long after Gopal Guru’s disappearance, Dhyana Chandra had to face a number of difficulties. The then king of Puri\[cxxvi\] ruled that since Kashi Mishra had been a servant of the king and had died without offspring, leaving no legal will, the land and buildings of the Math were therefore government property.

Moreover, though King Prataparudra had often requested Gopal Guru Goswami to accept bequests of land to help run the temple, Gopal had repeatedly refused these offers, being determined to serve Radha Kanta with spontaneous gifts of charity alone. Dhyana Chandra’s claims to succession were thus further weakened by the lack of any endowments in the Math’s name.

The king decided to occupy the Radha Kanta Math. He sent his bailiffs to barricade the door and ordered Dhyana Chandra and the other residents of the Math to vacate the premises immediately.

In the meantime, some Vaishnavas who had made a trip to Vrindavan were amazed when they saw Gopal Guru himself sitting under a papor tree in Vamshi Bata by the Yamuna, deeply absorbed in chanting japa. When some of them returned to Puri and gave this news to Dhyana Chandra, he took it as a sign. He decided to go immediately go to Vrindavan to see his guru, both because he found separation from him intolerable and because he hoped to bring him back to Puri to resolve the problems surrounding the ownership of the temple and the deities.

When he arrived in Vrindavan, Dhyana Chandra was astonished to find that his spiritual master was indeed engaged in intense bhajan in Vamshi Bata. Dhyana Chandra felt as though his life had been returned to him. He fell at his guru’s feet and recounted all the troubles that he had been having in Puri. He begged him to return with him to settle to dispute. Gopal Guru refused to leave Vraja Dham under any circumstances, however, but in order to calm his disciple, said, “In the garden by the Math, there is a neem tree. I will enter into that tree. Have an image of me made out of this tree and worship it. That will relieve the distress that you feel in my absence. Furthermore, I will enter into that murti and speak to the king through it. Then he will stop making trouble.”

Dhyana Chandra returned to Puri and set about following his spiritual master’s orders. The murti of Gopal Guru was made and installed next to Radha Kanta’s deity room and worshiped according to the procedures described in Dhyana Chandra’s *Paddhati*. Dhyana Chandra also installed a wooden image of Gopal Guru in Vrindavan in the place where he had seen him engaged in bhajan.\[cxxvii\]

Even though the king withdrew his claims over the property, Dhyana Chandra continued his guru’s policy of not accepting royal land endowments for the deities, prefering to serve the deities with the small gifts of lay devotees. This policy was only changed a few generations later under the mahant Govinda Sharan Das. Eventually, the Radha Kanta Math accumulated extensive land holdings in Ganjam, Puri, Cuttack and Visakhapatnam districts that brought an annual income of between fifty and ninety thousand rupees before Indian independence.

## Gopal Guru Goswami’s sūcaka kirtan

The following kirtan is sung on Gopal Guru’s disappearance day.

*āre mora gopāla guru bhakati kalapa taru*  
*makara-dhvaja nāma jāṅhāra \|*  
*śrī kṛṣṇa caitanya jāṅke gopāla baliye ḍāke*  
*dekhi śiśu caritra udāra \|\|1*  
*gaurāṅgera sevā-rase sadāi ānande bhāse*  
*gorā binu nāhi jāne ān*  
*tileka nā dekhi jāṅre dhairaja dharite nāre*  
*gorā jena gopālera prāṇ \|\|2*  
*gopāla śiśura prati śiksā dila eka rīti*  
*prabhu premāveśe ḍhuli ḍhuli*  
*kahe sabe āre āre āji haite gopālere*  
*ḍākibā gopāla guru bali \|\|3*  
*gopāle karuṇā dekhi sabāra sajala āṅkhi*  
*sukhera samudra uchalila*  
*sabe kahe anupāma śrī gopāla guru nāma*  
*prabhu datta jagate vyāpila \|\|4*  
*gopālera guru-bhakti kahite nāhika śakti*  
*sadāi prasanna vakreśvara*  
*mahāmatta nija-gīte nāhika upamā dite*  
*sarva cittākarṣa kalevara \|\|5*  
*dekhila sakala ṭhāṅi emana dayālu nāi*  
*kebā nā jagate yaśa ghoṣe*  
*sabe kaila prema-pātra haila vañcita mātra*  
*narahari nija karma doṣe \|\|6*

**1. O Gopal Guru, you are my devotional desire tree. Your name was previously Makaradhvaja, but Sri Krishna Chaitanya called you Gopal because your behavior as a child reminded him of Gopal Krishna.**  
**2. You were alway absorbed in the joy of serving Gauranga; indeed you knew nothing other than him. You could not tolerate being separated from the Lord for even a moment; it was as if Gaura was Gopal’s very life.**  
**3. One day, Gopal was explaining some devotional practices to another child. The Lord was so ecstatic when he saw this that he said to everyone, “From today on, I will call Gopal ‘guru’.”**  
**4. Tears filled the devotees’ eyes when they saw how merciful the Lord was to Gopal; it was as though the ocean of joy was overflowing. Everyone said that Gopal Guru was an extraordinary name and, as the Lord had given it, they all used it.**  
**5. I am incapable of describing Gopal’s devotion to his guru, Vakreshwara, who was always pleased with him. The incomparable Gopal Guru, whose appearance was attractive to everyone, was always intoxicated in singing devotional songs of his own composition.**  
**6. Everyone recognized that no one was as merciful as he. Who in the world did not sing his glories? He made everyone worthy of loving ecstasy; only I, Narahari, have been deprived of it because of my own misdeeds.**

## The Radha Kanta Math after Dhyana Chandra

Balabhadra succeeded Dhyana Chandra. He was selected by the Vaishnavas of the four sampradayas as their head, and consecrated him in this position by tying Lord Jagannath’s cloth around his head. It is said that the title “mahant” was conferred on the abbots of the Radha Kanta Math from this time.

Govinda Sharan, the fifth head of the Math, spread the faith of Mahaprabhu into southern Orissa. He made Jagannath Narayan Deva, the Raja of Parlakimedi his disciple. This king granted land to build a temple in his territory. His successors maintained their faith in Mahaprabhu for many generations. His descendant, the Maharaja of Parlakimedi, was the first chief minister of the Orissan legislative assembly. During the passing of the Utkal University Act in 1936, this distinguuished Vaishnava publicly declared, “We are firm believers in the religion that we follow, that is, the great teachings of Chaitanya.”\[cxxviii\] Many other rich landowners in Ganjam and further south followed the example of the Parlakimedi kings and took initiation from the mahants of Radha Kanta Math.

Since the time of Gopal Guru, practically ever single king of Puri made some kind of official declaration in favor of the Radha Kanta Math, with the result that it became integrally involved in the service of Lord Jagannath. The mahants of the Math thus have held the privilege of being able to directly offer the Lord flowers and fan Him in the temple, to fan Him on His boat during Chandan Yatra and on the chariot during Rathayatra. Whenever a mahant passes away, he is cremated with the sacred flame that comes from Lord Jagannath’s kitchen.

There are also royal edicts to the effect that, in the month of Karttika, the devotees of the Radha Kanta Math are to sing kirtan by the Garuda pillar every day after Lord Jagannath’s Bala bhoga. Royal edicts also give the Radha Kanta Math the right to do kirtan closest to the Rathayatra carts, to perform lila kirtan by the Lakshmi temple in the Boro Deul during the month of Karttika, and to do kirtan in front of Madan Mohan during the Chandan Yatra.

Ever since the time of Prataparudra, the kings themselves personally declare the abbots of Radha Kanta Math as mahant. According to the authorities at this Math, other math leaders only have the right to be called “adhikari,” whereas the title “mahant” is the unique property of the Radha Kanta Math abbot. Later, of course, use of the title “mahant” became generalized.

The mahant of the Radha Kanta Math is traditionally a Brahmin disciple of the previous mahant who has never been married and has taken the vows of renunciation. He is named by the previous mahant before his departure. On Vakreshwar Pandit and Gopal Guru Goswami’s disappearance days, the mahant of the Radha Kanta Math sits on a special seat next to the Gambhira and receives all the heads of the branch maths who come to swear their fealty by bringing gifts and so on.

The custom of taking ordination as a monk, or *bhek*, is done with the ritual wearing of one of the ordinating monk’s kaupin and bahirvas. Nevertheless, it is the regulation for even renounced babajis to wear their cloth folded through the legs in the householder style (*tri-kaccha*) whenever they are engaged in direct service to the deity or to Lord Jagannath in the temple. Naturally, the servants of Lord Jagannath wear their cloth in this style, as they are all householders, but so do the monks of the Radha Kanta Math when engaged in deity worship. At other times, of course, they wear the kaupin and bahirvas.

The Radha Kanta Math has a collection of some three hundred palm leaf manuscripts in Orissan script, most of which are unfortunately in poor condition. They also have a good library of printed books. Sad to say, the Math does not have any of the original handwritten manuscripts of the books written by Gopal Guru or Dhyana Chandra.

The Radha Kanta Math had an ancient hand-written manuscript of Dhyana Chandra’s *Paddhati*, but it was full of spelling mistakes and thus not particularly reliable.

When Sundarananda Vidyavinoda visited the Math in the 1940s, its mahant was Vishwambhar Dasji, who was very learned in Sanskrit and Vedanta, which he had studied in Kashi and Nabadwip. Besides this, he was a great student of music, for which he showed considerable talent. He was a promoter of education, and supported the study of *Harināmāmṛta-vyākaraṇa* and Vaishnava philosophy*,* as well as English and other subject, which were taught both in the Puri math and several of the branch maths. The current mahant is named Dhyana Chandra Das Goswami.

## Branch Maths

In all, the Radha Kanta Math’s mahants established more than fifty branch maths over the years. In each of the branches, deities named Radha Kanta are worshiped. In Puri itself, there are a number of branches. One of these is the nearby Giridhari Math, which was established during the time of Krishna Charan Das Mahant with donations from the queen of Sorguja.

The Boro Tarala and Sana Tarala Maths in the Bali Sahi neighborhood are also presently under the management of the Radha Kanta Math. Krishna Charan Das Goswami had two disciples, Gauranga Das and Nityananda Das. When he died, Krishna Charan made his senior disciple Gauranga Das his successor. Gauranga Das decided that he wanted to go on a lengthy pilgrimage and so turned over the responsibility for the math to his godbrother, Nityananda Das. When he returned from his pilgrimage, however, he was reinstated, but to show kindness to his godbrother, he established a separate math for him. The name Tarala comes from a region in the district of Visakhapatnam (Andhra Pradesh) whose kings were hereditary disciples and supporters of the two maths. This royal family later started taking initiation directly from the Radha Kanta Math mahants.

Both these temples have Radha Kanta deities, but there is no worship of Gauranga. The samadhis of the previous mahantas are on the grounds of the maths themselves.

Pancha Tattva Maha Mantra

For many years, the continuous chanting of the Holy Names has been carried out on the terrace in front of the Gambhira. The devotees of the Math chant the couplet:

*śrī kṛṣṇa caitanya prabhu nityānanda*  
*hare kṛṣṇa hare rāma śrī rādhe govinda*

Srila Bhakti Promode Puri Maharaj made the following comments on this practice after visiting the Gambhira in 1967:

We have heard that formerly the names of the entire Pancha Tattva used to be sung here. Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakur was the first to preach the chanting of the Pancha Tattva mantra,

*śrī kṛṣṇa caitanya prabhu nityānanda*  
*śrī advaita gadādhara śrīvāsādi-gaura-bhakta-vṛnda*

Ever since that time, the names of the Pancha Tattva have been sung separately from those of the Maha Mantra.

*hare kṛṣṇa hare kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa hare hare*  
*hare rāma hare rāma rāma rāma hare hare*

Even though Radha and Govinda are both present in their combined form as Gaurasundara, their names, forms, abodes, lila and associates, are eternally distinct and this distinction should be honored.

There are some people who think that the Maha Mantra should always be chanted while counting on beads and not sung aloud without counting. This kind of thinking should not be applied to the Maha Mantra, which is the all-powerful form of the Holy Name. Normally, mantras have a few distinguishing characteristics such as a seed syllable such as *om* and a sacred word such as *svāhā* or *namaḥ* indicating self-surrender. A mantra with such characteristics must be chanted according to strict rules including that of chanting a fixed number of times every day. The Maha Mantra is also to be chanted a fixed number of times, but is not restricted to this kind of chanting only. One may also chant it without counting; one may chant whether in a state of purity or impurity, silently or aloud. In fact, the chanting of the Holy Name is not bound by any restrictions. This has been clearly stated in the Chaitanya Charitamrita:

*khāite śuite jathā tathā nāma laya \|*  
*deśa-kāla niyama nāhi sarva siddhi haya \|\|*

**One can chant the Holy Name in any condition at all, whether eating or lying down. There are no rules governing the time and place for chanting; one can attain all perfections in any case. (CC** [**3.20.18**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-antya/20.18)**)**

This statement makes it quite clear that one can chant the Holy Name either counting on japa beads or not. The only rule is to chant constantly: *sarva-kṣaṇa bala ithe vidhi nāhi āra.* We have never seen the chanting of the Maha Mantra being restricted in any way anywhere in the teaching or personal example given by Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakur or by Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati.”\[cxxix\]

## Chapter 24 - Ganga Mata Math

The famous Ganga Mata Math stands on the southern side of the Shweta Ganga tank, which was described in chapter 21.

## Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya

Though the Shweta Ganga is an ancient holy site of great significance in the land of Purushottam Kshetra, it is of even greater significance to Gaudiya Vaishnavas for it was the home of Mahaprabhu’s beloved associate, Vasudeva Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya, and the site of many of the Lord’s pastimes.

Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya was a great scholar of Nyaya and Vedanta from Vidyanagar in Nabadwip, the son of another great scholar, Maheshwar Visharada. He came to live in Jagannath Puri before Mahaprabhu’s arrival, living there at the invitation of the king as the chief scholar of his court. According to *Gaura-gaṇoddeśa-dīpikā*, he was the incarnation of Brihaspati, the guru of the gods.

After taking sannyas at the age of twenty-four, Mahaprabhu left Nabadwip and came to Puri. When He arrived at Atharo Nala, the bridge with eighteen arches that marks the entrance to the town of Jagannath Puri, the Lord beheld the temple spire and had a vision of Krishna. He ran toward the temple in a trance of love and when He entered it, ran towards the deity of Jagannath in order to embrace Him. As He came close to the altar, He fell down in a faint. The temple watchmen and sevaites saw Him lying unconscious in the temple, and thinking Him to be a vagrant, prepared to beat Him and evict Him from the grounds.

Vasudeva Sarvabhauma happened to be present and he stopped them from committing this great offense. He had been impressed by the beauty of the Lord as well as by His manifestations of spiritual ecstasy on seeing Jagannath. He could understand that this was no ordinary person. With the help of some students and the temple guards, Vasudeva Sarvabhauma had the unconscious Lord transported to his own home. So this was one of the first places that Mahaprabhu came to in Jagannath Puri.

When Sarvabhauma learned of Mahaprabhu’s family background, he was very happy, for his father Maheshwar Visharada had been a good friend of Mahaprabhu’s maternal grandfather, Nilambar Chakravarti. Sarvabhauma himself was much older than the Lord and so felt protective toward Him. At the time, Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya was not a devotee, but a worshiper of the impersonal aspect of the Deity. He thus did not fully understand Mahaprabhu’s transcendental devotion, what to speak of His divinity. He felt that the Lord was a handsome young man and that if He wished to maintain His sannyas vows, He should study Vedanta diligently. This would awaken in Him the required attitude of renunciation from the world. Sarvabhauma thus invited the Lord to learn Vedanta from him. The Lord accepted and for the next seven days listened to Sarvabhauma discourse on Vedanta at his house.

The story of how Mahaprabhu converted Sarvabhauma to an understanding of the personal nature of the Supreme and the supremacy of devotion as a means for attaining Him has been recounted in all the biographies of Sri Chaitanya. After Sarvabhauma’s mind had been changed, Mahaprabhu graced him with a vision of His six-armed form. A wall painting of this form graces the walls of the Ganga Mata Math as a reminder of this vision. Unfortunately this old painting, like the rest of the property, has deteriorated considerably and can barely be made out.

Mahaprabhu regularly accepted invitations to take prasad at Sarvabhauma’s house. At first, Sarvabhauma invited Him to eat at his house for an entire month. The Lord refused, saying that it was against the principles of a sannyasi to take regular invitations in that way. Sarvabhauma reduced his invitation to twenty days, then to fifteen days, but the Lord continued to turn him down, agreeing to go only once. Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya continued to press Him to accept more than one invitation and finally the Lord agreed to come for five days a month. Sarvabhauma also had other guests amongst Mahaprabhu’s associates: Paramananda Puri would come for five days a month, Svarupa Damodar for four, and each of the Lord’s eight other sannyasi associates for two days each.

Once when Mahaprabhu came to eat at Sarvabhauma’s house, Amogha, the husband of Sarvabhauma’s daughter, Sathi, came to watch. Sarvabhauma knew Amogha’s fault-finding character and so had kept a stick to chase him away so that he would not disturb the Lord. However, Sarvabhauma was so absorbed in serving the Lord that Amogha managed to sneak in. When the young man saw the lavish feast that had been placed in front of the Lord, he immediately began to find fault:

**”There is enough food here to satisfy a dozen people! Is this sannyasi is going to eat it all by himself?” (Chaitanya Charitamrita** [**2.15.248**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/15.248)**)**

Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya flared up in anger, took the stick he had at the ready and went after Amogha who fled as fast as he could. Sarvabhauma’s wife, shocked on hearing her son-in-law insult the Lord, began to flail herself on the head and chest and cursed him, saying, “May Sathi become a widow!”

The Lord Himself laughed off Amogha’s trivial criticisms and tried to pacify Sarvabhauma and his wife. The next day, however, Amogha came down with cholera. Sarvabhauma thought that justice was being done, that it was a suitable punishment for his son-in-law’s offensive words. When Gopinath Acharya informed Mahaprabhu that Sarvabhauma and his wife were both fasting and that Amogha was on his deathbed with cholera, the merciful Lord immediately went to Amogha’s bedside, placed His hand on his chest and said,

**”Your Brahminical heart is holy by nature; it is thus a proper place for Krishna to reside. Why have you allowed crass envy to find a place there and allowed it to be contamined? Luckily, your sins have all been destroyed as a result of your relationship with Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya. One whose heart has been cleansed of all such contamination is able to chant the names of Krishna. So, get up, Amogha, and chant Krishna’s names! The Supreme Lord will bestow His mercy upon you before long.” (Chaitanya Charitamrita** [**2.15.274-7**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/15.274)**)**

The Lord’s touch and His compassionate words had an immediate effect on Amogha. He rose up and started chanting, “Krishna! Krishna!” The eight symptoms of ecstatic love manifested on his body. He remembered his offensive words to the Lord and in his remorse began to slap himself repeatedly on the cheeks until his face was swollen and Gopinath Acharya stopped him. The Lord again repeated that Amogha was dear to Him because of his relationship with Sarvabhauma.

**”I love everyone in Sarvabhauma’s house, even the servants. Even his household dog is dear to Me, so will I not have affection for his relatives? (Chaitanya Charitamrita** [**2.15.284**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/15.284)**)**

The Lord then went to Sarvabhauma’s house and asked him and his wife to forgive their son-in-law, whose offenses were just the result of immaturity. After bringing them around, He had them break their fast.

## Ganga Mata Goswamini

After the Lord’s earthly pastimes came to an end, Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya did not remain long in this world. With all the troubles that followed, Sarvabhauma’s house also was abandoned and neglected. As this was the place where Mahaprabhu chose to inaugurate His pastimes in Sri Kshetra, He decided to send one of His energies to revive it. That person was Ganga Mata Goswamini.

Ganga Mata Goswamini's original name was Sachi Devi. She was born in Puntia, which is in the Rajshahi district of present day Bangladesh, on the Shukla Dashami of Jyestha in AD 1601. Her father was an important zamindar or raja, whose name was Naresh Narayan. Sachi Devi was indifferent to family life and devoted to Krishna from her early childhood. Her parents saw this and wanted to see her married as soon as possible, but Sachi told them that she refused to accept any mortal as her husband. When she announced her determination to remain unmarried in this way, her parents were troubled but could do nothing to change her mind. After her mother died, Sachi Devi left home and set out on a pilgrimage that led her first to Puri and then to Vrindavan.

In Vrindavan, she took initiation from Hari Das Pandit Goswami, the head priest of the Govindaji temple. After being blessed by her guru, Sachi Devi began to engage in intense bhajan, subsisting through madhukari, that is, by begging for morsels of bread from door to door. She spent several years in Vrindavan and Radha Kund. When she had become very advanced in her devotional life, her guru sent her to Purushottam Kshetra to recover the home of Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya, which had fallen into disrepair. Taking the command of her spiritual master as her all in all, Sachi Devi came to Jagannath Puri and took the *kṣetra sannyāsa* vow. At that time, all that remained of Sarvabhauma's house was a single run down building that housed his Damodar Shalagram Shila.

Even while living at her home in Puntia, Sachi Devi had studied the scriptures. In Vrindavan, furthermore, she had thoroughly studied the Srimad Bhagavatam. Now, she set out to preach. With her transcendental qualities and her powerful discourses on the Bhagavata, she made such an impression on the public that she began to attract large audiences. It did not take long before her fame had spread so widely that the Gajapati king himself, Mukunda Deva II (king from 1655-1690), came to listen to her speak on the Bhagavatam. He too became a devoted follower after being impressed by her devotional qualities and her learning.

## How Sachi came to be known as Ganga Mata

Not long afterward, a miraculous occurrence took place. One Krishna Trayodasi, an opportune moment came for the Maha Varuni Ganges bath. Many people who seek to accumulate pious credits make the trip to the Ganges for this auspicious occasion. Indeed, many of Sachi Devi's friends asked her to accompany them, but she could not abandon her *kṣetra sannyāsa* vows nor her service to the deities, so she was obliged to plead that it was impossible for her to go.

Even though she really did not want to go, Jagannath Deva himself made arrangements for her to bathe in the Ganges. That night he appeared to her in a dream and told her to take bath in the Shweta Ganga in the middle of the night. Sachi Devi followed his instructions, but as soon as she entered the water, she had a vision of Ganga Devi herself. She was carried away in a strong river current that came from nowhere and suddenly found herself inside the Jagannath temple. At the same time, she continued to see herself bathing in the Ganges amongst her friends from Puri. She not only saw the Ganges and all those who were immersed in its waters, but could hear the joyful noise of the bathing crowds.

She was not the only one. The temple gatekeepers awakened on hearing this commotion and called Lord Jagannath's pujaris. They in turn gave a report to the King himself, who ordered them to open the temple doors. When they finally flung the doors open, they saw no one but Sachi Devi standing there alone. Jagannath's pujaris were confused and at first did not know what to do. They assumed that Sachi Devi had broken into the temple with the intention of robbing the Deities' valuables and that they had caught her red handed, but by their suspicions they committed an offense to this great devotee. As a result, they were attacked by various diseases and distresses—-so much so that the service to Jagannath was affected.

Jagannath Deva finally appeared to the King and told him what had really happened. Being influenced by Sachi Devi's pure devotional attitude, Lord Jagannath himself had made the Ganges flow from his feet to bathe Sachi Devi directly in the currents of his charanamrita. The King and the other servants of the Lord could only be freed from their offenses if they apologized to Sachi Devi and took mantra initiation from her.

King Mukunda Deva went to Sachi Devi with his entourage, the temple guards and servants. They paid her their prostrated obeisances and begged for her forgiveness. Though the King and all the pujaris asked her for initiation, she only gave the mantra to the King in obedience to Jagannath's order. The King wanted to give a large amount of land as *guru dakṣiṇā*, but Sachi Devi refused it. When the King continued to beg for an opportunity to render service, she finally said that every midday he could send two containers of Maha Prasad – one of rice and one of vegetables -- a cloth and 160 paisa for the service of the Vaishnavas. From that day onward, Sachi was known as Ganga Mata and Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya's house as Ganga Mata Math. To this day, these same items are sent to the Ganga Mata Math after the midday offering at the Jagannath temple.

One night, Mukunda Deva had a dream in which Jagannath Deva appeared to him and told him to give Sachi Devi the tract of land bordering on the Shweta Ganga. The next morning, the King came to see Sachi Devi and enthusiastically told her about the dream. Though she had no interest in increasing her worldly possessions, Sachi Devi decided to accept the King's gift for the sake of her guru given duty to improve the condition of Sarvabhauma's house. Prior to that she had had to beg for the necessary articles to serve the deities. Wherever there is true devotion to the Lord, the trouble which one has to take to serve him is not seen as trouble, but rather as an opportunity and a source of joy.

Another of those who were blessed by initiation from Ganga Mata Goswamini was a certain Smarta Brahmin named Mahirath Sharma from Dhananjayapur. He came, like many other pilgrims, to perform oblations to his ancestors at Shweta Ganga, but he had the opportunity to see Ganga Mata and to hear her speak on the Bhagavatam. As a result, he changed his mind about the goal of spiritual life and took diksha from her. He is said to have attained perfection doing bhajan near the Swarga Dwar. Later he went to preach pure devotion in the Ganjam district of Orissa, where he gained a large following.

## Rasika Ray

At present there are five pairs of deities in the Ganga Mata Math: Sri Sri Radha Rasika Ray, Sri Sri Radha Shyamasundar (Shyama Ray), Sri Sri Radha Madan Mohan (Mohan Ray), Sri Sri Radhavinoda (Vinoda Ray) and Sri Sri Radharaman. Other than these, the Damodar Shalagram Shila of Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya is worshiped on a separate silver throne along with a dancing figure of Sri Gauranga made of metal and a Gopal deity. The Rasika Ray deity is the most prominent figure on the altar. The deity is a beautiful wooden figure with two arms holding a flute, and long, attractive eyes. Rasika Ray is accompanied by Radha on His left and Lalita Sakhi on His right.

The story of how Rasika Ray came to accept Ganga Mata Goswamini’s service is told as follows: Once there was a resident of Jaipur in Rajasthan, Chandra Sharma (or Krishna Mishra, according to some), whose family had served the Rasika Ray deity for generations. As a result of *sevāparādha*, offenses in the performance of service to this deity, however, this Brahmin had no descendants to continue the family line. As a result, he had no idea what would happen to Rasika Ray when he died.

One day, Lord Jagannath appeared to Chandra Sharma in a dream and told him to bring Rasika Ray to Puri and to give Him to Ganga Mata if he wished to be rid of the effects of his offenses. The Brahmin did as he was told and placed the deity in a box along with Radharani and carried them all the way to Purushottam Kshetra. After the long journey, he appeared at Ganga Mata's door. When she saw Rasika Ray, Ganga Mata said, “This deity deserves service fit for a king. I live the life of a renunciate, subsisting on begging. Where and how could I keep such a deity? I would end up committing many offenses. You are a householder; you should keep and serve Him.”

As he had been ordered by Jagannath, the Brahmin did not know what to do when Ganga Mata refused his gift. So he simply hid Rasika Raya amongst the tulasi bushes and went away. That night, Rasika Ray appeared to Ganga Mata in a dream and said, “I have come all the way here simply to accept your service. The Brahmin has hidden Me amongst the tulusi bushes, so please put Me in a better place where you can render Me service.”

Once she had been so ordered, Ganga Mata took the deity in and joyfully organized a festival in His honor. In a short time, the deity’s worship was being conducted in a befitting manner.

Ganga Mata Goswamini served Rasika Ray with great devotion for many years. She spent twelve hours a day in one form or another of direct service to the deity; another six hours were spent in chanting the Holy Name and meditating on Krishna lila. The other six hours were dedicated to maintaining her body, eating, sleeping and cleaning herself.

In the beginning, Ganga Mata went out to beg from door to door, but after Rasika Ray came to live with her, she became so absorbed in His service that she would forget to go out. When Rasika Ray saw the trouble she was undergoing on His behalf, He found other ways for managing His own service. Devotees began to be attracted to Him and came for His darshan bringing gifts.

When she was very old, Ganga Mata began to worry that she was beginning to commit offenses to the Deity due to her inability to execute her duties properly. In great sadness, she prayed to the Lord to be relieved of her service. She said to her Lord, “My only desire is that I should leave this decrepit body while gazing upon Your beauty, hearing Your glories being sung, and smelling a garland of tulasi flowers that has been offered to Your lotus feet.”

Rasika Ray compassionately answered her prayer in a dream. He said, “Turn the responsibility for My service to one of your qualified disciples and I will grant your wish. You will join Me in My pastimes for all eternity.”

Ganga Mata had a disciple named Vrindavan Bhatta, a twenty-year-old Brahmin of the Kashyapa gotra, who despite his youth was learned in the scriptures and a humble and pure soul. On the Maghi Shukla Panchami, 1721, she gave him initiation and vesh and then placed him in the role of mahant, naming him Vanamali Das Mahant Goswami. Shortly thereafter, on the Shukla Ekadasi of Ashwin, in the midst of the chanting of the Holy Names, Ganga Mata Goswamini entered the eternal pastimes.

## The subsequent history of Ganga Mata Math

Vanamali Das was a powerful Vaishnava who made many disciples. One of his disciples was the king of Boro Kimedi, who at the time of his initiation donated two villages, Balijori and Bhuruki, and gold coins. Vanamali Das spent time in Radha Kund and Vrindavan where he established branch maths, installing deities of Gaura-Gadadhar.

Vanamali Das was succeeded by Gopal Das, another Brahmin. Gopal Das spent time preaching the Srimad Bhagavatam in Ganga Mata Goswamini’s homeland of Puntia. Among his disciples was the Athagarh king Madhusudan Jagaddeva, who gave the village of Shalbon to the Math. Another rich landowner from the district of Nayagarh also gave Gopal Das a village.

Gopal Das was followed by a Brahmin from Bangla Desh, Bhagavan Das. Bhagavan Das lived for some time on the beach in a bamboo hut, where he engage in intense bhajan, chanting the Holy Names. Afterward, he returned to manage the Math, and installed a deity of Radharani in the temple.

Bhagavan Das also preached and established branch maths outside of Puri, especially in Orissa’s Ganjam district, southwest of Puri. One of his disciples was the king of Dharakot in Ganjam, Ramachandra Singh, who spent a great deal of money to build the present Ganga Mata temple and dig a well for the Math. He also bestowed a village in Orissa to provide income for Rasika Ray’s service. Bhagavan Das installed Gaura Nitai deities in the king’s palace. He also installed the Mohan Ray Krishna deity in the Math. Bhagavan Das ended his days in Vrindavan.

Bhagavan Das’ successor was Madhusudan Das, who installed the deity of Gauranga and a Lalita deity to the right of Rasika Ray. He was followed by Nilambar Das, who also installed two Krishna deities, Vinoda Ray and Shyama Ray. He also placed a dancing form of Gauranga to the left of Rasika Ray.

Nilambar had many rich and influential disciples, including Raja Adikanda Deva, who gave the Math another village to provide income for the deities. The Maharaja of Nayagarh and the Raja of Athagarh, Chaitanya Jagaddeva, also became his disciples and brought him to their palaces. However, when Nilambar Das insisted that they ban the practice of animal sacrifice in their kingdoms, they refused to follow his order. As a result Nilambar Das rejected them.

Adikanda Deva became openly inimical toward his spiritual master and tried to take back the gifts of land he had given the Math. The case was taken to court and went on even after Nilambar Das’ death. His successor Narottam Das, however, won the case.

When Adikanda Deva’s brother Raghunath succeeded him on the throne, he made amends with Narottam Das and gave the village of Chakrapur to the Math as a sign of good faith. Similarly, Chaitanya Jagaddeva gave land and other gifts to the temple, including a deity of Sri Gopinath.

Narottam Das was followed by Pitambar Das. Two of his principal godbrothers, Achyuta Das and Paramananda Das, argued with Pitambar Das and left the Math. The queen of Biruli gave a village to Pitambar Das.

Pitambar Das was succeeded by Madhava Das, who was only a young boy at the time. Two of the temple servants, Manohar Das and Dinabandhu Das, acted as his wards and ran the Math until he came of age. The then king of Dharakot, Vraja Sundar Singh, had Madhava Das initiate his adopted son and crown prince, Madan Mohan, and gave him many valuable presents as guru dakshina. Madhava Das studied Sanskrit extensively, taking degrees in philosophy and poetics. He went on to become a very influential spiritual leader, with many wealthy disciples. He was able to purchase another large tract of land in the Math’s name from the gifts he received from his disciples and supporters. More villages were given the Math by Madan Mohan Singh of Dharakot and Raja Purushottam of Sana Kimedi. The subsequent mahantas were Radhakrishna Das and Vanamali Das.

There is a piece of land near the Lokanath temple called Samadhi Bagicha where the remains of the mahantas of the Ganga Mata Math are buried. The tradition here is that the bodies of the mahantas are cremated and their ashes are buried. This tradition is current throughout Puri. Sundarananda writes that he heard from Vanamali Das, who was mahanta when he did his research in 1945, that the samadhis of Lakshmipriya, Ganga Mata, Vanamali Das and Gopal Das had been washed away into the sea.

The Ganga Mata Math has used the Gauranga mantra and Gauranga gayatri mantra since the time of Gadadhar Pandit. The math has preserved the original Srimad Bhagavatam palm leaf manuscript used by Ganga Mata Goswamini. Unfortunately, many ancient manuscripts in handwritten Bengali script were so ruined by the ravages of time that they were thrown into the Shweta Ganga. They still have more than a hundred old manuscripts on palm leaf in the Orissan script, however. A traditional school or Tol was formerly held on the Math grounds, but this stopped more than fifty years ago.

The Math has one interesting tradition. In the Natya Mandir, an oil painting of the entire parampara up to the previous mahanta is always worshiped. After the disappearance of the living Mahanta, this oil painting is thrown into the ocean and replaced with a new one. The living Mahanta is not included in this painting.

The complete list of Mahantas on this painting is as follows:

(1) Lakshmipriya  
(2) Ganga Mata  
(3) Vanamali Das  
(4) Gopal Das  
(5) Bhagavan Das (Bangadeshi)  
(6) Madhusudan Das  
(7) Nilambar Das  
(8) Narottam Das  
(9) Pitambar Das  
(10) Madhava Das  
(11) Radhakrishna Das  
(12) Vanamali Das.

Branches of Ganga Mata’s Math are found in Jagannath Puri at the Haveli Math and Gopal Math, as well as the Gopal Math in Tangi village in Cuttack district. The Rajas of Dharakot, Sana Kimedi, Biruli, Athagarh, and Nayagarh were disciples from generation to generation of the Ganga Mata Math. The Math was thus one of the richest in Jagannath Puri, with an annual income of nearly Rs. 80,000 before Indian independence.

The current residents of the Ganga Mata Math say that there is a tunnel going from their temple to the main temple of Jagannath. They point out a very old looking hole lined with stones outside the room where Mahaprabhu heard from Sarvabhauma. This they say that Mahaprabhu used this tunnel every day to go to the Jagannath mandir. According to them it is now collapsed inside. The Pandas at Shweta Ganga also say that there is an underground channel connecting the Shweta Ganga and a pool inside the Jagannath temple.

## Chapter 25 - Siddha Bakul Math

The Siddha Bakul Math stands on the place where Hari Das Thakur used to live and chant the Lord’s holy names in the last years of his life. It was once accessible directly from the Radha Kanta Math, but nowadays must be approached through a small side road to the east of the Swarga Dwar Road.

## Krishna Das Kaviraj narrates how Hari Das came to live here:

After Mahaprabhu returned to Puri from His pilgrimage to southern India, word was immediately sent to Bengal and not long afterwards a large group of devotees set forth from Bengal to see Him. In the meantime, Snana Yatra had taken place and Lord Jagannath was absent from the temple during the Anasar. Mahaprabhu felt separation from Jagannath so intensely that He went to stay in Alalanath. However, when word came to Him that more than two hundred devotees had come from Bengal to see Him, He immediately returned to Kashi Mishra’s house where they were like a flood, overflowing the residence.

One by one, Mahaprabhu greeted all His Bengali associates, but when He failed to observe Hari Das, He inquired whether or not he had come. In fact, Hari Das was present there, but out of humility had been paying his obeisances from the other side of the road. The devotees went to Hari Das and told him that Mahaprabhu wanted to see him. Hari Das replied,

”I am a low-born person with no good qualities. I have no right to go near the temple. If I can find a solitary place in some garden somewhere, then I will pass my time there alone. That way there is no danger that the servants of Jagannath will accidentally touch me. This is my wish.” (*Chaitanya Charitāmṛta* [2.11.165-7](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/11.165))

The devotees came back to Mahaprabhu to report what Hari Das had said, and this wish pleased Him. So the Lord asked Kashi Mishra for another cottage near His own place of bhajan. He said,

*āmāra nikaṭe ei puṣpera udyāne*  
*eka-khāni ghara ache parama-nirjane*  
*sei ghara āmāke deha āche prayojana*  
*nibhṛte basiyā tāṅhā karibo smaraṇa*

**“There is an empty cottage in the flower garden next door, which is very secluded. Please give me this cottage, for I need it. I will go there to sit and meditate on the Lord.” (CC** [**2.11.175-6**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/11.175)**)**

Kashi Mishra was happy to have another chance to serve the Lord by making these arrangements according to His order. The Lord then went Himself to Hari Das, lifted him from the ground, embraced him, and began to extol his qualities. Hari Das answered, “I am an untouchable. Lord, you should not touch me!” The Lord, however, answered Him by saying:

**”I touch you just to become purified, for the standard of holiness you have achieved is far beyond Me. It is as though you are bathing at every moment in the waters of all holy places and performing all religious sacrifices, penances and charity. You are constantly performing the pious activity of studying the Veda. You are thus holier than any Brahmin or sannyasi.” (CC** [**2.11.189-191**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/11.189)**)**

**After saying this, the Lord took him to Kashi Mishra’s flower garden and gave him the solitary room there as a place to stay. “Stay here and chant the Holy Names. I will come here every day to visit you. From here, you can see the Lord’s discus on the pinnacle of the temple tower. Whenever you see it, pay your obeisances. I will arrange for Lord Jagannath’s prasad to be brought to you.” (CC** [**2.11.193-95**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/11.193)**)**

One can still see the pinnacle of the Jagannath temple from the Siddha Bakul Math, but it is not as easy as it once was, for though this was once a large secluded garden, a wall has been built around it and the neighborhood has also been built up and is now densely populated.

## The Siddha Bakul tree

The Siddha Bakul Math was once known by the name Mudra Math, but was subsequently renamed in honor of the ancient bakul tree that stands on the premises. There is a legend connected with this tree. Lord Jagannath’s sevakas give Jagannath, Balaram and Subhadra twigs to clean their teeth every morning. These twigs are usually taken from the kumbhatua tree. One day, however, one of the three twigs was lost and so the sevakas hurriedly replaced it with one from a bakul tree.
