*dāsaṅka śire bāndhi dele atibaṛa boli boile*  
*atibaṛa kathā kahile teṇu atibaṛa hoile*

**Mahaprabhu then took His upper cloth and wrapped it around Jagannath Das’ head and said, “You have said something very profound. Thus you shall be known from now on as ‘very great’ or Atiboro.” (*****Jagannātha-caritāmṛta,*** **chapter 3)**

Orthodox followers of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu remember that He ostracized Vallabha Bhatta for showing pride in his achievements as a scholar and superiority to Sridhar Swami, the great commentator on the Bhagavatam. Mahaprabhu disapproved of the Mayavadi custom of addressing a renunciate or sannyasi as “Narayan.” If anyone formally addressed Him in that way, or being overwhelmed by His spiritual power called Him “Krishna,” He would cover His ears and say,

*viṣṇu viṣṇu ihā nā kahibā*  
*jīvādhame kṛṣṇa jñāna kabhu nā karibā*  
*jei mūḍha kohe jīva īśvara haya sama*  
*sei to pāṣaṇḍī haya daṇḍe tāre yama*

**“O Vishnu, Vishnu! Don’t say such things. Never consider an ordinary conditioned soul to be Krishna. The fool who takes an ordinary living being to be the same as God is nothing more than an atheist who will be severely judged at the time of death.” (CC** [**2.18.111**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/18.111)**,** [**116**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/18.116)**)**

When Prakashananda Saraswati called Mahaprabhu “Bhagavan” and tried to touch His feet, the Lord showed how a jiva should behave when spoken to in this way:

*viṣṇu viṣṇu āmi kṣudra jīva hīna*  
*jīve kṛṣṇa māne ei aparādha cihna*  
*jīva viṣṇu buddhi kare je brahmā rudra sama*  
*nārāyaṇe māne tāre pāṣaṇḍe gaṇana*

**“O Vishnu! O Vishnu! I am an ordinary, fallen jiva. Anyone who thinks a jiva like Me is Krishna is committing an offense. The scriptures say that anyone who thinks even gods like Brahma or Rudra to be on the same level as Narayan is an atheist. This is true for someone who thinks any jiva is Vishnu.” (CC** [**2.25.75-77**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/25.75)**)**

Mahaprabhu made statements like these in order to give fair warning to those who confuse the individual soul with the Supreme Being. He did this despite being the Supreme Lord Himself. It is very hard to accept that He would have rewarded anyone for publicly claiming to be a manifestation of the Lord’s svarupa shakti, Srimati Radharani. Gaudiya Vaishnavas therefore do not accept the truth of Dibakar Das’s account. If Mahaprabhu did indeed say any such thing to Jagannath Das, it was surely sarcasm or deception. The Gaudiyas thus interpret Mahaprabhu’s words as meaning, "My dear sir, you have become too great (*ati baṛa*). An insignificant and fallen soul like Me can have nothing to do with you."

## Schism of Bengali and Orissan Vaishnavas

Dibakar Das writes that Mahaprabhu’s Bengali devotees became jealous of Jagannath Das because of the special favor that their master was bestowing on him. He goes on to say that the Bengali devotees made efforts to stop Mahaprabhu from giving the title Atiboro to Jagannath Das. The reason for this was that if he were to be somehow singled out in this way, their own status would be diminished. When the Bengali devotees were unable to convince Mahaprabhu to do as they asked, they asked Him to leave Puri. When Mahaprabhu refused, they themselves left Jagannath Puri to go to Vrindavan. Though from time to time they would return to meet Mahaprabhu during the Rathayatra, they were unable to abide seeing the influence Jagannath Das had over Him and so never remained there for long.

The feeling that Mahaprabhu’s Bengali devotees were jealous of His Orissan followers like Jagannath Das remains a source of friction to the present day. Sundarananda quotes the following article from the English-language newspaper, *New Orissa,* published in 1945:

“Mahapurush Jagannath Das was a personal friend of Chaitanya. It is written in Dibakar’s *Jagannātha-caritāmṛta* that Gaudiya Vaishnavas did not like that Chaitanya should hold Jagannath Das, the Oriya Brahmin saint, in high esteem. It was at their insistence that Chaitanya asked Balaram Das to formally initiate Jagannath Das, though as a perfect being he required no formal initiation. After that, when they saw Chaitanya still loving Jagannath Das and addressing him all the while as *atibaṛī*, the Gaudiya Vaishnavas had to leave Puri in a rage and go back to Bengal. They stayed for some time at Jajpur. Chaitanya went there to bring them back, but to their surprise they found Jagannath Das accompanying Chaitanya. They were so arrogant that they did not listen to Lord Chaitanya and so had to go to Bana Bishnupur and from there to Vrindavan. It is a pity that there is no mention of the names of Jagannath Das and the four Mahapurushas in Chaitanya Charitamrita by Krishna Das Kaviraj, Chaitanya Bhagavata by Vrindavan Das and Chaitanya Mangal by Lochan Das. They were all Bengali Vaishnavas. The Gaudiya Vaishnavas go so far as to say that Jagannath Das was a “Mayavadi” and was driven out by Chaitanya Chandra from his fold.”\[cxlvi\]

More recently, the Orissan historian K. C. Panigrahi has been even more explicit in leveling the same accusation:

The aforesaid great Vaishnava Oriya poets have not found mention in the Bengali Gaudiya literature. This narrow outlook of the Bengali Vaishnavas was the cause of antagonism between the Bengali and Oriya followers of the great saint, echoes of which have found mention in the *Jagannātha-caritāmṛta* of Dibakar Das.\[cxlvii\]

Mahaprabhu’s biographers were amongst His spiritually most advanced followers, and in their writing they demonstrated all the Vaishnava virtues, including freedom from envy. They showed no reticence in glorifying other Vaishnavas, whatever their race or caste, and repeatedly did so with great energy. Not being conditioned souls with all their lamentable characteristics, they showed no signs of misplaced nationalism or racial discrimination when writing about Mahaprabhu’s associations. In their love for Mahaprabhu, they transcended all these differences and created an atmosphere of harmony conducive to the service of the Lord.

Mahaprabhu’s Bengali followers never hesitated to glorify Orissa and its people, both directly and indirectly. Sanatan Goswami glorified Mahaprabhu in his *Līlā-stava* as *nīlācala-vibhūṣaṇa* – “the ornament of Nilachala,” and Rupa Goswami writes in his *Stava-mālā* that he desires to see Mahaprabhu as *nīlācala-vihārī*, “enjoying life in Nilachala.” In the *Stavāvalī*, Raghunath Das worships Mahaprabhu standing behind the Garuda pillar in the Jagannath temple and describes many of the Lord’s extraordinary activities in Nilachala in his *Gaurāṅga-stava-kalpa-vṛkṣa.*

In the *Sarva-saṁvādinī* to the *Tattva-sandarbha*, Jiva Goswami glorifies Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, stating that He was worshiped by devotees from Gauda, Varendra, Banga, Suhma and Utkala (Orissa).\[cxlviii\] In *Caitanya-candrodaya,* Kavi Karnapur writes that Mahaprabhu accepted the philosophy of Ramananda Raya, an Orissan, as being the only one that was wholly consistent (*niravadya siddhānta*).

Kaviraj Goswami goes even further in highlighting the Orissan devotees when he says that of Mahaprabhu’s four most intimate devotees, three were Orissans – Ramananda Ray, Sikhi Mahiti (a Deul Karan, or temple accountant) and his sister Madhavi Devi. Krishna Das describes the conversations between Ramananda and Chaitanya Mahaprabhu on the highest esoteric level of devotional understanding. He called Bhavananda Ray the incarnation of Pandu, his wife Kunti, and their five sons the five Pandavas.

Krishna Das identified Kanai Khuntia and Jagannath Mahanti as Lord Chaitanya’s eternal associates, imbued with the spirit of Krishna’s parents, Nanda and Yashoda (CC [2.15.19](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/15.19)). He named many of the Lord’s Orissan devotees, never shying away from glorifying them liberally: Maharaja Prataparudra, Kashi Mishra, Krishna Das, who would walk in front of Lord Jagannath holding a golden cane, Tulasi Paricha (the temple manager), Janardan (another temple Brahmin), Harichandan Mahapatra (a military officer and minister), Murari Mahiti (a temple accountant), Pradyumna Mishra (the head cook in the temple kitchen), Shivananda, Krishnananda, Paramananda Mahapatra, Singheshwar, Svapneshwar, Chandaneshwar and many others. But Krishna Das did not stop here; he even wrote with approval of an aged Orissan widow, who in her excitement to gaze upon the lotus-eyed Lord Jagannath, placed her foot on Mahaprabhu’s shoulder!

Far from leaving Nilachala in frustration with Mahaprabhu’s favoritism, the Bengali Vaishnavas flocked to Nilachala, as Vrindavan Das states in the Chaitanya Bhagavata:

*pratāparudrera prabhu sahita darśana*  
*ihā je śunaye tāre mile prema-dhana*  
*nīlācale janmilā jateka anucara*  
*sabe cinilena nija prāṇera īśvara*  
*paramānanda mahāpātra mahāśaya*  
*jāṅra tanu śrī-caitanya-bhakti-rasa-maya*  
*kāśī miśra parama vihvala kṛṣṇa-rase*  
*āpane rahilā prabhu jāṅhāra ābāse*  
*ei mata prabhu sarva bhṛtya kari saṅge*  
*niravadhi goṅāyena saṅkīrtana-raṅge*  
*jata jata udāsīna śrī-caitanya-dāsa*  
*sabe karilena āsi nīlācale vāsa*

**Anyone who hears about Mahaprabhu’s meeting with King Prataparudra will attain love for Krishna. All of Mahaprabhu’s eternal servants who took birth in Nilachala were able to recognize their lord and master. Amongst them were Paramananda Mahapatra, whose body was permeated with devotion to Lord Chaitanya, and another ecstatic devotee Kashi Mishra, in whose house Mahaprabhu made His residence. Mahaprabhu gathered all these devotees together and spent His time engaged in chanting the Holy Names in their company. All of Mahaprabhu’s sannyasi disciples came to Nilachala to reside near Him there. (Cbh** [**3.5.208-10**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cb-antya/5.208)**,** [**212-5**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cb-antya/5.212)**)**

Mahaprabhu’s sannyasi disciples included Svarupa Damodar Goswami, who had previously lived in Nabadwip but came to serve Mahaprabhu by staying near Him in Puri, where the two of them could share the most esoteric experiences of devotional life. There is no evidence anywhere that Svarupa Damodar ever thought of leaving Puri for Vrindavan.

Ishwar Puri’s disciple and servant, Govinda Das, came to Puri on his spiritual masters order in order to serve Mahaprabhu there. Paramananda Puri and other devotees who were Mahaprabhu’s seniors, including Namacharya Hari Das Thakur, came to live permanently in Nilachala. Gadadhar Pandit Goswami, Mahaprabhu’s shakti, took the vow of Kshetra sannyas – to never leave Jagannath Puri for even a day.

It is true that Mahaprabhu ordered Rupa and Sanatan Goswamis to go to Vrindavan in order to discover the lost sites of Krishna’s pastimes, establish deity worship, clarify the doctrines of Vaishnava theology and the standards of Vaishnava ethics and devotional practice. He thus “gave” them the land Vrindavan, which they never left, as it had become their *prabhu-datta-deśa*. It is difficult to understand how anyone could think that they or any other of Mahaprabhu’s followers would have gone to Vrindavan simply as a result of a personality clash with Jagannath Das or because Mahaprabhu had shown favoritism to him.

## Another incident from Jagannath Das’ life

In Ram Das’ *Dāḍhyatā Bhakti*, a later Orissan text of the Atibori sampradaya, another story is told about Jagannath Das that clearly illustrates the difference between the Atibori way of thinking and that of the Gaudiyas. After Jagannath had completed his Oriya translation of the Bhagavatam, he travelled throughout Orissa giving discourses in his sweet, musical voice. He attracted large numbers of people to his emotional performances and especially charmed the womenfolk, who flocked to hear him. These women showered him with money and gifts and often invited him into their homes for private Bhagavata classes, something that was clearly against the custom of the time. Hearing him sing and speak on the highest aspects of Krishna’s pastimes in the privacy of their own quarters, these women would be overcome with ecstatic symptoms, rolling on the ground and in general lost all sense of decorum despite being in mixed company. Furthermore, they served Jagannath Das in various other ways, by fanning him and massaging his feet. In particular, two extraordinarily powerful women named Medha and Sumedha became his close disciples.

The men in these women’s lives became uncomfortable with such goings-on and complained to Maharaj Prataparudra. The king sent his police to arrest Jagannath and bring him to court. He asked Jagannath angrily,

*kope boile dāsa śuna, eki tumbhara viḍambana*  
*chādiṇa puruṣa saṅgata, stirī madhyare gāa gīta*  
*niśi dibasa sabu bele, kebala thāa nāri mele*

**“What’s going on here, Jagannath Das? It seems that you no longer keep the company of men, but sing in the midst of women. You mix with them without any restriction, day and night. Is all this true?”**

Jagannath answered Prataparudra with the following words,

*svarūpa śuna daṇḍa-dhārī, āmbhe ta aṭu brahmacārī*  
*puruṣe puruṣa bolāuṅ, stirīṅka saṅge saṅgī heuṅ*

**“Here is the truth, O King. You have the power to punish me if you will, but my vow of celibacy is unbroken. When I am amongst men, I am a male, and when amongst women, I am one of them.”\[cxlix\]**

The king did not accept this argument as an adequate defense; indeed it confirmed his suspicions. He challenged Jagannath to show him proof of his female form and threw him in prison. Many of Jagannath’s women followers became quite distressed with the turn of events and stopped food and drink and even threatened to commit suicide if he were not released.

That night Jagannath Das fell to prayer, asking the Lord to save him from this calamity. Finally Lord Jagannath appeared to him in a dream and fulfilled his desire to have a female form whenever he liked.

*boile bāñchā siddha heu*  
*puruṣa tanu tora jāu*

**“May your wish be fulfilled and your male body be gone.”**

The next morning Jagannath Das astonished the Gajapati by appearing before him with feminine features. According to this account, it was then that the king asked Jagannath Das to initiate his chief queen, Gauri, in this female form.

Other accounts say that Jagannath appeared as a woman to the prison guards, who released him, thinking that a mistake had been made. In either case, though this tale is told in glorification of Jagannath Das’ spiritual attainments, those who are advanced in their understanding of Gaudiya siddhanta have misgivings about them. For them, the female spiritual body is something that is extremely private and meant for one’s most personal dealings with the Lord. It is most certainly not something to be publicly displayed for the sake of achieving personal goals like adoration, prestige or even personal freedom. It is for such flaunting of his spiritual achievements that Jagannath Das’ critics consider the title “Atibori” to be veiled mockery.

The question really comes down to this: if Jagannath Das could accept the title Mahaprabhu bestowed on him, why did he not wholeheartedly accept Mahaprabhu’s teachings? The sarcastic use of a word like “very great” is not unknown. Sanskrit dictionaries give *mahā paṇḍita* (“great scholar”) as a synonym for “fool.” In Bengal, Rupa Kaviraj was another person who was condemned by such a title. Srinivas Acharya’s daughter Hemalata Thakurani broke his tulasi necklace and named him *ati-baṛī.* Thenceforth he wore but one strand of tulasi beads around his neck. The Orissan Atibori Sampradaya similarly wore only one strand of beads for many centuries and have only taken to wearing three strands in recent years.

The essence of Mahaprabhu’s teaching about Vaishnava praxis is humility – *sarvottama haiyā āpnake māne tṛṇādham­ –* “Though superior to all, he considers himself lower than the straw.” Rupa, Sanatan, Hari Das Thakur, Krishna Das Kaviraj and Narottam Das – these devotees all personified this teaching. There is no evidence anywhere that any of Mahaprabhu’s devotees went about calling himself “very great.” Indeed, they consistently did the opposite. Despite the brilliance of his virtues, Krishna Das even said, “I am lower than a dung beetle; I am a greater sinner than even Jagai and Madhai.”

When Mahaprabhu complimented them or heaped praise on them, as He so often did, these devotees responded by showing an even more profound humility. If we are to believe the legends that have found life in the Atibori tradition, then the founder of their line was evidently an avid seeker of personal aggrandizement. If we believe or accept the truth of tales that say he took pride in a title that mocked such avidity, or that he made a public display of his intimate spiritual realizations and mystic achievements, then we do not glorify him as a truly great Vaishnava.

## Jagannath Das’ disciplic succession

There are differing opinions amongst the Atiboris about Matta Balaram Das’ disciplic succession, but Dibakar Das writes in his *Nitya-gupta-maṇi* (19.19-20) as follows –

*śrīmac-caitanya-devasya gaurī-dāsākhya-paṇḍitaḥ*  
*tasya śiṣyas tu gosvāmī hṛdayānanda-paṇḍitaḥ*  
*tac-chiṣyo matta-pūrvas tu balarāma iti smṛtaḥ*  
*mahān api jagannātha-dāsas tat-paricārakaḥ*

**This gives the disciplic succession as (1) Chaitanya Deva, (2) Gauri Das Pandit, (3) Hridayananda Pandit Goswami, (4) Matta Balaram Das, and (5) Jagannath Das. In Ishwar Das’ Orissan** ***Caitanya-bhāgavata*****, Vakreshwar Pandit is named as Hridayananda’s spiritual master.**

Dibakar’s version of the Boro Oriya Math’s disciplic succession is confirmed inside the temple itself. There, on one of the inner walls, paintings of the gurus in the line have been hung on the wall with their identities. The line of Mahants of the Math are given as follows:

Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu  
Gauri Das Pandit  
Hridayananda Pandit  
Balaram Das  
Atibori Jagannath Das  
Ramakrishna Das  
Murari Das Goswami  
Purushottam Das Goswami  
Mukunda Das Goswami  
Madhavananda Das Goswami  
Srinath Das Goswami  
Vamshidhar Das Goswami  
Shyamcharan Das Goswami  
Niladri Das Goswami  
Rasa Bihari Das Goswami  
Ramakrishna Das Goswami  
Vrindavan Das Goswami (Mahant during Sundarananda’s visit)

This disciplic succession is obviously problematic. The relationship of Gauri Das to Hridayananda is well known, as Shyamananda, the great apostle of the Goswamis’ message in Orissa, was his disciple. But it is also well known that Hridayananda never witnessed Mahaprabhu’s pastimes. If Jagannath Das was truly the grand-disciple of Hridayananda, he would have been Shyamananda’s junior, and certainly not a direct associate of Lord Chaitanya himself. We are left with two alternatives: either the disciplic succession as given is false, or the customary dates ascribed to Jagannath’s life (1490-1550) are incorrect. If the disciplic succession has been falsified, it still indicates that the Atibori line found it necessary to create a disciplic connection to Chaitanya Mahaprabhu for legitimation. If this line is genuine, then almost everything that has been written about Jagannath Das must be called into question. A third alternative – that the Gauri Das Pandit and Hridayananda named here are different from those found in Shyamananda’s guru parampara -- seems too great a coincidence to be considered.

Members of the Atibori sampradaya say that Jagannath Das’s name is mentioned in Devakinandan’s *Vaiṣṇava-vandanā*, one of the earliest sources of information about Mahaprabhu’s life. There the names of both Oriya Balaram Das and *saṅgīta paṇḍita* Jagannath Das are found. This seems to be incontrovertible evidence that these two were Mahaprabhu’s associates in Puri. However, tradition at the Siddha Bakul Math holds that a Siddha Jagannath Das was the first Mahant there after the departure of Hari Das Thakur. This Jagannath Das established the six-armed form of Mahaprabhu that is worshiped there as well as the image of Hari Das. Who is to say that this Jagannath is not the expert musician named in the *Vaiṣṇava-vandanā*? According to the Siddha Bakul traditions, this Jagannath Das was indeed an expert musician and often sang for Lord Jagannath in the temple.

The accusations of Jagannath Das’ followers that the universal absence of his name from all the accounts of Mahaprabhu’s life is due to friction between him and Mahaprabhu’s Bengali followers becomes meaningless if Jagannath Das was not Mahaprabhu’s contemporary, as indicated by the Boro Oriya Math’s disciplic succession.

## Why was Jagannath Das not mentioned in Mahaprabhu’s biographies?

Mahaprabhu’s biographers named many religious leaders of the period who met with Mahaprabhu, even those whose opinions differed from Mahaprabhu’s -- Vallabha Bhatta, Keshava Kashmiri, Ramadas Vishwas, Mukunda Saraswati, Prakashananda Saraswati, to name some of them. Kaviraj Goswami did not hesitate to speak the plain truth about all of these individuals, so what was to stop him from dealing with Jagannath Das if there were historical fact there?\[cl\]

There are many Orissan devotees described in the biographies of Chaitanya Deva and in the subsequent generations – Gopal Guru, Dhyana Chandra, and the Oriya poet Govinda Deva, to name but a few – who have accepted orthodox Gaudiya siddhanta in these matters. If Kavi Karnapur and other biographers of Mahaprabhu have not mentioned Jagannath Das’ name, it must be because He never met him, contrary to his biographers’ accounts. The proof is the guru pranali given in the Boro Oriya Math itself.

It is also a historical truth that for many generations, the Vaishnavas of the Atibori line were ostracized by the Gaudiya Vaishnavas of Puri. They would not share Maha Prasad with them, even in Jagannath Puri. If the Atiboris were such great friends of Mahaprabhu, then why this great division?

## Succession to Jagannath Das

Jagannath Das had sixteen chief disciples. In *Jagannātha-caritāmṛta*, the following verses name them,

*uddhavo rāmacandraś ca gopīnāthaś ca śrī-hariḥ*  
*nandanī vāmanī gaurā gopālākhaṇḍalas tathā*  
*janārdana-patiḥ kṛṣṇa-dāsaś ca vana-mālikaḥ*  
*govardhanas tathā kāhnu-khuṇṭikā na kramaṁ vadet*  
*punaḥ śiṣo jagannātha-dāsaś ca madhusūdanaḥ*

**(1) Uddhava, (2) Ramachandra, (3) Gopinath (4) Hari Das, (5) Nandani Acharya, (6) Vamani Mahapatra, (7) Srimati Gaura, (8) Gopal Das, (9) Akhandala Mekap, (10) Janardana Pati, (11) Krishna Das, (12) Vanamali Das, (13) Govardhan Das, (14) Kanai Khuntia, (15) Jagannath Das, (16) Madhusudan Das.**

One of Mahaprabhu’s followers, the author of *Mahābhāva-prakāśa,* was also named Kanai Khuntia. Krishna Das Kaviraj has mentioned him in several places and states that Mahaprabhu respected him like a father (CC [2.15.19](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/15.19), [29](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/15.29)). It is unlikely that Jagannath Das’ disciple of this name is the same person. Krishna Das Kaviraj does not mention Jagannath Das’ name in the Chaitanya Charitamrita, so it seems unlikely that he would name his disciple.

Sundarananda heard from the Math’s mahant, Vrindavan Dasji, that Purushottam Das, who was sixth in line of descent from Jagannath Das, had five principal disciples. Chief of these was Mukunda Das, who became the Mahant of the Boro Oriya Math. The other four disciples established branch maths, which are known as Sana (small) Oriya Maths. These are named (1) Sana Oriya Math, (2) Rama-Hari Das Math, (3) Vanamali Das Math, and (4) Bhagavata Das Math.

In the Kundhei Bent and Dandimal Sahis, there are between ten and twenty other maths belonging to this line, all of which accept the preeminence of the Boro Oriya Math. When it comes time for a new mahant to be ordained in any of these minor establishments, it is the head of the Boro Oriya Math who wraps the silk sari around his head. This sampradaya of Vaishnavas who follow Jagannath Das are spread throughout Orissa and connected maths who recognize its authority are found in the towns of Khandpara, Tigiria, Nilgiri, Athgarh, Barhamba, Narasinghapur, Dashpalla, Talcher, Dhenkanal, Nayagarh, Mayurbhanj, Ganjam and Midnapore.

## Bhaktivinoda Thakur and Bishikishan

When Bhaktivinoda Thakur was a deputy magistrate stationed in Jagannath Puri in the early 1870's, he arrested, judged and jailed a pseudo-incarnation of Maha Vishnu named Bishikishan, who claimed to belong to the Atibori apasampradaya. This man had mystic powers: he would sit near a fire and lean into the flames, then lift his head and make flames come out of his hair. He had two companions who went by the names Brahma and Shiva. Many wealthy and influential Hindus of Orissa came under his sway and sent him funds for constructing a temple; they even provided him with women for “rasa-lila.” Bishikishan boasted that he would drive the British out of Orissa and rule it as a divine king.

The incident prompted Bhaktivinoda to investigate the Atiboris as a result of which he wrote a letter, dated August 18, 1871, addressed to the editor of *Progress,* a Cuttack newspaper, in which he described the origin, philosophy and practices of the Atibori sect. Other than the points already covered above, the Thakur also questioned the genuineness of the Atiboris’ devotion to Lord Jagannath. He wrote,

“It is a source of pride among this group to claim that Lord Jagannath has personally revealed some truth or prophecy to them. Thus every respected Atibori can recite what they call their *mālikā*, or series of revelations from the Lord. A common prediction one will hear from them is the year the world will end...

“The Atiboris are mystics. They practice yoga and sometimes work magic, to cure diseases, for instance. They form a secret brotherhood, like the Freemasons in the West, and are also involved with drugs like marijuana and opium.”

The Thakur reckoned there were 15,000 Atiboris in Orissa during his stay there. At that time, they were often engaged in conspiracies against the government.

## Sat Lahari Math

The Sat Lahari Math is situated not far from the Hari Das Samadhi Math near the Swarga Dwar. It is the burial place of Atibori Jagannath Das. A shrine with an image of Jagannath Das once stood on this site. The followers of the Atibori Sampradaya say that this murti self-manifested twelve days after his disappearance, but it appears to have been installed much later. This figure was lost or stolen half a century ago and is no longer there.

The math is currently in serious difficulty and has been placed under the management of a committee under the chairmanship of the Puri district collector. When Sundarananda reported on it in *Śrī Kṣetra*, it was a totally abandoned to itinerant ascetics and stray dogs.

It is said that Jagannath Das once engaged a Mayavadi sannyasi named Brahmananda in debate and defeated him. He won recognition from Prataparudra who rewarded him with a math south of the Markandeya Sarovar, which became the Boro Oriya Math. Some critics of Jagannath Das say that Prataparudra became displeased with him and took this gift back, forcing him to go elsewhere. In view of the continued influence of the Boro Oriya Math in the Sri Mandir, this account seems unlikely.

The name of the math means “seven waves.” It comes from a legend that Jagannath Das used his mystic powers to move back the ocean the distance of seven waves in order to make room for a place to building.

According to legend, Jagannath Das lived at Sat Lahari Math until he was sixty years old (1550 AD). He then called all his disciples together and gave them last instructions and spiritual directions. He gave his wooden sandals to his chief disciple, Hari Das, and appointed him his successor. He then sat in a yogic posture and went into deep meditation and then left his body. His disciples buried his remains there and built a samadhi shrine in his memory.

## Sana Oriya Math

One of Jagannath Das’ sixteen principal disciples was Gopinath Das. He was the Mahant of the Sat Lahari Math. He was followed by Madhavananda Das who was succeeded by Murari and Dvarika Vallabh Das. Dvarika Vallabh Das established the Sana Oriya Math. One devotee of this math, Chaturbhuj Das converted many people to the Atibori Sampradaya throughout Orissa. Murari’s disciple was Ramakrishna Das, followed by Purushottam Das, Vamshidhar Das, Niladri Das, Rasavihari Das, Ramakrishna Das, and Vrindavan Das, who was the mahant when Sundarananda visited the Math in the mid-1940’s.

## Gandharva Math

This is the seat of Matta Balaram Das, situated near the Banki River in the Kundhei Bent Sahi.

Matta Balaram Das was the first of the Pancha Sakhas. According to Ishwar Das’ *Caitanya-bhāgavata*, Balaram Das met Mahaprabhu in Chandrapur while the Lord was on his way to Jagannath Puri.

*dekhi ānanda śrī caitanya*  
*subale kale sambhāṣaṇa*  
*premare jara jara hoi*  
*acchanti caitanya gosāñi*  
*rāma tāraka parama brahma*  
*kahile karṇe śrī caitanya*

**“With love overflowing, the Lord addressed him as Subala and imparted the** ***rāma-tāraka-parama-brahma*** **mantra into his ear.” (Chapter 46)**

Originally from Chandrapur, Balaram Das was a Karan by caste and fought for the rights of non-Brahmins. In one book, *Vedānta-sāra-gupta-gītā*, he wrote that the Brahmins resented his participation in discussions of the Vedanta in the Mukti Mandap. Balaram Das claimed that anyone he touched on the head would immediately be able to explain the Vedanta. A deaf and dumb beggar named Hari Das was brought from the Boro Danda, and true enough, upon being touched by Balaram Das’ hand, immediately began speaking Vedanta philosophy.\[cli\]

In his translation of the *Rāmāyaṇa,* Balaram Das also satirized the greedy priests in the temples visited by Rama and Sita during their exile. He was given the name Matta because of his madness in devotion. Balaram Das wrote several books including the *Amarakośa-gītā, Beṛha-parikramā* (a description of the shrines inside the Sri Mandir grounds), and *Brahmāṇḍa-bhūgola.*

## Balabhadri Akhra

Generally speaking, throughout Orissa monastic establishments are called maths. In this particular case, however, the term akhra (*akhaṛā*) has been used to describe the monastic institution. This comes from a different sense of mission, the residents of an akhara feel that their purpose is not so much to engage in worship themselves, but to protect genuine Vaishnavas from abuse and harassment by non-Vaishnavas.

The math gives a vague story of its beginnings in the distant past when a determined atheist took a vow not to drink water without having first destroyed some Vaishnava scriptures, destroy a temple or kill someone wearing the marks of devotion to Vishnu. If a day went by when he could not find a Vaishnava, he would take a clay statue of a Vaishnava and destroy it. The militant band of sadhus grew out of the need to counteract such demonic behavior and to protect the saintly devotees. Such akhras can be found in many other places, such as Vrindavan, Ujjain, Hardwar, etc. The sadhus who live here spend more time engaged in physical than in devotional culture.

They call themselves Gaudiya Jamayet, but members of any of the Vaishnava sampradayas can join them and become the Mahant of their establishments. The Mahant is named by the council of Mahants representing the four sampradayas in Puri.

The leaders of the city’s other maths also contribute to its upkeep, as visiting sadhus from all over India can come here and worship according to their own sampradaya’s rules. This system began about a century ago, when lawsuits set into motion by opposing interests destroyed the akhara’s material possessions, which were considerable at one time. In a rare case of cooperation, Puri’s Vaishnava mahants acted conjointly to keep the institution alive.

At the time Sundarananda visited the Balabhadri Akhara, the mahant was a monk of the Vakreshwar line, initiated at the Radha Kanta Math. Footprint shrines to the founders of the four great sampradayas – Ramanuja, Nimbarka, Vishnu Swami and Madhvacharya – have bee established on the akhara grounds, along with a shrine to Hanuman. Their temple also houses a deity of Patita Pavan Jagannath and Bal Gopal.

On Sept. 29, 1871, Bhaktivinoda Thakur wrote an article for the English-language paper, *Tajpore*, in which he gave an extensive description of many of Puri’s monastic establishments. On that occasion, he wrote that in the past, some maths changed their vocation from pure devotion to physical culture. This was due to the admixture of the modes of nature sullying the tradition of prema bhakti that had been established by the incarnation of the Supreme Lord Chaitanya.

## Kali Tilak Math

The Kali Tilak Math is situated in the Markandeya Sahi. It is said to have been established by the same Rupa Kaviraj who has been briefly mentioned above in connection with the Atiboris. It was once a wealthy establishment, but has fallen on harder times, even though it still has considerable land holdings. When Sundarananda visited the temple, its previous mahant, Sadananda Das, had just died and only an old woman and a hired pujari were living there. They told him that the Kali Tilak Math was a branch of the Singheshwar Math in Banpur village in Puri district. The samadhi remains of the fifteen previous mahants of the Math are all kept in one chamber of the math, which appears to be quite old, but neither of the residents could give him any information about their identities. One would have to go to Banpur to find out, they said. There is a small temple room in which are housed brass deities of Gaura-Nitai and Sri Sri Radha Madan Mohan. There is also a Shalagram Shila.

## Chapter 33 - The samadhi of Sal Beg

A small building in Balgandi, next to the Ramanandi sampradaya’s Balgandi Chata Math, is the burial place of the Muslim devotee of Jagannath, Sal Beg.

Srila Bhakti Promode Puri Maharaj writes –

Lord Jagannath is the friend of anyone, whether high or low, rich or poor, educated or illiterate. Even so, it seems that He shows a special preference for those who are the most fallen and helpless – *dīnere adhika dayā karen bhagavān* (CC [3.4.68](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-antya/4.68)). Of course, we are not talking of those who are simply fallen and helpless, but of those who have become meek and humble as a result, and turned to the Lord by taking up the process of self-surrender known as *śaraṇāgati*. To such people, He reveals Himself.\[clii\]

The Orissan poet Kavi Ram Das composed a book describing the lives of 64 devotees of Lord Jagannath, called *Dārḍhyatā-bhakti-rasāmṛta* (“The nectar of devotion performed with unflinching faith”), or *Dārḍhyatā-bhakti* for short. One of these devotees was Sri Sal Beg. The following account was given by the scholarly disciple of the late founder-acharya of the Chaitanya Gaudiya Math, Sri Sri Bhakti Dayita Madhava Goswami Maharaj, Srila Gati Krishna Das Adhikari.

Sal Beg’s father Lal Beg was a fierce general in the Mughal army under the leadership of the Emperor Akbar’s chief commander, Man Singh, and participated in the campaign to conquer Orissa in 1591-2. Lal Beg was in the village of Danda Mukundpur in the vicinity of Pipili when he saw a beautiful Brahmin child-widow walking on the road on her way to bathe in the village pond. He forcibly abducted the girl and carried her off to Cuttack where he married her. In 1593, she gave birth to a son, who was named Sal Beg. This Lal Beg’s house is still standing in Cuttack near the Lal Bag fort.

Lal Beg only remained in Cuttack for a short time before returning to Delhi, however. He was a good friend of Akbar’s son, Prince Selim. So Sal Beg was raised by his mother in Cuttack. Despite her forced conversion to Islam, his mother continued to have strong faith in Lord Jagannath and went on worshiping Him. She raised her son to similarly follow these practices, making sure he learned Sanskrit as a part of his education.

As he grew older, Sal Beg showed a desire to learn the military arts like his father. Though his mother was not enthusiastic, he showed great skill and soon mastered the various military skills.

In 1607, Orissa had gained a certain degree of autonomy under Mughal rule. Lal Beg was made Subadar of Bengal by the emperor Jahangir on May 30, 1607 and he remained in that position until his death on April 27, 1608. During this time, he brought his son to Bengal to help him fight the Afghans who opposed Mughal rule there. During one battle, Sal Beg was severely injured. Despite lengthy treatment, his condition deteriorated rather than improving. Indeed, he came to the point where he was no longer able to tolerate the pain and was ready to commit suicide. When his mother saw him in this terrible state, she was unable to bear his suffering, but all she could do was advise him to pray to Lord Jagannath.

Sal Beg did not have any great faith in the Vaishnava religion at that time, but he was in a state of despair. In the fear that he was about to die, he accepted his mother’s request. His mother said, “Child, if you can pray sincerely to Lord Jagannath, the deliverer of the most fallen, you will surely be healed within twelve days.” Sal Beg prayed for twelve days, but the wounds did not seem to heal, but rather continued to get worse. Naturally, he began to doubt that anything would come of his prayers.

However, on the last night of his vow, the merciful Lord Jagannath appeared to Sal Beg in a dream. Coming in the form of a young cowherd boy, the Lord touched His devotee’s entire body with His divine hand and it was immediately freed of infection. Very soon thereafter, Sal Beg’s handsome youthful body was restored to its former healthy state. Upon waking, Sal Beg felt an unshakable faith in Lord Jagannath and began to anxiously seek for another vision of the Lord.

Sal Beg began to chastise himself because even though the merciful Lord had cured him of his diseases, he was still unable to fix His image within his heart. Nevertheless, from that very moment, he surrendered completely to the Lord and felt spontaneous love for His lotus feet. No one but a devotee extremely blessed by the Lord could have possibly demonstrated the kind of determination and firmness in devotion that Sal Beg did with his songs and prayers in glorification of Lord Jagannath, all of which are filled with a deep, heart-felt expression of divine love.

Sal Beg gradually became unpopular among the Muslims who called him a Kafir for praying to Hindu idols. He had to suffer greatly for this, for he was eventually driven out of his house. Increasingly anxious to see his beloved Lord, he left Cuttack and set off on foot to Puri. On arriving there, however, not only was he not permitted to enter the temple to see Jagannath, but no math or Hindu household would give him shelter. Despite this rejection, the great devotee Sal Beg refused to swerve from his determination to serve his Lord. He built himself a little shelter of tal leaves at Balgandi on the Boro Danda and dedicated his entire being to the Lord’s bhajan. All the obstacles and prejudices he faced only served to strengthen his devotion and love for the Lord. He became a real saint – indifferent to both praise and insult – *tulya-nindā-stutir maunī santuṣṭo yena kenacit.* Out of a deep and genuine humility, he developed an equal vision in which all worldly taunts and jibes were manifestations of his worshipable lord’s blessings.

The refusal of the temple authorities to allow him to enter the temple did not produce resentment in him. Rather than blaming anyone, he considered it to be his worshipable lord’s benediction to teach him that he was in fact completely unworthy to enter the temple. So he wrote a song in which he prayed emotionally to the Lord and all the residents of the Dhama: “O residents of Nilachala, I am melting into an ocean of grief” (*ohe nīlācala-vāsi śoka-jaladhire gali bhāsi*).

When the Rathayatra came, Sal Beg was overjoyed that he would finally be able to see Lord Jagannath. During the Pahandi Vijaya, he gazed on the Lord without once turning his head. The affectionate Lord also felt great pleasure at finally seeing His surrendered devotee. Knowledgeable devotees will understand the joy that both the Lord and His devotee experience when they meet. The non-devotees of the world will have no understanding of this at all.

Most years, Sal Beg would waited for the raths to arrive in Balgandi near his shelter. First the Taladhvaja chariot of Lord Balabhadra came and stopped for a moment. Sal Beg saw Lord Balabhadra on the chariot and prayed to Him. The chariot then moved ahead. Then Mother Subhadra’s chariot arrived before his lean-to. She also stayed there for a while in order to extend darshan to her distinguished devotee. After a few minutes, her car also continued on its way. Sal Beg remained standing there in wait for the darshan of Lord Jagannath, anxiously singing prayers in his sweet voice.

After another hour or so, Jagannath’s car Nandighosh arrived nearby and came to an immediate halt. It thus appeared that all three Lords had a strong personal desire to extend darshan to their foremost devotee, Sal Beg. Lord Jagannath’s chariot stayed at Balgandi for an entire hour. Sal Beg utterly lost himself in a gulf of happiness as he enjoyed the presence of his desired Lord. His tears of happiness knew no bounds. In his melodious voice, he sang to the Lord, offering Him a garland of prayers he had composed himself.

It soon became apparent that Lord Jagannath was unwilling to leave His devotee and to proceed on His journey to the Gundicha temple without him. His chariot would not move an inch in spite of the efforts of all the people present. Finally the Pandas and Dayitas humbly entreated Sal Beg to pull the chariot ropes. As soon as he did so, the car started on its way again. Sal Beg felt overjoyed and filled with the feeling that he was truly beloved of Lord Jagannath.

In 1621, still during the rule of the Mughal emperor Jahangir, Begam Nur Jahan’s nephew Ahmed Beg was made Subadar of Cuttack. Not long afterward, he decided to attack and loot the Jagannath temple. The temple Pandas were afraid of the Subadar and hid Lord Jagannath on Parikuda island in Chilka Lake. Like all the devotees in Puri, Sal Beg feel great distress in Lord Jagannath’s separation. He sang the following lines:

*kene gheni jāucha jagannāthaṅku*  
*āmbhe darśana karibu kāṅhāṅku*

**Where can I go to see my Lord Jagannath? Who can we go to see?**

The Gajapati at the time was Narasingha Deva. When he heard Sal Beg’s emotional songs lamenting the separation from Jagannath, he was very moved. He gave Sal Beg permission to build a math in Balgandi. In the time that Sal Beg lived there, devotees from all over India began to come to visit him.

He wrote many songs, not only in Orissan, but also in Bengali and Brajabuli and other languages. Orissan Vaishnavas especially have great love for these moving songs, which they all know and sing, especially when on pilgrimage to Puri. Sal Beg’s songs are even sung with great reverence in the temple during Jagannath’s daily service.

Sal Beg himself remained absorbed in the worship of the Lord day and night. While living in Balgandi, his mother came to live out her final days in the abode of Lord Jagannath. When she finally left her body, Sal Beg carried it to the Swarga Dwar to fulfill her wish to have her body cremated. As they were both Muslims, this was considered to be an affront to the social custom of the day, and the priests even attacked his math to punish him for such insolence. As a result, Sal Beg decided to leave Jagannath Puri and went to Vrindavan where he spent some time engaged in bhajan. According to some, he practiced devotional service under the direction of Shyamananda Prabhu.

By this time Shah Jahan was sitting on the throne in Delhi, but even during his reign, his son Aurangzeb made an attempt to destroy the temples of Radha and Krishna in Vrindavan. This again caused Sal Beg to become depressed. He decided to leave Vraja and return to Puri, passing through Bengali so that he could bathe in the Ganges. His intention was to be in Puri for the Rathayatra festival. However, before he could leave Vrindavan, he fell ill. Hoping against hope that he could regain his health so that he could see his Lord, he sang,j

*agad-bandho he goṅsāi*  
*tumbha śrī-caraṇa binu āna gati nāi*  
*sāt śa’ pacāśa kośa cāli nā pāra-i*  
*moha jibā jāyeṅ nandīghoṣa thira bahi*

**O Lord, O friend of the universe, I have no shelter other than Your lotus feet. I will never be able to travel the 1500 miles to see you, but until I get there, please wait patiently on Nandighosh.**

Though Sal Beg was fifteen hundred miles away, Jagannath heard his prayer. Though the Lord’s ratha had proceeded as far as Balgandi, it would not move an inch further. For a full three months, the chariot remained there, motionless. Brahmins performed sacrifices, devotees chanted kirtan day and night, but the Lord’s chariot Nandighosh would not advance an inch. The strongest, most powerful men in the country were brought to pull on the ropes; hundreds of intoxicated elephants were harnessed, but to no avail. When Sal Beg finally arrived in Puri and appeared in front of the chariot to look at Lord Jagannath, the ratha suddenly started to rumble and move forward toward Gundicha.

*āpana icchāya ratha cale*  
*nā cale kāro bale*

**The chariot moves at the Lord’s desire and not by the strength of anyone’s arms.**

After this event, the Gajapati Narasingha Deva became convinced that Sal Beg was Lord Jagannath’s topmost devotee. He thought that as such, he should be allowed to enter the temple. Unfortunately, the priests of the Mukti Mandap would not allow the Gajapati to realize this liberal plan. They created so many disruptions to prevent it from taking place. Sal Beg, however, did not allow these disturbances to affect his devotional spirit. He took up residence at some distance from the temple and started chanting the Holy Names in seclusion with great determination. He never left Puri Dham again.

All the devotional songs written by Sal Beg make a deep impression on the heart. As soon as the devotees hear them, their hearts start to vibrate like a stringed instrument. From the heart, they proceed to the tongue where they dance in the form of sound. And that sound enters into the hearts of others and makes them vibrate in the same way. All his songs emphasize that Lord Jagannath is the Lord and friend of the entire world, who is present everywhere, the source of all auspiciousness, the all-powerful and all-compassionate Lord. Sal Beg wrote thousands of such songs, filling the storehouse of Orissan literature and forming one of its greatest treasures.

Unbiased admirers of virtue, whether Muslim or Hindu, were attracted to Sal Beg. Chanting aloud the Lord's names with great emotion, Sal Beg left this world for Lord Jagannath's abode in around 1646 or 1647. He was buried in Balgandi, where he had spent the last years of his saintly life. A small temple was constructed in his memory much later by the Balesore landlord Bhaskar Patra. This samadhi stands on the Grand Road in a walled area opposite the government hospital and adjacent to the Balgandi Chata Math of the Ramanandi sampradaya. It is under the jurisdiction of the Puri municipal government, but unfortunately is not being properly maintained. Because the gates are left wide open, animals can freely enter and contaminate the place. We call all pious people’s attention to this disgrace; for it is not appropriate that such a great devotee’s memorial should be so neglected.

The glories of Govinda’s prasad, of Govinda’s form, Govinda’s holy names and Govinda’s devotees, are still brightly present in the land of Sri Kshetra. Lord Jagannath appeared in His form as Nila Madhava to the fisherman caste of Shabaras, accepting the service of Visvavasu just to show that a devotee’s race and caste are unimportant to Him. The Shabaras are an untouchable caste, outside the scope of the Varnashram system, but Lord Jagannath is the Lord of every living being. He is the Lord of even the most fallen and helpless creature. Thus in order to bless those low castes who are prohibited from entering the temple, He appears in His Patita Pavana form on a high altar on the southern side of the Singha Dwar entrance, facing outside so that they can see Him from the public square.

## Two songs by Sal Beg

**1.**

*Jagabandhu he Gosāiṅ*  
*jagad-bandho he goṅsāi*  
*tumbha śrī-caraṇa binu āna gati nāi*  
*sāt śa’ pacāśa kośa cāli nā pāra-i*  
*moha jibā jāyeṅ nandīghoṣa thira bahi*

**O Lord, O friend of the universe, I have no shelter other than Your lotus feet. I will never be able to travel the 1500 miles to see you, but until I get there, please wait patiently on Nandighosh.**

*ratha cāri pāśe lambe mukutāra jharā*  
*jhala mala diśuthāi prabhu cakaḍolā*  
*bāiśī pāhacha tāle bikāhue bhāta*  
*darśana teṇiki thāu kaivalye mukata*

**O Prabhu Chakadola, whose round eyes are shaped like wheels! How brilliant you look on the chariot, with its streaming festoons. The rice that is scattered at the base of the twenty-two steps will bring me liberation – let Your darshan wait.**

*āge cale balabhadra madhye cānda muhiñre*  
*āsuchi kāliā pāche gahala lagāire*  
*kahe sālabega hīna jātīre yavana*  
*ehīmate ājñā heo śiri bṛndāvana*

**Balabhadra rides in front, followed by the moon-faced Subhadra and the black Lord Jagannath comes in the rear, creating a stir. The lowly Sal Beg, born a Muslim, prays – “Give me Your permission to leave Vrindavan.”**

**2.**

*Jagannātha he, kichi māgunahiṅ*  
*jagannātha he, kichi māgunāhiṅ muñ tote*  
*māgunāhiṅ dhana, māgunāhiṅ jana*  
*māguchi śaradhā bāliru hāte*

**O Jagannath! I ask for nothing from You – I ask not for wealth, I ask not for followers. All I ask is for a few inches of land at Shraddha Balu.**

*āna daraśana na loṛe nayana eka tumbha dekhā binā*  
*śuṇibāku kāna nāicche āna tumbha carita kāmanā*

**My eyes want nothing but to see Your glorious form, My ears want nothing but to hear the recitation of Your glories.**

*jihva na bāñchai grāmya gīta gāibāku rajanī dibasa*  
*tumbha nāmāvalī kebala saṅkhāli hoi thāu pīta-vāsa*

**My tongue has no desire to sing songs of worldly love, neither by day or night; Your holy names, O yellow-robed Lord, are my only hope.**

*nāsa mora tṛpti na labhai āna subāsa dravya āghrāṇe*  
*tava chaṛā māla tulasī kusuma candana karpūra dhyāne*

**My nose finds no satisfaction in any other sweet fragrant substance but meditates on the scent of Your tulasi and flower garlands, Your camphor-mixed sandalwood paste.**

*mo hasta aṅguli rāma vanamāli japu thāu hare kṛṣṇa*  
*kahe sālabega jātire yavana to tīrthe jāu mora prāṇa*

**O Rama! O Vanamali! My hands want only to finger my beads as I chant the Hare Krishna mantra.**

Sal Beg, born a Muslim, says, “Let me die in this holy land.”

## Chapter 34 - Maths of other sampradayas

## Maths of the Shankara Sampradaya

Govardhan Math

Shankaracharya, the incarnation of Lord Shiva, established Govardhan Math, or Bhogavardhan Math, probably near the beginning of the ninth century. One tradition holds that the name *bhoga-vardhana* results from Shankara’s influence in increasing the amount of food offerings given to Lord Jagannath.

This is without a doubt the oldest math in Jagannath Puri. The ground level of Govardhan Math is several feet below the level of its surroundings. This is also true of several of the Shiva temples, such as Markandeshwar, Lokanath and Yameshwar, all of which are older than the present Jagannath temple itself.

A marble murti of Shankara housed in the Govardhan Math with a seat (*gadi*), indicating that this is the residence of the Shankaracharya, or representative of the sampradaya’s founder. The monks at Govardhan Math also worship a deity of Krishna in the form of a cowherd boy, but since the Shankara school does not accept the eternal nature of the Supreme Lord’s form, they are not recognized as Vaishnavas. There is also a Shiva linga called Ardhanarishwar in the temple.

Math records indicate that 144 different abbots have been heads of the Govardhan Math since its founding. The present abbot is named Swami Niranjan Deva Tirtha.

## Shankara’s role in the establishment of Jagannath Puri

The Vaishnava scriptures say that Shankaracharya was an incarnation of Lord Shiva who came to bewilder the atheists, to turn them away from Lord Vishnu. In fact, history shows that Shankara played a pivotal role in reinstating Hinduism in India and driving Buddhism out of the subcontinent, thus setting the stage for the revival of Vaishnavism.

Emphasis is usually placed on Shankara’s philosophical contributions and it is often forgotten that he was also the founder of the Smarta school of worship. The essence of Smarta worship is that one worships five gods – Shiva, Vishnu, Ganapati, Surya and Shakti. In the time prior to Shankara, these different Hindu sects were often in conflict with each other, and the syncretic system of worship established by Shankara under the banner of the Advaita philosophy made it possible for a type of neo-Hinduism or neo-Brahmanism to take shape.

In order to spread his teachings, Shankaracharya set up religious headquarters in the four corners of India: Dwaraka in the west, Rameshwar in the south, Badarikashram in the north and Sri Kshetra in the east. The Govardhan Math historically played a very important role in the affairs of the Jagannath temple until a very recent time. The temple priests have traditionally been Smartas, who emphasize again and again that the Jagannath temple is a great center of syncretism, uniting all streams of Hinduism in the figure of Jagannath.

According to the *Mādalā-pañjī*, when Shankara came to Sri Kshetra, he found no Jagannath deity there. The influence of the Buddhists was very strong and Shankara set about debating with their scholars and defeating them. He heard from local people that Lord Jagannath had been hidden in the Chilika Lake. Using his mystic power, he found the deity under a banyan tree and reinstalled Him in the temple with all the suitable rites. He also installed the deities of Balaram (to represent Shiva) and Subhadra (to represent Shakti) so that “all the sects would be satisfied.”

*Mādalā-pañjī* further states that Shankara placed the Brahma-padartha (Nabhi Brahma) inside Lord Jagannath, and placed Shalagram Shilas he brought with him from his travels to Nepal inside Lord Baladeva and Lady Subhadra. He also established the Nrisingha temple in the temple compound, where an image of Shankara can still be seen at the feet of Sri Sri Lakshmi Nrisingha.

Inside the temple, there is a depiction of Shankaracharya in painting on one of the pillars in the Jagamohan. A legend has it that before the present temple was built, the Govardhan Math of Shankaracharya was located in the very place where the present Jagamohan now stands. The acharyas of the Math were in charge of Lord Jagannath’s worship. In those days, the sannyasis’ ashram was in Bali Sahi. When plans were made for the construction of the massive temple, it was necessary to move the Govardhan Math to the site in Bala Sahi. The painting of Shankara was left as a memento.

## The continued influence of the Shankara sect

Only Smarta Brahmins from the sixteen settlements and sannyasis of Shankara’s order have the right to sit on the Mukti Mandap council. This right is denied the heads of even the most influential and powerful Vaishnava maths. In the District Collector’s report made in 1805, just after the British took over in Orissa, it is emphatically stated that the sannyasis of Shankaracharya’s order must be consulted on all affairs related to the temple.

In the *Karmāṅgī* of *Mādalā-pañjī*, in which the temple rituals are described, the following directive is found: “Gurus are of three types: the first are the sannyasis of Shankaracharya’s order. The head of the Govardhan Math is also called the Shankaracharya. He is the foremost preceptor. He is to receive a pot of Maha Prasad and a plate of Khichuri after it has been offered to the goddess Bimala Devi. He has the right to sit within the sanctum of the temple. He is authorized to personally render any service to the Deity, as he wishes. The priests of the temple enter service only when he presents them after examination. The priests are to daily serve his personal Nrisingha deity. He is the original preceptor.”

During the Maratha period (ca. 1750-1800) of influence in Puri, the Ramanandi sadhu Baba Govinda Brahmachari undertook repairs to Jagannath’s Ratna Singhasan. Up until that time, images of Shankaracharya and Padmapada, the first acharya of Govardhan Math, stood on the altar. These statues were shifted from the Ratnavedi while the repairs were being made. Before they could be reinstated on the altar, some Vaishnavas snatched them away and threw them into the sea. The Govardhan Math sannyasis petitioned the authorities several times, but they thought it prudent not to take an anti-Vaishnava position at that time, so they were never replaced.

The abbot of Govardhan Math still has a prestigious position as can be inferred from the fact that he is the permanent head (or nayaka) of the Mukti Mandap council. Temple authorities traditionally consult him in religious and ritual matters whenever necessary.

Padmapada Tirtha wrote several books glorifying Sri Purushottam, including *Puruṣa-vivṛtti,* in which the following verse is found:

*na mātā na pita na ca sṛṣṭi-hetuḥ*  
*na cākṛtir vā prakṛti-viśeṣaḥ*  
*na ca prapañca-svarūpānuvṛttiḥ*  
*sa hi vareṇyaḥ puruṣottamottamaḥ*

**Lord Purushottam is not our mother, nor our father. Nor is He the cause of the creation. He is neither formless, nor is He a manifestation of nature. His actions are not dictated by an identity born of material nature. He is the supreme being, the greatest of all conscious entities, the supreme person. (verse 1)**

When Sundarananda first visited Govardhan Math, Madhusudhan Tirtha was the abbot there. Sundarananda was shown the Math’s extensive manuscript library by Madhusudan Tirtha and gave an account of it in the first volume of *Vaiṣṇava-mañjuṣā-samāhṛti.*

When Srila Prabhupada Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati visited Puri, he was also introduced to Madhusudan Tirtha, with whom he had many philosophical discussions. Tirtha Swami held Srila Prabhupada in high esteem.

## Gopal Tirtha Math

The Gopal Tirtha math is situated near the ruins of the Puruna Nahar in Bali Sahi. It was established by a sannyasi in the Shankara line named Gopal Tirtha. The deity worshiped here is a form of the goddess named Bhuvaneshwari.

This math is involved in Jagannath Deva’s service by contributing a part of the Hati Vesh on the Snana Purnima day and Makara Sankranti days and offers panti bhoga to the Lord. It has branches in Bhubaneshwar and elsewhere, but they are under the control of the OHREC.

## Shankarananda Saraswati Math

This math is situated close to the Gopal Tirtha Math. It has a close connection to the Sringeri Math in South India. Nrisingha Deva is the ishta deva of this math. It is also called the Shankaranandi Math. It has a branch in Bhubaneswar.

According to some, this was the ashram of the great expounder of the Bhagavata, Sridhar Swami.

## Shiva Tirtha Math

At the time Sundarananda wrote *Sri Kshetra*, this math, situated next door to the Gopal Tirtha Math, was no longer functioning as a residence for sannyasis. The abbot was living in Bhubaneswar and had turned over the worship of the temple deities to a professional Brahmin.

## Mahi Prakash Brahmachari Math

Situated in the Harchandi Sahi neighbhorhood.

## Lakshmibhadra Math or Nanguli Math

This math, situated in the Lakshmi Bazaar, is run by sannyasis with the Puri title. It is also called Dash Nami Math. Apparently the sannyasis of this math used to practice castration as a part of their sadhana.

## Maths of the Ramanuja Sampradaya

**Emar Math**

There are as many as fifty maths of the Sri Vaishnava sampradaya in Jagannath Puri, the most important of which is Emar Math, which Sri Ramanujacharya, the great teacher of the *viśiṣṭādvaita* doctrine, established in the 11th century.

Ramanuja came to Puri from South India at around the same time that the Ganga dynasty established itself in Orissa. This was also the time that Lord Jagannath’s great temple was built. It is generally accepted that Ramanuja had a great influence on Anantavarman Chodaganga Deva, whose devotion to Shiva had always been greater than to Jagannath before meeting him. A sign of the influence of Ramanuja on the temple is that the tilak of the Sri Sampradaya appears on the temple and the deities.

Ramanuja preached the glories of the Daru Brahma to the entire world. He established a math of his own close to the Singha Dwar entrance of the Jagannath temple. This place is known as Sri Ramanuja Kota. His disciple Govinda was the first abbot of this math. This Govinda’s name in Tamil was Embarumanar. The Tamil word *embāra* is made up of *emba* and *āra,* and means “my lord.” This word has been corrupted to *emār*, and the math is now popularly called Emar Math. It also goes by the names Raj Gopal Math and Srinivas Kot.

Of all the Vaishnava maths in Puri, the Emar Math one has traditionally been the most richly endowed. This temple makes flower garlands for the deities’ Boro Sringar Vesh every evening. In particular, they make the guna and jhampa garlands for the Lord’s nose and the alaka garland for His forehead.

It appears that in some respects, Ramanujacharya was not able to make the changes he wished to make on Lord Jagannath’s worship. All his biographers seem to agree on one thing, which is also found in the *Madala Panji*: when Ramanuja tried to use his influence with the king to establish the Pancharatra rites in Jagannath worship, he met with failure.

Two traditions were entrenched in the Lord Jagannath temple: on the one hand the Pandas were Smartas (as mentioned in the the article on Govardhan Math above), on the other, the temple had many rites centred on the participation of the Dayitas and other descendents of the original worshipers of Nila Madhava. All these parties resisted Ramanuja’s attempts to establish a purely Pancharatra style of worship.

They prayed to Lord Jagannath who confirmed the local tradition. One of Ramanuja’s biographies, *Prapannamritam,* states that Lord Jagannath appeared to Ramanuja in a dream and asked him not to disturb the prevailing system. Ramanuja then tried to convince Lord Jagannath that the Pancharatra Agamas were superior!

The next morning, the Acharya was surprised to find himself far away in Srikurmam in Andhra Pradesh, without his danda and kamandalu. The *Madala Panji* says he was taken there by Garuda on Lord Jagannath's orders.\[cliii\]

During the time of Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati, the mahant of Emar Math, Gadadhar Ramanuja Das, often came to visit Srila Prabhupada and hear Hari katha from him.

## Sri Ram Das Math

This math is situated opposite the southern entrance to the Jagannath temple. Ram Das was the guru of the Maratha governor, and thus his math received rich endowments from the Marathas during their reign over Orissa.

## Dakshin Parshwa Math (Sri Raghava Das Math)

This math is situated opposite the southern entrance (“the horse gate”) to the Jagannath temple. It participates in a number of different services to Lord Jagannath: it supplies tahia on the Snana Purnima, Rathayatra, Bahuda and Niladri Vijaya days. It also furnishes part of the Hati Vesh, cotton for the Pahandi Vijaya, sandalwood for the the Sarvanga niti on Khadilagi Ekadasi. It also supplies flower garlands for Navanka Bedha and adhara pana bhoga and panti bhoga on certain festive days.

The devotees of this math also make a special bamboo parasol used for the deities during the Anasar period. This special service came as a result of the mercy shown by the Lord to Raghava Das. This legendary saint is said to have lived in the 13th century. He meditated in a standing position on the hot beach without regard for the weather. Some kind people took pity on him and tried to protect him from the sun and rain by placing a parasol over him, but the wind would always come and blow these attempts at giving him shade away. Finally, one of the temple sevakas decided to try giving him one of Lord Jagannath’s used parasols. Amazingly, this one remained fixed in the sand, even when there was a storm. Ever since then, the followers of Raghava Das have supplied the Lord’s parasol during the Anasar period.

## Uttara Parshva Math

Situated near the temple’s northern or elephant’s gate.

## Trimali Math

This very old math is located near the Uttara Parshva Math. This math supplies camphor for the arati lamps and frankincense resin (*jhuna*).

## Samadhi Math

This math is situated in Kalika Devi Sahi, southeast of the temple. The math received its name from a Vaishnava sadhaka named Jayaram Das who once lived there. He would remain absorbed in mystic trance or samadhi from Dvadasi until Dasami, in other words, for 13 days every fortnight.

Two sadhus named Vasudeva Ramanuja Das and Damodar Ramanuja Das used to live together here at this math. Vasudeva Ramanuja Das was a renunciate monk, but wore white cloth. He introduced Saraswati Thakur to a book called *Kṣamā-ṣoḍaśī*, a Ramanuji treatise on the renounced order of life. He disappeared in 1933.

Vasudeva would unfailingly recite the Sanskrit verses of the Srimad Bhagavatam every day. After so doing, he would distribute maha prasad to the Vaishnavas, Brahmins and other guests. He would also go to worship in the Jagannath temple next to a Hanuman shrine at the southern gate. Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakur and Siddhanta Saraswati Thakur would come to pay their respects to him and take maha prasad in his company. They often discussed the Srimad Bhagavatam with him. Vasudeva Maharaj, as he was known, would always respond with great humility when someone paid obeisances to him. He would answer “*dāso’smi*” and prostrate himself in return. \[cliv\]

Damodar Ramanuja Das was also a staunch Vaishnava. He spent a great deal of money improving the gardens inside the temple grounds. Bhaktivinoda Thakur approved of this project and also collected money from Calcutta to help him. Vasudeva Ramanuja Das also built a small temple to Narasingha near the six-armed form of Gauranga inside the south entrance to the temple.

## Nrisinghachari and Venkatachari Maths

The Mahants of both these maths in Bali Sahi are married householders with the surname Achari. It is said that Ramanuja Acharya had eight chief disciples who established centres in South India. Five of these were renunciates and three householders. The Nrisinghachari and Venkatachari Maths were founded by the descendants of two of these three householder disciples of Ramanuja. These are also called the Achari Maths.

## Other Maths of the Ramanuja Sampradaya

Some other maths of the Ramanuja line are the Regsa Math, located near the Uttara Parshva Math, Pandit Math in Kundhei Bent Sahi, Siddha Math in Dol Mandap Sahi, Jiyar Swami Math and Giri Swami Math in Bali Sahi, Rangama Math in Suar Sahi, Ketki Math in Markandeshwar Sahi, Rima Chatra near the police station on the Boro Danda..

Lakshmi Narayan is worshiped in all the Maths of the Ramanuja sampradaya.

## Maths of the Ramanandi sampradaya

Ramananda was a 14th century saint, initiated in the Sri Sampradaya as a follower in the 23rd generation after Ramanuja. Those who follow him have a number of differences from the rest of the Ramanuja line in matters concerning the object of worship, ritual, and doctrine. Some of the differences between the two sampradayas are as follows: The Ramanandis worship Sita Rama rather than Lakshmi Narayan. They wear tulasi mala around their necks all the time, whereas most Ramanujis usually put tulasi on only when they are recited their sandhya mantras. They do not observe tridandi sannyasa on retiring from household life, but wear white kaupin and bahirvas.

The followers of Ramananda belong to two different groups, one holding him to be a complete incarnation of Ramachandra, the other considering him to be only a partial incarnation. The latter group give more importance to the connection of their line to Ramanujacharya.

Unless otherwise stated, all the Ramanandi maths have Sita Ram deities installed.

## Boro Chata Math and Sana Chata Math

Situated north of the Singha Dwar on the Boro Danda. Sadhus from the Boro Chata Math sing kirtan at the time of Mangal Arati, Pahuda Arati and Bala Dhupa. They also supply the Lord’s Padma Vesha. The Ghumasar Math in Kundhei Bent Sahi and Angira Chata or Angira Ashram in Dol Mandap Sahi are currently under the management of the Boro Chata Math.

## Balaram Kot

In Bali Sahi. This was formerly part of the Achari Math,\[clv\] but was turned over to the Ramanandis at the end of the 19th century. The deities worshiped here are a Nrisingha Shalagram Shila and Lakshmi Narayan. The Panjabi Math is also in Bali Sahi. It has Sita Ram and Lakshman deities.

## Harija Khandi Math

This math, which is situated by the Shweta Ganga, is one of the most affluent in Puri. It has many branches throughout southern India. Besides Sita Ram, Radha-Krishna, Jagannath and Lakshmi, and Narasingha Shalagram are worshiped here.

## Swarga Dwar Chata

This math has been built beside a wide-branched banyan tree. During the time of Bhaktivinoda Thakur, a very old sadhu who continuously repeated the holy syllable *om* had his residence here. Bhaktivinoda was impressed with the spirituality of this devotee and went to visit him on January 17, 1903, spending the time discussing the Srimad Bhagavatam with him.

## Papudia Math

This math stands directly in front of the King’s palace. The name of the math comes from its founder, a south Indian known as Papudia Jagannath Das, a Ramanandi sadhu with a beard and long, matted locks of hair.

Papudia Jagannath Das lived in Puri at the turn of the 20th century. It is said that when he came to Puri, Orissa was in the throes of a drought that had lasted twelve years. As soon as he arrived, however, rain began to fall. This brought him immediate fame in the region.

Papudia Jagannath Das was a great ascetic and scholar, who had memorized the entire Bhagavatam. While Bhaktivinoda Thakur was living at the Bhajan Kuti, Jagannath Das often came to visit him to discuss scripture and Krishna katha. He also invited Bhaktivinoda Thakur to feasts and festivals in his math. He was fun loving and whenever he saw a carriage full of pilgrims, he would jokingly call out, “*Sādhu khilāo* – Feed the ascetics!” \[clvi\]

## Other Ramanandi Maths

The Kaushalya Das Math near the main temple’s southern gate; Neul Das Math in Dol Mandap Sahi; Boro Akhra or Digambar Akhra, also known as Pancha Ramanandiya Digambar Baithak situated near the Singha Dwar; Chauni Math, just south of the Singha Dwar; Nirbani Baithak, situated near the Chandan Pukur; Mahanirbani Baithak near the Boro Shankha; Niralambi Baithak near the Gundicha temple; Maniram Math in Kundhei Bent Sahi, near the king’s palace; Balgandi Chata, ear Balgandi on the Boro Danda (Besides Sita Ram, Lord Jagannath’s Patita Pavana murti and Sri Nrisinghadeva Shalagram are worshiped here.); Sundar Ram Math (Sundar Das Math), in Kundhei Bent Sahi; Nua Math, near Sundar Ram Math. Maluka Chaura Math, near Ananta Shayan at Swarga Dwar (There is a murti of Vidura here.); Boro Santa Math, Markandeshwar Sahi; Puruna Nahar Chata, near the ruins of the ancient palace.

## Maths of the Nimbarka Sampradaya

Unless otherwise stated, all Nimbarka maths have deities of Radha and Krishna. There are the Sri Radha Vallabha Math on the eastern side of the Boro Danda, next to the Singha Dwar. Deities of Sri Sri Radha and Krishna are worshiped here, but most of the rooms in this math are rented out to pilgrims. Sri Ramaji Math is in the Chudanga Sahi; Chikiti Math in Bali Sahi; Dukhi Shyam Chata is on the road to the Lokanath temple; and Chauliya Math in Balgandi.

## Vishnuswami Maths

The Vishnu Swami Akhra near Markandeya Sarovar is the main math of this sampradaya. They worship Hanumanji in thei temple. There are also two other akhras on the road to the Gundicha temple.

## Sant Sampradaya Maths

There are two significant maths belonging to the Nirakari Sant sampradaya.

## Kabir Chaura Math

This math is in the Svarga Dwar area. It is associated with the Kabir sect. Kabir (1440-1518) was a mystic poet of Muslim birth who became a disciple of Ramananda, but then started his own spiritual path and inspired the other mystics who went by the name of Sants. Though fundamentally devotional in their sadhana, these mystics are nirakaris, that is, they do not believe in God’s divine form. They are also famous for their rejection of caste distinctions and their fusion of various Islamic and Hindu elements in their conception of God and spirituality. Kabir supposedly stayed here when he came to Jagannath Puri.

## Bauli Math

This math is situated in Bali Sahi Also known as Nanak Chaura Math as it is associated with the name of Guru Nanak. Guru Nanak (1469-1539), the founder of the Sikh religion and contemporary of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, was also a Sant in his doctrine. It is written in his biography that when he visited the Jagannath temple, he came at the time of evening arati. Nanak stood silent, not participating because, he said, mere lamps and flowers were not homage enough to the glory and wonder of God, to whom Nature paid a far more sublime tribute. The verse he sang have been immortalized in the Guru Granth Sahib:

“In the salver of the sky  
The Sun and Moon shine like lamps,  
The galaxy of stars are scattered like pearls;  
The chandan-scented winds waft as Thine incense,  
The forests are Thy flowers.  
(Thus) is Thy arati (adoration) performed,  
O, Thou Destroyer of fear!”

But it is also written in his biography that he met Chaitanya Mahaprabhu while in Puri and danced with him in Harinam sankirtan. Nanak’s visit to Puri probably took place sometime around 1518.

## Mangu Math

Located next to the Emar Math. Interestingly, this math supplies a ram for sacrifice to the goddess Bimala each year on the Maha Navami night of Durga Puja.

## Non-traditional Hindu sampradayas

A number of other maths and ashrams have sprung up in Puri over the past century, associated with modern gurus who do not belong to any specific tradition, Vaishnava or other. Some of these are named here --

• Bijay Krishna Goswami Ashram (Narendra Sarovar) Bijay Krishna Goswami was a descendant of Advaita Acharya who became a member of the Brahmo Samaj. He was a contemporary of Bhaktivinoda Thakur and debated with him on at least one occasion. He was later initiated by Lokanath Brahmachari and his doctrine is an eclectic one, leaning to yoga with a mixture of bhakti.

• Advaita Brahma Ashram (Girnar Banta)  
• Nilachala Ashram of Sitaram Omkarnath (Svarga Dwar)  
• Karar Ashram (founded by the yogi Yukteshwar Giri, spiritual master of Paramahamsa Yogananda (1893-1952), known in the west as the founder of the Divine Life Fellowship, practicing kriya yoga. (Svarga Dwar)  
• Pranavananda Ashram (Chakra Tirtha), belonging to the Bharata Sevashram Sangha.  
• Sat Sangha Ashram (Chakra Tirtha)  
• Nigamananda Ashram (Lokanath Temple Road)  
• Divya Dham Yoga Ashram (Chakra Tirtha Road)  
• Ma Anandamayi Ashram (Svarga Dwar). Anandamayi Ma (1896-1982) was a Bengal ecstatic, who is considered by her followers to be an incarnation of the Mother Goddess, Kali. She had an extremely wide following all over India. She also has an eclectic doctrine.  
• Abhiram Paramahamsa Ashram (Marich Kot Lane)  
• Languli Math (Grand Road, opposite Snana Vedi)  
• Ramakrishna Math (Collectoriate Road)  
• Bhagavata Ashram (near bus stand)  
• Hari Das Ashram (Sarvodaya Nagar)
